school-c12-business-a.title: Class 12 Business Studies — Principles & Functions of Management (Part A)
school-c12-business-a.description: Class 12 Business Studies Part 1 chapter by chapter: management, principles, business environment, planning, organising, staffing, directing and controlling — with case-based practice.

courses.title: Ch 1 · Nature and Significance of Management
courses.summary: Concept of management, efficiency and effectiveness, characteristics, objectives and importance, management as science/art/profession, levels and functions of management, and coordination as the essence of management.
outcomes: Learners can define management and distinguish efficiency from effectiveness
Learners can explain the characteristics, objectives and importance of management
Learners can evaluate management as an art, science and profession
Learners can describe levels and functions of management
Learners can explain coordination and why it is the essence of management

scenes.text: Class 12 must run the annual fest with ₹50,000 and 40 volunteers.
Some teams finish early; others waste money.
Ms. Rao says: the fest needs management.

steps.title: Meaning
steps.body:
**Management** is the process of getting things done with the aim of achieving goals **effectively** and **efficiently**.
- **Effectiveness** = completing the task / achieving the goal on time (doing the right task)
- **Efficiency** = doing the task with minimum cost/resources (doing the task right)
Both are needed; a firm can be effective but inefficient (goal met at high cost) or efficient but ineffective (cheap but late).

steps.title: Characteristics
steps.body:
- Goal-oriented process
- All-pervasive (business, school, hospital, government)
- Multidimensional: management of work, people and operations
- Continuous process
- Group activity
- Dynamic function (adapts to environment)
- Intangible force (felt in the results)

steps.title: Solved case 1
steps.body: A factory meets its target of 10,000 units by the deadline but spends 20% more than budget on overtime. → **Effective but not efficient.**

steps.title: Solved case 2
steps.body:
"Management is practised in hospitals, schools and NGOs as much as in companies." → Characteristic: **all-pervasive**.
"The manager changed the product mix after a new competitor entered." → **dynamic**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Swapping the meanings of efficiency and effectiveness.
- Writing "management is tangible" — it is intangible.
- Listing objectives when the question asks for characteristics.

activity.prompt: Efficiency or effectiveness?

items.text: Launching the product on the planned date
Producing the same output with fewer labour hours

quiz.why: Efficiency is concerned with doing the task right, so it compares inputs and outputs, i.e. cost and resources used.

options: Completing the right task on time
quiz.why: Effectiveness means completing the right task, achieving the goal, and doing so on time. It is about the end result, not the cost.

quiz.q: "Management is practised in all types of organisations." Characteristic:
quiz.why: Management is needed in every type of organisation (business, hospitals, schools, clubs), so it is all-pervasive.

quiz.q: Management of work, people and operations shows that it is:
quiz.why: Management involves the management of work, people and operations, so it has many dimensions: it is multidimensional.

quiz.q: Management cannot be seen but its presence is felt. It is:
quiz.why: Management cannot be seen, but its effects (like order and results) can be felt, so it is intangible.

scenes.text: A shoe company wants profit and growth.
The town expects clean water and jobs.
Workers want fair pay and growth.

steps.title: Objectives
steps.body:
- **Organisational:** survival, profit, growth
- **Social:** creating benefits for society — eco-friendly methods, employment for disadvantaged sections, schools/crèches
- **Personal:** competitive salaries, peer recognition, personal growth, meeting diverse needs of employees

steps.title: Importance
steps.body:
- Helps achieve group goals
- Increases efficiency
- Creates a dynamic organisation (helps adapt to change)
- Helps achieve personal objectives
- Helps in development of society

steps.title: Solved case 1
steps.body: A company sets up a sewage treatment plant and employs differently-abled persons. → **Social objectives.**

steps.title: Solved case 2
steps.body: A firm increases its sales by 25% and opens two new branches. → **Organisational objective: growth.**

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Writing "profit" as a social objective.
- Listing importance points when asked for objectives — read the question.

activity.prompt: Classify each objective

items.text: Earning enough revenue to cover costs (survival)
Running a school for workers' children

quiz.why: Survival, profit and growth are the economic objectives an organisation aims for, so they are organisational objectives.

quiz.q: Employment to disadvantaged sections is a:
quiz.why: Providing employment to disadvantaged sections of society is a benefit to society, so it is a social objective.

quiz.q: Management creates a dynamic organisation by:
quiz.why: A dynamic organisation adapts to change, and management helps by changing plans and structure as the environment changes.
Peer recognition satisfies an individual's own needs, so it is a personal objective.

quiz.q: Which is NOT an importance of management?
quiz.why: Management helps to achieve group goals, increase efficiency and develop society, but it cannot guarantee profit.

lessons.title: Management as an art, science and profession

story.title: Is a manager like a doctor?

scenes.text: A brilliant manager seems to have a natural flair.
But she also uses proven principles.
Is management a profession like medicine?

steps.title: As an art
steps.body: Features of art: existence of theoretical knowledge, personalised application, based on practice and creativity. **Management satisfies all** → it is an art.

steps.title: As a science
steps.body: Features of science: systematised body of knowledge, principles based on experimentation, universal validity. Management has systematic knowledge and principles from experimentation, but they are not exact or universal because it deals with human behaviour → **inexact (soft) science**.

steps.title: As a profession
steps.body: Features: well-defined body of knowledge ✓; restricted entry (exam/degree) ✗ (anyone can be a manager); professional association ✓ but membership not compulsory (e.g. AIMA); ethical code ✗ not binding; service motive — partly. → **Not a full-fledged profession.**

steps.title: Solved case 1
steps.body: "A manager uses principles creatively according to the situation." → management as an **art** (personalised application).

steps.title: Solved case 2
steps.body: "Anyone can be appointed manager without a compulsory degree." → feature of profession **not** satisfied: restricted entry.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling management an exact science.
- Claiming management is a full profession because MBA degrees exist — entry is not legally restricted.

activity.prompt: Match the feature to art / science / profession

options: Art and inexact science; not a full profession
quiz.why: Management is an art and an inexact science, but it is not a full profession as it lacks some features such as restricted entry.

quiz.q: Which profession feature does management lack?
quiz.why: A full profession has restricted entry (a qualification is compulsory), but anyone can become a manager, so management lacks this.

quiz.q: Management principles are not universal because they deal with:
quiz.why: Principles of management deal with human behaviour, which varies from person to person, so they are not universal like laws of physics.

quiz.q: Creativity in applying knowledge relates to management as:
quiz.why: Using knowledge creatively to suit the situation is the mark of an art, so management is an art.
AIMA (All India Management Association) is a professional association of managers. Membership is not compulsory.

scenes.text: CEO sets direction; plant head runs operations; foreman guides workers.
Three levels, five functions.
Every manager performs all functions in different degrees.

steps.title: Levels
steps.body:
- **Top:** CEO, MD, chairman, board — set objectives and policies, responsible for welfare and survival, coordinate departments
- **Middle:** division/department heads, plant superintendents — interpret policies, ensure staffing, assign duties, motivate, cooperate with other departments
- **Supervisory/operational:** foremen, supervisors — directly oversee workers, maintain quality, minimise wastage, link between management and workers

steps.title: Functions
steps.body: **Planning** (deciding in advance) → **Organising** (assigning duties, grouping tasks, allocating resources) → **Staffing** (right people in right jobs) → **Directing** (leading, motivating, communicating) → **Controlling** (monitoring performance and correcting deviations).

steps.title: Solved case 1
steps.body: "Ravi interprets the policies framed by the board and assigns work to supervisors." → **middle-level** manager.

steps.title: Solved case 2
steps.body: "The manager compares actual output with the target and takes corrective action." → function: **controlling**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying only top managers plan — every level plans.
- Confusing organising (structure) with staffing (people).

activity.prompt: Put the functions of management in their usual order

quiz.why: Foremen and supervisors work at the supervisory (operational) level, where they oversee workers directly.

quiz.q: Framing overall policies is done by:
quiz.why: Top-level management frames the organisation's overall objectives and policies.

quiz.q: Right person for the right job is:
quiz.why: Staffing is the function of placing the right person on the right job.
Directing includes motivating, leading and guiding employees to do their work.
Middle management interprets the policies framed by top management and passes them to supervisors for implementation.

scenes.text: Forty musicians, each excellent.
Without a conductor, it is noise.
Coordination makes the parts work as one.

steps.title: Meaning
steps.body: **Coordination** is the force that binds all other functions of management; the process of synchronising activities of different departments.

steps.title: Characteristics
steps.body:
- Integrates group efforts
- Ensures unity of action
- Continuous process
- All-pervasive function
- Responsibility of all managers
- Deliberate function

steps.title: Why it is the essence
steps.body: Needed in all functions and at all levels. Importance rises with: **growth in size**, **functional differentiation** (departments pursue their own goals), **specialisation** (specialists think they are the best judge).

steps.title: Solved case 1
steps.body: Production makes 10,000 units while sales can sell only 7,000 → poor coordination between departments. Remedy: integrate the production plan with the sales forecast.

steps.title: Solved case 2
steps.body: "Coordination is not a separate function; it is the essence of management." Reason: it is required in planning, organising, staffing, directing and controlling — and at top, middle and lower levels.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling coordination a separate sixth function.
- Saying it is only the job of top management.

statements.s: Coordination is a deliberate function.
Only top managers coordinate.
Coordination is a one-time activity.
Specialisation increases the need for coordination.
statements.why: Specialists may not accept others' views.

quiz.why: Coordination is the force that binds all the functions of management together, so it is called the essence of management.

quiz.q: Which increases the need for coordination?
quiz.why: Functional differentiation (many specialised departments) pulls people in different directions, so it increases the need for coordination.
Coordination ensures unity of action, as the different departments and people work together toward the common goal.
Coordination is the responsibility of every manager at all levels, not just the CEO or HR.
Coordination is a continuous process that is needed as long as the organisation operates.

questions.q: Effectiveness is about:
questions.why: Effectiveness is about completing the task and achieving the goal (doing the right task). It is not about minimum cost.

questions.q: Management is a ___ process.
questions.why: Management is a continuous process: its functions are carried on constantly as long as the organisation exists.

questions.q: Profit is a/an ___ objective.
questions.why: Profit is an economic objective of the business, so it is an organisational objective.

questions.q: Supervisors belong to ___ level.
questions.why: Supervisors work at the operational (supervisory) level, directly overseeing workers.

questions.q: Management is an inexact science because:
questions.why: Management is an inexact science because it deals with human behaviour, so its principles do not give the same result every time.

questions.q: Assertion: Coordination is the essence of management. Reason: It is needed in every function and at every level.
questions.why: Both are true. Coordination is needed in every function and at every level to hold them together, which is why it is called the essence of management.

questions.q: Which feature of profession is fully satisfied by management?
questions.why: Management has a well-defined body of knowledge (principles, theories, books and courses), a feature of a profession. It lacks restricted entry and a binding code.

questions.q: Case: A company achieved its production target but at a cost 30% over budget. This shows:
questions.why: The company achieved its goal (effective) but spent 30% over budget (not efficient), so it shows effectiveness without efficiency.

questions.q: Case: "Mr Sen sets the long-term direction and is responsible for the survival of the company." Level:
questions.why: Setting the long-term direction and being responsible for the company's survival are tasks of top-level management.

questions.q: Case: The R&D team designed a premium product that marketing cannot sell at that price. What is lacking?
questions.why: If R&D's product cannot be sold by marketing at that price, the departments did not work together, which shows a lack of coordination.

questions.q: Case: A firm provides crèche facilities and plants trees around the factory. Objective:
questions.why: Providing creche facilities and planting trees benefit employees' families and society, so they serve a social objective.

questions.q: Case: An HR manager notices that employees value recognition from colleagues and introduces "Employee of the Month". Which objective is served?
questions.why: Recognition from colleagues satisfies the employees' personal needs, so introducing 'Employee of the Month' serves the personal objective.

questions.q: Case: A manager applies the same principle differently in two branches because their workers differ. This shows management as:
questions.why: Applying the same principle differently to suit different workers shows creativity and personalised application, which is the mark of art.

questions.q: Case: In a large company with 12 departments, each department head pursues his own targets. The factor increasing the need for coordination:
questions.why: In a large firm with many departments, each pursuing its own targets, the functional differentiation raises the need for coordination.

questions.q: Case: "Our company increased output by 10% with the same workforce but missed the launch date by two months." Choose the best evaluation.
questions.why: Increasing output with the same workforce means resources were used well (efficient), but missing the launch date means the goal was not achieved on time (not effective).

questions.q: Case: A consultant claims management is a full profession because many managers have MBAs. The best counter-argument:
options: Entry is not legally restricted to degree holders
questions.why: Having an MBA is not compulsory to become a manager, since entry to management is not legally restricted, so management is not a full profession.

questions.q: Which is NOT a characteristic of management?
questions.why: Management is intangible. It cannot be seen, though its effects can be felt. Group activity, dynamic and goal-oriented are its characteristics.

courses.title: Ch 2 · Principles of Management
courses.summary: Nature and significance of management principles; Taylor's scientific management — principles and techniques (functional foremanship, standardisation, method/motion/time/fatigue study, differential piece wage); Fayol's 14 principles; Taylor vs Fayol.
outcomes: Learners can explain the nature and significance of principles of management
Learners can explain Taylor's principles and techniques
Learners can apply Fayol's 14 principles to cases
Learners can compare Taylor and Fayol

scenes.text: An old supervisor runs the factory "the way it was always done".
A new manager brings tested principles.
Waste falls; output rises.

steps.title: Meaning
steps.body: A **principle of management** is a broad and general guideline for decision-making and behaviour. Principles are not rigid like those of pure science; they are flexible and applied with judgement.

steps.title: Nature
steps.body:
- Universal applicability
- General guidelines (not ready-made solutions)
- Formed by practice and experimentation
- Flexible
- Mainly behavioural
- Cause-and-effect relationships
- Contingent (depend on the situation)

steps.title: Significance
steps.body:
- Provide managers with useful insights into reality
- Optimum utilisation of resources and effective administration
- Scientific decisions
- Meeting changing environment requirements
- Fulfilling social responsibility
- Management training, education and research

steps.title: Solved case 1
steps.body: "Principles are modified by a manager according to the situation." → nature: **flexible / contingent**.

steps.title: Solved case 2
steps.body: "Principles help reduce wastage and avoid trial-and-error." → significance: **optimum utilisation of resources**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Writing that principles are rigid like science.
- Mixing "principles" (guidelines) with "techniques" (procedures).

statements.s: Management principles are rigid.
Principles are developed through practice and experimentation.
Principles mainly deal with human behaviour.
Principles give ready-made solutions to every problem.

quiz.why: Principles of management are flexible guidelines to action, not rigid rules, and managers adapt them to the situation.

quiz.q: Contingent nature means application depends on:
quiz.why: Contingent means that their use depends on the situation, so a principle may be applied differently in different cases.

quiz.q: Which is NOT a nature of principles?
quiz.why: Principles of management are general guidelines, not absolute or exact, since they deal with human behaviour.
Principles give managers a basis for reasoned, scientific decisions instead of random or biased ones.
Principles are used in management training, education and research, since they form a body of knowledge.

scenes.text: F. W. Taylor (1856–1915) studied work at steel plants.
He timed and analysed each task.
He said: replace rule of thumb with science.

steps.title: Four principles
steps.body:
1. **Science, not rule of thumb** — find the one best way by scientific enquiry
2. **Harmony, not discord** — complete change in mental attitude of workers and management ("mental revolution")
3. **Cooperation, not individualism** — management and workers cooperate; workers' suggestions welcomed
4. **Development of each and every person to his/her greatest efficiency and prosperity** — scientific selection and training

steps.title: Solved case 1
steps.body: Workers and management share gains from higher productivity instead of fighting over the surplus → **Harmony, not discord** (mental revolution).

steps.title: Solved case 2
steps.body: A company rewards workers for useful suggestions and managers share responsibility with them → **Cooperation, not individualism**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Writing "Harmony" when the case is about suggestion schemes (that is cooperation).
- Attributing the 14 principles to Taylor (they are Fayol's).

activity.prompt: Match each case to Taylor's principle
pairs: Finding the best way to pack boxes by experiment
Workers and managers stop seeing each other as rivals
Scientific selection and training of workers
Development of each person to greatest efficiency

quiz.why: Mental revolution means a change in attitude between workers and management, under the principle of harmony, not discord.
F.W. Taylor is called the father of scientific management.

quiz.q: Rule of thumb is replaced by:
quiz.why: Taylor wanted the scientific method to replace the rule of thumb (trial-and-error guesswork).

quiz.q: Scientific selection and training relates to:
quiz.why: Scientific selection and training help each worker to reach maximum efficiency, which is Taylor's principle of development of each and every person.
Taylor developed his ideas through experiments at the shop-floor (factory) level to improve productivity.

scenes.text: Taylor suggested splitting a foreman's job among specialists.
One plans the route; another fixes machines.
Efficient workers earn a higher rate per piece.

steps.title: Functional foremanship
steps.body: Separate planning and execution. **Planning in-charge:** instruction card clerk, route clerk, time and cost clerk, disciplinarian. **Production in-charge:** speed boss, gang boss, repair boss, inspector. (This violates Fayol's unity of command.)

steps.title: Other techniques
steps.body:
- **Standardisation and simplification of work** (standard tools, methods; eliminating unnecessary varieties)
- **Method study** — best way of doing a job
- **Motion study** — eliminate unnecessary movements
- **Time study** — standard time for a well-defined job
- **Fatigue study** — rest intervals
- **Differential piece wage system** — higher rate for those meeting the standard

steps.title: Solved example 1 — differential piece wage
steps.body:
Standard: 10 units/day. Rate ₹50 per unit at or above standard; ₹40 below.
Worker A makes 11 → 11 × 50 = **₹550**. Worker B makes 9 → 9 × 40 = **₹360**. The gap (₹190) for just 2 units motivates B to improve.

steps.title: Solved case 2
steps.body:
A company finds that a worker bends 12 times to pick parts; rearranging the bench reduces it to 4. → **Motion study**.
A company decides the standard time to assemble a fan is 18 minutes. → **Time study**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Confusing method study (overall method) with motion study (movements).
- Forgetting that functional foremanship has 8 specialists (4 + 4).

activity.prompt: Standard 20 units. Rate ₹30/unit if standard met, ₹25/unit otherwise. Worker X makes 19 units. Earnings (₹)?

quiz.q: Number of specialists in functional foremanship:
quiz.why: Under functional foremanship, there are eight specialist foremen, four in the planning department and four in the production department.
The speed boss is one of the four specialists in the production department, under the production in-charge.
Fatigue study decides the rest intervals and their frequency, so that workers can work at best efficiency.

quiz.q: Eliminating unnecessary varieties of products is:
quiz.why: Simplification removes unnecessary varieties and sizes of products to cut costs. Standardisation fixes standards for products or processes.
Under differential piece-rate wages, efficient workers (those meeting the standard) are paid a higher rate to reward them.

scenes.text: Henri Fayol (1841–1925) managed a French mining company.
He wrote 14 principles for the whole organisation.
They apply at the top as much as on the floor.

steps.title: Principles 1–7
steps.body:
1. **Division of work** — specialisation
2. **Authority and responsibility** — balance between them
3. **Discipline** — obedience to rules and agreements, by both superiors and subordinates
4. **Unity of command** — one boss for each employee
5. **Unity of direction** — one head and one plan for a group of activities with the same objective
6. **Subordination of individual interest to general interest**
7. **Remuneration of employees** — fair and just pay

steps.title: Solved case 1
steps.body: A salesman gets conflicting orders from the sales manager and the production manager → violation of **unity of command**.

steps.title: Solved case 2
steps.body: A company making shampoos and biscuits has separate divisions, each with its own head and plan → **unity of direction**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Confusing unity of command (one boss per person) with unity of direction (one plan per activity group).
- Thinking discipline applies only to workers.

activity.prompt: Unity of command or unity of direction?

items.text: Each worker reports to only one supervisor
Each product line has its own plan and head

quiz.why: Unity of command means each employee should receive orders from one boss only.
Authority and responsibility must be balanced, and a person given responsibility needs matching authority.
Henri Fayol is known as the father of general (modern) management theory.

quiz.q: Employees put organisational goals above personal ones:
quiz.why: Subordination of individual interest to general interest means employees put the organisation's goals above their personal ones.
Specialisation is the basis of division of work, since each person does the work that suits them best.

lessons.title: Fayol's principles (8–14) and Taylor vs Fayol

scenes.text: A clerk needs urgent approval from a clerk in another department.
Going up and down the chain takes days.
Fayol's "gang plank" allows a direct route in emergencies.

steps.title: Principles 8–14
steps.body:
8. **Centralisation and decentralisation** — balance
9. **Scalar chain** — formal line of authority from top to bottom; **gang plank** allows direct communication between same-level employees in emergencies (with superiors' knowledge)
10. **Order** — a place for everything and everyone
11. **Equity** — kindness and justice; no discrimination
12. **Stability of tenure of personnel**
13. **Initiative** — encourage employees to make and carry out plans
14. **Esprit de corps** — team spirit; use "we" not "I"

steps.title: Taylor vs Fayol
steps.body:
- Perspective: shop-floor (Taylor) vs top management (Fayol)
- Unity of command: Taylor's functional foremanship ignores it; Fayol insists on it
- Applicability: specialised situations vs universal
- Basis: observation and experimentation vs personal experience
- Focus: productivity vs improving overall administration
- Personality: scientist vs practitioner

steps.title: Solved case 1
steps.body: A company keeps changing staff every few months; costs of training rise and morale falls → violation of **stability of tenure**.

steps.title: Solved case 2
steps.body: Female workers are paid less than male workers for the same work → violation of **equity** (and of law).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Confusing order (right place) with discipline (obeying rules).
- Forgetting that gang plank needs superiors' knowledge.

activity.prompt: Match the case to the Fayol principle violated/applied
pairs: Direct contact between two supervisors in an emergency
Tools kept in fixed, labelled places
Manager says "we did it", not "I did it"
Same pay for same work regardless of caste or gender

quiz.why: The gang plank is a shortcut for direct communication across the same level, used within the scalar chain.
'A place for everything and everyone, and everything and everyone in its place' is Fayol's principle of order.
Team spirit, harmony and unity among employees is esprit de corps.
Taylor focused on improving productivity at the shop-floor (operational) level, using scientific methods.
In functional foremanship, a worker receives orders from eight specialists, which violates Fayol's principle of unity of command.

questions.q: Principles of management are:
questions.why: Management principles are flexible guidelines, not rigid rules, so managers adapt them to situations.

questions.q: Fayol gave ___ principles.
questions.why: Henri Fayol gave 14 principles of management.

questions.q: "One best way of doing a job" is found by:
questions.why: Method study finds the one best way of doing a job, by studying the different ways and choosing the best.

questions.q: Esprit de corps means:
questions.why: Esprit de corps means team spirit, unity and harmony among team members.

questions.q: Mental revolution is part of:
questions.why: Taylor's mental revolution is part of the principle 'harmony, not discord', which asks workers and management to cooperate.

questions.q: Assertion: Functional foremanship violates unity of command. Reason: A worker receives orders from eight specialists.
questions.why: Both are true. A worker under functional foremanship takes orders from eight specialists, so there is more than one boss. This violates unity of command.

questions.q: Route clerk is under:
questions.why: The route clerk is one of the four specialists in the planning department, under the planning in-charge.

questions.q: Case: A manager shouts at workers who arrive late but himself ignores meeting deadlines. Principle violated:
questions.why: A manager who punishes lateness but ignores deadlines himself breaks the principle of discipline, which applies to superiors and subordinates alike.

questions.q: Case: Two divisions of a company make similar products, each with separate plans and heads, and both compete for the same customers. Which principle is being violated?
questions.why: Unity of direction means one head and one plan for a group of activities with the same objective. Two divisions chasing the same customers with separate plans and heads break this principle.

questions.q: Case: A factory finds that a task takes 40 minutes on average and sets this as standard. Technique:
questions.why: Measuring the time taken to do a task and fixing a standard time is time study.

questions.q: Standard 50 units; ₹10/unit if achieved, ₹8 if not. Worker makes 49 units. Earnings:
questions.why: The worker makes 49 units, which is below the standard of 50, so the lower rate applies to all units: 49 × ₹8 = ₹392.

questions.q: Case: A marketing executive is told by two managers to visit two different cities on the same day. Violation and consequence:
questions.why: Getting orders from two managers for the same day violates unity of command and confuses the employee.

questions.q: Case: A company standardises bulb sizes to three and stops making 12 other variants. Technique:
questions.why: Cutting bulbs to three standard sizes is standardisation, and dropping the other 12 variants is simplification.

questions.q: Case: Workers are encouraged to make suggestions and a reward scheme is introduced. Which Taylor principle AND Fayol principle fit?
questions.why: Encouraging suggestions shows Taylor's principle of cooperation, not individualism, and Fayol's principle of initiative.

questions.q: Which pair is correctly matched?
options: Taylor — shop floor; Fayol — top management
questions.why: Taylor focused on shop-floor efficiency, while Fayol focused on top management and the overall administration.

questions.q: Rest intervals are fixed by:
questions.why: Fatigue study determines the rest intervals so that workers do not get too tired.

questions.q: Balance between concentration and dispersal of authority:
questions.why: The balance between concentration and dispersal of authority is centralisation and decentralisation.

courses.title: Ch 3 · Business Environment
courses.summary: Meaning, features and importance of business environment; its dimensions (economic, social, technological, political, legal); India's economic reforms of 1991 (liberalisation, privatisation, globalisation) and their impact on business, with managerial responses.
outcomes: Learners can define business environment and explain its features
Learners can explain the importance of understanding the environment
Learners can classify forces into the five dimensions
Learners can explain the 1991 reforms and their impact on business

scenes.text: A phone maker sees cheaper rivals arrive overnight.
Laws, tastes and technology keep changing.
Together these are the business environment.

steps.title: Meaning
steps.body: **Business environment** = the sum total of all individuals, institutions and other forces that are **outside the control** of a business enterprise but that may affect its performance.

steps.title: Features
steps.body:
- Totality of external forces
- Specific forces (investors, customers, competitors, suppliers) and general forces (economic, social, political, legal, technological)
- Inter-relatedness
- Dynamic nature
- Uncertainty
- Complexity
- Relativity (differs from country to country, region to region)

steps.title: Solved case 1
steps.body: "Demand for sarees is high in one region but low in another." → **Relativity**.

steps.title: Solved case 2
steps.body: "Rising health awareness increased demand for organic food, which led to new government standards for labelling." → **Inter-relatedness** (social and legal forces affect each other).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Including internal factors (like the firm's own employees' skill) as environment — the environment is external.
- Confusing complexity (hard to understand) with uncertainty (hard to predict).

activity.prompt: Match the case to the feature
pairs: Fashion trends cannot be predicted reliably
Political change leads to new taxes and affects prices
Hard to know exactly how a policy will affect demand
Demand for woollens differs between Punjab and Kerala

quiz.q: Business environment consists of forces that are:
quiz.why: The business environment is made up of external forces (economic, social, political, etc.) that are largely beyond a firm's control.
Customers and competitors directly affect a particular firm, so they are specific forces.

quiz.q: Environment varies from country to country:
quiz.why: Business environment differing from one country or region to another is the feature of relativity.
An environment that keeps changing is dynamic.
Economic and political conditions affect all firms alike, so they are general forces.

scenes.text: A firm noticed early that people wanted UPI-based payments.
It launched before rivals and grabbed the market.
Watching the environment pays.

steps.title: Importance
steps.body:
- Enables the firm to **identify opportunities** and get **first mover advantage**
- Helps to **identify threats** and early warning signals
- Helps in **tapping useful resources**
- Helps in **coping with rapid changes**
- Assists in **planning and policy formulation**
- Helps in **improving performance**

steps.title: Solved case 1
steps.body: A two-wheeler company learnt that an international rival would enter India and immediately improved its after-sales service. → **Identifying threats / early warning**.

steps.title: Solved case 2
steps.body: A company that studies market trends continuously and adapts its strategy outperforms rivals. → **Improving performance**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: - Mixing "identify opportunities" and "identify threats" in cases — check if the news is good or bad for the firm.

activity.prompt: Opportunity or threat for a petrol-car maker?

quiz.why: A firm that identifies opportunities early can use them before its competitors, which gives it a first-mover advantage.
Early warning signals alert the firm to threats before they become serious, so it can prepare.
The environment is the source from which a firm obtains useful resources, such as raw materials, capital and labour.
Understanding the environment helps managers in planning and policy-making.

quiz.q: Firms that continuously monitor the environment:
quiz.why: Firms that keep watching the environment can adapt and so improve their performance.

scenes.text: Interest rates change (economic).
Families want healthier food (social).
AI tools arrive (technological); new laws pass (legal); a new government forms (political).

steps.title: Five dimensions
steps.body:
- **Economic:** interest rates, inflation, incomes, stock markets, government economic policies
- **Social:** customs, traditions, values, lifestyle, health consciousness, demographics
- **Technological:** new inventions, methods of production, digital payments, e-commerce
- **Political:** political stability, government attitude towards business
- **Legal:** legislation, court judgments, regulations (e.g. Companies Act 2013, Consumer Protection Act 2019, rules on advertising)

steps.title: Solved case 1
steps.body: "The RBI raised the repo rate, making loans costlier." → **Economic** dimension.

steps.title: Solved case 2
steps.body: "Many people now prefer to order groceries via apps." → **Technological** (and social — changing lifestyle). In exams, choose the most direct cause.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling a new law "political" — it is **legal**.
- Calling a change in government's stability "legal" — it is **political**.

activity.prompt: Classify each change into its dimension

quiz.why: The repo rate is set by the RBI and affects interest rates and credit, so it is an economic factor.
Health consciousness is a change in people's attitudes and lifestyles, so it is a social factor.

quiz.q: A court judgment affecting business is:
quiz.why: A court judgment that affects business is part of the legal environment.
Political stability concerns the government and its policies, so it is part of the political dimension.
Growth of digital payments is due to new technology, so it is a technological factor.

lessons.title: Economic reforms of 1991 and their impact

scenes.text: India faced a balance-of-payments crisis.
The New Industrial Policy (1991) launched big reforms.
Liberalisation, privatisation and globalisation changed business forever.

steps.title: LPG
steps.body:
**Liberalisation:** freeing business from unnecessary controls — abolishing licensing for most industries, freedom to decide scale, freedom in movement of goods, reduced tax rates, simplified import/export, easier foreign capital and technology.
**Privatisation:** giving the private sector a greater role and reducing the public sector — disinvestment, fewer industries reserved for the public sector, BIFR referral for sick units.
**Globalisation:** integrating the economy with the world — reduced tariffs, freer flow of trade, capital, technology and people.

steps.title: Impact on business
steps.body:
- Increasing competition
- More demanding customers
- Rapidly changing technological environment
- Necessity for change
- Need for developing human resources
- Market orientation (produce what customers want)
- Loss of budgetary support to the public sector

steps.title: Solved case 1
steps.body: After reforms, foreign brands entered the Indian car market, and domestic firms had to improve quality and service. → Impact: **increasing competition** and **more demanding customers**.

steps.title: Solved case 2
steps.body: A PSU must now earn its own funds instead of relying on government budget support → **loss of budgetary support to the public sector**.

steps.title: Managerial responses
steps.body: Firms became customer-focused, invested in R&D and technology, trained employees, and adopted flexible strategies to survive in a dynamic environment.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying globalisation means only exporting.
- Confusing liberalisation (removing controls) with privatisation (reducing state ownership).

activity.prompt: Which reform does each measure belong to?

items.text: Abolishing industrial licensing for most industries
Disinvestment of government shares in PSUs
Reducing industries reserved for public sector
Freedom to fix scale of business
Free flow of technology across countries

quiz.q: The New Industrial Policy was announced in:
quiz.why: The New Industrial Policy, which started India's economic reforms, was announced in 1991.
Disinvestment is the sale of government shares in public sector units, which is part of privatisation.
Reducing import duties opens the economy to the rest of the world, which is globalisation.

quiz.q: One impact of reforms on business:
quiz.why: After the reforms, many new firms (including foreign ones) entered the market, so competition increased.
Market orientation means producing what customers want, instead of selling whatever is produced.

questions.q: Business environment is:
questions.why: The business environment is external to the firm and beyond its control.

questions.q: Competitors are:
questions.why: Competitors affect a particular firm directly, so they are specific forces.

questions.q: Repo rate is a/an ___ factor.
questions.why: The repo rate is the rate at which the RBI lends to banks, so it is an economic factor.

questions.q: Liberalisation means:
questions.why: Liberalisation means removing unnecessary controls and restrictions on business, such as licensing.

questions.q: Inability to predict changes is:
questions.why: The inability to predict how the environment will change is uncertainty.

questions.q: Assertion: Environment helps identify threats. Reason: Early warning signals allow firms to prepare.
questions.why: Both are true. Early warning signals show threats in good time, so firms can prepare for them.

questions.q: New labelling law for food packaging is:
questions.why: A law on food-packaging labels is part of the legal environment.

questions.q: Case: A firm launched sugar-free products after noticing rising diabetes awareness. Dimension:
questions.why: Rising health awareness is a change in people's attitudes, so launching sugar-free products responds to a social factor.

questions.q: Case: After 1991, an Indian PSU had to raise funds from the market. Impact:
options: Loss of budgetary support to public sector
questions.why: After 1991, public sector units lost the government's budgetary support and had to raise funds from the market themselves.

questions.q: Case: A company that first launched an e-wallet captured a large market share. Importance shown:
questions.why: The first firm to launch a new product gains a large share before rivals, which is first-mover advantage.

questions.q: Case: Demand for heaters rises in Shimla but not in Chennai. Feature:
questions.why: Heaters are in demand in cold Shimla but not in warm Chennai, which shows that the environment differs by place: relativity.

questions.q: Case: A government decision to cut corporate tax increased investment and also changed hiring. Features shown:
questions.why: A government's tax decision affecting investment and also hiring shows that parts of the environment are inter-related.

questions.q: Case: After globalisation, Indian firms invested heavily in training staff. Impact:
questions.why: After globalisation, competition is stronger, so firms need skilled people, which creates the need to develop human resources.

questions.q: Which is NOT part of liberalisation (1991)?
questions.why: Liberalisation lowers import tariffs and removes licences. Raising import tariffs would be the opposite.

questions.q: Case: A cosmetics firm must reformulate products after a court bans an ingredient, while consumer preference also shifts to herbal products. Dimensions involved:
questions.why: A court banning an ingredient is a legal factor, and customers shifting to herbal products is a social factor.

questions.q: Case: Consumers now demand fast delivery, better quality and lower prices because of more choices. Which impact of reforms and which LPG element mainly caused it?
questions.why: With globalisation and liberalisation, customers get many choices and so demand better quality, speed and prices. This is the 'more demanding customers' impact.

questions.q: Specific forces affect:
questions.why: Specific forces directly affect an individual firm or industry, for example customers, competitors and suppliers. General forces affect all firms.

courses.title: Ch 4 · Planning
courses.summary: Meaning, importance, features and limitations of planning; the planning process; and types of plans — objectives, strategy, policy, procedure, method, rule, programme and budget.
outcomes: Learners can explain the importance and features of planning
Learners can explain the limitations of planning
Learners can describe the steps in the planning process
Learners can identify types of plans in cases

scenes.text: The class plans a trip to Jaipur.
They decide dates, budget, transport and backups in advance.
Fewer surprises, less waste.

steps.title: Meaning
steps.body: **Planning** is deciding in advance what to do and how to do it. It bridges the gap from where we are to where we want to be.

steps.title: Importance
steps.body:
- Provides **direction**
- **Reduces the risks of uncertainty**
- **Reduces overlapping and wasteful activities**
- **Promotes innovative ideas**
- **Facilitates decision-making**
- **Establishes standards for controlling**

steps.title: Solved case 1
steps.body: A company sets a target of 20% sales growth so every department knows what to work towards. → **Provides direction.**

steps.title: Solved case 2
steps.body: A firm compares actual output with planned targets every month. → Planning **establishes standards for controlling**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying planning *eliminates* uncertainty — it only reduces the risk.
- Treating planning as a one-time activity.

activity.prompt: Match the case to the importance of planning
pairs: Everyone knows the target and works towards it
Backup supplier lined up in case of a strike
Two departments stop doing the same survey
Managers brainstorm new ways to reach goals
Targets become the yardstick for review

options: In advance what to do and how
quiz.why: Planning is deciding in advance what to do, how to do it and who will do it.
Planning reduces the risk of uncertainty, since it forecasts the future and prepares for it.
Planning gives the targets and standards used for controlling, so it provides the basis for controlling.
Planning facilitates decision-making, as the manager has goals and alternatives in front of them.

options: Where we are and where we want to be
quiz.why: Planning is the bridge between where we are now and where we want to be.

scenes.text: A detailed plan assumed fuel prices would stay steady.
Prices doubled.
Plans help — but they have limits.

steps.title: Features
steps.body:
- Focuses on achieving objectives
- Primary function of management (precedes other functions)
- Pervasive (all levels, all departments)
- Continuous
- Futuristic
- Involves decision-making (choosing among alternatives)
- A mental exercise (requires thinking, foresight and judgement)

steps.title: Limitations
steps.body:
- Leads to **rigidity**
- May not work in a **dynamic environment**
- **Reduces creativity** (middle managers just follow)
- Involves **huge costs**
- Is a **time-consuming** process
- **Does not guarantee success** (can create false sense of security)

steps.title: Solved case 1
steps.body: "Managers followed last year's plan exactly although customers' tastes had changed." → limitation: **rigidity** / does not work in dynamic environment.

steps.title: Solved case 2
steps.body: "Planning is done at the top, middle and lower levels." → feature: **pervasive**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Writing "planning guarantees success".
- Confusing "primary function" with "pervasive".

activity.prompt: Feature or limitation of planning?

quiz.q: Planning precedes other functions — it is:
quiz.why: Planning comes before all the other functions (organising, staffing, directing, controlling), so it is primary.

quiz.q: Planning is done at all levels — it is:
quiz.why: Planning is needed at all levels of management and in all departments, so it is pervasive.
Rigidity is a limitation of planning, as plans may not be changed when the situation changes.
Planning looks ahead and prepares for the future, so it is futuristic.

quiz.q: Planning requires choosing among alternatives, so it:
quiz.why: Planning means choosing the best from various alternatives, so it involves decision-making.

scenes.text: Goal: open 10 new stores this year.
Assume demand rises 8% (premise).
Compare options, choose, act, review.

steps.title: Steps
steps.body:
1. **Setting objectives**
2. **Developing premises** (assumptions about the future — forecasts)
3. **Identifying alternative courses of action**
4. **Evaluating alternative courses** (pros and cons)
5. **Selecting an alternative**
6. **Implementing the plan**
7. **Follow-up action** (monitoring)

steps.title: Solved case 1
steps.body: "The manager assumed that the government would not change the GST rate in the coming year." → step: **developing premises**.

steps.title: Solved case 2
steps.body: "The team compared three locations on cost, footfall and rent." → step: **evaluating alternative courses**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Putting "selecting an alternative" before "evaluating".
- Forgetting follow-up action as the last step.

activity.prompt: Arrange the steps of the planning process

quiz.why: Planning premises are assumptions about the future conditions under which the plan will operate.
The first step of the planning process is setting objectives, since everything else depends on them.

quiz.q: Comparing pros and cons of alternatives:
quiz.why: Comparing the merits and demerits of the different alternatives is evaluating the alternatives.
Checking and monitoring the plan after implementation is the follow-up action.
Putting the chosen plan into action is implementing the plan.

scenes.text: "Increase sales by 10%" is an objective.
"No smoking in the factory" is a rule.
"Steps to process a refund" is a procedure.

steps.title: Single-use vs standing plans
steps.body:
**Single-use plans:** for a one-time event — programmes, budgets, specific projects.
**Standing plans:** used repeatedly — policies, procedures, methods, rules.

steps.title: Eight types
steps.body:
- **Objectives:** end results (e.g. 15% return on investment)
- **Strategy:** comprehensive plan to achieve objectives, considering environment (e.g. enter rural markets with small packs)
- **Policy:** general statement guiding decisions (e.g. "we sell only for cash")
- **Procedure:** chronological steps to carry out an activity
- **Method:** prescribed way of performing a task (best way)
- **Rule:** specific statement of what must/must not be done — no discretion
- **Programme:** detailed statement of a project: objectives, policies, procedures, rules, tasks, resources
- **Budget:** plan stated in numerical terms (e.g. sales budget)

steps.title: Solved case 1
steps.body: "No employee shall use a mobile phone on the shop floor; violation attracts a fine." → **Rule**.

steps.title: Solved case 2
steps.body: "Recruitment: (1) receive application, (2) screen, (3) test, (4) interview, (5) offer." → **Procedure**. "Our company will recruit only through campus placements." → **Policy**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Confusing policy (flexible guide) with rule (rigid, no discretion).
- Confusing procedure (sequence of steps) with method (way of doing one step).

activity.prompt: Match each example to the type of plan
pairs: Steps for processing a purchase order
Expected sales of ₹2 crore next year
Launch small sachets for rural markets to beat a rival

quiz.q: A plan with no scope for discretion:
quiz.why: A rule is a specific statement of what must be done, and it allows no discretion.

quiz.q: Budget is a plan expressed in:
quiz.why: A budget is a plan expressed in numerical terms.

quiz.q: Chronological steps to perform a routine activity:
quiz.why: A procedure lays down the chronological sequence of steps to perform a routine activity.
Programmes and budgets are made for a specific purpose and are not repeated, so they are single-use plans.
A strategy is made after considering the business environment (competitors, customers and other forces).

questions.q: Planning is a ___ function.
questions.why: Planning comes before other functions of management, so it is a primary function.

questions.q: Premises are:
questions.why: Planning premises are assumptions about the future, which form the base of the plan.

questions.q: Rule allows:
questions.why: A rule is a rigid directive that leaves no scope for discretion.

questions.q: Planning reduces:
questions.why: Planning reduces the risk of uncertainty by forecasting and preparing for changes.

questions.q: Last step of planning process:
questions.why: The last step of the planning process is the follow-up action, which checks whether the plan is working.

questions.q: Assertion: Planning may lead to rigidity. Reason: Managers may be unable to change plans as circumstances change.
questions.why: Both are true. A plan fixed in advance can become rigid if managers cannot change it as circumstances change.

questions.q: Budget is a ___ plan.
questions.why: A budget is made for a specific period or purpose and is not reused as such, so it is a single-use plan.

questions.q: Case: "Our company will give 10% discount to bulk buyers." Type of plan:
questions.why: A general guideline for decision-making, such as giving a 10% discount to bulk buyers, is a policy.

questions.q: Case: The company forecasted that the monsoon would be normal and demand for tractors would rise. Step:
questions.why: Assuming a normal monsoon and rising tractor demand is forecasting future conditions, which is developing premises.

questions.q: Case: A detailed plan for opening a new plant includes tasks, resources, steps and timelines. Type:
questions.why: A detailed plan with tasks, resources, steps and timelines is a programme.

questions.q: Case: Middle managers stopped suggesting new ideas because everything was decided by the plan. Limitation:
questions.why: When plans leave no room for fresh ideas, managers stop thinking creatively. That is the limitation 'reduces creativity'.

questions.q: Case: A firm spent ₹10 lakh and three months on market research before planning a launch, but a sudden lockdown made the plan useless. Limitations shown:
options: Huge cost, time-consuming, may not work in dynamic environment
questions.why: The planning cost a lot (₹10 lakh), took time (three months) and failed because the environment changed suddenly. All three limitations are shown.

questions.q: Case: The manager told staff that "the best way to stitch this collar is in 6 standard moves." Type:
questions.why: A prescribed way of doing a particular task (6 standard moves) is a method.

questions.q: Case: Faced with a new rival, a firm decides to launch a cheaper brand and expand into tier-2 cities. Type of plan:
questions.why: A plan to deal with a rival (a cheaper brand and expansion) is a strategy, which is made keeping the environment and competitors in mind.

questions.q: Which pair is correctly matched?
options: Policy — no discretion; Rule — guide to thinking
Policy — guide to thinking; Rule — no discretion
questions.why: A policy is a general guide to thinking in decision-making, whereas a rule is a rigid statement that leaves no discretion. Budget is a single-use plan.

questions.q: Case: Planning is done by the CEO for the company, by the marketing head for her department and by supervisors for daily shifts. Features shown:
questions.why: Planning done by the CEO, department heads and supervisors at different levels shows it is pervasive. It goes on every day, so it is also continuous.

questions.q: Planning is a mental exercise because it requires:
questions.why: Planning is a mental exercise because it needs thinking, foresight and judgement instead of physical effort.

courses.title: Ch 5 · Organising
courses.summary: Meaning, steps and importance of organising; organisation structure and span of management; functional and divisional structures; formal and informal organisation; delegation and decentralisation.
outcomes: Learners can explain the steps and importance of organising
Learners can compare functional and divisional structures
Learners can distinguish formal and informal organisation
Learners can explain elements of delegation
Learners can explain decentralisation and compare it with delegation

lessons.title: Meaning, steps and importance of organising

scenes.text: The fest has 40 volunteers and 20 tasks.
Group tasks into teams: stage, food, tickets.
Each team gets a head and clear duties.

steps.title: Meaning
steps.body: **Organising** is the process of identifying and grouping the work to be done, defining and delegating responsibility and authority, and establishing relationships so that people work together most effectively towards objectives.

steps.title: Steps
steps.body:
1. **Identification and division of work**
2. **Departmentalisation** (grouping similar activities)
3. **Assignment of duties**
4. **Establishing reporting relationships**

steps.title: Importance
steps.body:
- Benefits of specialisation
- Clarity in working relationships
- Optimum utilisation of resources
- Adaptation to change
- Effective administration
- Development of personnel
- Expansion and growth

steps.title: Solved case 1
steps.body: "Activities of similar nature were grouped into Purchase, Production and Sales departments." → step: **departmentalisation**.

steps.title: Solved case 2
steps.body: "Each employee knows to whom he reports." → importance: **clarity in working relationships** (and step: establishing reporting relationships).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Mixing organising (structure) with staffing (filling posts).
- Getting the order of steps wrong.

activity.prompt: Arrange the steps of organising

quiz.why: Grouping similar or related activities into departments is departmentalisation.
Organising avoids duplication and overlapping of work, so resources are used to the best advantage. This is optimum utilisation of resources.
The last step of the organising process is establishing reporting relationships, which says who reports to whom.

options: Work is divided into manageable tasks
quiz.why: Organising divides work into small, manageable tasks and assigns them to people, which leads to specialisation.

options: Adding new departments and positions easily
quiz.why: A good organisation structure lets the firm add new departments and positions easily, which helps growth.

scenes.text: A small shoe firm has Purchase, Production and Sales heads.
It now makes shoes, bags and belts.
Should it switch to product divisions?

steps.title: Structure and span
steps.body: **Organisation structure** = framework within which managerial and operating tasks are performed. **Span of management** = number of subordinates a manager can effectively manage; it decides the levels in the structure.

steps.title: Functional structure
steps.body:
Grouping by functions (production, marketing, finance, HR).
**Suitable:** large firms with a single product line; need for specialisation.
**Advantages:** specialisation, coordination within a function, managerial efficiency, minimal duplication, training of specialists, focus on functions.
**Disadvantages:** functional objectives over organisational objectives, inter-departmental coordination problems, conflict of interests, inflexibility (narrow perspective).

steps.title: Divisional structure
steps.body:
Grouping by products/markets; each division has its own functions.
**Suitable:** diversified firms with many product lines.
**Advantages:** product specialisation and development of managers, fixing accountability (division as profit centre), flexibility and quick decisions, easy expansion (new division).
**Disadvantages:** conflict among divisions over resources, duplication of functions/costs, divisional managers may ignore organisational interests.

steps.title: Solved case 1
steps.body: A company manufactures only steel and needs deep specialisation → **functional structure**.

steps.title: Solved case 2
steps.body: A company makes cement, textiles and software → **divisional structure** (each division accountable for its own profits).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Choosing functional structure for a highly diversified company.
- Saying divisional structure avoids duplication — it causes duplication.

activity.prompt: Functional or divisional structure?

items.text: Each unit is a profit centre
Easy to add a new product unit
Departments may chase their own goals

options: Number of subordinates under a manager
quiz.why: Span of management is the number of subordinates who report directly to one manager.
A company with diversified products suits the divisional structure, where each product has its own division.

quiz.q: Accountability is easy to fix in:
quiz.why: In the divisional structure, each division's performance is clear, so accountability is easy to fix.

quiz.q: Functional structure is grouped on the basis of:
quiz.why: A functional structure groups jobs by function, such as production, marketing and finance.
Each division in a divisional structure needs its own functional departments, which duplicates activities and raises costs.

scenes.text: The org chart shows who reports to whom.
At lunch, friends from different departments share news.
Rumours spread faster than circulars.

steps.title: Formal organisation
steps.body:
Structure deliberately designed by management; clearly defined roles and relationships; follows rules, chain of command.
**Advantages:** easy to fix responsibility, no duplication, unity of command, clear objectives, stability.
**Limitations:** delays (procedures), may ignore human needs, rigid, does not capture all relationships.

steps.title: Informal organisation
steps.body:
Network of social relationships that arises from interaction among employees; no written rules; communication through the **grapevine**; independent channels.
**Advantages:** fast communication, fulfils social needs, complements formal organisation (feedback).
**Limitations:** spreads rumours, may resist change, pressure to conform to group norms.

steps.title: Solved case 1
steps.body: Employees from different departments form a cricket team and share work tips informally. → **Informal organisation**.

steps.title: Solved case 2
steps.body: A rumour about layoffs spreads quickly; management uses the informal network to quickly correct it. → Managers can use informal organisation to **complement** formal communication.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying informal organisation is created by management.
- Claiming informal organisation has no advantages.

activity.prompt: Formal or informal organisation?

quiz.why: The grapevine, the informal network of communication, belongs to the informal organisation.
A formal organisation is deliberately created by management, with defined roles and relationships.
A limitation of informal organisation is that it can spread rumours (and distort information).
An informal organisation gives employees social satisfaction and a sense of belonging.
Formal organisation follows set procedures, which can cause delays in getting things done.

scenes.text: The sales head cannot visit every client.
She gives her deputy authority to approve discounts up to 5%.
But she remains answerable to the CEO.

steps.title: Meaning
steps.body: **Delegation** is the downward transfer of authority from a superior to a subordinate. It is necessary for effective functioning but does not mean abdication — the manager is still accountable.

steps.title: Elements
steps.body:
- **Authority:** right to give commands; flows **downward**; can be delegated
- **Responsibility:** obligation of a subordinate to perform the duty; flows **upward**; arises from superior–subordinate relationship; cannot be entirely delegated
- **Accountability:** answerability for the final outcome; flows **upward**; **cannot be delegated**
Authority should match responsibility.

steps.title: Importance
steps.body: Effective management (frees managers for important work), employee development, motivation, facilitation of growth, basis of management hierarchy, better coordination.

steps.title: Solved case 1
steps.body: The production manager gives a supervisor authority to hire temporary workers but the supervisor hires the wrong people. The production manager still answers to the CEO. → **Accountability cannot be delegated.**

steps.title: Solved case 2
steps.body: A subordinate is asked to cut costs by 10% but is not allowed to change suppliers → authority not matching responsibility.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying accountability can be delegated.
- Saying authority flows upward.

activity.prompt: Match the element of delegation to its feature
pairs: Answerability for outcome; cannot be delegated

quiz.why: Accountability cannot be delegated. A manager remains answerable for the work even after delegating it.
Authority flows from superiors to subordinates, that is downward.
Responsibility arises from the superior–subordinate relationship, because a subordinate is bound to carry out the assigned duty.
Delegation gives employees chances to take decisions and use their skills, so it helps them to develop.
Even after delegating a task, the manager remains accountable for the result.

scenes.text: A retail chain has 200 stores across India.
Store managers decide local promotions.
Head office decides only major policies.

steps.title: Meaning
steps.body: **Decentralisation** is the systematic delegation of authority to all levels, keeping only the most important decisions (policy, major investments) at the top. No organisation is completely centralised or decentralised; a balance is needed.

steps.title: Importance
steps.body:
- Develops initiative among subordinates
- Develops managerial talent for the future
- Quick decision-making
- Relief to top management
- Facilitates growth
- Better control (performance at each level can be evaluated)

steps.title: Delegation vs decentralisation
steps.body:
- Delegation: compulsory for work to be done; decentralisation: optional policy decision of top management
- Delegation: narrow scope (superior → immediate subordinate); decentralisation: wide (all levels)
- Delegation: more control by superior; decentralisation: less control by top
- Delegation: a process/technique; decentralisation: the result of the policy of systematic delegation

steps.title: Solved case 1
steps.body: "Branch managers can now approve loans up to ₹10 lakh without asking head office." → **Decentralisation** → quick decisions.

steps.title: Solved case 2
steps.body: "Only the board decides on new plants; everything else is decided at plant level." → decentralisation with major policy decisions retained at the top.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Treating delegation and decentralisation as identical.
- Saying decentralisation is compulsory.

activity.prompt: Delegation or decentralisation?

items.text: Compulsory for any manager to get work done
An optional policy of top management
Spread of authority to all levels
Between a superior and immediate subordinate
Develops managerial talent across the organisation

quiz.why: Decentralisation is optional. Top management decides how much authority to spread across the organisation.
Decentralisation puts decision-making near the point of action, which gives quicker decisions.
Delegation of authority is narrow in scope. Decentralisation is a wider, systematic spread of authority at all levels.
Decentralisation relieves top management of routine decisions, so they can focus on strategy.
Complete decentralisation would mean no control by top management, so it is neither possible nor desirable.

questions.q: Departmentalisation is a step in:
questions.why: Departmentalisation, grouping similar activities, is a step in the process of organising.

questions.q: Grapevine is part of:
questions.why: The grapevine is an informal communication network that is part of the informal organisation.

questions.q: Accountability:
questions.why: Accountability cannot be passed on to anyone. It remains with the delegating manager.

questions.q: Functional structure suits:
questions.why: A functional structure suits firms with a single product or a few related products, where specialisation by function is important.

questions.q: Span of management determines:
questions.why: The span of management (number of subordinates per manager) determines how many levels there are in the structure.

questions.q: Assertion: Decentralisation is an optional policy. Reason: Top management decides how far authority is spread.
questions.why: Both are true. Top management decides how far authority is spread, so decentralisation is optional.

questions.q: Case: A company making cosmetics, garments and food items. Best structure:
questions.why: A company that makes cosmetics, garments and food items has diversified products, so the divisional structure suits it.

questions.q: Case: Employees of different departments started a book club and share information quickly. This is:
questions.why: A group that forms out of social interaction (a book club) and shares information quickly is an informal organisation.

questions.q: Case: The marketing head was asked to raise sales but not given authority to spend on promotion. Principle ignored:
questions.why: The marketing head was given responsibility but not the authority to spend on promotion. This breaks the rule that authority must match responsibility.

questions.q: Case: Plant managers of a company can now hire workers and buy materials independently; top management only decides expansion. Concept:
questions.why: When plant managers can take decisions on hiring and purchases and top management only decides expansion, authority is spread downward. This is decentralisation.

questions.q: Case: In a functional structure, the production and marketing heads blame each other for falling sales. Disadvantage:
questions.why: In a functional structure, departments can blame each other and pursue their own interests, which gives coordination problems and conflict.

questions.q: Case: A divisional company finds that each division has its own accounts and HR teams, raising costs. Disadvantage:
questions.why: Each division having its own accounts and HR teams repeats functions, which raises costs. This is duplication of functions.

questions.q: Case: A manager delegated authority to an assistant, who made an error causing a loss. The CEO holds the manager answerable. Element:
questions.why: Even after delegating, the manager is still answerable to the CEO for the loss. That is accountability.

questions.q: Which is TRUE?
options: Authority flows downward; accountability flows upward
questions.why: Authority flows downward from superior to subordinate, while accountability flows upward, as the subordinate is answerable to the superior.

questions.q: Case: A growing firm adds a new "Kids' wear" unit with its own production and sales team without disturbing other units. Advantage illustrated:
questions.why: A divisional structure lets a firm add a new product division with its own team without disturbing the others, so it facilitates expansion.

questions.q: Organising helps optimum utilisation of resources by:
questions.why: Organising avoids duplication and overlapping of work, so resources are used fully and effectively.

questions.q: Informal organisation arises from:
questions.why: The informal organisation arises from the social interaction among employees, and is not designed by management.

courses.title: Ch 6 · Staffing
courses.summary: Meaning and importance of staffing, staffing as part of human resource management, the staffing process, recruitment (internal and external sources), the selection process, and training and development methods.
outcomes: Learners can explain the meaning and importance of staffing
Learners can list the steps of the staffing process
Learners can compare internal and external sources of recruitment
Learners can describe the selection process
Learners can distinguish training, development and education and classify training methods

lessons.title: Meaning, importance and process of staffing

scenes.text: A new café is ready — but has no baristas.
The owner estimates she needs 6 staff.
Then she must find, choose, train and keep them.

steps.title: Meaning
steps.body: **Staffing** is filling and keeping filled the positions in the organisation structure — through estimating manpower needs, recruitment, selection, placement, training, appraisal, promotion and compensation. It is a function of every manager and is part of **Human Resource Management** (HRM).

steps.title: Importance
steps.body:
- Obtains competent personnel
- Ensures higher performance (right person in the right job)
- Ensures continuous survival and growth (succession planning)
- Optimum utilisation of human resources (avoids over/under-manning)
- Improves job satisfaction and morale

steps.title: Staffing process
steps.body:
1. **Estimating manpower requirements** (workload analysis — number and type needed; workforce analysis — number available)
2. **Recruitment** (searching and stimulating candidates to apply)
3. **Selection** (choosing the best)
4. **Placement and orientation**
5. **Training and development**
6. **Performance appraisal**
7. **Promotion and career planning**
8. **Compensation**

steps.title: Solved case 1
steps.body: "The HR manager compared the workers needed for next year's production with those available." → step: **estimating manpower requirements** (workload + workforce analysis).

steps.title: Solved case 2
steps.body: "New employees were introduced to colleagues and shown the rules on their first day." → **orientation** (induction).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Confusing placement (putting the selected person in the job) with orientation (introducing to the organisation).
- Thinking staffing is only the HR department's job — every manager staffs.

activity.prompt: Arrange the staffing process

options: Number and type of employees needed
quiz.why: Workload analysis estimates how much work there is, and so how many people and what types of people are needed.

options: Introducing new employee to the organisation
quiz.why: Orientation (induction) introduces a new employee to the organisation, its rules, people and work.
Staffing is the responsibility of every manager, since every manager has to select, train and appraise the people working under them, even though HR may help.

quiz.q: Right person in the right job leads to:
quiz.why: Putting the right person in the right job means the person has the right skills for it, so work is done better and performance rises.
Performance appraisal means evaluating an employee's actual performance against the standards set for the job.

scenes.text: A senior accountant post falls vacant.
An internal clerk is promoted, creating another vacancy.
For the clerk's post, the firm advertises online.

steps.title: Meaning
steps.body: **Recruitment** is the process of searching for prospective employees and stimulating them to apply. It is a **positive** process (increases the pool of applicants); selection is **negative** (rejects many).

steps.title: Internal sources
steps.body:
**Transfer** (shifting an employee to another job of similar status) and **Promotion** (shifting to a higher position).
Merits: motivates employees, simpler and cheaper selection, tool of training, shifting of workforce from surplus to deficient departments.
Limitations: limits fresh talent, may reduce competition among employees, frequent transfers lower productivity, new enterprise cannot use it.

steps.title: External sources
steps.body:
Direct recruitment (notice at gate), casual callers, advertisement, employment exchange, placement agencies and management consultants, campus recruitment, recommendations of employees, labour contractors, web publishing (job portals).
Merits: qualified personnel, wider choice, fresh talent, competitive spirit.
Limitations: dissatisfaction among existing staff, lengthy process, costly.

steps.title: Solved case 1
steps.body: "Unskilled workers were hired for a sudden rush by putting a notice at the factory gate." → **Direct recruitment**.

steps.title: Solved case 2
steps.body: "Final-year students of a business school were interviewed on campus." → **Campus recruitment**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling recruitment a negative process.
- Listing promotion as an external source.

activity.prompt: Internal or external source?

quiz.why: Recruitment is a positive process because it attracts as many suitable candidates as possible to apply.
A transfer moves an existing employee from one job or place to another within the organisation, so it is an internal source of recruitment.
Filling posts from within the organisation does not bring in new ideas and talent, so internal sources limit fresh talent.
External sources give a wider choice and bring in fresh talent and new ideas.

quiz.q: Applications kept on file from job seekers who walk in:
quiz.why: Job seekers who walk in without being called and leave applications are 'casual callers', and their applications are kept on file for future vacancies.

scenes.text: 200 applications for 3 posts.
Tests, interviews, checks.
Three people get offers.

steps.title: Steps
steps.body:
1. **Preliminary screening**
2. **Selection tests:** intelligence, aptitude, personality, trade (skill), interest tests
3. **Employment interview**
4. **Reference and background checks**
5. **Selection decision**
6. **Medical examination**
7. **Job offer**
8. **Contract of employment**

steps.title: Types of tests
steps.body:
- **Intelligence test:** IQ, mental ability
- **Aptitude test:** potential to learn new skills
- **Personality test:** emotions, maturity, value system
- **Trade test:** existing skills/knowledge
- **Interest test:** pattern of interests/involvement

steps.title: Solved case 1
steps.body: "Candidates for a typist post were asked to type a letter to check speed and accuracy." → **Trade test**.

steps.title: Solved case 2
steps.body: "The firm checked with the candidate's previous employer about his conduct." → **Reference and background checks**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Confusing aptitude (potential) with trade (existing skill).
- Placing medical examination before the selection decision (NCERT order: decision → medical → job offer).

activity.prompt: Match the situation to the selection test
pairs: Checking how fast a driver can learn a new truck model
Checking a welder's current welding skill
Finding which activities a candidate enjoys

quiz.why: Selection is called a negative process because it rejects many candidates in order to choose the few suitable ones.

quiz.q: A test of existing skill is:
quiz.why: A trade test checks the existing skills of a candidate, while an aptitude test checks potential to learn.
The first step of selection is preliminary screening, which quickly removes unsuitable applicants from the list.
The last step of the selection process is the contract of employment, signed after the job offer is accepted.

quiz.q: Potential to learn is measured by:
