quiz.why: An aptitude test measures an individual's potential to learn new skills.

scenes.text: A new technician works under a master craftsman for two years.
Managers attend a leadership workshop.
Both grow — differently.

steps.title: Training, development, education
steps.body:
**Training:** increasing knowledge and skills of an employee for doing a particular job (job-oriented).
**Development:** overall growth of the employee (career-oriented).
**Education:** increasing general knowledge and understanding of the environment.

steps.title: Benefits
steps.body:
To organisation: less wastage, higher productivity, prepares future managers, lower absenteeism and turnover, helps adapt to change.
To employees: better career, higher earnings, safer handling of machines, higher morale.

steps.title: Methods
steps.body:
**On-the-job:** apprenticeship programmes, coaching, internship training, job rotation.
**Off-the-job:** classroom lectures/conferences, films, case studies, computer modelling, **vestibule training** (dummy workplace with similar equipment), programmed instruction.

steps.title: Solved case 1
steps.body: "Workers practise on equipment set up in a separate room that copies the shop floor." → **Vestibule training**.

steps.title: Solved case 2
steps.body:
"A trainee electrician works under a master worker for a fixed period." → **Apprenticeship**.
"Management trainees spend 3 months each in production, sales and finance." → **Job rotation**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling vestibule training an on-the-job method — it is off-the-job.
- Treating training and development as the same.

activity.prompt: On-the-job or off-the-job method?

quiz.why: Training is job-oriented: it improves the skills and knowledge needed to do a particular job.
Development is career-oriented and aims at the overall growth of the employee, not only at one job.
Vestibule training happens away from the actual workplace in a simulated setting, so it is an off-the-job method.
Moving trainees from one department or job to another to give wide experience is job rotation.

quiz.q: A benefit of training to the organisation:
quiz.why: Trained employees make fewer mistakes, so training reduces wastage of materials.

questions.q: Staffing fills positions in the:
questions.why: Staffing fills the positions created in the organisation structure by placing suitable people in them.

questions.q: Promotion is a/an ___ source.
questions.why: A promotion moves an existing employee to a higher post, so it is an internal source of recruitment.

questions.q: Recruitment is:
questions.why: Recruitment is positive because it encourages many people to apply, in contrast to selection, which rejects.

questions.q: Vestibule training is:
questions.why: Vestibule training takes place off the job, in a place that copies the work conditions.

questions.q: Workforce analysis estimates:
questions.why: Workforce analysis estimates the supply, the number of people available. Workload analysis estimates how many are needed.

questions.q: Assertion: Selection is called a negative process. Reason: It rejects more candidates than it accepts.
questions.why: Both are true. Selection rejects many candidates and chooses only a few, so it is called a negative process.

questions.q: Case: A company asks applicants for a pilot post to take a test of hand–eye coordination potential. Test:
questions.why: A test of potential (such as hand–eye coordination) that predicts how well someone will learn a skill is an aptitude test.

questions.q: Case: Temporary workers were hired through a contractor for a short project. Source:
questions.why: Temporary workers hired through a contractor for a short project come from labour contractors, an external source.

questions.q: Case: Employees are dissatisfied because outsiders were hired for senior posts. Limitation of:
questions.why: Employees feel dissatisfied if outsiders get senior posts they hoped for, which is a limitation of external sources.

questions.q: Case: Trainees learn by working under a senior who guides and gives feedback daily. Method:
questions.why: Learning on the job under a senior who guides and gives feedback regularly is coaching.

questions.q: Case: A newly selected employee is shown the canteen, rules and team members. Step:
questions.why: Introducing the new employee to the workplace, rules and colleagues is orientation (induction).

questions.q: Case: A firm found it had 40 surplus workers in one plant and a shortage in another and shifted them. Source/merit:
options: Transfer — shifting workforce from surplus to deficient departments
questions.why: Moving the workforce from a surplus plant to one with a shortage is a transfer, which is used to meet shortages from within.

questions.q: Case: A firm uses an online portal to post jobs and screen CVs. Source:
questions.why: Posting jobs and screening CVs on an online portal is web publishing, a source of external recruitment.

questions.q: Correct order:
options: Selection decision → Medical examination → Job offer
questions.why: The selection decision is made first, followed by the medical examination, and then the job offer.

questions.q: Case: A firm wants to prepare employees for future leadership roles through workshops on strategy and conflict management. This is:
questions.why: Preparing employees for future leadership with workshops on strategy and conflict is development, which is career-oriented and long-term.

questions.q: Job rotation is a/an ___ method.
questions.why: Job rotation takes place at the workplace as the trainee moves between jobs, so it is an on-the-job method.

questions.q: Staffing is a part of:
questions.why: Staffing deals with the people in an organisation, so it is a part of Human Resource Management.

courses.title: Ch 7 · Directing
courses.summary: Meaning, importance and principles of directing; its elements — supervision, motivation (Maslow's need hierarchy; financial and non-financial incentives), leadership (styles and qualities) and communication (process, formal/informal, barriers and how to overcome them).
outcomes: Learners can explain the meaning, importance and principles of directing
Learners can explain Maslow's need hierarchy and incentives
Learners can describe leadership styles and qualities
Learners can explain the communication process, networks and barriers

lessons.title: Meaning, importance and principles of directing; supervision

scenes.text: The plan is ready; staff are hired.
Now someone must instruct, guide, motivate and lead.
That is directing.

steps.title: Meaning
steps.body: **Directing** = instructing, guiding, communicating and inspiring people to achieve objectives. It initiates action, takes place at every level, is continuous and flows from top to bottom.

steps.title: Importance
steps.body: Initiates action; integrates employees' efforts; motivates to realise potential; facilitates introduction of changes; brings stability and balance.

steps.title: Principles
steps.body: Maximum individual contribution; harmony of objectives; unity of command; appropriateness of direction technique; managerial communication; use of informal organisation; leadership; follow-through.

steps.title: Supervision
steps.body: Overseeing subordinates at work. A **supervisor** maintains day-to-day contact, is a link between workers and management, maintains group unity, ensures performance, provides on-the-job training, builds morale and gives feedback.

steps.title: Solved case 1
steps.body: A manager convinces employees to accept new software by explaining its benefits → importance: **facilitates introduction of changes**.

steps.title: Solved case 2
steps.body: A manager regularly checks whether his instructions are being followed and helps solve problems → principle: **follow-through**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying directing happens only at top level.
- Forgetting that supervision is an element of directing, not a separate function.

activity.prompt: Match the case to the principle of directing
pairs: Each worker gets orders from only one boss
Manager checks implementation of orders and helps
Personal goals of staff aligned with company goals
Manager uses the grapevine to spread correct information
Choose motivation technique suited to the person

quiz.why: Directing is the function that initiates action: it gets people to start working according to plans.
Directing flows from top to bottom, with each manager directing their subordinates.
A supervisor is the link between the workers and the management, passing orders down and workers' problems up.

quiz.q: Which is an element of directing?
quiz.why: The elements of directing are supervision, motivation, leadership and communication. Recruitment and budgeting belong to other functions.

options: Reducing resistance through communication and motivation
quiz.why: Good directing, through communication, motivation and leadership, reduces employees' resistance to change.

scenes.text: A new worker first needs a salary for food and rent.
Then job security.
Later, recognition and growth matter more.

steps.title: Meaning
steps.body: **Motivation** is the process of stimulating people to act to achieve desired goals. Key terms: **motive** (inner state that energises behaviour), **motivation** (process), **motivators** (techniques like pay, bonus, recognition). Motivation is an internal feeling; it is complex and can be positive or negative.

steps.title: Maslow's need hierarchy (lowest to highest)
steps.body:
1. **Physiological:** food, shelter — basic salary
2. **Safety/security:** job security, stability of income, pension
3. **Affiliation/belonging:** friendship, acceptance
4. **Esteem:** self-respect, status, recognition
5. **Self-actualisation:** becoming what one is capable of — growth, self-fulfilment
Assumptions: needs are hierarchical; a satisfied need no longer motivates; a person moves to the next level only when the lower is satisfied.

steps.title: Solved case 1
steps.body: "An employee with a good salary and job security now wants to be part of a friendly team." → next need: **affiliation/belonging**.

steps.title: Solved case 2
steps.body: "A senior scientist is offered challenging projects to reach her full potential." → **self-actualisation**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Putting esteem below affiliation (order: physiological → safety → affiliation → esteem → self-actualisation).
- Saying a satisfied need still motivates.

activity.prompt: Order Maslow's needs from lowest to highest

quiz.why: Self-actualisation, the need to achieve one's full potential, is the highest level in Maslow's hierarchy.
Job security gives protection against future loss or harm, so it satisfies safety needs.
Recognition and status give self-respect and respect from others, which are esteem needs.
Basic salary pays for food, clothing and shelter, so it satisfies physiological needs.
According to Maslow, a need that is already satisfied no longer motivates a person. Only the next unsatisfied need does.

scenes.text: The bonus was nice but lasted a month.
Being named "Employee of the Year" stayed with Priya for years.
Good firms use both.

steps.title: Financial incentives
steps.body: Pay and allowances; productivity-linked wage incentives; bonus; profit sharing; co-partnership/employee stock option; retirement benefits (provident fund, pension, gratuity); perquisites (car, housing, medical aid).

steps.title: Non-financial incentives
steps.body: Status; organisational climate; career advancement opportunity; **job enrichment** (more challenging, varied, autonomous work); employee recognition programmes; job security; employee participation (joint committees, suggestion schemes); employee empowerment (more autonomy and power).

steps.title: Solved case 1
steps.body: "Employees get shares of the company at a lower price." → **Co-partnership / Employee Stock Option** (financial).

steps.title: Solved case 2
steps.body: "A designer's job is redesigned to include planning and client handling, with more freedom." → **Job enrichment** (non-financial; satisfies higher-order needs).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling job security a financial incentive — it is non-financial.
- Confusing job enrichment (more depth/responsibility) with job rotation (moving between jobs).

activity.prompt: Financial or non-financial incentive?

quiz.why: A stock option gives employees shares at a fixed price, which is a monetary reward, so it is a financial incentive.
Job enrichment gives more responsibility and challenging work, which satisfies higher-order needs like esteem and self-actualisation.
A good organisational climate (positive work environment) is a non-financial incentive.
Retirement benefits like pension and provident fund are monetary, so they are financial incentives.
Employee participation involves workers in decisions through suggestion schemes, joint committees and worker directors.

scenes.text: Captain A decides everything alone.
Captain B asks the team before deciding.
Captain C lets players decide on their own.

steps.title: Meaning and importance
steps.body: **Leadership** is the process of influencing the behaviour of people to make them strive voluntarily towards group goals. Importance: influences behaviour, maintains personal relations, introduces changes, handles conflicts, trains subordinates.

steps.title: Leadership styles
steps.body:
- **Autocratic (authoritarian):** gives orders, expects obedience; one-way communication; quick decisions; suits unskilled staff/emergencies
- **Democratic (participative):** consults subordinates; two-way communication; encourages ideas
- **Laissez-faire (free-rein):** minimal leader role; subordinates decide; suits highly skilled, self-motivated teams

steps.title: Qualities of a good leader
steps.body: Physical features, knowledge, integrity, initiative, communication skills, motivation skills, self-confidence, decisiveness, social skills.

steps.title: Solved case 1
steps.body: "The manager allows his research team of experts to set their own targets and methods." → **Laissez-faire**.

steps.title: Solved case 2
steps.body: "During a fire drill the supervisor gave clear orders and expected instant compliance." → **Autocratic** (appropriate for emergencies).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying one style is always best — the right style depends on the situation.
- Confusing leadership (influence) with supervision (overseeing work).

a.text: A machine breaks down and there is a risk of injury. Workers are confused. Which style should the supervisor use right now?

choices.label: Autocratic — give clear orders immediately
choices.feedback: Right: in an emergency quick, clear commands are needed.

choices.label: Laissez-faire — let workers figure it out
choices.feedback: Risky — confusion in an emergency can cause injury.

b.text: Next month the supervisor leads a team of experienced engineers designing a new process. Which style now?

choices.label: Democratic or free-rein — involve and trust the experts
choices.feedback: Yes: skilled, motivated people respond well to participation and freedom.

choices.label: Autocratic — dictate every step
choices.feedback: This may kill creativity among experts.

c.text: The situation worsens. The supervisor must act.

choices.label: Take charge and give clear orders

end1.text: Great leaders change style to fit the situation and the people.

end2.text: The engineers feel unheard; ideas dry up. Style must fit the team.

quiz.why: A democratic leader consults subordinates and involves them in decisions.
Laissez-faire (free-rein) leadership gives group members freedom, and works with highly skilled and self-motivated teams.
An autocratic leader gives orders and expects obedience, with communication flowing one way (from leader to followers).

options: Influence people to work willingly towards goals
quiz.why: Leadership is the ability to influence people so that they work willingly and enthusiastically towards the goals.

quiz.q: Which is a quality of a good leader?
quiz.why: Integrity (honesty and fairness) is a quality of a good leader. Rigidity, secrecy and indecisiveness are weaknesses.

scenes.text: A manager emails "Do the needful ASAP".
Three people understand three different things.
Communication failed — why?

steps.title: Process elements
steps.body: Sender → Message → **Encoding** → Media/channel → **Decoding** → Receiver → **Feedback**; **Noise** = any obstruction (poor connection, ambiguous words, gestures).

steps.title: Formal and informal communication
steps.body:
**Formal:** follows official chain; vertical (upward/downward) or horizontal (same level). Networks: single chain, wheel, circular, free flow, inverted V.
**Informal (grapevine):** no official channel; spreads fast; may distort. Grapevine networks: single strand, gossip, probability, cluster.

steps.title: Barriers
steps.body:
- **Semantic:** badly expressed message, symbols with different meanings, faulty translation, unclarified assumptions, technical jargon, body language
- **Psychological/emotional:** premature evaluation, lack of attention, loss by transmission and poor retention, distrust
- **Organisational:** rigid policy, rules and regulations, status, complex structure, lack of facilities
- **Personal:** fear of challenge to authority, lack of confidence of superior in subordinates, unwillingness to communicate, lack of proper incentives

steps.title: Improving communication
steps.body: Clarify ideas before communicating; communicate according to the needs of the receiver; consult others before communicating; be aware of language, tone and content; convey things of help and value to listeners; ensure proper feedback; communicate for present as well as future; follow up; be a good listener.

steps.title: Solved case 1
steps.body: A manager uses heavy technical terms with new workers who do not understand them → **semantic barrier (technical jargon)**.

steps.title: Solved case 2
steps.body: A subordinate hesitates to share a problem because he fears the boss → **personal barrier** (or psychological — distrust). A worker forms an opinion before the speaker finishes → **premature evaluation** (psychological).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling "status differences" a semantic barrier — it is organisational.
- Forgetting feedback in the communication process.

activity.prompt: Classify the barrier

quiz.why: Encoding is the process of turning the sender's message into words, symbols or gestures.
The grapevine is an informal communication channel that works outside the official hierarchy.
Differences in status between sender and receiver affect how openly information flows, and this is an organisational barrier.
Feedback from the receiver shows whether the message was understood as intended.

quiz.q: Body language and gesture decoding errors are:
quiz.why: Errors in decoding body language and gestures are semantic barriers (about the meaning of symbols).

questions.q: Directing takes place at:
questions.why: Directing is done by managers at all levels, because every manager has subordinates to guide.

questions.q: Lowest need in Maslow's hierarchy:
questions.why: Physiological needs (food, water, shelter) are at the lowest level of Maslow's hierarchy.

questions.q: Bonus is a/an:
questions.why: A bonus is extra money paid to employees, so it is a financial incentive.

questions.q: Grapevine spreads:
questions.why: The grapevine spreads quickly and in all directions, because it works through people talking to each other.

questions.q: Democratic leaders:
questions.why: Democratic leaders consult subordinates before taking decisions.

questions.q: Assertion: A satisfied need does not motivate. Reason: Behaviour is driven by unsatisfied needs (Maslow).
questions.why: Both are true. Per Maslow, behaviour is driven by unsatisfied needs, so a satisfied need no longer motivates.

questions.q: Technical jargon is a ___ barrier.
questions.why: Technical jargon that the receiver cannot understand is a semantic barrier, since it relates to meaning and language.

questions.q: Case: Employees are given more autonomy and challenging tasks. Incentive:
questions.why: Giving employees more autonomy and challenging tasks is job enrichment.

questions.q: Case: A worker who now has a secure job and friendly team wants a better designation and respect. Need:
questions.why: Once safety (secure job) and affiliation (friendly team) are satisfied, the worker looks for recognition and a better designation, which are esteem needs.

questions.q: Case: A new manager refuses to let staff share their views; workers obey but morale is low. Style:
questions.why: A manager who refuses to let staff share their views and expects obedience is autocratic.

questions.q: Case: A message sent through five levels got distorted by the time it reached workers. Barrier:
questions.why: A message passed through many levels loses or changes content, which is loss by transmission and poor retention (a psychological barrier).

questions.q: Case: A company lets workers form a committee that advises management on safety. Incentive:
questions.why: A committee of workers that advises management on safety is employee participation, a non-financial incentive.

questions.q: Case: The manager uses informal gatherings to understand employees' concerns and to pass on correct information. Principle of directing:
questions.why: Using informal gatherings to understand concerns and pass on correct information is the principle of making use of the informal organisation.

questions.q: Case: A supervisor says "excellent!" with a frown; workers think he is unhappy. Barrier:
questions.why: The supervisor's words say 'excellent' but his frown says otherwise, so workers misread him. This is a body-language decoding problem, a semantic barrier.

questions.q: Case: A team of expert designers is given broad goals and left to decide methods themselves; the leader only provides resources. Style and suitability:
questions.why: Broad goals, freedom to decide the methods and a leader who only provides resources describe laissez-faire leadership, which suits skilled and self-motivated teams.

questions.q: Which is correctly matched?
options: Pension — safety needs; Recognition — esteem needs
questions.why: A pension gives security, so it satisfies safety needs, and recognition gives esteem. The other pairs mismatch the needs.

questions.q: Supervision is an element of:
questions.why: Supervision, motivation, leadership and communication are the elements of directing.

courses.title: Ch 8 · Controlling
courses.summary: Meaning, importance and limitations of controlling; the relationship between planning and controlling; and the controlling process including critical point control and management by exception.
outcomes: Learners can explain the meaning and importance of controlling
Learners can state the limitations of controlling
Learners can explain the relationship between planning and controlling
Learners can describe each step of the controlling process

scenes.text: The school bus must reach by 7:45.
The transport head checks arrival times daily.
When buses run late, routes are changed.

steps.title: Meaning
steps.body: **Controlling** means ensuring that activities in an organisation are performed as per plans. It compares actual performance with standards, finds deviations and takes corrective action. It is a **goal-oriented**, **pervasive** (all levels, all organisations), **backward-looking** and **forward-looking** function.

steps.title: Importance
steps.body:
- Accomplishing organisational goals
- Judging accuracy of standards
- Making efficient use of resources
- Improving employee motivation
- Ensuring order and discipline
- Facilitating coordination in action

steps.title: Solved case 1
steps.body: "Regular checks revealed that the target of 500 units/day was too high given machine capacity; the standard was revised." → **Judging accuracy of standards**.

steps.title: Solved case 2
steps.body: "Strict monitoring reduced theft and dishonest behaviour." → **Ensuring order and discipline**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying controlling is only a post-mortem — it is also forward-looking (improves future plans).
- Thinking only top management controls.

activity.prompt: Match the case to the importance of controlling
pairs: Standard revised after checking it was unrealistic
Waste of raw material detected and reduced
Employees know they will be evaluated, so they work better
All departments work to common standards

quiz.q: Controlling ensures that activities are performed:
quiz.why: Controlling ensures that activities are carried out as per the plans, by measuring and correcting deviations.
Controlling looks backward, to review past performance, and forward, since lessons help plan the future.

options: It is needed at all levels and in all organisations
quiz.why: Controlling is pervasive because it is needed at all levels of management and in all types of organisations.
By comparing actual with standards, controlling shows whether the standards were accurate.

options: Employees know what is expected and how they will be judged
quiz.why: When employees know what is expected and how they will be judged, they work with more clarity, which improves motivation.

scenes.text: A plan says where to go.
Control checks if we are on the way.
Without one, the other is useless.

steps.title: Limitations
steps.body:
- **Difficulty in setting quantitative standards** (e.g. employee morale, job satisfaction)
- **Little control over external factors** (government policy, technology, competition)
- **Resistance from employees** (e.g. CCTV, close monitoring)
- **Costly affair** (expense, time, effort — should be worth the benefit)

steps.title: Relationship between planning and controlling
steps.body:
- Planning is the basis of controlling; controlling is meaningless without planning; planning is meaningless without controlling.
- "Planning is looking ahead; controlling is looking back" — but controlling also looks ahead because it improves future planning.
- Both are forward- and backward-looking. They are **inseparable twins of management**.

steps.title: Solved case 1
steps.body: A company cannot measure "customer delight" accurately in numbers → limitation: **difficulty in setting quantitative standards**.

steps.title: Solved case 2
steps.body: A firm installs GPS trackers on salespeople's phones; staff protest → **resistance from employees**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying controlling is only backward-looking.
- Saying controlling can control external factors.

statements.s: Planning is meaningless without controlling.
statements.why: No way to know if plans are achieved.

statements.s: Controlling is only backward-looking.
Managers can fully control external factors like government policy.
statements.why: That is a limitation of controlling.

statements.s: A small firm should avoid a control system that costs more than its benefits.
statements.why: Controlling is costly; benefits must exceed costs.

quiz.why: Planning sets the standards and controlling checks against them. They depend on each other, so they are called inseparable twins.
A limitation of controlling is that a firm has little control over external factors such as government policy, competition and technology.

quiz.q: Standards for morale are hard to set because:
quiz.why: Standards for qualitative areas like morale or job satisfaction are not easily quantifiable, so they are hard to set and measure.
Controlling compares actual performance against the standards that are set in planning.
If employees resist a control measure such as CCTV, that is resistance from employees, which is a limitation of controlling.

scenes.text: Standard: 1,000 units per day.
Actual: 920 units.
Why? A machine was faulty → repair it.

steps.title: Steps
steps.body:
1. **Setting performance standards** (quantitative — cost, units, time; or qualitative — goodwill, morale)
2. **Measurement of actual performance** (personal observation, sample checking, reports)
3. **Comparing actual performance with standards** → deviation
4. **Analysing deviations** — using **critical point control** (focus on key result areas) and **management by exception** (only significant deviations reported to top management)
5. **Taking corrective action** (if deviation is beyond acceptable range); otherwise no action needed

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: Standard 1,000 units; actual 920. Acceptable deviation ±5% (950–1,050). Deviation 8% → significant → analyse cause (machine breakdown) → corrective action: repair/replace machine.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: Corrective actions by cause: defective material → change quality parameters/supplier; obsolete machinery → replace; defective process → modify process; defective physical conditions → improve; untrained workers → train; unrealistic standards → revise standards.

steps.title: Critical point control and MBE
steps.body:
**Critical point control:** focus on key result areas (KRAs) — e.g. a 5% rise in labour cost matters more than a 15% rise in postage.
**Management by exception:** "an attempt to control everything results in controlling nothing" — only significant deviations go to top management. Saves time and effort.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Taking corrective action for every tiny deviation.
- Setting standards that cannot be measured.
- Confusing critical point control (what to watch) with management by exception (what to report).

activity.prompt: Arrange the steps of the controlling process

quiz.why: Setting performance standards is the first step of the controlling process.

quiz.q: Focusing on key result areas is:
quiz.why: Concentrating control on the key result areas that affect performance most is critical point control.

quiz.q: Only significant deviations are reported to top management:
quiz.why: In management by exception, only the significant deviations from standards are reported to top management.

quiz.q: If actual performance is within the acceptable range:
quiz.why: If performance is within the acceptable limits, there is no need for corrective action.

quiz.q: Untrained workers cause deviation — corrective action:
quiz.why: If deviations are due to untrained workers, the right corrective action is training.

scenes.text: Case studies ask you to spot the step or importance.
Look for keywords: standard, measure, compare, deviation, correct.
Quote the line and name the concept.

steps.title: Solved case 1
steps.body:
"Kiran Ltd. set a target of producing 200 units of a product per day. Actual production was 180. The manager found that two workers were untrained and arranged a training programme."
Steps: setting standards (200), measuring (180), comparing (deviation 20), analysing (untrained workers), corrective action (training).

steps.title: Solved case 2
steps.body: "The production manager of a cake shop notices that the cost of flour has risen by 2%, while the cost of electricity has risen by 12%. He focuses on flour because it is 60% of total cost." → **Critical point control** (focus on key result area).

steps.title: How to answer
steps.body: Quote the exact line from the case in quotation marks, then name the step/importance/limitation and explain briefly.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Naming only one step when the case shows several.
- Explaining theory without referring to the case lines.

a.text: Target: 500 shirts/day. Today: 470. Acceptable range: ±2%. What do you do first?

choices.label: Compare and check whether the deviation is significant
Ignore it — it is close enough

b.text: You find the main cause is a new batch of poor-quality thread. Corrective action?

choices.label: Lower the target to 470
choices.feedback: Standards should be revised only if they were unrealistic.

c.text: Next week output falls to 440. Now?

end2.text: The real problem remains hidden. Always analyse causes before revising standards.

quiz.q: In case 1, "arranged a training programme" is:
quiz.why: Arranging a training programme to fix a deviation is the corrective action step of controlling.

quiz.q: In case 2, focusing on flour cost is:
quiz.why: Focusing on the flour cost (the key area for a bakery) is critical point control.
Deviation is the difference between actual performance and the standard.
Standards should be revised if they are found to be unrealistic. They need not be changed for every deviation.

quiz.q: Sample checking is a method of:
quiz.why: Sample checking is a technique of measuring actual performance.

questions.q: Controlling compares actual performance with:
questions.why: Controlling compares actual performance with the standards set in planning.

questions.q: First step of controlling process:
questions.why: Setting standards is the first step of the controlling process, followed by measurement, comparison, finding deviations and action.

questions.q: Planning and controlling are:
questions.why: Planning and controlling are inseparable: planning sets the standards and controlling checks against them.

questions.q: Management by exception means:
options: Only significant deviations reported to top
questions.why: Management by exception means only the significant deviations are brought to the notice of top management.

questions.q: Controlling is:
questions.why: Controlling is backward-looking (it reviews past performance) and forward-looking (lessons guide future plans).

questions.q: Assertion: Controlling cannot be effective without planning. Reason: Planning provides the standards against which performance is measured.
questions.why: Both are true. Planning provides the standards against which performance is measured, so controlling cannot work without it.

questions.q: Case: Introducing CCTV led to protests by employees. Limitation:
questions.why: Employees protesting against the introduction of CCTV is an example of resistance from employees to control.

questions.q: Case: A sudden change in import duty raised costs; the company could do little. Limitation:
questions.why: A sudden change in import duty is beyond the firm's control, so this shows the limitation of little control over external factors.

questions.q: Case: Target 1,200 units; actual 1,140; acceptable deviation 3%. Is corrective action needed?
questions.why: The shortfall is 60 units, 60/1,200 = 5%, which exceeds the acceptable 3% deviation, so corrective action is needed.

questions.q: Case: Monitoring showed raw material wastage of 8% versus a 3% standard; the firm changed its cutting process. Steps shown last:
questions.why: Finding that wastage is 8% against a standard of 3% and changing the cutting process shows analysing the deviation and taking corrective action.

questions.q: Case: A manager focuses on deviations in labour cost (60% of total cost) and ignores a large % change in stationery cost. Concept:
questions.why: Focusing on labour cost, which is the major part of total cost, and ignoring the small item is critical point control.

questions.q: Case: A small grocery shop considers buying expensive software to monitor two employees. Which limitation should it weigh?
questions.why: Expensive monitoring software for two employees may cost more than the benefit, so the shop should weigh that controlling is costly.

questions.q: Case: The CEO receives reports only on deviations above 10% while managers handle smaller ones. Concept and benefit:
options: Management by exception; saves top managers' time
questions.why: Reporting only deviations above 10% to the CEO is management by exception, which saves top managers' time for important matters.

questions.q: Case: The standard of 50 calls/hour at a call centre was found impossible; it was changed to 30. Importance shown:
questions.why: Changing an impossible standard shows how controlling helps to judge whether the standards are accurate.

questions.q: Personal observation is used for:
questions.why: Personal observation is a technique of measuring the actual performance of employees.

questions.q: Controlling is a ___ function.
questions.why: Controlling is pervasive: it is needed at all levels and in all types of organisations.

school-c12-business-b.title: Class 12 Business Studies — Business Finance & Marketing (Part B)
school-c12-business-b.description: Class 12 Business Studies Part 2 chapter by chapter: financial management, financial markets, marketing and consumer protection, plus Revision & Practice with mock papers.

courses.title: Ch 9 · Financial Management
courses.summary: Meaning, role and objectives of financial management; investment, financing and dividend decisions with their factors; financial planning; capital structure and trading on equity; fixed and working capital and the factors affecting them.
outcomes: Learners can explain the role and primary objective of financial management
Learners can explain the three financial decisions and their determinants
Learners can explain financial planning and its importance
Learners can compute EPS under different capital structures and explain trading on equity
Learners can state factors affecting fixed and working capital

story.title: Where does money come from — and go?

scenes.text: A juice company wants a new bottling plant.
Should it borrow or issue shares?
And how much profit should it keep vs pay out?

steps.title: Meaning
steps.body: **Business finance** = money required for carrying out business activities. **Financial management** is concerned with optimal procurement as well as usage of finance — at minimum cost and with acceptable risk.

steps.title: Role
steps.body: Financial decisions affect: size and composition of fixed assets; quantum of current assets and their break-up; amount of long-term and short-term financing; break-up of long-term financing into debt and equity; all items in the Profit & Loss account (interest, depreciation, etc.).

steps.title: Objective
steps.body: **Wealth maximisation** of equity shareholders — maximising the market value of equity shares. A decision is good if it increases the market price of shares, i.e. benefits exceed cost.

steps.title: Solved case 1
steps.body: A company chooses a project that gives higher long-term value, though short-term profits are lower. → consistent with **wealth maximisation** (not mere profit maximisation).

steps.title: Solved case 2
steps.body: "Financial manager decides how much to keep in inventory and receivables" → role: **quantum of current assets and their break-up**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Writing "profit maximisation" as the main objective.
- Thinking financial management is only about raising money — it is also about using it well.

statements.s: The primary objective of financial management is maximising shareholders' wealth.
statements.why: Measured by the market price of equity shares.

statements.s: Financial management only deals with raising funds.
statements.why: Also deals with investment and usage.

statements.s: Financial decisions affect the composition of fixed assets.
Higher risk always means a better financial decision.
statements.why: Return must be balanced with acceptable risk.

quiz.why: The primary objective of financial management is to maximise the wealth of shareholders, which shows up as a higher share price.
Shareholders' wealth is shown by the market price of the equity shares. A higher price means greater wealth.
Financial management is about the procurement (raising) and the effective use of funds in the business.

quiz.q: Break-up of long-term funds into debt and equity is part of:
quiz.why: Deciding the mix of debt and equity for long-term funds is the financing decision.
A good financial decision increases the value of the firm: its benefits are more than its costs.

scenes.text: Where to invest? (investment decision)
How to raise the money? (financing decision)
How much profit to distribute? (dividend decision)

steps.title: Investment decision
steps.body: Long-term (**capital budgeting**) and short-term (working capital) investments. **Factors:** cash flows of the project, rate of return, investment criteria (techniques such as payback, NPV, IRR), risk involved.

steps.title: Financing decision
steps.body: Quantum of funds from various long-term sources (debt and equity). Debt is cheaper (interest is tax-deductible) but riskier (fixed obligation). **Factors:** cost, risk, floatation costs, cash flow position, fixed operating costs, control considerations, state of capital markets.

steps.title: Dividend decision
steps.body: How much of profit to distribute and how much to retain. **Factors:** amount of earnings, stability of earnings, stability of dividends, growth opportunities, cash flow position, shareholders' preference, taxation policy, stock market reaction, access to capital market, legal constraints (Companies Act), contractual constraints (loan agreements).

steps.title: Solved case 1
steps.body: "A company with many profitable growth projects decided to pay a low dividend." → factor: **growth opportunities**.

steps.title: Solved case 2
steps.body: "The promoters did not want to dilute their control, so the company raised debt rather than issuing new shares." → financing decision factor: **control considerations**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling capital budgeting a financing decision — it is investment.
- Forgetting that floatation cost is higher for equity than for debt in general.

activity.prompt: Which decision does the factor relate to?

items.text: Rate of return of a project

quiz.why: Capital budgeting means choosing long-term investments, so it is part of the investment decision.

quiz.q: Interest on debt is tax-deductible, so debt is:
quiz.why: Interest on debt is deducted before tax, which reduces the tax paid. This makes debt cheaper than equity.

quiz.q: A company with unstable earnings tends to pay:
quiz.why: A company with unstable earnings keeps more profit for safety, so it tends to pay a lower dividend.
Equity brings in new owners and dilutes control, so a firm afraid of losing control prefers debt.

quiz.q: Restrictions in loan agreements on dividend are:
quiz.why: Restrictions placed on dividends by loan agreements are contractual constraints on dividend decisions.

scenes.text: Next year's expansion needs ₹5 crore.
The CFO forecasts sales, cash needs and sources.
Funds arrive just when needed.

steps.title: Meaning and objectives
steps.body: **Financial planning** = preparing a financial blueprint of future operations. Objectives: (1) ensure **availability of funds** whenever required; (2) see that the firm does **not raise resources unnecessarily** (avoids idle funds). Usually covers 3–5 years (long-term) and one year or less (short-term budgets).

steps.title: Importance
steps.body:
- Anticipates future requirements; prepares for different situations
- Helps avoid business shocks and surprises
- Coordinates various business functions (sales, production)
- Reduces waste and duplication
- Links the present with the future
- Links investment and financing decisions
- Makes evaluation of actual performance easier

steps.title: Solved case 1
steps.body: "The CFO forecast a cash shortfall in December and arranged a bank credit line in advance." → **availability of funds when required; avoiding shocks**.

steps.title: Solved case 2
steps.body: "A company raised ₹10 crore but used only ₹6 crore, paying interest on idle money." → lack of financial planning — violates objective of **not raising resources unnecessarily**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Confusing financial planning (blueprint) with financial management (whole function).
- Forgetting the dual objective (availability + avoiding excess).

activity.prompt: A good financial plan should…
items: Ensure funds are available when needed
Allow comparison of actual with planned figures

options: Availability of funds and avoiding unnecessary funds
quiz.why: The twin objectives of financial planning are to ensure funds are available when needed and to avoid raising unnecessary funds.
Financial planning covers long-term plans (3–5 years) and short-term plans (up to 1 year).
Financial planning links the investment and financing decisions on a continuous basis.
Idle excess funds earn nothing but still carry a cost (such as interest), so they cause unnecessary cost.
Planning for the firm's funds in advance helps to avoid business shocks and surprises.

lessons.title: Capital structure and trading on equity

scenes.text: Project needs ₹30 lakh; expected EBIT ₹4 lakh.
Option B: ₹20 lakh debt at 10%.
Does debt raise EPS? Only if return > interest rate.

steps.title: Capital structure
steps.body:
**Capital structure** = mix of owners' funds (equity, retained earnings) and borrowed funds (debt). Financial leverage = proportion of debt (Debt/Equity or Debt/(Debt+Equity)).
**Trading on equity:** using fixed-cost debt to increase EPS. It is **favourable** only when **ROI > rate of interest** on debt.

steps.title: Solved example 1 — favourable
steps.body:
Total ₹30 lakh; EBIT ₹4 lakh (ROI 13.33%); tax 30%; shares of ₹10.
**Plan A** (all equity, 3 lakh shares): EBT 4,00,000; tax 1,20,000; EAT 2,80,000; **EPS ₹0.93**.
**Plan B** (₹10 lakh equity = 1 lakh shares; ₹20 lakh debt @10%): interest 2,00,000; EBT 2,00,000; tax 60,000; EAT 1,40,000; **EPS ₹1.40**.
ROI 13.33% > 10% → debt **raises** EPS.

steps.title: Solved example 2 — unfavourable
steps.body:
Same, but EBIT ₹2 lakh (ROI 6.67%).
Plan A: EAT 1,40,000 → EPS ₹0.47. Plan B: interest 2,00,000 → EBT 0 → **EPS ₹0**.
ROI < interest → debt **reduces** EPS.

steps.title: Factors affecting choice of capital structure
steps.body: Cash flow position, interest coverage ratio (ICR), debt service coverage ratio (DSCR), return on investment, cost of debt, tax rate, cost of equity, floatation costs, risk consideration (operating + financial), flexibility, control, regulatory framework, stock market conditions, capital structure of other companies in the industry.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting to deduct interest before tax.
- Using total capital instead of number of equity shares for EPS.
- Saying debt always increases EPS.

activity.prompt: Capital ₹50 lakh: ₹20 lakh equity (₹10 shares) + ₹30 lakh debt @ 8%. EBIT ₹6 lakh; tax 25%. EPS (₹)?

quiz.q: Trading on equity is favourable when:
quiz.why: Trading on equity is beneficial when the return on investment is higher than the rate of interest, since debt then raises EPS.

options: Proportion of debt in capital structure
quiz.why: Financial leverage refers to the proportion of debt in the firm's capital structure.
Interest is deducted from profit before tax is calculated, so it reduces the tax liability.
A high interest coverage ratio means profits easily cover the interest, so the firm can safely take more debt.
EPS = EAT/number of shares = 1,20,000/60,000 = ₹2.

scenes.text: Machines last 10 years — fixed capital.
Raw material and cash for wages — working capital.
Each needs different financing.

steps.title: Fixed capital
steps.body:
Investment in long-term assets (capital budgeting decisions). Importance: long-term growth, large amounts, risky, irreversible.
**Factors:** nature of business (trading needs less, manufacturing more), scale of operations, choice of technique (capital- vs labour-intensive), technology upgradation, growth prospects, diversification, financing alternatives (leasing reduces need), level of collaboration (sharing facilities).

steps.title: Working capital
steps.body:
**Gross WC** = current assets; **Net WC** = current assets − current liabilities.
**Factors:** nature of business, scale of operations, business cycle (boom needs more), seasonal factors, production cycle (longer cycle → more WC), credit allowed, credit availed, operating efficiency, availability of raw material, growth prospects, level of competition, inflation.

steps.title: Solved case 1
steps.body:
"An ice-cream maker needs more working capital in summer." → factor: **seasonal factors**.
"A shipbuilder takes 2 years to build each ship." → **long production cycle** → high working capital.

steps.title: Solved case 2
steps.body:
"A company leases machines instead of buying them." → **financing alternatives** reduce fixed capital needs.
"A restaurant (service) needs less fixed capital than a steel plant." → **nature of business**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying credit allowed reduces working capital — it increases it.
- Saying credit availed increases WC — it reduces it.

activity.prompt: Does the factor INCREASE or DECREASE working capital required?

quiz.why: Net working capital = current assets − current liabilities.

quiz.q: Trading concerns need ___ fixed capital than manufacturing.
quiz.why: A trading concern needs less investment in fixed assets than a manufacturing firm, so less fixed capital.
Leasing assets instead of buying them reduces the fixed capital the firm needs to invest.
A capital-intensive method uses more machinery, so it needs more fixed capital.

quiz.q: In a boom, working capital needed:
quiz.why: In a boom, sales and production rise, so more working capital is needed.

questions.q: Primary aim of financial management:
questions.why: The primary aim of financial management is wealth maximisation of the shareholders.

questions.q: Capital budgeting relates to:
questions.why: Capital budgeting deals with decisions on long-term investment in assets.

questions.q: Net working capital =
questions.why: Net working capital = current assets − current liabilities.

questions.q: Debt is cheaper than equity because:
questions.why: Interest on debt is deductible for tax, so the effective cost of debt is lower than that of equity.

questions.q: Trading on equity raises EPS when:
questions.why: Trading on equity raises EPS when the return on investment is greater than the cost of debt.

questions.q: Assertion: Companies with stable earnings can pay higher dividends. Reason: Stable earnings reduce uncertainty about future cash flows.
questions.why: Both are true. Stable earnings reduce the uncertainty about future cash flows, so the company can pay higher dividends.

questions.q: Case: A sugar mill needs more working capital just after harvest season when it buys cane. Factor:
questions.why: A sugar mill buys sugarcane just after harvest, so it needs more working capital then. This is the effect of seasonal factors and raw material availability.

questions.q: Case: A company's loan agreement prevents it from paying dividends above 20%. Factor:
questions.why: A loan agreement that caps dividends is a contractual constraint, which limits the dividend decision.

questions.q: Case: Promoters want to keep control; market is bearish. Preferred source:
questions.why: Promoters wanting to keep control and a bearish market (low share prices) make debt the preferred source.

questions.q: EBIT ₹5 lakh; debt ₹20 lakh @ 10%; tax 30%; 1 lakh shares. EPS:
questions.why: Interest = 10% of 20 lakh = 2 lakh. PBT = 5 − 2 = 3 lakh, tax at 30% leaves 2.1 lakh. EPS = 2.1 lakh/1 lakh shares = ₹2.10.

questions.q: Case: Total capital ₹40 lakh; EBIT ₹3 lakh; debt available at 9%. Should the firm use heavy debt?
questions.why: ROI = 3/40 = 7.5%, which is lower than the 9% cost of debt. Heavy debt would reduce returns for shareholders.

questions.q: Case: A firm allows customers 90 days credit while suppliers allow it only 15 days. Effect on working capital:
questions.why: If customers pay after 90 days but the firm has to pay suppliers in 15 days, cash is tied up for longer, so more working capital is needed.

questions.q: All-equity plan: EBIT ₹6 lakh, tax 25%, 4 lakh shares → EPS ₹1.125. Levered plan with ₹20 lakh debt @ 12% and 2 lakh shares: EPS?
questions.why: Interest = 12% of 20 lakh = 2.4 lakh. PBT = 6 − 2.4 = 3.6 lakh. After 25% tax, 2.7 lakh. EPS = 2.7 lakh/2 lakh shares = ₹1.35.

questions.q: Case: Despite high profits, a startup with huge growth opportunities pays no dividend. Which factor and decision?
questions.why: A startup with big growth opportunities keeps its profits for investment, so it pays no dividend. The growth factor decides the dividend decision.

questions.q: Floatation cost is a factor in:
questions.why: Floatation cost, the cost of issuing securities, is a factor in the choice of the source of funds, which is the financing decision.

questions.q: Financial planning ensures:
options: Funds are available when needed without excess
questions.why: Financial planning ensures funds are available at the right time, and that excess funds are not raised.

courses.title: Ch 10 · Financial Markets
courses.summary: Concept and functions of financial markets; money market and its instruments; capital market — primary and secondary; methods of floatation; stock exchange functions, depositories and dematerialisation; SEBI's objectives and functions.
outcomes: Learners can explain the functions of financial markets
Learners can describe money market instruments
Learners can distinguish money and capital markets, and primary and secondary markets
Learners can explain methods of floatation and stock exchange functions
Learners can describe SEBI's objectives and functions

lessons.title: Financial markets and the money market

scenes.text: Families save money in banks and funds.
Companies need funds to grow.
Financial markets connect them.

steps.title: Concept and functions
steps.body:
A **financial market** links savers and investors by mobilising funds between them.
**Functions:** mobilisation of savings and channelling them into productive uses; facilitating **price discovery**; providing **liquidity** to financial assets; **reducing cost of transactions** (time, effort, money).

steps.title: Money market (short-term, up to one year)
steps.body:
Participants: RBI, commercial banks, NBFCs, state governments, large corporates, mutual funds.
**Instruments:**
- **Treasury bill** — short-term borrowing by the Government of India, issued by RBI; issued at a discount and repaid at par (zero-coupon); maturities currently 91, 182 and 364 days
- **Commercial paper** — short-term unsecured promissory note issued by large creditworthy companies, at a discount; used for working capital/bridge financing
- **Call money** — very short-term (overnight to a few days) inter-bank borrowing, often to meet reserve requirements; rate = call rate
- **Certificate of deposit** — unsecured, negotiable short-term instrument issued by banks/financial institutions in bearer form
- **Commercial bill** — bill of exchange used to finance working capital of firms; can be discounted with banks

steps.title: Solved case 1
steps.body: "A bank short of funds to meet its cash reserve requirement borrowed from another bank overnight." → **Call money**.

steps.title: Solved case 2
steps.body: "A large company raised short-term funds for 6 months through an unsecured promissory note issued at a discount." → **Commercial paper**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling T-bills interest-bearing — they are issued at a discount (zero-coupon).
- Saying any small company can issue commercial paper — only large creditworthy companies.

activity.prompt: Match the instrument to its description
pairs: Government short-term borrowing at a discount, issued by RBI
Unsecured promissory note of large companies
Negotiable bearer instrument issued by banks
Bill of exchange that can be discounted by banks

quiz.q: Money market deals in funds for:
quiz.why: The money market deals in short-term funds, with maturity up to one year.
Treasury bills are issued at a discount and redeemed at face value with no interest, so they are zero-coupon instruments.

options: Market determines prices through demand and supply
quiz.why: Price discovery means that prices are decided by the interaction of demand and supply in the market.
Commercial paper is an unsecured, short-term promissory note issued by large creditworthy companies.
Call money is the overnight borrowing and lending among banks.

scenes.text: A company sells new shares to the public — primary market.
Investors later trade them among themselves — secondary market.
Both form the capital market.

steps.title: Capital market
steps.body: Market for **medium and long-term** funds — equity, debentures, bonds, long-term loans. Includes banks, financial institutions and stock exchanges.

steps.title: Capital vs money market
steps.body: Participants (capital: financial institutions, banks, corporates, foreign investors, retail investors; money: RBI, banks, corporates mainly), instruments (shares, debentures vs T-bills, CP, CD), investment outlay (small denominations vs large), duration (long vs up to 1 year), liquidity (less vs high), safety (riskier vs safer), expected return (higher vs lower).

steps.title: Primary vs secondary market
steps.body:
**Primary (new issues):** sale of new securities by companies; directly promotes capital formation; securities sold by company to investors; no fixed place.
**Secondary (stock market):** trading of existing securities; indirectly promotes capital formation; investors trade among themselves; located at stock exchanges; prices determined by demand and supply.

steps.title: Methods of floatation (primary market)
steps.body: Offer through prospectus · offer for sale (via intermediaries) · private placement · rights issue (to existing shareholders in proportion) · e-IPO (online through stock exchange).

steps.title: Solved case 1
steps.body: "A company offered new shares first to its existing shareholders in the ratio of 1 new for every 4 held." → **Rights issue**.

steps.title: Solved case 2
steps.body: "A company sold shares to a few institutional investors without a public issue." → **Private placement**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying the secondary market directly raises capital for the company.
- Confusing offer for sale (through intermediaries) with offer through prospectus (direct to public).

activity.prompt: Primary or secondary market?

items.text: Buying shares through a broker on NSE
Prices set by demand and supply among investors

quiz.why: The capital market deals in medium- and long-term funds.
New securities are issued and sold to investors in the primary market.

quiz.q: Offering new shares to existing shareholders:
quiz.why: Offering new shares to existing shareholders in proportion to their holding is a rights issue.
The secondary market does not give funds to companies directly, but it gives liquidity, which encourages investment. So it promotes capital formation indirectly.

quiz.q: Compared to money market, capital market instruments are:
quiz.why: Capital market instruments are riskier than money market ones, but investors expect higher returns.

scenes.text: Earlier, share certificates were paper.
Now shares sit in a demat account.
Trades happen electronically on NSE and BSE.

steps.title: Stock exchange
steps.body:
An institution that provides a platform for buying and selling existing securities. Functions:
- Provides **liquidity and marketability** to existing securities
- **Pricing of securities** (by demand and supply)
- **Safety of transactions** (regulated)
- Contributes to **economic growth** (channelises savings)
- **Spreading of equity cult** (encourages investment)
- Provides **scope for speculation** (within limits)

steps.title: Depositories and demat
steps.body: **Dematerialisation** = converting physical certificates into electronic form. **Depositories** in India: **NSDL** and **CDSL**. Investors deal through **Depository Participants (DPs)** — banks/brokers. Trading procedure (broad): open trading and demat accounts (with PAN) → place order through broker → order executed on screen-based trading → contract note → settlement (shares/money transferred).

steps.title: Solved case 1
steps.body: "Anil wants to sell his shares quickly and can do so any working day on the exchange." → function: **liquidity and marketability**.

steps.title: Solved case 2
steps.body: "Savings of millions of households flow into companies through share purchases on exchanges." → **contributes to economic growth**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying stock exchanges sell new shares for companies (that is the primary market).
- Confusing depositories (NSDL/CDSL) with stock exchanges (NSE/BSE).

activity.prompt: Arrange the basic steps an investor follows to buy shares
items: Open a trading account and a demat account (with PAN)
Place a buy order through a registered broker
Order is matched on the exchange's electronic system
Settlement: money paid and shares credited to the demat account

quiz.why: NSDL and CDSL are depositories that hold securities in electronic form.

quiz.q: Converting physical shares to electronic form:
quiz.why: Converting physical share certificates into electronic form is dematerialisation.
A stock exchange gives liquidity to existing securities by providing a place to buy and sell them.

quiz.q: An investor deals with a depository through a:
quiz.why: An investor deals with a depository through a Depository Participant (DP), such as a bank or broker.

quiz.q: Encouraging people to invest in shares is called:
quiz.why: Encouraging more people to invest in shares is spreading the equity cult.

lessons.title: SEBI — Securities and Exchange Board of India

scenes.text: A company hides losses in its prospectus.
Investors lose money.
SEBI exists to stop such abuses.

steps.title: Establishment
steps.body: Set up in **1988** (as a non-statutory body); given **statutory powers** through the **SEBI Act, 1992**.

steps.title: Objectives
steps.body:
- Regulate stock exchanges and the securities industry for orderly functioning
- Protect the rights and interests of investors (especially small investors)
- Prevent trading malpractices and achieve a balance between self-regulation and statutory regulation
- Regulate and develop a code of conduct and fair practices by intermediaries (brokers, merchant bankers)

steps.title: Functions
steps.body:
**Protective:** prohibit fraudulent and unfair trade practices, check price rigging and **insider trading**, promote fair practices, educate investors.
**Developmental:** training of intermediaries, conducting research, promoting activities of stock exchanges, flexible approach (e.g. permitting internet trading, underwriting optional).
**Regulatory:** registration and regulation of brokers, sub-brokers, merchant bankers, mutual funds; levying fees; conducting inquiries and audits; regulation of takeovers.

steps.title: Solved case 1
steps.body: "SEBI penalised a director who bought shares using unpublished price-sensitive information." → **Protective function (insider trading)**.

steps.title: Solved case 2
steps.body: "SEBI registers and inspects stockbrokers and mutual funds." → **Regulatory function**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Writing SEBI was set up in 1992 — that is when it became statutory; it was set up in 1988.
- Mixing developmental (training, research) and regulatory (registration, inspection) functions.

activity.prompt: Classify SEBI's function

quiz.why: SEBI (Securities and Exchange Board of India) was established in 1988 as a non-statutory body.
SEBI was given statutory powers in 1992 through the SEBI Act.

quiz.q: Insider trading control is a ___ function.
quiz.why: Prohibiting insider trading protects investors, so it is a protective function of SEBI.

quiz.q: Registering mutual funds is a ___ function.
quiz.why: Registering and regulating mutual funds is a regulatory function of SEBI.
A main objective of SEBI is to protect the interests of investors in securities.

questions.q: Money market deals in funds up to:
questions.why: The money market deals in short-term funds, with a maturity of up to one year.

questions.q: Treasury bills are issued by RBI on behalf of:
questions.why: The RBI issues treasury bills on behalf of the Government of India.

questions.q: SEBI was set up in:
questions.why: SEBI was set up in 1988 and given statutory powers in 1992.

questions.q: Depositories in India:
questions.why: The two depositories in India are NSDL (National Securities Depository Ltd) and CDSL (Central Depository Services Ltd).

questions.q: Stock exchange deals in:
questions.why: A stock exchange deals in existing (already issued) securities. New issues are sold in the primary market.

questions.q: Assertion: Primary market directly promotes capital formation. Reason: Companies receive funds from investors when they issue new securities.
questions.why: Both are true. In the primary market, companies get funds from investors directly when they issue new securities, so it directly promotes capital formation.

questions.q: Commercial paper is issued by:
questions.why: Commercial paper is issued by large, creditworthy companies as an unsecured short-term instrument.

questions.q: Case: A company sells shares to an issuing house, which then sells them to the public. Method:
questions.why: When a company sells shares to an issuing house, which then resells them to the public, it is an offer for sale.

questions.q: Case: An investor sells shares on Monday and receives money quickly. Function of stock exchange:
questions.why: A stock exchange lets investors sell shares quickly and get money, which is liquidity and marketability.

questions.q: Case: A bank issued a negotiable, unsecured bearer instrument for 6 months to raise funds. Instrument:
questions.why: A negotiable, unsecured instrument issued by a bank to raise short-term funds is a certificate of deposit.

questions.q: Case: SEBI holds workshops to train brokers and promotes new trading technology. Function:
questions.why: Training brokers and promoting new trading technology develops the market, so it is a developmental function.

questions.q: Case: A company director bought shares before announcing a big contract, using confidential information. SEBI action falls under:
questions.why: Trading on confidential information is insider trading. SEBI's action to stop it is a protective function.

questions.q: Case: A firm issues new shares online through the exchange's system. Method:
questions.why: Issuing new shares online through the exchange's system is an e-IPO.

questions.q: Which pair is correct?
options: Money market — low risk, low return; Capital market — higher risk, higher return
questions.why: The money market has low risk and low returns, while the capital market has higher risk and higher returns.

questions.q: Case: A seller of goods draws a bill on the buyer, which the seller then discounts with a bank to get cash early. Instrument and market:
questions.why: A bill drawn by the seller on the buyer and discounted with a bank is a commercial bill, a short-term instrument of the money market.

questions.q: Case: An investor's shares bought through a broker are credited electronically through a DP linked to a depository. This shows:
questions.why: Shares credited electronically through a Depository Participant are held in dematerialised form, which is through the depository system.

questions.q: Price discovery is a function of:
questions.why: Price discovery, deciding prices through demand and supply, is a function of financial markets.

courses.title: Ch 11 · Marketing
courses.summary: Concept of marketing, marketing vs selling, marketing philosophies, functions of marketing, and the marketing mix — product (branding, packaging, labelling), price (factors), place (channels and physical distribution) and promotion (advertising, personal selling, sales promotion, public relations).
outcomes: Learners can explain the marketing concept and compare marketing with selling
Learners can explain the five marketing philosophies
Learners can list the functions of marketing
Learners can explain branding, packaging and labelling
Learners can explain factors affecting price and choice of channel
Learners can compare elements of the promotion mix

lessons.title: Concept of marketing and marketing philosophies

scenes.text: A shampoo maker used to make one big bottle for everyone.
Research showed rural buyers wanted small, cheap sachets.
Sachets became a huge success.

steps.title: Concept
steps.body: **Marketing** is a social process by which individuals and groups obtain what they need and want through creating, offering and freely exchanging products and services of value with others. Features: needs and wants, creating a market offering, customer value, exchange mechanism.

steps.title: Marketing vs selling
steps.body:
Selling: part of marketing; focus on transfer of title; seller's needs; product first; ends with sale; aims at profit through volume.
Marketing: wider (includes selling); focus on customer satisfaction; customer's needs; begins before production and continues after sale; profit through customer satisfaction.

steps.title: Marketing philosophies
steps.body:
- **Production concept:** availability and affordability (produce efficiently, distribute widely)
- **Product concept:** quality, performance and features
- **Selling concept:** aggressive selling and promotion
- **Marketing concept:** identify customer needs and satisfy them better than competitors
- **Societal marketing concept:** customer satisfaction + long-term welfare of society (environment, ethics)

steps.title: Solved case 1
steps.body: "A company stopped using plastic packaging and switched to biodegradable materials even though it cost more." → **Societal marketing concept**.

steps.title: Solved case 2
steps.body: "A firm believes customers will buy if offered the best-quality product with many features." → **Product concept**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying marketing and selling are the same.
- Confusing marketing concept (customer satisfaction) with societal concept (plus social welfare).

activity.prompt: Match the case to the marketing philosophy
pairs: Make it cheap and available everywhere
Best quality and features will sell
Find what customers want and deliver it better
Satisfy customers and protect the environment

quiz.why: Marketing starts before production, with market research to find out what customers want.

options: Seller's need to convert product into cash
quiz.why: The selling concept focuses on the seller's need to convert the product into cash, often by aggressive selling.
Societal marketing adds concern for the long-term welfare of society to customer satisfaction.
The production concept assumes customers prefer products that are widely available and affordable, so it stresses production and distribution.
Marketing is wider than selling, as it includes research, product design, pricing, promotion and after-sales service.

lessons.title: Functions of marketing and the marketing mix

scenes.text: Research what people want.
Design, package, brand, price, promote, deliver.
The marketer does all of it.

steps.title: Functions of marketing
steps.body: Gathering and analysing market information · marketing planning · product designing and development · standardisation and grading · packaging and labelling · branding · customer support services · pricing of products · promotion · physical distribution · transportation · warehousing.

steps.title: Standardisation vs grading
steps.body: **Standardisation:** producing goods of predetermined specifications (uniformity). **Grading:** classifying products into groups by quality, size, etc. (mainly for agricultural products like wheat, cotton).

steps.title: Marketing mix (4 Ps)
steps.body: **Product** (what is offered), **Price** (amount paid), **Place** (physical distribution and channels), **Promotion** (informing and persuading).

steps.title: Solved case 1
steps.body: "A rice company sorts rice into premium, standard and broken categories." → **Grading**.

steps.title: Solved case 2
steps.body: "A mobile company provides free home service and 24×7 helplines." → **Customer support services**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Confusing standardisation with grading.
- Listing "people" as one of the 4 Ps in NCERT's framework (that is from the extended services mix).

activity.prompt: Match the activity to the function of marketing
pairs: Giving the product a name and symbol

quiz.why: Grading is the classification of products into groups based on quality, size and so on. It is mainly used for agricultural products.
Standardisation fixes standards for products (like size and quality), which ensures uniformity of quality.
The 4 Ps of the marketing mix are Product, Price, Place and Promotion.
Warehousing keeps goods until they are needed, so it creates time utility.
Transportation moves goods to where they are needed, which creates place utility.

story.title: A name, a box, a label

scenes.text: A biscuit has a name, a logo and a colourful pack.
The pack protects and sells.
The label tells weight, price, date, ingredients.

steps.title: Product and its classification
steps.body: A **product** is anything of value offered to a market — goods, services, ideas. Consumer products: convenience, shopping, speciality; durable/non-durable. Industrial products: raw materials, components, plant, supplies, business services.

steps.title: Branding
steps.body:
**Brand** = name, term, sign, symbol, design or combination identifying a seller's products. **Brand name** = the part that can be spoken. **Brand mark** = symbol/design (cannot be spoken). **Trade mark** = a brand or part of it given legal protection (registered).
Advantages: differentiation, helps advertising, differential pricing, ease in introducing new products; for customers — identification, quality assurance, status.

steps.title: Packaging
steps.body: Levels: **primary** (immediate container, e.g. tube), **secondary** (additional layer, e.g. carton), **transportation packaging** (for storage/transport, e.g. corrugated boxes). Functions: product identification, product protection, convenience, facilitating promotion. Importance: rising health/sanitation standards, self-service retail, innovation opportunity, product differentiation.

steps.title: Labelling
steps.body: Functions: describe the product and its contents; identify the product/brand; grading; help in promotion; provide information required by law (e.g. MRP, net quantity, date of manufacture, expiry, statutory warnings).

steps.title: Solved case 1
steps.body: "The swoosh symbol" is a **brand mark**; the spoken name of the brand is the **brand name**; once registered it is a **trade mark**.

steps.title: Solved case 2
steps.body: "A toothpaste tube inside a carton, packed in boxes of 100 for shipping" → primary, secondary and transportation packaging respectively.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Confusing brand mark (symbol) with trade mark (legally protected brand).
- Thinking labels are only decorative — many details are legally required.

activity.prompt: Level of packaging

items.text: Cardboard box around a perfume bottle

quiz.q: A brand that is legally registered:
quiz.why: A brand (or part of it) that has been given legal protection through registration is a trade mark.

quiz.q: Part of a brand that can be spoken:
quiz.why: The part of a brand that can be spoken, such as a word or letters, is the brand name.
Primary packaging is the product's immediate container, such as the tube holding toothpaste.

quiz.q: Labels may show legally required info like:
quiz.why: Labels carry legally required information such as MRP, date of expiry and ingredients.
Branding differentiates the firm's product from competitors' products.

lessons.title: Price and place (channels and physical distribution)

scenes.text: A new juice is priced at ₹30 — rival is ₹28.
It must reach 10,000 shops before summer.
Through distributors and retailers.

steps.title: Factors affecting price
steps.body: Product cost (fixed, variable, semi-variable) · utility and demand (elasticity) · extent of competition · government and legal regulations (price controls for essentials) · pricing objectives (profit maximisation, market share, survival, product quality leadership) · marketing methods used (distribution, advertising, packaging, credit, customer services).

steps.title: Channels of distribution
steps.body:
- **Zero level (direct):** manufacturer → customer (e.g. online direct sales, door-to-door)
- **One level:** manufacturer → retailer → customer
- **Two level:** manufacturer → wholesaler → retailer → customer
- **Three level:** manufacturer → agent → wholesaler → retailer → customer
**Factors in choice:** product (perishable/technical/industrial → short channel), company (financial strength, degree of control), competition, market (size, concentration, customers' buying pattern), environment.

steps.title: Physical distribution components
steps.body: **Order processing** · **Transportation** · **Warehousing** · **Inventory control**.

steps.title: Solved case 1
steps.body: "A bakery sells cakes only through its own outlets because they are perishable." → **zero-level/short channel** due to product factor (perishability).

steps.title: Solved case 2
steps.body: "The government fixed a ceiling price for life-saving drugs." → factor affecting price: **government and legal regulations**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Counting the manufacturer and customer as levels — levels = number of intermediaries.
- Forgetting inventory control as a component of physical distribution.

activity.prompt: Arrange a THREE-level channel from producer to customer

quiz.why: A manufacturer → retailer → consumer chain has one intermediary, so it is a one-level channel.
Perishable goods spoil quickly, so they need short channels to reach the consumer fast.

quiz.q: Price ceilings on essential drugs relate to:
quiz.why: Price ceilings on essential drugs are set by the government, so they relate to government regulation.

quiz.q: Which is NOT a component of physical distribution?
quiz.why: The components of physical distribution are order processing, transportation, warehousing and inventory control. Branding is a product decision.

quiz.q: Inelastic demand allows the firm to:
quiz.why: When demand is inelastic, customers keep buying even at higher prices, so the firm can charge a relatively high price.

scenes.text: A TV ad reaches millions.
A salesperson explains a home water purifier in person.
"Buy 2 get 1 free" pushes quick sales.

steps.title: Advertising
steps.body:
Impersonal, paid form of communication by an identified sponsor. Merits: mass reach, enhances customer satisfaction and confidence, expressiveness, economy (low cost per person). Limitations: less forceful, lack of feedback, inflexibility, low effectiveness amid clutter.
Objections: adds to cost, undermines social values (materialism), confuses buyers, encourages sale of inferior products, some ads are in bad taste. Counter-arguments exist (e.g. larger sales reduce per-unit cost).

steps.title: Personal selling
steps.body: Oral presentation in face-to-face conversation with prospective buyers. Features: personal form, develops relationship, two-way, flexible, immediate feedback. Important for business (effective, flexible, minimises wasted effort, consumer attention, lasting relationships), customers and society (employment, mobility of sales people).

steps.title: Sales promotion
steps.body: Short-term incentives to encourage immediate purchase. Techniques: rebate, discount, refunds, product combinations, quantity gift, instant draws and assured gift, lucky draw, usable benefit, full finance at 0%, sampling, contests.

steps.title: Public relations
