steps.body: Managing communication to build a favourable image and goodwill — press relations, product publicity, corporate communication, lobbying, counselling. Publicity is unpaid.

steps.title: Solved case 1
steps.body: "Free toothbrush with every 200 g toothpaste" → **Product combination** (sales promotion). "₹10 off on MRP for 1 week" → **Discount**.

steps.title: Solved case 2
steps.body: "A car company's sales executive takes customers on test drives and answers their questions." → **Personal selling** (two-way, immediate feedback).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling publicity a type of advertising — publicity is not paid.
- Confusing discount (price reduction) with rebate (reduction on clearing excess stock / special offer).

activity.prompt: Which element of the promotion mix?

items.text: Salesperson demonstrating a vacuum cleaner at home
Press conference about a new eco-friendly plant
Newspaper ad by an identified sponsor
Company sponsoring a sports event to build image

quiz.why: Advertising is a paid, impersonal form of communication through the mass media.

quiz.q: Immediate feedback is a feature of:
quiz.why: In personal selling the seller talks to the buyer face to face, so immediate feedback is possible.
A free sample is a short-term incentive to try a product, so it is a sales promotion technique.
Publicity is non-paid communication, for example through news stories.
Advertising is impersonal, so it does not give immediate feedback.

questions.q: Marketing concept focuses on:
questions.why: The marketing concept puts the customer first: the firm tries to satisfy customer needs.

questions.q: Sorting products by quality is:
questions.why: Grading is sorting products into classes by quality, size and so on.

questions.q: Brand mark is:
questions.why: A brand mark is the part of a brand that is a symbol, design or colour (it cannot be spoken).

questions.q: Two-level channel has:
questions.why: A two-level channel has two intermediaries between the producer and consumer, the wholesaler and the retailer.

questions.q: Advertising is a ___ form of communication.
questions.why: Advertising is a paid, impersonal form of communication through mass media.

questions.q: Assertion: Selling is a part of marketing. Reason: Marketing includes activities before production and after sale besides selling.
questions.why: Both are true. Marketing includes research and product development before production and service after the sale, so selling is just a part of marketing.

questions.q: Case: A company stopped using CFC gases in refrigerators to protect the ozone layer. Philosophy:
questions.why: Dropping CFC gases to protect the ozone layer shows concern for society's long-term welfare, which is the societal marketing concept.

questions.q: Case: "Buy a refrigerator now and pay in 12 EMIs at 0% interest." Technique:
questions.why: Offering to finance the purchase in EMIs at 0% interest is a sales promotion technique called full finance at 0%.

questions.q: Case: A detergent firm puts a warning "Keep away from children" and directions for use on the pack. Function:
questions.why: Directions for use and warnings on the pack are information given on the label, as required by law.

questions.q: Case: A heavy machinery maker sells directly to factories through its own sales team. Channel and reason:
questions.why: A heavy machinery maker selling directly to factories uses a zero-level channel, which suits technical industrial products.

questions.q: Case: A firm cuts price to win market share from rivals. Factor in pricing:
questions.why: Cutting the price to win market share from rivals reflects the pricing objective and competition, which are factors in pricing.

questions.q: Case: Toothpaste tube (A), carton (B), box of 100 cartons (C). Levels:
options: A secondary, B primary, C transportation
A primary, B secondary, C transportation
questions.why: The toothpaste tube is the primary package, the carton is the secondary package and the box of 100 cartons is for transportation.

questions.q: Case: A company publishes a press release about winning an environmental award, gaining free media coverage. Tool:
questions.why: A press release that gains free media coverage is publicity (public relations).

questions.q: Case: A brand's name and logo are registered under the Trade Marks Act, so others cannot use them. This is a:
questions.why: A brand's name and logo that are legally registered are a trade mark.

questions.q: Case: A firm believes that if it produces a lot at low cost and distributes widely, customers will buy. Critics say it ignores customer needs. Philosophy:
questions.why: Producing a lot at low cost and distributing widely, while ignoring customers' needs, is the production concept.

questions.q: Components of physical distribution:
options: Order processing, transportation, warehousing, inventory control
questions.why: The components of physical distribution are order processing, transportation, warehousing and inventory control.

questions.q: Transportation creates ___ utility.
questions.why: Transportation moves goods to where they are needed, creating place utility.

courses.note: topic order may differ by edition

courses.title: Ch 12 · Consumer Protection
courses.summary: Importance of consumer protection; the Consumer Protection Act 2019 — who is a consumer, consumer rights and responsibilities; ways and means of protection; the three-tier redressal machinery, reliefs and appeals; role of consumer organisations and NGOs.
outcomes: Learners can explain the importance of consumer protection from consumers' and business points of view
Learners can define a consumer under the Consumer Protection Act 2019
Learners can list consumer rights and responsibilities
Learners can describe the redressal machinery, who can file, reliefs and appeals
Learners can explain the role of consumer organisations and NGOs

scenes.text: Asha's new pressure cooker leaks on the first day.
The shop refuses to replace it.
Who protects Asha?

steps.title: Why consumers need protection
steps.body: Consumers face unsafe products, adulteration, false and misleading advertising, overcharging, hoarding, black marketing, short weights, poor after-sales service.

steps.title: Importance from consumers' point of view
steps.body: Consumer ignorance (of rights and remedies); unorganised consumers; widespread exploitation of consumers.

steps.title: Importance from business point of view
steps.body: Long-term interest of business (satisfied customers return); business uses society's resources; social responsibility; moral justification; avoiding government intervention (self-regulation builds trust).

steps.title: Solved case 1
steps.body: "Customers were not aware they could get a refund for a defective product." → **Consumer ignorance**.

steps.title: Solved case 2
steps.body: "A company voluntarily recalled a faulty batch of cars to retain customer trust." → business view: **long-term interest of business / social responsibility**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: - Saying consumer protection is only the government's job — business, consumers and organisations all play a role.

activity.prompt: Consumer point of view or business point of view?

items.text: Consumers do not know their rights

quiz.q: Consumers often lack information about rights — this is:
quiz.why: Consumers often do not know their rights or how to use them, which is consumer ignorance.

quiz.q: From business view, consumer protection serves:
quiz.why: From a business point of view, protecting consumers builds trust and brings repeat sales, which serve the firm's long-term interest.

quiz.q: Misleading advertising is an example of:
quiz.why: Misleading advertising gives consumers false information, so it is an example of consumer exploitation.
Unorganised consumers lack the collective bargaining strength that businesses have.
When businesses regulate themselves and follow ethical practices, the government has less reason to intervene.

lessons.title: Consumer Protection Act 2019: consumer, rights and responsibilities

scenes.text: The Consumer Protection Act, 2019 replaced the 1986 Act.
It covers offline and online purchases.
It lists six consumer rights.

steps.title: Who is a consumer?
steps.body: Under the **Consumer Protection Act, 2019**, a consumer is a person who **buys goods or hires/avails services for a consideration** (paid, promised or partly paid, or under deferred payment), including users with the buyer's approval, and including transactions **online** (e-commerce, teleshopping, direct selling, multi-level marketing). A person who obtains goods **for resale or for any commercial purpose** is **not** a consumer (except goods/services used exclusively for earning livelihood by self-employment).

steps.title: Consumer rights
steps.body:
1. **Right to safety** (against hazardous goods)
2. **Right to be informed** (quality, quantity, purity, price, standard, date of manufacture, etc.)
3. **Right to choose**
4. **Right to be heard** (complaints considered by appropriate forums)
5. **Right to seek redressal** (relief against unfair trade practices)
6. **Right to consumer education**

steps.title: Consumer responsibilities
steps.body: Be aware of goods/services; buy standardised goods (ISI, Agmark, Hallmark, FPO); learn risks and follow instructions; read labels; be assertive to get a fair deal; be honest (buy only from legal sources); ask for a cash memo; file complaints with genuine claims; form consumer societies; respect the environment.

steps.title: Solved case 1
steps.body: "A buyer purchased 50 mobile phones to resell in his shop; one was defective." → He is **not a consumer** under the Act for this purchase (commercial purpose/resale).

steps.title: Solved case 2
steps.body: "A medicine strip shows no expiry date." → violation of **right to be informed**. "A shopkeeper forces a customer to buy only one brand" → **right to choose**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting that online purchases are covered under the 2019 Act.
- Treating a buyer for resale as a consumer.

activity.prompt: Match the situation to the consumer right
pairs: Electric iron gives a shock due to faulty wiring
Pack does not show ingredients and expiry
Shop forces you to buy only its house brand
You get compensation for a defective TV

quiz.q: The current consumer law is the Consumer Protection Act of:
quiz.why: The Consumer Protection Act, 2019, replaced the 1986 Act and is the present law.

quiz.q: Goods bought for resale — buyer is:
options: Not a consumer under the Act
quiz.why: A person who buys goods for resale or a commercial purpose is not a consumer under the Act.
Hallmark shows the purity of gold and silver jewellery.
Asking for a cash memo is a consumer responsibility because it is evidence of purchase.
The 2019 Act covers online (e-commerce) purchases as well.

scenes.text: Asha files a complaint against the cooker company.
Which commission hears it?
She can even file online (e-Daakhil).

steps.title: Who can file a complaint
steps.body: A consumer; any registered voluntary consumer association; the Central or State Government; the Central Consumer Protection Authority; one or more consumers on behalf of numerous consumers with the same interest; legal heir/representative of a deceased consumer; parent/guardian of a minor consumer.

steps.title: Three-tier machinery
steps.body:
**District Commission**, **State Commission**, **National Commission** — jurisdiction based on the **value of goods/services paid as consideration**.
The Act (2019) originally set: District up to ₹1 crore; State ₹1–10 crore; National above ₹10 crore. The **Consumer Protection (Jurisdiction…) Rules, 2021** revised these to: District up to **₹50 lakh**; State **₹50 lakh–₹2 crore**; National **above ₹2 crore**. (Check which figures your exam board uses.)

steps.title: Appeals
steps.body: District → State Commission within **45 days**; State → National within **30 days**; National → **Supreme Court** within **30 days** (time limits as in the Act; delay may be condoned for sufficient cause).

steps.title: Reliefs available
steps.body: Remove defect; replace goods; refund price; pay compensation for loss/injury; pay punitive damages; discontinue unfair/restrictive trade practice; not offer hazardous goods for sale; withdraw hazardous goods; cease manufacture of hazardous goods; pay sum to a consumer welfare fund; issue corrective advertisement; pay adequate costs.

steps.title: Solved case 1
steps.body: Consideration paid ₹40,000 for a defective laptop → **District Commission** (under both the original and revised limits).

steps.title: Solved case 2
steps.body: A builder failed to deliver a flat bought for ₹1.5 crore → under the 2021 Rules, **State Commission** (₹50 lakh–₹2 crore).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using the claim amount (compensation demanded) instead of the **value of consideration paid** to decide jurisdiction.
- Mixing up 45 days (first appeal) and 30 days (later appeals).

activity.prompt: Under the 2021 Rules, what is the maximum value of consideration (in ₹ lakh) for a complaint to be filed in a District Commission?

options: Value of goods/services paid as consideration
quiz.why: Under the Act, the jurisdiction of the District, State and National Commissions depends on the value of the goods or services paid as consideration.

quiz.q: Appeal against District Commission goes to:
quiz.why: An appeal against an order of the District Commission goes to the State Commission.

quiz.q: Appeal against the National Commission goes to:
quiz.why: An appeal against an order of the National Commission goes to the Supreme Court.
Corrective advertising, ordering the seller to publish a correction, is one of the reliefs available under the Act.
A registered consumer association can file a complaint on behalf of consumers.

lessons.title: Ways and means; consumer organisations and NGOs

scenes.text: Companies set up grievance cells.
Consumer groups run awareness drives.
Government passes laws and sets standards.

steps.title: Ways and means of consumer protection
steps.body:
- **Self-regulation by business** (codes of conduct, grievance cells)
- **Business associations** (e.g. FICCI, CII codes of conduct)
- **Consumer awareness**
- **Consumer organisations**
- **Government** (laws like the Consumer Protection Act 2019, Legal Metrology Act, Food Safety and Standards Act, BIS standards)

steps.title: Role of consumer organisations and NGOs
steps.body: Educating the public about rights (training, workshops); publishing periodicals and reports; testing products in labs and publishing results; encouraging consumers to protest and act against exploitation; providing legal assistance; filing complaints in commissions on behalf of consumers; taking initiative to file cases in the general interest of the public.

steps.title: Solved case 1
steps.body: "A voluntary group tested 10 brands of honey and published adulteration results." → role: **comparative testing and publishing results**.

steps.title: Solved case 2
steps.body: "An NGO filed a complaint on behalf of many residents against a builder." → **filing complaints on behalf of consumers**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying only government can protect consumers.
- Forgetting that NGOs can file complaints in the general public interest.

activity.prompt: Before you buy, a smart consumer…
items: Checks for standard marks (ISI, Agmark, Hallmark, BIS)
Reads the label: MRP, net quantity, expiry, ingredients
Keeps warranty card and bill safely
Knows that complaints can be filed online too

quiz.why: The ISI mark is given by the Bureau of Indian Standards (BIS) for quality of industrial and consumer products.
Self-regulation means that businesses voluntarily follow ethical and quality standards, without being forced by law.

Consumer organisations educate and help buyers by comparatively testing products and publishing the results. Making laws, running courts and printing currency are functions of the legislature, the judiciary and the central bank, not of consumer groups.

quiz.q: A government means of consumer protection:
options: Passing laws like the Consumer Protection Act
quiz.why: The government protects consumers mainly through legislation such as the Consumer Protection Act, which creates rights, authorities and redressal forums. Selling, branding and advertising are business activities, not protection measures.

options: On behalf of consumers / in public interest
quiz.why: Registered consumer associations and NGOs can file complaints on behalf of consumers or in the public interest, not only for themselves. This lets many affected consumers get redress together.

questions.q: The consumer law currently in force:
questions.why: The Consumer Protection Act, 2019 replaced the 1986 Act and is the law now in force. The Companies Act and SEBI Act deal with companies and securities markets, not consumer rights.

questions.q: Right to safety protects against:
questions.why: The right to safety protects consumers from goods and services that are hazardous to life and property, such as faulty appliances. Price, queues and advertising are different issues covered by other rights.

questions.q: Which mark is for agricultural products?
questions.why: Agmark certifies the quality of agricultural products. Hallmark is for gold and silver jewellery, ISI is for industrial products and FPO is for processed fruit products.

questions.q: A buyer for resale is:
options: Not a consumer under the Act
questions.why: Under the Act, a person who buys goods for resale or for a commercial purpose is not a consumer. Only buyers for personal use, or for self-employment livelihood, are covered.

questions.q: Appeal from State to National Commission within:
questions.why: An appeal against a State Commission order to the National Commission must be filed within 30 days. The 45-day limit applies to appeals from the District Commission to the State Commission.

questions.q: Assertion: Consumer protection is in the long-term interest of business. Reason: Satisfied customers lead to repeat sales and goodwill.
questions.why: Both statements are true. Satisfied customers buy again and spread goodwill, so protecting consumers benefits the business in the long run; the reason therefore explains the assertion.

questions.q: Case: A packet of chips shows no net weight. Right violated:
questions.why: Not showing the net weight denies the buyer information about quantity. This violates the right to be informed about the quantity, quality and price of goods.

questions.q: Case: Ritu bought a phone online; it was defective. Is she covered?
questions.why: The Act covers purchases of goods and services made online as well as in shops, so Ritu can complain about the defective phone. The 2019 Act expressly includes e-commerce.

questions.q: Case: An ad claimed a drink increases height; the commission ordered a correction. Relief:
questions.why: A misleading ad is corrected by ordering the advertiser to issue a corrective advertisement. Refund, replacement and removal of defect relate to a faulty product, not a false claim.

questions.q: Case: Consideration paid ₹25 lakh. Under the 2021 Rules, forum:
questions.why: Under the 2021 Rules the District Commission hears cases where the consideration paid is up to ₹50 lakh. ₹25 lakh is below that limit, so the District Commission is the forum.

questions.q: Case: A consumer, unhappy with the District Commission's order, wants to appeal. Within what time and where?
questions.why: An order of the District Commission can be appealed to the State Commission within 45 days. Appeals from the State Commission to the National Commission have a 30-day limit.

questions.q: Case: Consideration ₹3 crore for a defective machine bought for a home workshop used for self-employment. Forum under 2021 Rules:
questions.why: Under the 2021 Rules, consideration above ₹2 crore goes to the National Commission. A machine used for self-employment livelihood is still a consumer purchase, so the complaint is valid.

questions.q: Case: A consumer group publishes test results showing which helmets meet safety standards. Role:
questions.why: Publishing test results that compare helmets is comparative product testing, a typical role of consumer organisations. Making laws and fixing prices are not their functions.

questions.q: Case: A company sells a heater that caught fire; the commission orders it to withdraw all such heaters and pay damages. Reliefs:
options: Withdraw hazardous goods and pay compensation/punitive damages
questions.why: For a dangerous product the commission can order the goods withdrawn from sale and award compensation or punitive damages. A refund, replacement or corrective ad alone would not remove the danger or punish the seller.

questions.q: Case: Customers had to keep visiting the shop for a refund and finally got it through a commission. Which rights were ultimately exercised?
options: Right to be heard and right to seek redressal
questions.why: Customers who were heard in the commission and finally got their refund used the right to be heard and the right to seek redressal. Choice, safety and education are not the rights involved here.

questions.q: Consumer responsibility includes:
questions.why: A responsible consumer asks for a cash memo as proof of purchase, which helps in any later complaint. Ignoring instructions, false complaints and black-market buying are irresponsible acts.

questions.q: Who can file a complaint?
options: Consumer, registered consumer association, Central/State Government, CCPA
questions.why: The Act lets a consumer, a registered consumer association, the Central or State Government, or the CCPA file a complaint. The other options wrongly limit this to one group.

courses.title: Revision & Practice — Class 12 Business Studies
courses.summary: Quick-revision sheets for all twelve chapters and two mock papers (as a 20-question test) with case-based and assertion–reason questions.
outcomes: Learners can recall key lists (principles, steps, functions) quickly
Learners can identify concepts in case studies
Learners can attempt mixed mock questions under time pressure

scenes.text: Lists are the backbone of Business Studies.
Learn them with a keyword for each.

steps.title: Ch 1
steps.body: Effectiveness (goal) vs efficiency (cost) · features: goal-oriented, pervasive, multidimensional, continuous, group, dynamic, intangible · objectives: organisational, social, personal · art ✓, inexact science, not full profession · levels: top, middle, supervisory · coordination = essence

steps.title: Ch 2
steps.body: Nature: universal, general, practice-based, flexible, behavioural, cause-effect, contingent · Taylor: science, harmony, cooperation, development; techniques: functional foremanship (8), standardisation/simplification, method/motion/time/fatigue study, differential piece wage · Fayol 14: DAD-UU-SRC-SOE-SIE

steps.title: Ch 3
steps.body: Features: totality, specific & general, inter-related, dynamic, uncertain, complex, relative · importance: opportunities, threats, resources, change, planning, performance · dimensions: economic, social, technological, political, legal · 1991: LPG; impacts: competition, demanding customers, technology, change, HR, market orientation, less budget support to PSUs

cards.back: Division, Authority, Discipline, Unity of command, Unity of direction, Subordination, Remuneration, Centralisation, Scalar chain, Order, Equity, Stability, Initiative, Esprit de corps
Planning: instruction card clerk, route clerk, time & cost clerk, disciplinarian · Production: speed boss, gang boss, repair boss, inspector

quiz.why: Mental revolution means a change in attitude of workers and managers, from conflict to cooperation. This is Taylor's principle of harmony, not discord.

quiz.q: New law on e-waste is a ___ dimension.
quiz.why: A new law is a legal rule that businesses must follow, so it belongs to the legal dimension of the business environment.
Middle management links top and lower levels; it interprets the policies framed by top management and passes them down for execution. Framing policies is top management's work.
Motion study observes the movements of a worker to eliminate unnecessary and wasteful ones, so the job is done faster and with less fatigue.
Disinvestment means the government sells part of its stake in public sector units, which is a key part of privatisation under the 1991 reforms.

scenes.text: Plan → Organise → Staff → Direct → Control.
Control feeds back into planning.

steps.title: Ch 4 Planning
steps.body: Importance: direction, uncertainty, overlapping, innovation, decisions, standards · features: objectives, primary, pervasive, continuous, futuristic, decision-making, mental · limitations: rigidity, dynamic env, creativity, cost, time, no guarantee · process: objectives → premises → alternatives → evaluate → select → implement → follow-up · types: objective, strategy, policy, procedure, method, rule, programme, budget

steps.title: Ch 5 Organising
steps.body: Steps: identify/divide work, departmentalise, assign duties, reporting · functional vs divisional · formal vs informal (grapevine) · delegation: authority ↓, responsibility ↑, accountability (not delegable) · decentralisation optional

steps.title: Ch 6 Staffing
steps.body: Process: estimate → recruit → select → place/orient → train → appraise → promote → compensate · internal: transfer, promotion · selection: screening, tests, interview, references, decision, medical, offer, contract · training on-job: apprenticeship, coaching, internship, rotation; off-job: lectures, films, case study, computer modelling, vestibule, programmed instruction

steps.title: Ch 7 Directing
steps.body: Elements: supervision, motivation (Maslow 5; financial & non-financial incentives), leadership (autocratic, democratic, laissez-faire), communication (process, formal/informal, barriers: semantic, psychological, organisational, personal)

steps.title: Ch 8 Controlling
steps.body: Process: standards → measure → compare → analyse (CPC, MBE) → correct · limitations: quantitative standards, external factors, resistance, cost · planning & controlling inseparable

cards.back: Only significant deviations reported to top
Rule: no discretion · Policy: guide with discretion

quiz.q: Developing premises is a step in:
quiz.why: Developing premises means making assumptions about the future conditions under which plans will work. This forecasting is a step of the planning process.
The grapevine is the informal network of communication that arises from social relations. It is part of informal organisation, not of the official structure.
In Maslow's hierarchy, self-actualisation, the need to realise one's full potential, sits at the top. Safety is lower, and esteem comes just below it.
Status differences between superior and subordinate come from the organisation's structure and hierarchy, so they are an organisational barrier to communication.
Critical point control concentrates on key result areas, where a deviation would seriously affect the whole organisation. It does not try to control every activity.

scenes.text: Three decisions and two markets.
Plus SEBI.

steps.title: Ch 9
steps.body: Objective: wealth maximisation · investment (cash flows, return, criteria, risk) · financing (cost, risk, floatation, cash flow, fixed operating cost, control, market) · dividend (earnings, stability, growth, cash, preference, tax, market reaction, access, legal, contractual) · trading on equity favourable if ROI > interest · fixed & working capital factors

steps.title: Ch 10
steps.body: Functions: mobilise savings, price discovery, liquidity, low transaction cost · money market: T-bill, CP, call money, CD, commercial bill · capital market: primary (prospectus, offer for sale, private placement, rights, e-IPO) & secondary · stock exchange functions · NSDL/CDSL · SEBI 1988, statutory 1992: protective, developmental, regulatory

steps.title: Exam strategy
steps.body: For numericals, set out EBIT → interest → EBT → tax → EAT → EPS in a table for each plan.

steps.title: Top mistakes to avoid
steps.body: Writing "profit maximisation" as the objective; confusing primary and secondary markets; mixing SEBI's function types.

cards.back: (EBIT − Interest)(1 − tax) ÷ number of equity shares
Zero-coupon, issued at discount by RBI for GoI
New shares offered first to existing shareholders

quiz.why: Debt raises EPS only when the return on investment is greater than the interest rate, because then borrowed funds earn more than they cost. If ROI is lower, debt reduces EPS.

quiz.q: Long production cycle means ___ working capital.
quiz.why: A long production cycle keeps money locked in raw material and work-in-progress for longer, so more working capital is needed.

quiz.q: Price rigging check is SEBI's ___ function.
quiz.why: Checking price rigging protects investors from unfair practices, so it is SEBI's protective function. Regulatory covers rules for market players and developmental covers promotion of the market.
The secondary market, or stock exchange, is where existing securities are bought and sold. New issues are handled by the primary market.
Issuing equity or rights shares dilutes control, but debt holders get no voting rights. So when keeping control is a concern, debt is favoured.

scenes.text: 4 Ps and 5 philosophies.
6 rights, 3 commissions.

steps.title: Ch 11
steps.body: Philosophies: production, product, selling, marketing, societal · functions: info, planning, design, standardisation/grading, packaging/labelling, branding, support, pricing, promotion, physical distribution, transport, warehousing · brand name/mark/trade mark · packaging levels: primary, secondary, transportation · price factors · channels 0–3 levels · physical distribution: order processing, transport, warehousing, inventory · promotion: advertising, personal selling, sales promotion, PR

steps.title: Ch 12
steps.body: CPA 2019 consumer definition (excludes resale/commercial) · rights: safety, informed, choose, heard, redressal, education · responsibilities · ways: self-regulation, business associations, awareness, consumer organisations, government · District/State/National Commission (2021 Rules: ≤₹50 lakh / ₹50 lakh–₹2 crore / >₹2 crore) · appeals 45/30/30 days

steps.title: Exam strategy
steps.body: For case questions, quote the line, name the concept, then explain in one sentence.

steps.title: Top mistakes to avoid
steps.body: Confusing brand mark with trade mark; counting manufacturer/consumer as channel levels; using compensation claimed instead of consideration paid for jurisdiction.

quiz.why: A free gift given with a product is a short-term incentive to boost sales, which is sales promotion. Advertising and PR do not give such direct incentives.
The societal marketing concept adds social welfare to customer satisfaction, so firms also consider the long-term good of society.
An appeal against an order of the District Commission must be made to the State Commission within 45 days.
The law requires the label to show the MRP, the maximum retail price inclusive of all taxes. Costs, profit and employee names are not required there.
Personal selling is face-to-face, so the seller and buyer talk both ways and get immediate feedback. Advertising and publicity are one-way mass communication.

questions.q: Mock A1 · Coordination is:
questions.why: Coordination binds all activities together toward common goals, so it is called the essence of management. It is needed at every level, not a separate function.

questions.q: Mock A2 · Which is NOT a Fayol principle?
questions.why: Differential piece wage is a technique of Taylor's scientific management. Order, equity and initiative are Fayol's principles.

questions.q: Mock A3 · Premises are:
questions.why: Premises are assumptions about the future conditions in which plans will operate. Budgets, rules and programmes are types of plans.

questions.q: Mock A4 · Case: A diversified company makes cars, tractors and bikes. Structure:
questions.why: A firm with separate product lines (cars, tractors, bikes) groups its work by product, which is the divisional structure. A functional structure groups by function.

questions.q: Mock A5 · Case: Candidates are tested on their ability to learn a new software quickly. Test:
questions.why: A test of how quickly one can learn a new skill checks potential to learn, which is an aptitude test. Interest and personality tests measure other traits.

questions.q: Mock A6 · Case: The manager uses jargon; new staff misunderstand. Barrier:
questions.why: Jargon that new staff cannot understand is a problem of language and meaning, so it is a semantic barrier.

questions.q: Mock A7 · Assertion: Controlling is forward-looking too. Reason: Its findings improve future planning.
questions.why: Both statements are true. Controlling compares actual with planned results, and the findings help improve future plans, so it is forward-looking as well; the reason explains the assertion.

questions.q: Mock A8 · EBIT ₹8 lakh; debt ₹40 lakh @ 10%; tax 30%; 2 lakh shares. EPS:
questions.why: Interest = 10% of 40 lakh = 4 lakh. EBT = 8 − 4 = 4 lakh; after 30% tax, 4 × 0.7 = 2.8 lakh. EPS = 2.8 lakh ÷ 2 lakh shares = ₹1.40.

questions.q: Mock A9 · Case: Unskilled workers hired via notice at factory gate for urgent order. Source:
questions.why: Hiring unskilled workers through a notice at the factory gate is direct recruitment, since candidates apply directly to the firm. No intermediary like an exchange or campus is involved.

questions.q: Mock A10 · Case: Supervisor A and B communicate directly to solve an urgent issue, informing their bosses. Principle:
questions.why: Gang plank is a shortcut that lets people at the same level in different chains communicate directly in an emergency, while informing their superiors. It is an exception to the scalar chain.

questions.q: Mock B1 · SEBI got statutory status in:
questions.why: SEBI was set up in 1988 but was given statutory status by the SEBI Act in 1992.

questions.q: Mock B2 · Right to choose is violated when:
questions.why: The right to choose means being able to select from a variety of goods. A shop that forces one brand takes this freedom away.

questions.q: Mock B3 · Sachet packs for rural buyers reflect:
questions.why: Making small sachet packs that rural buyers can afford starts from customer needs, which is the marketing concept. The selling concept focuses on pushing existing products.

questions.q: Mock B4 · Bank overnight borrowing to meet reserves:
questions.why: Call money is very short-term borrowing, for one day or up to fifteen days, used by banks to meet reserve requirements.

questions.q: Mock B5 · Case: Company issues new shares to existing holders 1:5. Method:
questions.why: New shares offered to existing shareholders in proportion to their holding (1 for every 5) is a rights issue.

questions.q: Mock B6 · Case: In a boom, a firm needs more raw material and credit sales rise. Effect:
questions.why: In a boom, sales and credit sales rise and more raw material is needed, so more money is tied up in current assets. Working capital requirement therefore increases.

questions.q: Mock B7 · Case: Consideration ₹1.2 crore for a defective machine (personal use). Forum under 2021 Rules:
questions.why: Under the 2021 Rules the State Commission hears cases with consideration above ₹50 lakh and up to ₹2 crore. ₹1.2 crore falls in that range.

questions.q: Mock B8 · Case: Employees get the option to buy company shares at a lower price after 3 years. Incentive:
questions.why: Giving employees the right to buy shares later at a lower price is an employee stock option, a financial incentive that links their reward to company performance.

questions.q: Mock B9 · Case: A firm pays low dividends because it has many profitable projects and wants to avoid costly borrowing. Factors:
options: Growth opportunities and access to capital market
questions.why: A firm with many profitable projects keeps profits for growth, and easy access to capital markets is not the issue here. Growth opportunities and capital market access explain a low dividend.

questions.q: Mock B10 · Case: A detergent maker sponsors a river-cleaning drive and issues a press release; media cover it free. Tool:
questions.why: A press release about a cleaning drive that the media cover free is publicity, a form of public relations. Unlike advertising, the firm does not pay for the coverage.

school-c12-chemistry-a.title: Class 12 Chemistry · Part A (Ch 1–5)
school-c12-chemistry-a.description: Class 12 Chemistry, chapters 1–5: solutions, electrochemistry, chemical kinetics, d- and f-block elements and coordination compounds — with solved numericals and chapter tests.

courses.title: Ch 1 · Solutions
courses.summary: Types of solutions, every concentration term, solubility and Henry's law, vapour pressure and Raoult's law, ideal and non-ideal solutions with azeotropes, the four colligative properties, and abnormal molar masses with the van't Hoff factor — with fully solved numericals. Independent practice material; not affiliated with or endorsed by any board or exam body.
outcomes: Learners can convert between mass %, mole fraction, molarity and molality.
Learners can apply Henry's law and Raoult's law, and classify deviations from ideality.
Learners can use ΔT_b = K_b m, ΔT_f = K_f m and π = CRT to find molar masses.
Learners can calculate and interpret the van't Hoff factor for dissociation and association.

lessons.title: Types of solutions and concentration terms

scenes.text: When little Tanu had diarrhoea, the doctor said: one ORS packet in exactly one litre of clean water.
Too little water makes the solution too concentrated; too much makes it too weak to help.
Chemists express 'how much is dissolved' in several precise ways — each useful for a different job.

steps.title: What is a solution
steps.body: A **homogeneous mixture** of two or more components. The component in larger amount is usually the **solvent**; the rest are **solutes**. Binary solutions can be gaseous (air), liquid (sugar in water, O₂ in water, ethanol in water) or solid (alloys like brass; H₂ in palladium; amalgam of Hg in Na).

steps.title: Concentration terms
steps.body:
- **Mass %** = (mass of component/mass of solution) × 100.
- **Volume %**; **mass by volume %** (g per 100 mL).
- **ppm** = (parts of component/total parts) × 10⁶ — for trace amounts (e.g. fluoride in water).
- **Mole fraction** xᵢ = nᵢ/Σn; Σx = 1.
- **Molarity M** = moles of solute per litre of solution (changes with temperature).
- **Molality m** = moles of solute per kg of solvent (temperature-independent, since it uses masses).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Ex 1.** 4 g NaOH (M = 40) in 250 mL solution.
- n = 0.1 mol; M = 0.1/0.25 = **0.4 mol/L**.

**Ex 2.** 2.5 g ethanoic acid (M = 60) in 75 g benzene.
- n = 0.0417 mol; m = 0.0417/0.075 = **0.556 mol/kg**.

**Ex 3.** Mole fraction of ethylene glycol (C₂H₆O₂, M = 62) in a 20% by mass aqueous solution.
- In 100 g: 20/62 = 0.323 mol glycol; 80/18 = 4.444 mol water
- x(glycol) = 0.323/4.767 ≈ **0.068**; x(water) ≈ 0.932.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using volume of *solvent* instead of *solution* for molarity.
- Using mass of solution instead of solvent for molality.
- Forgetting to convert g to kg (molality) and mL to L (molarity).

steps.title: Molarity ↔ molality
steps.body: For a solution of density d (g/mL), molarity M and solute molar mass M₂: **m = 1000M/(1000d − M·M₂)**.

activity.prompt: Find the molality of a solution containing 9 g glucose (M = 180 g/mol) in 250 g water (mol/kg).

quiz.q: Which concentration term is independent of temperature?
quiz.why: Molality uses mass of solute per kg of solvent, and masses do not change with temperature. Molarity uses volume, which changes with temperature.

quiz.q: Sum of mole fractions of all components is
quiz.why: The mole fractions of all components of a mixture add up to exactly 1, since each is a fraction of the total moles.
Brass is zinc dissolved in copper, a solid in a solid, forming a solid solution (alloy).

quiz.q: Molarity is defined as moles of solute per
quiz.why: Molarity is moles of solute per litre of solution. Per kg of solvent is molality.
Parts per million expresses very small amounts, so it is used for trace quantities such as pollutants in air or water.

sources: NCERT Class 12 Chemistry (topic reference, own wording)

lessons.title: Solubility and Henry's law

scenes.text: When Rohit opens a chilled soda bottle there is a gentle hiss; a warm one sprays everywhere.
CO₂ is dissolved under high pressure; opening the cap lowers the pressure and gas escapes.
Warmer liquid holds less gas — Henry's law and temperature explain both.

steps.title: Solubility of solids
steps.body:
Solubility is the maximum amount that dissolves in a given amount of solvent at a given temperature (a saturated solution is in dynamic equilibrium with undissolved solute).
- 'Like dissolves like': ionic and polar solutes dissolve in polar solvents; non-polar in non-polar.
- Endothermic dissolution (ΔH > 0): solubility rises with temperature; exothermic: falls (Le Chatelier).
- Pressure has almost no effect (solids and liquids are nearly incompressible).

steps.title: Henry's law (gases in liquids)
steps.body:
**The partial pressure of a gas in vapour is proportional to its mole fraction in solution:**
**p = K_H x**
- Higher K_H ⇒ lower solubility.
- Solubility of gases **decreases with temperature** (K_H increases), because dissolution is exothermic.

Applications: soda bottles sealed under high CO₂ pressure; **scuba divers** breathe air diluted with helium to reduce N₂ dissolved in blood ('bends' on rapid surfacing); **anoxia** at high altitude because of low O₂ partial pressure.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Ex 1.** K_H for CO₂ in water at 298 K is 1.67×10⁸ Pa. Mole fraction under 2.53×10⁵ Pa:
- x = p/K_H = 2.53×10⁵/1.67×10⁸ ≈ **1.52×10⁻³**.
- In 500 mL water (27.8 mol): n(CO₂) ≈ 1.52×10⁻³ × 27.8 ≈ **0.042 mol ≈ 1.85 g**.

**Ex 2.** If the partial pressure of O₂ above water is halved, its solubility **halves** (direct proportion).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking larger K_H means higher solubility — it is the opposite.
- Applying Henry's law to gases that react with water strongly (e.g. NH₃, HCl) — deviations are large.
- Forgetting that gas solubility falls on heating (fish suffer in warm water).

statements.s: Solubility of gases in water increases with temperature.
A gas with higher K_H is less soluble.
Pressure has a large effect on the solubility of solids in liquids.
statements.why: Solids and liquids are nearly incompressible.

statements.s: Scuba tanks use helium-diluted air to reduce the bends.
statements.why: Helium is much less soluble in blood.

options: partial pressure and mole fraction of a gas in solution
quiz.why: Henry's law says the partial pressure of a gas above a solution is proportional to its mole fraction in the solution: p = K_H x.

quiz.q: Raising temperature makes O₂ in water
quiz.why: Gas solubility falls as temperature rises, because K_H increases. So O₂ is less soluble in warm water.

quiz.q: The 'bends' in divers are caused by
quiz.why: At high pressure, extra nitrogen dissolves in blood. On a rapid ascent pressure falls and the N₂ forms bubbles, causing the bends.

quiz.q: Soda bottles are sealed under high pressure of
quiz.why: By Henry's law, more CO₂ dissolves in the drink at high CO₂ pressure, giving a fizzy soda when the bottle is opened.

quiz.q: 'Like dissolves like' predicts that iodine dissolves best in
quiz.why: Like dissolves like: non-polar iodine dissolves best in non-polar CCl₄. Water and salt water are polar.

lessons.title: Vapour pressure, Raoult's law and non-ideal solutions

scenes.text: Aunt Neelam notices her perfume smells different near the end of the bottle.
More volatile components evaporate faster, so the vapour is richer in them.
Raoult's law tells us exactly how much each component contributes to the vapour.

steps.title: Raoult's law
steps.body:
For a solution of two volatile liquids: **p₁ = x₁p₁°**, **p₂ = x₂p₂°** and total **p = p₁° + (p₂° − p₁°)x₂** — a straight line against x₂.

Vapour composition: **y₁ = p₁/p** — the vapour is richer in the more volatile component.

For a non-volatile solute in a solvent: p = x₁p₁° (only the solvent contributes). Raoult's law is a special case of Henry's law where K_H = p°.

steps.title: Ideal and non-ideal solutions
steps.body:
**Ideal:** obeys Raoult's law at all compositions; **ΔH_mix = 0, ΔV_mix = 0**; A–B interactions ≈ A–A and B–B (n-hexane + n-heptane; benzene + toluene).

**Positive deviation:** A–B interactions weaker; p higher than predicted; ΔH_mix > 0, ΔV_mix > 0. Examples: ethanol + acetone, ethanol + water, CS₂ + acetone.

**Negative deviation:** A–B interactions stronger (e.g. H-bonding between components); p lower; ΔH_mix < 0, ΔV_mix < 0. Examples: chloroform + acetone, nitric acid + water, phenol + aniline.

steps.title: Azeotropes
steps.body:
Mixtures that boil at constant composition (liquid and vapour have the same composition), so they cannot be separated by fractional distillation.
- **Minimum-boiling** (large positive deviation): ethanol–water at about 95% ethanol by volume.
- **Maximum-boiling** (large negative deviation): nitric acid–water at about 68% HNO₃ by mass.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Ex 1.** p°_A = 450 mmHg, p°_B = 700 mmHg, x_A = 0.4.
- p_A = 0.4 × 450 = 180; p_B = 0.6 × 700 = 420
- **p = 600 mmHg**; y_A = 180/600 = **0.30** (vapour richer in B).

**Ex 2.** Mixing acetone and chloroform warms the mixture. ⇒ ΔH_mix < 0 ⇒ **negative deviation** (H-bond between CHCl₃ and C=O).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using liquid mole fractions for the vapour composition.
- Swapping signs: positive deviation ⇒ ΔH_mix positive (endothermic), volume expands.
- Thinking azeotropes are compounds — they are mixtures.

activity.prompt: Classify each mixture.

quiz.q: For an ideal solution, ΔH_mix is
quiz.why: In an ideal solution the A–B interactions equal A–A and B–B ones, so no heat is absorbed or released and ΔH_mix = 0.
Ethanol molecules are H-bonded; adding water breaks some of these bonds, weakening interactions. Vapour pressure becomes higher than Raoult's law predicts, a positive deviation.
Negative deviation means stronger A–B attractions and lower vapour pressure, so the mixture boils at a higher temperature, giving a maximum-boiling azeotrope.

quiz.q: Vapour above a solution is richer in
quiz.why: The more volatile component has higher vapour pressure, so it contributes more to the vapour, which is richer in it than the liquid.

quiz.q: Raoult's law for a non-volatile solute gives p =
quiz.why: With a non-volatile solute only the solvent evaporates, so the vapour pressure is the solvent's mole fraction times its pure vapour pressure: p = x₁p₁°.

lessons.title: Relative lowering of vapour pressure and elevation of boiling point

scenes.text: Dev's mother adds salt to the pasta water and jokes that it boils hotter now.
It does — but by only a fraction of a degree for a pinch.
The rise depends only on the number of dissolved particles, not their identity: a colligative property.

steps.title: Colligative properties
steps.body: Depend on the **number of solute particles**, not their nature (for dilute solutions of non-volatile solutes): RLVP, ΔT_b, ΔT_f and osmotic pressure.

steps.title: Relative lowering of vapour pressure
steps.body:
(p₁° − p₁)/p₁° = x₂ = n₂/(n₁ + n₂) ≈ n₂/n₁ (dilute).
So **(p° − p)/p° = (w₂M₁)/(M₂w₁)** — gives the molar mass M₂ of the solute.

steps.title: Elevation of boiling point
steps.body:
A solution has lower vapour pressure, so it must be heated more to reach atmospheric pressure.
**ΔT_b = K_b m** where K_b (ebullioscopic constant) is in K kg mol⁻¹ (water 0.52, benzene 2.53).
**M₂ = (1000 × K_b × w₂)/(ΔT_b × w₁)** (w in g).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using molarity in ΔT_b = K_b m (it needs molality).
- Forgetting the 1000 when solvent mass is in grams.
- Applying colligative formulas to electrolytes without the van't Hoff factor.

activity.prompt: A solution of 3 g of a non-volatile solute in 100 g water boils at 373.26 K (pure water 373.00 K; K_b = 0.52 K kg/mol). Find the molar mass (g/mol).

quiz.why: Colligative properties depend only on the number of solute particles, not on their nature or identity.

quiz.q: Relative lowering of vapour pressure equals
quiz.why: By Raoult's law, (p° − p)/p° = x₂, the mole fraction of the solute.
The ebullioscopic constant K_b of water is 0.52 K kg mol⁻¹. 1.86 is K_f of water and 5.12 is K_f of benzene.

quiz.q: Boiling point of a solution compared with the pure solvent is
quiz.why: The solute lowers the vapour pressure, so the solution must be heated more to boil. Its boiling point is higher than the pure solvent's.

quiz.q: ΔT_b for 0.2 m urea in water is
quiz.why: ΔT_b = K_b × m = 0.52 × 0.2 = 0.104 K. Urea does not dissociate, so i = 1.

lessons.title: Depression of freezing point and osmotic pressure

story.title: Salt on icy roads and saline drips

scenes.text: In snowy Himalayan towns, workers sprinkle salt on icy roads so ice melts below 0 °C.
In a hospital, a patient gets a drip of 0.9% saline — never pure water.
Pure water would rush into blood cells by osmosis and burst them.

steps.title: Depression of freezing point
steps.body:
At the freezing point, solid and liquid have the same vapour pressure. The solution's lower vapour pressure makes it freeze at a lower temperature.
**ΔT_f = K_f m**; K_f (cryoscopic constant): water 1.86, benzene 5.12 K kg mol⁻¹.
**M₂ = (1000 × K_f × w₂)/(ΔT_f × w₁)**. Antifreeze (ethylene glycol) in car radiators uses this.

steps.title: Osmosis and osmotic pressure
steps.body:
**Osmosis:** solvent flows through a **semipermeable membrane** from pure solvent (or dilute solution) into a more concentrated solution.
**Osmotic pressure π** = the extra pressure that just stops it: **π = CRT = (n₂/V)RT**, R = 0.083 L bar mol⁻¹ K⁻¹.
- Measured at room temperature and gives large values even for tiny concentrations ⇒ **best method for molar masses of proteins and polymers**.
- **Isotonic** solutions have equal π (0.9% NaCl ≈ blood); **hypertonic** makes cells shrink; **hypotonic** makes them swell.
- **Reverse osmosis:** apply pressure > π to push solvent out of the solution through the membrane — used for **desalination** and home RO purifiers.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using V in mL with R = 0.083 L bar mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ (convert to litres).
- Saying solute moves in osmosis — solvent moves.
- Expecting ΔT_f to be positive in the final temperature — the solution freezes *below* the solvent.

a.text: Red blood cells are placed in three beakers: 0.9% NaCl, 2% NaCl and pure water. What happens in pure water?

choices.label: Cells swell and may burst
choices.feedback: Right — water is hypotonic; it flows into the cells.

choices.label: Cells shrink
choices.feedback: Shrinking happens in a hypertonic solution.

a2.text: Water moves from lower to higher solute concentration. Pure water has less solute than the cell. Which way does water move?

choices.label: Cells shrink (plasmolysis-like crenation)
choices.feedback: Correct — 2% is hypertonic; water leaves the cells.

b2.text: 2% has more solute than blood. Where will water go?

choices.label: Out of the cells — they shrink

end.text: That is why drips use isotonic 0.9% saline: no net osmosis, cells stay healthy.

quiz.why: The cryoscopic constant K_f of water is 1.86 K kg mol⁻¹. The value 0.52 is K_b, and 5.12 is for benzene.
Van't Hoff's equation for osmotic pressure is π = CRT, which is like the ideal gas equation.

quiz.q: Molar masses of proteins are best found by
quiz.why: Osmotic pressure gives large, easily measured values even for dilute solutions at room temperature, so it suits large molecules like proteins that are unstable on heating.

quiz.q: Desalination by RO needs applied pressure
quiz.why: In reverse osmosis, pressure larger than the osmotic pressure is applied on the salt-water side to push water through the membrane to the pure side.

quiz.q: A cell placed in a hypertonic solution
quiz.why: In a hypertonic solution the outside concentration is higher, so water moves out of the cell by osmosis and it shrinks.

lessons.title: Abnormal molar masses and the van't Hoff factor

story.title: Why salt lowers freezing point twice as much

scenes.text: In the lab, Leena finds that 0.1 m NaCl freezes at nearly twice the depression of 0.1 m glucose.
NaCl splits into Na⁺ and Cl⁻ — twice as many particles.
Van't Hoff introduced a factor i to correct the colligative formulas for such cases.

steps.title: The van't Hoff factor
steps.body:
**i = observed colligative property / calculated (normal) value = normal molar mass / observed molar mass = total particles after / particles before.**
Modified equations: **ΔT_b = iK_b m**, **ΔT_f = iK_f m**, **π = iCRT**, RLVP = i x₂.
- Dissociation (electrolytes): i > 1 (NaCl → 2, K₂SO₄ → 3, ideal limit).
- Association: i < 1 (ethanoic acid dimerises in benzene via H-bonds ⇒ i ≈ 0.5).
- Observed molar mass is lower than true for dissociation, higher for association: hence 'abnormal'.

steps.title: Degree of dissociation / association
steps.body:
- Dissociation into n ions: **α = (i − 1)/(n − 1)**.
- Association into (A)ₙ: **α = (1 − i)/(1 − 1/n)**; for dimers α = 2(1 − i).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Ex 1.** ΔT_f of 0.1 m NaCl (complete dissociation): ΔT_f = 2 × 1.86 × 0.1 = **0.372 K**.

**Ex 2.** 2 g ethanoic acid (M = 60) in 100 g benzene (K_f = 5.12) lowers f.p. by 0.89 K.
- Calculated ΔT_f = 5.12 × (2/60)/0.1 ≈ 1.71 K
- i = 0.89/1.71 ≈ **0.52**
- α (dimerisation) = 2(1 − 0.52) ≈ **0.96** ⇒ about 96% associated.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using i = 2 for weak electrolytes — they dissociate only partly.
- Forgetting that association makes i < 1.
- Using α = (i − 1)/n instead of (i − 1)/(n − 1).

activity.prompt: Match each solute (ideal, complete dissociation or association) to its i.

quiz.q: van't Hoff factor for Al₂(SO₄)₃ (complete dissociation) is
quiz.why: Al₂(SO₄)₃ gives 2 Al³⁺ and 3 SO₄²⁻ on complete dissociation, so 5 ions per formula unit and i = 5.

quiz.q: Association of solute particles makes i
quiz.why: Association joins particles into larger units, so there are fewer particles than expected and i is less than 1.

quiz.q: Observed molar mass of NaCl from ΔT_f is
quiz.why: NaCl dissociates into two ions, so the observed colligative effect is larger than for undissociated NaCl. Since M ∝ 1/ΔT_f, the calculated molar mass is lower than 58.5.

quiz.q: The solution with the lowest freezing point (same molality):
quiz.why: At equal molality, CaCl₂ gives three ions (i = 3), the most particles, so it lowers the freezing point most. NaCl gives 2, and glucose and urea give 1.

quiz.q: A weak acid HA is 20% dissociated. i =

questions.q: Molality is expressed in
questions.why: Molality is moles of solute per kilogram of solvent, so its unit is mol/kg.

questions.q: Which is a colligative property?
questions.why: Osmotic pressure depends on the number of solute particles, so it is a colligative property. Density does not depend only on particle count.

questions.q: Amalgam of mercury with sodium is a solution of
questions.why: In sodium amalgam, mercury (a liquid) dissolves in sodium (a solid), which is a liquid in solid solution.

questions.q: Assertion: Molality is preferred over molarity for colligative properties. Reason: Molality does not change with temperature.
options: Both true; reason does not explain
questions.why: Both statements are true. Molality is based on masses, which do not change with temperature, and colligative properties are measured at varying temperatures; so the reason explains the assertion.

questions.q: Which aqueous solution has the highest boiling point?
questions.why: Boiling point elevation depends on i × m. BaCl₂ gives three ions (i = 3), more than NaCl (2) or the non-electrolytes glucose and urea (1).

questions.q: Chloroform and acetone mixture shows
questions.why: Chloroform and acetone form hydrogen bonds with each other, so A–B attraction is stronger than in the pure liquids. Vapour pressure is lower than expected, a negative deviation.

questions.q: The molarity of pure water is about
questions.why: 1 L of water is about 1000 g, which is 1000/18 ≈ 55.5 mol, so its molarity is about 55.5 M.

questions.q: Case: p°(benzene) = 0.850 bar. A solution of 0.5 g non-volatile solute in 39 g benzene has p = 0.845 bar. Molar mass of solute (M_benzene = 78) is about
Liquids A and B form an ideal solution: p°_A = 200 mmHg, p°_B = 600 mmHg, x_A = 0.5. Mole fraction of A in vapour:
questions.why: p_A = 0.5 × 200 = 100 and p_B = 0.5 × 600 = 300 mmHg, so total p = 400. Mole fraction of A in vapour = 100/400 = 0.25.

questions.q: Assertion: A 0.9% NaCl solution is isotonic with blood. Reason: Isotonic solutions have the same osmotic pressure.
options: Both true; reason does not explain
questions.why: Both are true. Isotonic solutions have equal osmotic pressure, and 0.9% NaCl matches blood, so the reason explains why it is isotonic.

questions.q: The osmotic pressure of 0.1 M glucose at 300 K (R = 0.083 L bar mol⁻¹ K⁻¹):
questions.why: π = CRT = 0.1 × 0.083 × 300 = 2.49 bar. Glucose does not dissociate, so i = 1.

questions.q: 10 g of a solute in 200 g water lowers f.p. by 0.93 K (K_f = 1.86). Molar mass:
Case: An aqueous solution freezes at −0.186 °C. Its boiling point is (K_f = 1.86, K_b = 0.52)
questions.why: ΔT_f = 0.186 K, so m = 0.186/1.86 = 0.1. Then ΔT_b = 0.52 × 0.1 = 0.052, so the boiling point is 100.052 °C.

questions.q: K_H values (in kbar) of gases A, B, C are 20, 40, 60 at the same T. Most soluble gas:
questions.why: By Henry's law, solubility is inversely proportional to K_H. Gas A has the lowest K_H (20 kbar), so it is the most soluble.

questions.q: A 0.01 m solution of a salt AB₂ shows ΔT_f = 0.0558 K (K_f = 1.86). Degree of dissociation:
questions.why: ΔT_f = i K_f m gives i = 0.0558/(1.86 × 0.01) = 3. For AB₂ ⇌ A + 2B, i = 1 + 2α = 3, so α = 1.

questions.q: Case: A weak acid HX (0.1 m) has ΔT_f = 0.2046 K (K_f = 1.86). Its degree of dissociation is
Assertion: Fractional distillation cannot separate an azeotrope. Reason: Its liquid and vapour have the same composition.
options: Both true; reason does not explain
questions.why: Both are true. At the azeotropic composition the vapour has the same composition as the liquid, so distillation cannot change it and cannot separate the components.

questions.q: Which pair of solutions is isotonic (same T)?
questions.why: Isotonic solutions have equal i × C. Glucose gives 0.2 × 1 = 0.2 and NaCl gives 0.1 × 2 = 0.2, so their osmotic pressures match.

lessons.title: Galvanic cells and electrode potentials

scenes.text: For the science fair, Arnav pushes a zinc nail and a copper coin into a lemon and lights a tiny LED with three of them.
Zinc gives up electrons more readily than copper, so electrons flow through the wire.
Every battery turns a spontaneous redox reaction into electricity — this is a galvanic cell.

steps.title: Galvanic (voltaic) cell
steps.body:
Converts the chemical energy of a **spontaneous redox reaction** into electrical energy.
**Daniell cell:** Zn(s) + Cu²⁺(aq) → Zn²⁺(aq) + Cu(s), E° = 1.10 V.
- **Anode** (−): oxidation — Zn → Zn²⁺ + 2e⁻.
- **Cathode** (+): reduction — Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu.
- **Salt bridge** (KCl or KNO₃ in agar) completes the circuit and keeps both solutions neutral.
**Cell notation:** Zn(s) | Zn²⁺(aq) || Cu²⁺(aq) | Cu(s) — anode on the left, cathode on the right.

steps.title: Electrode potential and SHE
steps.body:
The potential difference between an electrode and its solution is the **electrode potential**; by convention we use **reduction potentials**. Absolute values cannot be measured, so we compare with the **standard hydrogen electrode (SHE)**: Pt | H₂(g, 1 bar) | H⁺(aq, 1 M), assigned **E° = 0.00 V** at all temperatures.

**E°cell = E°cathode − E°anode = E°right − E°left**.

Some values: Li⁺/Li −3.05 V; K⁺/K −2.93; Mg²⁺/Mg −2.36; Zn²⁺/Zn −0.76; Fe²⁺/Fe −0.44; Cu²⁺/Cu +0.34; Ag⁺/Ag +0.80; F₂/F⁻ +2.87 V.
- Higher (more positive) E° ⇒ stronger oxidising agent (F₂ strongest); lower E° ⇒ stronger reducing agent (Li strongest).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Ex 1.** Zn | Zn²⁺ || Cu²⁺ | Cu: E° = 0.34 − (−0.76) = **1.10 V**.

**Ex 2.** Cu | Cu²⁺ || Ag⁺ | Ag: E° = 0.80 − 0.34 = **0.46 V**; reaction Cu + 2Ag⁺ → Cu²⁺ + 2Ag.

**Ex 3.** Can a copper vessel store AgNO₃ solution? E°cell for Cu + 2Ag⁺ is +0.46 V > 0 ⇒ reaction is spontaneous ⇒ **no**, copper would dissolve and silver deposit.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Multiplying E° by stoichiometric coefficients — E° is intensive and never multiplied.
- Calling the anode positive in a galvanic cell (it is negative; in electrolysis the anode is positive).
- Writing the cathode on the left in cell notation.

activity.prompt: Find E°cell for Mg | Mg²⁺ || Ag⁺ | Ag. Use E°(Mg²⁺/Mg) = −2.36 V and E°(Ag⁺/Ag) = +0.80 V.

quiz.q: In a galvanic cell oxidation occurs at the
quiz.why: In a galvanic cell oxidation takes place at the anode (An Ox) and reduction at the cathode (Red Cat).

quiz.q: The SHE is assigned a potential of
quiz.why: The standard hydrogen electrode is the reference, and its potential is defined as 0.00 V; other electrodes are measured against it.

quiz.q: The function of a salt bridge is to
options: complete the circuit and maintain neutrality
quiz.why: The salt bridge lets ions move between the half-cells, completing the circuit and keeping each solution electrically neutral. It does not supply electrons.

quiz.q: The strongest oxidising agent among these is
quiz.why: F₂ has the highest standard reduction potential, so it gains electrons most readily and is the strongest oxidising agent.

quiz.q: If E°cell is positive, the cell reaction is
quiz.why: ΔG° = −nFE°, so a positive E°cell gives a negative ΔG°, which means the reaction is spontaneous.

lessons.title: The Nernst equation, ΔG and equilibrium constant

scenes.text: Ishita's torch dims slowly over weeks, not all at once.
As the battery reacts, product ions build up and reactants run low.
Nernst showed how cell voltage depends on concentrations — and why it finally drops to zero at equilibrium.

steps.title: Nernst equation
steps.body:
For an electrode Mⁿ⁺ + ne⁻ → M: E = E° − (RT/nF) ln(1/[Mⁿ⁺]).
For a cell aA + bB → cC + dD:
**E = E° − (2.303RT/nF) log Q**, and at 298 K **E = E° − (0.059/n) log Q**, Q = [C]ᶜ[D]ᵈ/[A]ᵃ[B]ᵇ (pure solids = 1).

steps.title: E°, ΔG° and K
steps.body:
- **ΔG = −nFE** and **ΔG° = −nFE°** (F = 96 487 ≈ 96 500 C mol⁻¹).
- At equilibrium E = 0 and Q = K: **E° = (0.059/n) log K** at 298 K ⇒ **log K = nE°/0.059**.
- Positive E° ⇒ negative ΔG° ⇒ K > 1.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Ex 1.** Zn | Zn²⁺ (0.001 M) || Cu²⁺ (0.1 M) | Cu, E° = 1.10 V, n = 2.
- Q = [Zn²⁺]/[Cu²⁺] = 0.01; log Q = −2
- E = 1.10 − (0.059/2)(−2) = **1.159 V**.

**Ex 2.** ΔG° for the Daniell cell: −2 × 96500 × 1.10 = **−212.3 kJ/mol**.

**Ex 3.** K for the Daniell reaction: log K = 2 × 1.10/0.059 ≈ 37.3 ⇒ **K ≈ 2×10³⁷** — the reaction goes essentially to completion.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Writing Q upside down (products on top, reactants below).
- Using n = 1 for a 2-electron reaction.
- Including concentrations of solids in Q.

steps.title: Concentration cell
steps.body: Same electrodes, different concentrations: E = (0.059/n) log(C_cathode/C_anode) — the more concentrated side is the cathode.

activity.prompt: For Ni | Ni²⁺ (0.01 M) || Ag⁺ (0.1 M) | Ag, E° = 1.05 V and n = 2. Find E at 298 K (V). Q = [Ni²⁺]/[Ag⁺]².

quiz.why: At 298 K, 2.303RT/F = 2.303 × 8.314 × 298/96500 ≈ 0.059 V, which is the constant in the Nernst equation.

quiz.q: When a cell reaches equilibrium, E is
quiz.why: At equilibrium there is no net reaction and no driving force, so the cell potential E falls to zero.

quiz.q: ΔG° = −nFE°. If E° = 0.5 V and n = 2, ΔG° is
log K = nE°/0.059 at 298 K. For n = 1, E° = 0.118 V, K =
In the Nernst equation, solids have activity
quiz.why: Pure solids and liquids have constant concentration and are taken as unit activity, so they are written as 1 in the Nernst equation.

lessons.title: Conductance of electrolytic solutions

scenes.text: An RO technician dips a little meter into Aman's tap water and reads its 'TDS'.
The meter actually measures conductivity: dissolved ions carry current.
Chemists define conductivity and molar conductivity to compare solutions fairly.

steps.title: Resistance, conductivity and cell constant
steps.body:
- R = ρl/A; **conductance G = 1/R** (siemens, S).
- **Conductivity κ = 1/ρ = G × (l/A)** — S m⁻¹ (or S cm⁻¹).
- **Cell constant G* = l/A = κR** — found using a standard KCl solution of known κ.
- Measured with AC (to avoid electrolysis) in a Wheatstone-bridge-type circuit.

steps.title: Molar conductivity
steps.body:
**Λm = κ/c** — conductivity of the volume containing 1 mol of electrolyte between electrodes 1 cm apart (conceptually).
- With κ in S cm⁻¹ and c in mol/L: **Λm (S cm² mol⁻¹) = 1000κ/c**.
- With κ in S m⁻¹ and c in mol m⁻³: Λm in S m² mol⁻¹ (1 S m² mol⁻¹ = 10⁴ S cm² mol⁻¹).

steps.title: Variation with concentration
steps.body:
- **κ decreases** on dilution (fewer ions per unit volume).
- **Λm increases** on dilution.
- **Strong electrolytes** (KCl, NaCl): Λm rises slowly, linearly with √c — **Debye–Hückel–Onsager: Λm = Λ°m − A√c**; extrapolate to c → 0 to get Λ°m.
- **Weak electrolytes** (CH₃COOH): Λm rises steeply at low c because the degree of dissociation increases; Λ°m cannot be found by extrapolation.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Ex 1.** A cell filled with 0.1 M KCl (κ = 1.29 S m⁻¹) has R = 100 Ω.
- G* = κR = **129 m⁻¹**.

**Ex 2.** The same cell with 0.02 M solution has R = 520 Ω.
- κ = G*/R = 129/520 = **0.248 S m⁻¹**
- c = 0.02 mol/L = 20 mol m⁻³ ⇒ Λm = 0.248/20 = **0.0124 S m² mol⁻¹ = 124 S cm² mol⁻¹**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Mixing units of c (mol/L vs mol m⁻³).
- Saying conductivity increases on dilution — molar conductivity does; conductivity falls.
- Using DC to measure solution conductance (causes electrolysis and polarisation).

activity.prompt: A 0.05 M solution has κ = 0.0055 S cm⁻¹. Find its molar conductivity (S cm² mol⁻¹).

quiz.why: Conductivity κ = 1/ρ, where resistivity is in Ω m, so κ has unit S m⁻¹.

quiz.q: On dilution, the molar conductivity of an electrolyte
quiz.why: On dilution, ions are farther apart and, for weak electrolytes, more dissociation occurs. So molar conductivity increases.
The cell constant is the distance between the electrodes divided by their area, l/A, in cm⁻¹.

quiz.q: Λ°m of a weak electrolyte cannot be found by extrapolation because
options: Λm rises steeply at low concentration
quiz.why: For a weak electrolyte, Λm rises very steeply at low concentration and the curve is not linear, so it cannot be extrapolated to give Λ°m.

quiz.q: AC is used for conductance measurement to
quiz.why: Direct current would cause electrolysis and polarisation at the electrodes, changing the solution. Alternating current avoids this.

lessons.title: Kohlrausch's law and its applications

scenes.text: Priya cannot measure Λ°m of acetic acid directly; the graph shoots up at low concentration.
Kohlrausch noticed each ion contributes a fixed amount at infinite dilution.
So she adds known values from strong electrolytes to get the weak one.

steps.title: Kohlrausch's law of independent migration
steps.body:
At infinite dilution each ion contributes independently: **Λ°m = ν₊λ°₊ + ν₋λ°₋**.
Examples (S cm² mol⁻¹): λ°(H⁺) = 349.6, λ°(OH⁻) = 199.1, λ°(Na⁺) = 50.1, λ°(K⁺) = 73.5, λ°(Cl⁻) = 76.3, λ°(CH₃COO⁻) = 40.9. H⁺ and OH⁻ are exceptionally mobile (proton hopping in water).

steps.title: Applications
steps.body:
1. **Λ°m of a weak electrolyte** from strong ones:
Λ°(CH₃COOH) = Λ°(HCl) + Λ°(CH₃COONa) − Λ°(NaCl).
2. **Degree of dissociation** α = Λm/Λ°m.
3. **Dissociation constant** Ka = cα²/(1 − α).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Adding instead of subtracting the common salt term.
- Forgetting stoichiometric coefficients: Λ°(CaCl₂) = λ°(Ca²⁺) + 2λ°(Cl⁻).
- Using Λm in place of Λ°m in α = Λm/Λ°m.

activity.prompt: Using λ°(Mg²⁺) = 106.0 and λ°(Cl⁻) = 76.3 S cm² mol⁻¹, find Λ°m of MgCl₂ (S cm² mol⁻¹).

quiz.why: Kohlrausch's law states that at infinite dilution each ion contributes independently to the molar conductivity.
Λ°(CH₃COOH) = Λ°(CH₃COO⁻) + Λ°(H⁺) = Λ°(HCl) + Λ°(CH₃COONa) − Λ°(NaCl), because Na⁺ and Cl⁻ cancel.
The degree of dissociation of a weak electrolyte is the ratio of molar conductivity at the given concentration to that at infinite dilution: α = Λm/Λ°m.

quiz.q: The ion with the highest limiting molar conductivity in water is
quiz.why: H⁺ has the highest limiting molar conductivity because it moves by proton hopping between water molecules (Grotthuss mechanism).

quiz.q: Ka of a weak acid from conductance is
quiz.why: For HA ⇌ H⁺ + A⁻, Ka = cα²/(1 − α) by Ostwald's dilution law, with α = Λm/Λ°m.

lessons.title: Electrolysis and Faraday's laws

scenes.text: Meera's 'gold' earrings are actually brass coated with a thin layer of gold.
The jeweller passed current through a gold-salt solution with the earrings as the cathode.
Faraday's laws tell exactly how much metal a given current deposits.

steps.title: Electrolytic cell
steps.body: External electrical energy drives a **non-spontaneous** reaction. Here the **anode is positive** (oxidation) and the **cathode is negative** (reduction). Uses: electroplating, refining copper, extracting Na, Mg, Al, making NaOH and Cl₂.

steps.title: Faraday's laws
steps.body:
1. **First law:** mass deposited is proportional to charge passed: **m = ZQ = ZIt** (Z = electrochemical equivalent).
2. **Second law:** for the same charge, masses are in the ratio of their equivalent masses (M/n).
- 1 mole of electrons carries **1 F = 96 487 ≈ 96 500 C**.
- **m = (M × I × t)/(n × F)**.

steps.title: Products of electrolysis
steps.body:
Depend on the state of electrolyte, electrodes and competing reactions (E° and overpotential):
- **Molten NaCl:** Na at cathode, Cl₂ at anode.
- **Aqueous NaCl:** H₂ at cathode (water reduced, since Na⁺ has very negative E°); Cl₂ at anode (O₂ formation needs a large overpotential); NaOH remains.
- **Dilute H₂SO₄:** H₂ at cathode, O₂ at anode.
- **Aqueous CuSO₄ with copper electrodes:** Cu dissolves at anode and deposits at cathode (electrorefining).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Ex 1.** 2 A for 965 s through CuSO₄ solution.
- Q = 1930 C = 0.02 F
- Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu ⇒ 0.01 mol Cu = **0.635 g**.

**Ex 2.** 1.5 A for 30 min through AgNO₃.
- Q = 1.5 × 1800 = 2700 C ⇒ 0.028 mol e⁻ ⇒ 0.028 mol Ag = **3.02 g**.

**Ex 3.** Charge to reduce 1 mol MnO₄⁻ to Mn²⁺: 5 F = **4.83×10⁵ C**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting n (electrons per ion) in m = MIt/nF.
- Expecting Na from aqueous NaCl — water is reduced instead.
- Using minutes instead of seconds for t.

activity.prompt: How many grams of aluminium (M = 27, Al³⁺) are deposited by 9650 C?

quiz.why: One faraday is the charge carried by one mole of electrons, about 96 500 C.

quiz.q: In an electrolytic cell the anode is
quiz.why: In an electrolytic cell the anode is connected to the positive terminal of the battery, so it is positive, and oxidation occurs there.

quiz.q: Electrolysis of aqueous NaCl gives at the cathode
quiz.why: In aqueous NaCl, water is reduced more easily than Na⁺, so H₂ is liberated at the cathode, not sodium.

quiz.q: Charge needed to deposit 1 mol Cu from Cu²⁺ is
quiz.why: Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu needs 2 mol of electrons per mole of copper, so 2 F of charge.
By Faraday's first law, the mass deposited is proportional to the quantity of charge passed.
