lessons.title: Batteries, fuel cells and corrosion

story.title: The rusty gate and the e-rickshaw

scenes.text: Outside Ravi's house, an e-rickshaw charges its lead-acid batteries overnight.
Nearby, the iron gate shows orange rust where the paint has chipped.
Both are electrochemistry: one stores energy usefully, the other slowly eats metal.

steps.title: Primary batteries (not rechargeable)
steps.body:
- **Dry (Leclanché) cell:** zinc container anode, carbon rod cathode with MnO₂; paste of NH₄Cl + ZnCl₂. ~1.5 V.
- **Mercury cell:** Zn–Hg amalgam anode, HgO + carbon cathode, KOH + ZnO paste. Overall Zn(Hg) + HgO → ZnO + Hg; constant **1.35 V** (no ions in overall reaction) — used in hearing aids and watches.

steps.title: Secondary batteries (rechargeable)
steps.body:
**Lead storage battery** (vehicles, inverters): anode Pb, cathode PbO₂, electrolyte ~38% H₂SO₄.
- Anode: Pb + SO₄²⁻ → PbSO₄ + 2e⁻
- Cathode: PbO₂ + SO₄²⁻ + 4H⁺ + 2e⁻ → PbSO₄ + 2H₂O
- Overall: Pb + PbO₂ + 2H₂SO₄ → 2PbSO₄ + 2H₂O. Charging reverses it.
**Nickel–cadmium** cells have longer life. (Lithium-ion cells power phones and EVs.)

steps.title: Fuel cells
steps.body:
Reactants supplied continuously. **H₂–O₂ fuel cell** (used in Apollo missions):
- Anode: 2H₂ + 4OH⁻ → 4H₂O + 4e⁻
- Cathode: O₂ + 2H₂O + 4e⁻ → 4OH⁻
- Overall: 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O. Efficiency ~70% (vs ~40% for thermal plants); only water as product.

steps.title: Corrosion
steps.body:
An electrochemical process. In rusting, a spot on iron acts as **anode**: Fe → Fe²⁺ + 2e⁻; another spot is the **cathode**: O₂ + 4H⁺ + 4e⁻ → 2H₂O (H⁺ from dissolved CO₂). Fe²⁺ is further oxidised to hydrated Fe₂O₃·xH₂O (rust). Moisture and salts speed it up.
**Prevention:** paint, oil, grease; **galvanising** (zinc coat); **sacrificial anode** (Mg or Zn blocks on ship hulls and pipelines); alloying (stainless steel).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling a fuel cell a battery that stores fuel — it is fed continuously.
- Saying zinc protects iron only as a barrier — it also corrodes preferentially (more negative E°).
- Writing rusting without oxygen and water.

activity.prompt: Match each cell to its key feature.

quiz.q: Electrolyte in a lead storage battery is
quiz.why: The lead storage battery uses about 38% sulfuric acid as the electrolyte.

quiz.q: The mercury cell gives constant voltage because
options: no ions appear in the overall reaction
quiz.why: In the mercury cell no ions appear in the overall reaction, so electrolyte concentration does not change. The reaction quotient stays constant and so does the voltage.

quiz.q: Product of an H₂–O₂ fuel cell is
quiz.why: In the H₂–O₂ fuel cell the overall reaction is 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O, so the only product is water.
In rusting iron is oxidised (Fe → Fe²⁺ + 2e⁻), so that spot acts as the anode.

quiz.q: A sacrificial anode for iron pipes is usually
quiz.why: Magnesium or zinc have more negative E° than iron, so they are oxidised in preference and protect the iron.

sources: NCERT Class 12 Chemistry (topic reference, own wording)

questions.q: Unit of molar conductivity is
questions.why: Molar conductivity = κ/c, so its unit is S cm² mol⁻¹. S cm⁻¹ is the unit of conductivity.

questions.q: The cathode in a galvanic cell is
questions.why: In a galvanic cell the cathode is the positive electrode where reduction occurs, since electrons arrive there.

questions.q: Which metal can displace Cu from CuSO₄ solution?
questions.why: A metal displaces another from solution if its E° is lower. Zn has lower E° than Cu, so it reduces Cu²⁺. Pt, Ag and Au are less reactive.

questions.q: Assertion: E° is an intensive property. Reason: Multiplying a half-reaction by 2 does not change its E°.
options: Both true; reason does not explain
questions.why: Both are true. E° is intensive, and doubling a half-reaction doubles ΔG but not the potential, which shows E° does not depend on the amount.

questions.q: E°cell for Fe | Fe²⁺ || Ag⁺ | Ag (E°Fe = −0.44, E°Ag = 0.80) is
questions.why: Silver has the higher E°, so it is the cathode: E°cell = E°cathode − E°anode = 0.80 − (−0.44) = 1.24 V.

questions.q: Charge required to produce 1 mol O₂ from water is
questions.why: 2H₂O → O₂ + 4H⁺ + 4e⁻ needs 4 mol of electrons per mole of O₂, so 4 F.

questions.q: Λm of a strong electrolyte varies with concentration as
questions.why: For strong electrolytes Λm = Λ°m − A√c (Debye–Hückel–Onsager), giving a straight line against √c.

questions.q: Case: A current of 0.5 A flows for 2 hours through molten AlCl₃. Mass of Al deposited (M = 27):
For a reaction with n = 2 and E°cell = 0.295 V at 298 K, log K is
The Nernst equation for Zn²⁺/Zn at 298 K and [Zn²⁺] = 0.01 M gives E =
Assertion: Λm of a weak electrolyte increases sharply on dilution. Reason: Its degree of dissociation increases on dilution.
options: Both true; reason does not explain
questions.why: Both are true. A weak electrolyte dissociates more on dilution, giving more ions per mole, so Λm rises sharply; the reason explains the assertion.

questions.q: Case: The resistance of a conductivity cell with 0.1 M KCl (κ = 0.0129 S cm⁻¹) is 100 Ω. With 0.05 M NaCl it is 200 Ω. Λm of the NaCl solution:
ΔG° for a cell with E° = 1.0 V and n = 1 is about
Which product forms at the anode when aqueous CuSO₄ is electrolysed with platinum electrodes?
questions.why: With inert Pt electrodes, water is oxidised at the anode (2H₂O → O₂ + 4H⁺ + 4e⁻), so O₂ is released. Copper is deposited at the cathode.

questions.q: A concentration cell Cu | Cu²⁺ (0.01 M) || Cu²⁺ (0.1 M) | Cu has E at 298 K of
questions.why: For a concentration cell E = (0.059/n) log(c₂/c₁) = (0.059/2) log(0.1/0.01) = 0.0295 × 1 = 0.0295 V.

questions.q: Case: Λ°(NH₄Cl) = 129.8, Λ°(NaOH) = 248.1, Λ°(NaCl) = 126.4 S cm² mol⁻¹. Λ°(NH₄OH) is
questions.why: By Kohlrausch's law, Λ°(NH₄OH) = Λ°(NH₄Cl) + Λ°(NaOH) − Λ°(NaCl) = 129.8 + 248.1 − 126.4 = 251.5.

questions.q: How long must 5 A flow to deposit 2.16 g of Ag (M = 108)?
Why does a galvanised iron bucket not rust even when scratched?
options: Zinc has more negative E° and is oxidised preferentially
questions.why: Zinc has a more negative E° than iron, so it is oxidised first and protects the iron as a sacrificial metal, even where the coating is scratched.

courses.title: Ch 3 · Chemical Kinetics
courses.summary: Rate of a reaction (average and instantaneous), factors affecting rate, rate law, order and molecularity, units of k, integrated rate equations for zero- and first-order reactions with half-lives, pseudo-first-order reactions, the Arrhenius equation, activation energy, catalysis and collision theory. Independent practice material; not affiliated with or endorsed by any board or exam body.
outcomes: Learners can express rate in terms of any reactant or product.
Learners can determine order from data and give units of k.
Learners can apply integrated rate laws and half-life formulas for zero- and first-order reactions.
Learners can use the Arrhenius equation to find Ea or k at another temperature.

lessons.title: Rate of a chemical reaction

scenes.text: On Diwali night, a firework explodes in a fraction of a second.
Meanwhile, the iron railing outside rusts over years.
Chemical kinetics measures how fast reactions go — and why.

steps.title: Average and instantaneous rate
steps.body: For R → P: **average rate = −Δ[R]/Δt = +Δ[P]/Δt** (mol L⁻¹ s⁻¹). The **instantaneous rate** is the slope of the concentration–time curve at a point: −d[R]/dt. Rates usually fall as reactants are used up.

steps.title: Stoichiometry and rate
steps.body:
For aA + bB → cC + dD:
**Rate = −(1/a)d[A]/dt = −(1/b)d[B]/dt = +(1/c)d[C]/dt = +(1/d)d[D]/dt**.
For gases, partial pressures can replace concentrations (atm s⁻¹).

steps.title: Factors affecting rate
steps.body: Concentration (or pressure) of reactants, temperature, catalyst, surface area (powders react faster), nature of reactants, and radiation for photochemical reactions.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Ex 1.** 2N₂O₅ → 4NO₂ + O₂. [N₂O₅] falls from 0.40 to 0.36 mol/L in 5 min.
- Rate of disappearance of N₂O₅ = 0.04/5 = **0.008 M min⁻¹**
- Rate of reaction = ½ × 0.008 = **0.004 M min⁻¹**
- Rate of formation of NO₂ = 4 × 0.004 = **0.016 M min⁻¹**; of O₂ = **0.004 M min⁻¹**.

**Ex 2.** For N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃, if −d[N₂]/dt = 0.1 M s⁻¹ then d[NH₃]/dt = **0.2 M s⁻¹** and −d[H₂]/dt = **0.3 M s⁻¹**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting the minus sign for reactants (rate is always positive).
- Forgetting to divide by stoichiometric coefficients.
- Treating average rate over a long interval as the instantaneous rate.

activity.prompt: For 2A → 3B, the rate of formation of B is 0.09 M s⁻¹. What is the rate of disappearance of A (M s⁻¹)?

quiz.q: Unit of rate of reaction is
quiz.why: Rate is the change in concentration per unit time, so its unit is mol L⁻¹ s⁻¹.

options: the average over the whole reaction
the slope of the tangent to the conc.–time curve
quiz.why: The instantaneous rate at a moment is the slope of the tangent to the concentration–time curve at that point.
For 2HI → H₂ + I₂, each rate is divided by its coefficient, so rate = −½ d[HI]/dt = d[H₂]/dt.

quiz.q: Powdered marble reacts with acid faster than chips because
quiz.why: Powder has a larger surface area than chips, giving more contact with the acid, so the reaction is faster.

quiz.q: As a reaction proceeds, its rate usually
quiz.why: As reactants are used up their concentrations fall, so the rate usually decreases with time.

sources: NCERT Class 12 Chemistry (topic reference, own wording)

lessons.title: Rate law, order and molecularity

scenes.text: In a lab, Sameer changes the concentration of one reactant at a time and records the initial rates.
Doubling [A] quadruples the rate; doubling [B] changes nothing.
The rate law can only be found from experiment — never just from the balanced equation.

steps.title: Rate law
steps.body:
**Rate = k[A]ˣ[B]ʸ** — x and y are found experimentally (may be 0, fractions or integers) and need not match the stoichiometric coefficients.
- **Order** = x + y (overall); x is the order w.r.t. A.
- **k** (rate constant) depends on temperature and catalyst, not on concentration.
- **Units of k:** (mol L⁻¹)^(1−n) s⁻¹ ⇒ zero order mol L⁻¹ s⁻¹; first s⁻¹; second L mol⁻¹ s⁻¹.

steps.title: Molecularity and mechanism
steps.body:
**Molecularity** = number of species colliding in an **elementary** step: unimolecular, bimolecular, rarely termolecular. Always a whole number (1, 2, 3), defined only for elementary reactions, theoretical.

Complex reactions occur in steps; the **slowest step is rate-determining**. Example: 2H₂O₂ → 2H₂O + O₂ in alkaline I⁻ is first order in each of H₂O₂ and I⁻: step 1 H₂O₂ + I⁻ → H₂O + IO⁻ (slow), step 2 H₂O₂ + IO⁻ → H₂O + I⁻ + O₂ (fast). I⁻ is a catalyst; IO⁻ an intermediate.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Ex 1.** Rate = k[A]²[B]. Doubling [A] ⇒ rate × **4**; doubling both ⇒ × **8**; overall order **3**.

**Ex 2.** Data: [A] = 0.1 M → rate 2×10⁻³; [A] = 0.2 M → 8×10⁻³ M s⁻¹ ([B] fixed). (2)ˣ = 4 ⇒ **x = 2**.

**Ex 3.** Units of k for rate = k[A]^(1/2)[B]: overall order 3/2 ⇒ **mol^(−1/2) L^(1/2) s⁻¹**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Taking orders from the balanced equation.
- Saying molecularity can be zero or fractional.
- Mixing up order (experimental) with molecularity (theoretical, elementary steps).

activity.prompt: Order or molecularity?

quiz.q: Units of k for a first-order reaction are
quiz.why: For first order rate = k[A], so k = rate/conc = (mol L⁻¹ s⁻¹)/(mol L⁻¹) = s⁻¹.
Overall order is the sum of the powers in the rate law: 1 + 2 = 3.

quiz.q: Molecularity of a reaction can be
quiz.why: Molecularity is the number of molecules colliding in an elementary step, so it is a whole number like 1, 2 or 3, never zero, negative or a fraction.
The slowest step limits how fast products form, like a bottleneck, so it is the rate-determining step.

quiz.q: If units of k are L mol⁻¹ s⁻¹, the order is
quiz.why: The unit of k is (mol L⁻¹)^(1−n) s⁻¹. L mol⁻¹ s⁻¹ corresponds to 1 − n = −1, so n = 2.

sources: NCERT Class 12 Chemistry (topic reference, own wording)

lessons.title: Integrated rate equations: zero and first order

scenes.text: A doctor tells Kavya's grandfather to take a tablet every 8 hours.
The drug's concentration in blood falls by the same fraction every few hours — first-order behaviour.
Half-life calculations decide safe and effective dosing schedules.

steps.title: Zero-order reactions
steps.body:
Rate = k[R]⁰ = k (independent of concentration).
**[R] = [R]₀ − kt**; graph of [R] vs t is a straight line with slope −k.
**t½ = [R]₀/(2k)** — proportional to initial concentration.
Examples: decomposition of NH₃ on hot platinum at high pressure; decomposition of HI on gold (surface saturated).

steps.title: First-order reactions
steps.body:
Rate = k[R] ⇒ **k = (2.303/t) log([R]₀/[R])**, or [R] = [R]₀e^(−kt).
- Graph of log[R] vs t: straight line, slope −k/2.303; ln[R] vs t slope −k.
- **t½ = 0.693/k** — independent of initial concentration.
- After n half-lives, [R] = [R]₀/2ⁿ. **Time for 99.9% completion ≈ 10 t½**.
Examples: radioactive decay, N₂O₅ decomposition, hydrogenation of ethene (C₂H₄ + H₂ → C₂H₆, rate = k[C₂H₄]).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Ex 1.** First order, k = 1.15×10⁻³ s⁻¹: t½ = 0.693/1.15×10⁻³ ≈ **603 s**.

**Ex 2.** A first-order reaction is 30% complete in 40 min.
- k = (2.303/40) log(100/70) = 0.0576 × 0.155 ≈ **8.9×10⁻³ min⁻¹**
- t½ = 0.693/0.0089 ≈ **78 min**.

**Ex 3.** Zero order, [R]₀ = 0.8 M, k = 0.02 M min⁻¹: t½ = 0.8/0.04 = **20 min**; complete reaction at 40 min.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using t½ = 0.693/k for zero order.
- Using log instead of ln with the factor 2.303 dropped (or both).
- Writing the fraction *remaining* where the fraction *reacted* is given: 30% complete ⇒ 70% left.

activity.prompt: A first-order reaction has t½ = 20 min. What percentage of the reactant remains after 60 min?

quiz.q: Half-life of a first-order reaction is
quiz.why: For a first-order reaction t½ = 0.693/k, which does not depend on the initial concentration.

quiz.q: For a zero-order reaction, the plot of [R] vs t is
quiz.why: For zero order [R] = [R]₀ − kt, so the plot of [R] against t is a straight line with slope −k.

quiz.q: If t½ of a reaction doubles when [R]₀ doubles, the order is
quiz.why: For zero order t½ = [R]₀/2k, which is proportional to [R]₀. Doubling [R]₀ doubles t½, so the order is 0.

quiz.q: Time for 99.9% completion of a first-order reaction is about
quiz.why: t = (2.303/k) log 1000 = 6.909/k, and t½ = 0.693/k. Their ratio is about 10, so about 10 t½.

quiz.q: For first order, a straight line is obtained by plotting
quiz.why: For first order log[R] = log[R]₀ − kt/2.303, so a plot of log[R] against t is a straight line with slope −k/2.303.
Each half-life halves the amount, so after 3 half-lives the fraction left is (1/2)³ = 1/8.

sources: NCERT Class 12 Chemistry (topic reference, own wording)

lessons.title: Pseudo-first-order and gas-phase kinetics

scenes.text: When cane sugar is boiled with a little acid, it slowly turns into glucose and fructose.
Water is a reactant too, but there is so much of it that its concentration hardly changes.
The reaction then behaves as if it were first order — a pseudo-first-order reaction.

steps.title: Pseudo-first-order reactions
steps.body:
A reaction of higher order behaves as first order when one reactant is in large excess.
- **Acid hydrolysis of ethyl acetate:** CH₃COOC₂H₅ + H₂O → CH₃COOH + C₂H₅OH; rate = k'[ester], with k' = k[H₂O].
- **Inversion of cane sugar:** C₁₂H₂₂O₁₁ + H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ (glucose) + C₆H₁₂O₆ (fructose), H⁺ catalysed; rate = k[sucrose].

steps.title: First-order gas reactions with pressures
steps.body:
For A(g) → B(g) + C(g) starting with pressure p₀: at time t, if A has fallen by x, total pt = p₀ + x ⇒ **p_A = 2p₀ − pt**.
**k = (2.303/t) log[p₀/(2p₀ − pt)]**.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Ex 1.** SO₂Cl₂(g) → SO₂(g) + Cl₂(g), p₀ = 0.5 atm; after 100 s, pt = 0.6 atm.
- p_A = 2(0.5) − 0.6 = 0.4 atm
- k = (2.303/100) log(0.5/0.4) = 0.02303 × 0.0969 ≈ **2.23×10⁻³ s⁻¹**.

**Ex 2.** For the same reaction, total pressure when p_A has fallen to 0.25 atm: x = 0.25 ⇒ pt = 0.5 + 0.25 = **0.75 atm**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using total pressure directly as the reactant pressure.
- Forgetting that pseudo-first-order k' contains the constant concentration of the excess reactant.
- Getting the stoichiometry wrong in p_A for reactions like 2A → B + C (then p_A = p₀ − 2x).

statements.s: Inversion of cane sugar is truly a first-order reaction in every reactant.
statements.why: It is pseudo-first-order; water is in excess.

statements.s: For A(g) → B(g) + C(g), p_A = 2p₀ − pt.
statements.why: pt = p₀ + x and p_A = p₀ − x.

statements.s: Acid hydrolysis of ethyl acetate is pseudo-first-order.
In a pseudo-first-order reaction the excess reactant's concentration changes greatly.

quiz.q: A pseudo-first-order reaction is actually of
options: higher order with one reactant in excess
quiz.why: A pseudo-first-order reaction is really of higher order, but one reactant is in large excess, so its concentration stays almost constant and the rate depends only on one reactant.
Inversion of cane sugar is its hydrolysis into glucose and fructose, and the optical rotation changes sign.

quiz.q: For A(g) → 2B(g), if p₀ = 1 atm and pt = 1.4 atm, p_A =
quiz.why: A → 2B: if x of A reacts, total pressure = p₀ − x + 2x = p₀ + x. So x = 1.4 − 1 = 0.4 and p_A = 1 − 0.4 = 0.6 atm.

quiz.q: In acid hydrolysis of an ester, H⁺ acts as
quiz.why: H⁺ speeds up ester hydrolysis but is regenerated, so it is a catalyst and not used up.

quiz.q: k' in a pseudo-first-order reaction has units
quiz.why: The constant k' = k[excess reactant] includes the constant concentration, so it behaves like a first-order constant with unit s⁻¹.

lessons.title: Temperature, activation energy and catalysis

scenes.text: Milk left on the kitchen counter in summer sours by evening; in the fridge it lasts days.
A 10 °C rise roughly doubles the rate of many reactions.
Arrhenius explained why: only molecules with enough energy to climb an activation barrier react.

steps.title: Arrhenius equation
steps.body:
**k = A e^(−Ea/RT)**; A = frequency (pre-exponential) factor, Ea = activation energy.
- ln k = ln A − Ea/RT ⇒ plot of **log k vs 1/T** is a line of **slope −Ea/(2.303R)**.
- Between two temperatures: **log(k₂/k₁) = [Ea/(2.303R)] × (T₂ − T₁)/(T₁T₂)**.
- e^(−Ea/RT) is the fraction of molecules with energy ≥ Ea (Maxwell–Boltzmann distribution); raising T widens the high-energy tail, increasing this fraction sharply.

steps.title: Catalysts
steps.body: A catalyst provides an **alternative pathway of lower Ea**; it is not consumed. It **does not change ΔG, ΔH or K** — it speeds forward and backward reactions equally, so equilibrium is reached sooner. It cannot make a non-spontaneous reaction occur.

steps.title: Collision theory
steps.body:
Molecules must **collide** with enough energy (≥ threshold) and the **proper orientation**:
**Rate = P Z_AB e^(−Ea/RT)**, where Z_AB = collision frequency and P = probability (steric) factor.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Ex 1.** Rate doubles from 298 K to 308 K. Find Ea.
- log 2 = [Ea/(2.303 × 8.314)] × 10/(298 × 308)
- Ea = 2.303 × 8.314 × 0.301 × 9178 ≈ **52.9 kJ/mol**.

**Ex 2.** Slope of log k vs 1/T is −5000 K. Ea = 2.303 × 8.314 × 5000 ≈ **95.7 kJ/mol**.

**Ex 3.** Ea = 0 ⇒ k = A at all temperatures — rate independent of T.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using °C instead of K in Arrhenius calculations.
- Using R = 0.0821 (L atm) instead of 8.314 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ with Ea in joules.
- Saying catalysts shift equilibrium.

bands.text: +10 °C: rate roughly × 2 — the classic rule of thumb for Ea ≈ 50 kJ/mol.
+30 °C: rate roughly × 8 — why food spoils fast in summer.

quiz.q: In the Arrhenius equation, A is the
quiz.why: In k = A e^(−Ea/RT), A is the frequency (pre-exponential) factor, related to the collision frequency and orientation.
A catalyst offers an alternative path with lower activation energy, so more molecules can react. It does not change temperature or ΔG.

quiz.q: Slope of log k versus 1/T is
quiz.why: log k = log A − Ea/(2.303RT), so plotting log k against 1/T gives a straight line of slope −Ea/2.303R.
A catalyst changes the pathway and so lowers Ea. K, ΔG and ΔH depend only on initial and final states, so they stay the same.

quiz.q: According to collision theory, effective collisions need
quiz.why: Effective collisions need both sufficient energy (at least the threshold) and proper orientation of the molecules; either alone is not enough.

questions.q: Rate of a zero-order reaction is
questions.why: For zero order rate = k[R]⁰ = k, so the rate does not depend on the reactant concentration.

questions.q: Unit of k for a second-order reaction is
questions.why: For second order, k = rate/conc² = (mol L⁻¹ s⁻¹)/(mol L⁻¹)² = L mol⁻¹ s⁻¹.

questions.q: Which can be fractional?
questions.why: Order is found from experiments and can be a fraction. Molecularity counts molecules in an elementary step, so it is always a whole number.

questions.q: Assertion: The half-life of a first-order reaction is independent of initial concentration. Reason: t½ = 0.693/k.
options: Both true; reason does not explain
questions.why: Both are true. Since t½ = 0.693/k has no [R]₀ term, half-life does not depend on the initial concentration, so the reason explains the assertion.

questions.q: For 2NO + O₂ → 2NO₂, rate = k[NO]²[O₂]. If the volume is halved, rate becomes
questions.why: Halving the volume doubles every concentration. Rate ∝ [NO]²[O₂] becomes 2² × 2 = 8 times.

questions.q: For 4NH₃ + 5O₂ → 4NO + 6H₂O, if rate of formation of NO is 3.6×10⁻³ M s⁻¹, rate of disappearance of O₂ is
questions.why: Rate of O₂ disappearance = (5/4) × rate of NO formation = 1.25 × 3.6×10⁻³ = 4.5×10⁻³ M s⁻¹.

questions.q: A first-order reaction has k = 0.0693 min⁻¹. Its t½ is

questions.why: Doubling [A] doubles the rate, so order in A is 1. Doubling [B] makes it 4 times, so order in B is 2. Rate = k[A][B]².

questions.q: From the case above, k equals
questions.why: Using the first run: 1×10⁻⁴ = k(0.1)(0.1)² = k × 10⁻³, so k = 0.1 L² mol⁻² s⁻¹.

questions.q: A first-order reaction takes 40 min for 75% completion. Its t½ is
questions.why: 75% completion means 25% is left, which is two half-lives. So 2t½ = 40 min and t½ = 20 min.

questions.q: Assertion: A catalyst does not alter the equilibrium constant. Reason: It lowers activation energy of forward and backward reactions equally.
options: Both true; reason does not explain
questions.why: Both are true. A catalyst speeds up the forward and backward reactions equally, so equilibrium is reached sooner but K does not change.

questions.q: Case: Rate constant rises from 2×10⁻³ to 8×10⁻³ s⁻¹ between 300 K and 320 K. Ea is about (log 4 = 0.602)
Gas-phase A → B + C is first order. p₀ = 0.4 atm; after 10 min, pt = 0.6 atm. k =
questions.why: A → B + C: pt = p₀ + x = 0.6, so x = 0.2 and p_A = 0.2, half of p₀. So t½ = 10 min and k = 0.693/10 = 0.0693 min⁻¹.

questions.q: For a zero-order reaction with [R]₀ = 1 M and k = 0.05 M s⁻¹, time for completion is
questions.why: For zero order, [R] = [R]₀ − kt reaches zero at t = [R]₀/k = 1/0.05 = 20 s.

questions.q: Hydrogenation of ethene C₂H₄ + H₂ → C₂H₆ has rate = k[C₂H₄]. Its order is
questions.why: The rate law rate = k[C₂H₄] has power 1 on one reactant, so the order is 1. Order comes from the rate law, not from the stoichiometry.

questions.q: The rate constant of a reaction becomes 0 when
questions.why: In k = A e^(−Ea/RT), as T → 0 K the exponent tends to −∞, so k → 0.

questions.q: Case: A first-order drug decays with t½ = 4 h. Starting at 80 mg in the body, after 10 h about how much remains?
questions.why: Number of half-lives = 10/4 = 2.5. Amount left = 80 × (1/2)^2.5 = 80 × 0.177 ≈ 14 mg.

courses.title: Ch 4 · The d- and f-Block Elements
courses.summary: Position and electronic configuration of transition elements, trends in radii, ionisation enthalpy, oxidation states and electrode potentials of the 3d series, magnetic moments, colour, catalysis, interstitial compounds and alloys, lanthanoids, lanthanoid contraction and actinoids — plus K₂Cr₂O₇ and KMnO₄ as a JEE/NEET extension. Independent practice material; not affiliated with or endorsed by any board or exam body.
outcomes: Learners can write configurations of 3d elements and their ions, including Cr and Cu.
Learners can explain trends in oxidation states and E° values using stability of d⁰, d⁵ and d¹⁰.
Learners can calculate spin-only magnetic moments and explain colour.
Learners can explain lanthanoid contraction and its consequences and compare lanthanoids with actinoids.

lessons.title: Transition elements: position, configuration and physical properties

story.title: Why the scooter frame is steel

scenes.text: Kunal's scooter frame is steel; the switch contacts are copper; the bulb filament is tungsten.
All three are d-block metals — strong, conducting and with very high melting points.
Their partly filled d orbitals give them a whole set of special properties.

steps.title: Position and definition
steps.body:
The d-block lies between groups 2 and 13 (groups 3–12) in four series: 3d (Sc–Zn), 4d (Y–Cd), 5d (La, Hf–Hg), 6d (Ac, Rf–Cn).
**Transition element:** an element with an incompletely filled d subshell in its ground state or in any common oxidation state. So **Zn, Cd and Hg** (d¹⁰ in both) are *not* regarded as transition elements; Cu is (Cu²⁺ is d⁹).

steps.title: Electronic configuration
steps.body:
General: **(n−1)d¹⁻¹⁰ ns¹⁻²**. 3d series: Sc 3d¹4s², Ti 3d²4s², V 3d³4s², **Cr 3d⁵4s¹**, Mn 3d⁵4s², Fe 3d⁶4s², Co 3d⁷4s², Ni 3d⁸4s², **Cu 3d¹⁰4s¹**, Zn 3d¹⁰4s².
Cr and Cu are exceptions because half-filled and completely filled d subshells have extra stability (exchange energy). Ions lose **4s electrons first**: Fe²⁺ = [Ar]3d⁶, Fe³⁺ = [Ar]3d⁵.

steps.title: Physical properties and radii
steps.body:
- Typical metals: hard, high melting and boiling points (strong metallic bonding involving many unpaired d electrons); melting points peak near the middle (d⁵) of each series — W has the highest m.p. among metals; Zn, Cd, Hg are low (Hg is liquid).
- Atomic radii decrease slowly across a series (added d electrons shield poorly), then level off.
- 4d and 5d elements of a group have almost equal radii (Zr 160 pm, Hf 159 pm) because of **lanthanoid contraction**.
- Densities increase across the series (Ti to Cu).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Ex 1.** Configuration of Mn²⁺ (Z = 25): [Ar]3d⁵ — five unpaired electrons.

**Ex 2.** Is Sc a transition element? Sc = 3d¹4s²: partly filled d in the ground state ⇒ **yes** (though Sc³⁺ is d⁰).

**Ex 3.** Why is Zn's m.p. low? Its d¹⁰ electrons do not take part in metallic bonding ⇒ weaker metallic bonds.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Removing 3d electrons before 4s when forming ions.
- Writing Cr as 3d⁴4s² or Cu as 3d⁹4s².
- Calling zinc a transition metal.

activity.prompt: Match each species to its configuration.

quiz.q: General configuration of d-block elements is
quiz.why: d-block elements are filling the (n−1)d subshell, so their general configuration is (n−1)d¹⁻¹⁰ ns¹⁻².

quiz.q: Which is NOT a transition element?
quiz.why: Zn has a completely filled d¹⁰ configuration both in the ground state and in its common +2 state, so it is not a true transition element.
Cr is 3d⁵4s¹, not 3d⁴4s², because a half-filled d subshell is extra stable.

quiz.q: Zr and Hf have nearly the same radius due to
quiz.why: Zr and Hf have nearly the same radius because of lanthanoid contraction: poor shielding by 4f electrons pulls outer electrons in before Hf.

quiz.q: When Fe forms Fe²⁺, electrons are removed from
quiz.why: In transition metals the 4s electrons are lost first, so Fe²⁺ is formed by removing both 4s electrons.

lessons.title: Ionisation enthalpy, oxidation states and electrode potentials

scenes.text: In the lab, Niharika sees manganese compounds in many colours: pale pink Mn²⁺, brown MnO₂, green manganate and deep purple permanganate.
Manganese shows oxidation states from +2 to +7.
Which state is stable depends on configuration and on the energy balance of ionisation and hydration.

steps.title: Ionisation enthalpy
steps.body:
Increases gradually across a series (rising nuclear charge, poor d shielding) but less steeply than for main-group elements. Irregularities come from extra stability of d⁵ and d¹⁰:
- **2nd IE** is unusually high for **Cr** and **Cu** (removing an electron from d⁵ and d¹⁰).
- **3rd IE** is high for **Mn** (Mn²⁺ is d⁵) and **Zn** (d¹⁰).

steps.title: Variable oxidation states
steps.body:
Because (n−1)d and ns energies are close, both can be used.
- Mn shows the most: +2 to +7 (MnO₄⁻).
- Sc mainly +3; Zn only +2.
- Highest states appear with **O and F** (most electronegative; O also forms multiple bonds): CrO₄²⁻, MnO₄⁻, VF₅, CrF₆.
- Low states (0, +1) are found in complexes with π-acceptor ligands such as CO: Ni(CO)₄, Fe(CO)₅.

steps.title: Electrode potentials
steps.body:
**E°(M²⁺/M):** negative for the 3d series except **Cu (+0.34 V)** — Cu's high atomisation and ionisation enthalpies are not balanced by hydration enthalpy, so Cu does not liberate H₂ from acids. Mn, Ni and Zn are more negative than the trend predicts (stable d⁵ Mn²⁺, d¹⁰ Zn²⁺, very negative hydration enthalpy of Ni²⁺).

**E°(M³⁺/M²⁺):** Mn³⁺/Mn²⁺ = +1.57 V and Co³⁺/Co²⁺ = +1.97 V are high ⇒ Mn³⁺ and Co³⁺ are strong oxidising agents; Cr³⁺/Cr²⁺ = −0.41 V ⇒ Cr²⁺ is a strong reducing agent; Fe³⁺/Fe²⁺ = +0.77 V.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Ex 1.** Why is Cr²⁺ reducing while Mn³⁺ is oxidising (both d⁴)? Cr²⁺ → Cr³⁺ gives stable **t₂g³** (d³); Mn³⁺ → Mn²⁺ gives stable **d⁵**.

**Ex 2.** Why is E°(Mn³⁺/Mn²⁺) much more positive than E°(Fe³⁺/Fe²⁺)? Mn²⁺ (d⁵) is very stable, but for iron the d⁵ configuration is Fe³⁺, so Fe²⁺ → Fe³⁺ is easy.

**Ex 3.** Oxidation state of Mn in KMnO₄: +1 + x − 8 = 0 ⇒ **x = +7**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying all 3d metals react with dilute acids to give H₂ — Cu does not.
- Forgetting that stability depends on configuration *and* enthalpy terms.
- Assuming highest oxidation states form with all ligands — they need O or F.

statements.s: Manganese shows oxidation states from +2 to +7.
E°(Cu²⁺/Cu) is negative like the other 3d metals.
Co³⁺ is a strong oxidising agent in water.
Highest oxidation states are usually shown in fluorides and oxides.
statements.why: F and O are highly electronegative; O forms multiple bonds.

quiz.q: Which 3d metal does NOT liberate H₂ from dilute HCl?
quiz.why: Cu has a positive E° (Cu²⁺/Cu = +0.34 V), so it cannot reduce H⁺ and does not release H₂ from dilute HCl.

quiz.q: The 3rd ionisation enthalpy of Mn is high because
quiz.why: Mn²⁺ has the stable half-filled 3d⁵ configuration, so removing a third electron needs a lot of energy.

quiz.q: Oxidation state of Cr in K₂Cr₂O₇ is
quiz.why: In K₂Cr₂O₇: 2(+1) + 2x + 7(−2) = 0, so 2x = 12 and x = +6.

quiz.q: Which is a strong reducing agent?
quiz.why: Cr²⁺ readily loses an electron to become the stable d³ Cr³⁺, so it is a strong reducing agent. The others tend to gain electrons.

quiz.q: Ni(CO)₄ contains Ni in oxidation state
quiz.why: CO is a neutral ligand, so Ni in Ni(CO)₄ has oxidation state 0.

lessons.title: Magnetic properties, colour, catalysis and alloys

scenes.text: Aditi grows beautiful blue copper sulphate crystals for her project.
When she heats them, they turn white as water is driven off.
The blue colour comes from d electrons jumping between split d orbitals — which needs water ligands around Cu²⁺.

steps.title: Magnetic properties
steps.body:
Unpaired electrons make substances **paramagnetic**; all paired ⇒ **diamagnetic**.
**Spin-only magnetic moment μ = √(n(n + 2)) BM** (n = number of unpaired electrons).
- n = 1: 1.73; n = 2: 2.83; n = 3: 3.87; n = 4: 4.90; n = 5: 5.92 BM.

steps.title: Colour
steps.body:
In a complex, ligands split the d orbitals. Absorbing visible light promotes an electron from a lower to a higher d orbital (**d–d transition**); the colour seen is the **complement** of the absorbed colour. Ions with d⁰ (Sc³⁺, Ti⁴⁺) or d¹⁰ (Zn²⁺, Cu⁺) are **colourless**.
Aquated ions: Ti³⁺ purple, V³⁺ green, Mn²⁺ pale pink, Fe³⁺ yellow, Co²⁺ pink, Ni²⁺ green, Cu²⁺ blue.

steps.title: Complexes, catalysts, interstitial compounds and alloys
steps.body:
- **Complex formation:** small, highly charged ions with vacant d orbitals: [Fe(CN)₆]³⁻, [Cu(NH₃)₄]²⁺.
- **Catalysts** (variable oxidation states and surfaces): V₂O₅ in the Contact process, finely divided Fe in the Haber process, Ni in hydrogenation of oils; Fe³⁺ catalyses I⁻ + S₂O₈²⁻ by switching between Fe³⁺ and Fe²⁺.
- **Interstitial compounds:** small atoms (H, C, N) trapped in metal lattices — TiC, Mn₄N, Fe₃H; non-stoichiometric, very hard, high m.p., retain metallic conductivity, chemically inert.
- **Alloys:** similar radii allow substitution — brass (Cu–Zn), bronze (Cu–Sn), stainless steel (Fe–Cr–Ni).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Ex 1.** μ for Fe²⁺ (3d⁶, 4 unpaired): √(4 × 6) = √24 ≈ **4.90 BM**.

**Ex 2.** μ = 3.87 BM for a 3d ion of charge +3: n = 3 ⇒ d³ ⇒ **Cr³⁺**.

**Ex 3.** Why is Ti⁴⁺ colourless but Ti³⁺ purple? Ti⁴⁺ is d⁰ (no d–d transition); Ti³⁺ is d¹.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Counting electrons instead of *unpaired* electrons in μ.
- Forgetting the 4s-first rule before counting d electrons of an ion.
- Saying anhydrous CuSO₄ is blue — it is white (no ligand field splitting by water).

activity.prompt: Calculate the spin-only magnetic moment (BM) of Mn²⁺ (Z = 25).

quiz.q: Spin-only moment of an ion with 2 unpaired electrons is
quiz.why: μ = √(n(n+2)) = √(2 × 4) = √8 = 2.83 BM for n = 2 unpaired electrons.

quiz.q: Which ion is colourless in water?
quiz.why: Zn²⁺ is d¹⁰, with no vacant d orbital to allow d–d transitions, so it is colourless. The other ions have partly filled d orbitals.

quiz.q: V₂O₅ is used as a catalyst in
quiz.why: V₂O₅ catalyses the oxidation of SO₂ to SO₃ in the Contact process for sulfuric acid.
Small atoms like H, C, N in the voids of the metal lattice make interstitial compounds very hard and give them high melting points.

quiz.q: Colour of transition metal ions is due to
quiz.why: Transition metal ions are coloured because electrons jump between split d orbitals (d–d transitions), absorbing visible light.

lessons.title: Lanthanoids and actinoids

story.title: The rare earths in your earphones

scenes.text: Raghav's wireless earphones contain tiny but powerful neodymium magnets.
Neodymium is a lanthanoid — one of the 'rare earths' found in monazite sand, including on India's Kerala coast.
Lanthanoids are so alike chemically that separating them is one of chemistry's hardest jobs.

steps.title: Lanthanoids (Ce, Z = 58 to Lu, Z = 71)
steps.body:
Configuration: [Xe]4f¹⁻¹⁴5d⁰⁻¹6s². Common oxidation state **+3**. Also **Ce⁴⁺** (f⁰, strong oxidising agent), **Eu²⁺** and **Yb²⁺** (f⁷, f¹⁴; reducing).
Properties: silvery-white soft metals; react with water to give H₂; with acids; burn in O₂ giving Ln₂O₃; hydroxides Ln(OH)₃ are basic. Many Ln³⁺ ions are coloured (f–f transitions); La³⁺ and Lu³⁺ (f⁰, f¹⁴) are colourless.
Uses: **misch metal** (~95% lanthanoid metals, ~5% Fe, traces of S, C, Ca, Al) in Mg-based alloys for bullets, shells and lighter flints; mixed oxides as catalysts in petroleum cracking; phosphors in screens.

steps.title: Lanthanoid contraction
steps.body:
A steady decrease in atomic and ionic (Ln³⁺) radii from La to Lu, because 4f electrons shield each other poorly from the increasing nuclear charge.
**Consequences:**
- 4d and 5d elements of the same group have nearly identical radii (Zr/Hf, Nb/Ta) and very similar properties.
- Lanthanoids are difficult to separate.
- Basic strength of hydroxides **decreases** from La(OH)₃ to Lu(OH)₃ (smaller cation, more covalent).

steps.title: Actinoids (Th, Z = 90 to Lr, Z = 103)
steps.body:
Configuration: [Rn]5f¹⁻¹⁴6d⁰⁻¹7s². All are **radioactive**; elements beyond U are man-made.
- **Wider range of oxidation states** (+3 to +7; e.g. Np and Pu up to +7) because 5f, 6d and 7s energies are close.
- **Actinoid contraction** is greater than lanthanoid contraction (5f shielding is even poorer).
- Chemistry is complicated by radioactivity and short half-lives.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Ex 1.** Why is Ce⁴⁺ a good oxidising agent? It tends to return to the common +3 state (E°(Ce⁴⁺/Ce³⁺) ≈ +1.74 V).

**Ex 2.** Which is more basic: La(OH)₃ or Lu(OH)₃? **La(OH)₃** — La³⁺ is larger, so the M–OH bond is more ionic.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying lanthanoid contraction means radii fall sharply — it is a small, steady decrease.
- Thinking actinoids show fewer oxidation states than lanthanoids — they show more.
- Calling lanthanoids rare in abundance — 'rare earths' are not all that rare, just hard to separate.

activity.prompt: Lanthanoids or actinoids?

quiz.q: The common oxidation state of lanthanoids is
quiz.why: The common and most stable oxidation state of lanthanoids is +3, giving Ln³⁺ ions.
The 4f electrons shield the nuclear charge poorly, so effective nuclear charge increases along the series and the size shrinks. This is the lanthanoid contraction.

quiz.q: Which lanthanoid ion is a strong oxidising agent?
quiz.why: Ce⁴⁺ tends to gain an electron to reach the more stable +3 state, so it is a strong oxidising agent. Eu²⁺ and Yb²⁺ are reducing.

quiz.q: Actinoids show a wider range of oxidation states because
quiz.why: The 5f, 6d and 7s energies are close, so electrons from several subshells can take part in bonding. This gives actinoids many oxidation states.
Misch metal, an alloy mainly of lanthanoids with iron, gives sparks on striking, so it is used in lighter flints.

lessons.title: Potassium dichromate and potassium permanganate (JEE/NEET extension)

scenes.text: Older police breath analysers used orange acidified dichromate that turned green when alcohol was present.
Dichromate oxidised ethanol and was itself reduced to green Cr³⁺.
Permanganate's purple colour vanishing works the same way in titrations — the reagent is its own indicator.

steps.title: Potassium dichromate, K₂Cr₂O₇
steps.body:
**Preparation from chromite (FeCr₂O₄):**
1. Fuse with Na₂CO₃ in air: 4FeCr₂O₄ + 8Na₂CO₃ + 7O₂ → 8Na₂CrO₄ + 2Fe₂O₃ + 8CO₂.
2. Acidify: 2Na₂CrO₄ + 2H⁺ → Na₂Cr₂O₇ + 2Na⁺ + H₂O.
3. Add KCl: Na₂Cr₂O₇ + 2KCl → K₂Cr₂O₇ + 2NaCl.
**Chromate ⇌ dichromate** depends on pH: 2CrO₄²⁻ (yellow) + 2H⁺ ⇌ Cr₂O₇²⁻ (orange) + H₂O.
**Oxidising action (acid):** Cr₂O₇²⁻ + 14H⁺ + 6e⁻ → 2Cr³⁺ + 7H₂O (E° = 1.33 V); oxidises I⁻ → I₂, Fe²⁺ → Fe³⁺, H₂S → S, Sn²⁺ → Sn⁴⁺.

steps.title: Potassium permanganate, KMnO₄
steps.body:
**Preparation:** fuse MnO₂ with KOH and an oxidant (KNO₃) → K₂MnO₄ (green); in neutral/acidic solution manganate disproportionates: 3MnO₄²⁻ + 4H⁺ → 2MnO₄⁻ + MnO₂ + 2H₂O. Commercially, alkaline manganate is oxidised electrolytically.
**Oxidising action:**
- Acidic: MnO₄⁻ + 8H⁺ + 5e⁻ → Mn²⁺ + 4H₂O (oxidises Fe²⁺, C₂O₄²⁻, I⁻, NO₂⁻, H₂S).
- Neutral/weakly alkaline: MnO₄⁻ + 2H₂O + 3e⁻ → MnO₂ + 4OH⁻ (e.g. I⁻ → IO₃⁻; Mn²⁺ → MnO₂).
Permanganate is a self-indicator in titrations (purple disappears at the end point). Shapes: MnO₄⁻ tetrahedral; Cr₂O₇²⁻ two tetrahedra sharing one O (Cr–O–Cr).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Ex 1.** Moles of Fe²⁺ oxidised by 1 mol of MnO₄⁻ in acid: MnO₄⁻ gains 5e⁻; each Fe²⁺ loses 1e⁻ ⇒ **5 mol**.

**Ex 2.** Moles of Fe²⁺ oxidised by 1 mol of Cr₂O₇²⁻: 6e⁻ ⇒ **6 mol**.

**Ex 3.** Oxalate: 2MnO₄⁻ + 5C₂O₄²⁻ + 16H⁺ → 2Mn²⁺ + 10CO₂ + 8H₂O.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using HCl to acidify KMnO₄ titrations — HCl is oxidised to Cl₂; dilute H₂SO₄ is used.
- Forgetting that the number of electrons differs in acid (5) and neutral (3) media.
- Calling chromate orange (it is yellow; dichromate is orange).

steps.title: Note on syllabus
steps.body: Recent rationalised NCERT editions trimmed these compounds from the chapter; they remain useful for competitive exams and practical chemistry. Check your current syllabus.

activity.prompt: Complete the half-reactions in acidic medium.

quiz.q: Colour of the chromate ion is
quiz.why: Chromate (CrO₄²⁻) is yellow, while dichromate (Cr₂O₇²⁻) is orange. They interconvert with change in pH.

quiz.q: In acid, MnO₄⁻ is reduced to
quiz.why: In acidic medium MnO₄⁻ takes up 5 electrons and is reduced to Mn²⁺: MnO₄⁻ + 8H⁺ + 5e⁻ → Mn²⁺ + 4H₂O.
Chromite, FeCr₂O₄, is the main ore from which chromates and dichromates are made.

quiz.q: KMnO₄ titrations are acidified with dilute H₂SO₄, not HCl, because
quiz.why: HCl is oxidised to Cl₂ by KMnO₄, which would use up permanganate and give wrong results. Dilute H₂SO₄ is not oxidised.
The manganate ion, MnO₄²⁻, is green, while permanganate MnO₄⁻ is purple.

sources: NCERT Class 12 Chemistry (topic reference, own wording)

questions.q: Which element has configuration [Ar]3d¹⁰4s¹?
questions.why: [Ar]3d¹⁰4s¹ is the configuration of copper, where a full d subshell is extra stable.

questions.q: Most common oxidation state of lanthanoids:
questions.why: Lanthanoids most commonly form the +3 oxidation state, Ln³⁺.

questions.q: Which ion is coloured?
questions.why: V³⁺ is d², with partly filled d orbitals, so it is coloured. Cu⁺ is d¹⁰, and Sc³⁺ and Ti⁴⁺ are d⁰, so they are colourless.

questions.q: Assertion: Zn is not regarded as a transition element. Reason: Zn has completely filled d orbitals in its ground state and in its common oxidation state.
options: Both true; reason does not explain
questions.why: Both are true. A transition element has an incomplete d subshell in its atom or ions, and Zn has completely filled d¹⁰ in both, so the reason explains the assertion.

questions.q: Number of unpaired electrons in Co²⁺ (Z = 27) is
questions.why: Co²⁺ is 3d⁷. In high-spin form the d electrons fill as t₂g⁵eg² with 3 unpaired electrons.

questions.q: The spin-only moment of Cu²⁺ is
questions.why: Cu²⁺ is d⁹ with one unpaired electron: μ = √(1 × 3) = 1.73 BM.

questions.q: Which shows the maximum number of oxidation states in the 3d series?
questions.why: Mn shows oxidation states from +2 to +7, the widest range in the 3d series, because it has five unpaired d electrons plus 4s electrons.

questions.q: Case: A 3d metal ion M²⁺ has μ = 4.90 BM. M could be
questions.why: μ = 4.90 BM means 4 unpaired electrons, since √(4 × 6) = 4.90. Fe²⁺ (d⁶ high spin) has 4. Mn²⁺ has 5, Ni²⁺ has 2 and Zn²⁺ has 0.

questions.q: Why does E°(Mn³⁺/Mn²⁺) exceed E°(Cr³⁺/Cr²⁺) greatly?
options: Mn²⁺ is d⁵ (stable); Cr³⁺ is d³ (stable)
questions.why: Mn³⁺ readily gains an electron to become the stable half-filled d⁵ Mn²⁺, giving a large positive E°. Cr³⁺ is a stable d³, so Cr³⁺ is reluctant to gain one and E° is negative.

questions.q: Assertion: Transition metals form interstitial compounds. Reason: Small atoms like H, C, N fit into voids of their lattices.
options: Both true; reason does not explain
questions.why: Both are true. Small atoms like H, C and N fit into the voids of the metal lattice, which is how interstitial compounds form.

questions.q: Which pair has nearly the same atomic radius?
questions.why: Zr and Hf have almost identical radii because of the lanthanoid contraction between them.

questions.q: Basic character of lanthanoid hydroxides
questions.why: Ionic size falls from La³⁺ to Lu³⁺, so the M–OH bond becomes more covalent and basic character decreases.

questions.q: Case: In acidic solution, how many moles of KMnO₄ are needed to oxidise 1 mol of FeC₂O₄ completely (Fe²⁺ → Fe³⁺, C₂O₄²⁻ → CO₂)?
questions.why: Fe²⁺ → Fe³⁺ loses 1 electron and C₂O₄²⁻ → 2CO₂ loses 2, so 3 electrons per FeC₂O₄. Each MnO₄⁻ takes 5, so 3/5 = 0.6 mol are needed.

questions.q: Which is the strongest reducing agent?
questions.why: Cr²⁺ has E°(Cr³⁺/Cr²⁺) = −0.41 V, so it loses an electron easily to form the stable d³ Cr³⁺ and is the strongest reducing agent.

questions.q: Actinoid contraction is greater than lanthanoid contraction because
options: 5f electrons shield even more poorly than 4f
questions.why: 5f electrons shield the nucleus even more poorly than 4f electrons, so the contraction across actinoids is greater.

questions.q: Case: An aqueous ion is colourless and diamagnetic. Which could it be?
questions.why: Zn²⁺ is d¹⁰, so there are no d–d transitions, and all electrons are paired, so it is colourless and diamagnetic. The others have unpaired d electrons.

questions.q: Why is the second ionisation enthalpy of Cu unusually high?
questions.why: Removing a second electron from Cu⁺ means breaking the stable, completely filled 3d¹⁰ subshell, which takes a lot of energy.

courses.title: Ch 5 · Coordination Compounds
courses.summary: Werner's theory, key terms (ligands, denticity, chelates, coordination number and sphere), IUPAC nomenclature, structural and stereoisomerism, valence bond theory, crystal field theory with colour and magnetism, metal carbonyls, and applications in biology, analysis, medicine and industry. Independent practice material; not affiliated with or endorsed by any board or exam body.
outcomes: Learners can explain Werner's theory and deduce formulas from AgCl precipitation data.
Learners can name and write formulas of complexes by IUPAC rules.
Learners can identify linkage, ionisation, coordination, solvate, geometrical and optical isomers.
Learners can apply VBT and CFT to predict geometry, magnetism and colour.

lessons.title: Werner's theory and key terms

story.title: Green and violet from the same formula

scenes.text: In 1893 Alfred Werner puzzled over cobalt chloride–ammonia compounds of different colours.
Adding silver nitrate precipitated different amounts of AgCl from each, even though they had similar formulas.
His explanation — two kinds of valence — won the Nobel Prize in 1913 and founded coordination chemistry.

steps.title: Werner's theory
steps.body:
1. Metals show **primary valence** (ionisable; = oxidation state; satisfied by anions) and **secondary valence** (non-ionisable; = coordination number; satisfied by ligands — neutral molecules or anions).
2. Secondary valences point in fixed directions, giving definite geometry (octahedral, tetrahedral, square planar).

Evidence: moles of AgCl precipitated per mole of complex:
- CoCl₃·6NH₃ → 3 AgCl ⇒ [Co(NH₃)₆]Cl₃ (yellow)
- CoCl₃·5NH₃ → 2 AgCl ⇒ [CoCl(NH₃)₅]Cl₂ (purple)
- CoCl₃·4NH₃ → 1 AgCl ⇒ [CoCl₂(NH₃)₄]Cl (green and violet isomers)
**Double salts** (e.g. Mohr's salt FeSO₄·(NH₄)₂SO₄·6H₂O) dissociate completely into simple ions in water; **complexes** keep the complex ion intact.

steps.title: Key terms
steps.body:
- **Coordination entity / sphere:** central atom + attached ligands, written in [ ]; ions outside are **counter ions**.
- **Ligand:** ion or molecule donating electron pairs. **Denticity:** unidentate (Cl⁻, H₂O, NH₃), didentate (en = H₂NCH₂CH₂NH₂, C₂O₄²⁻), polydentate (EDTA⁴⁻, hexadentate).
- **Chelate:** a polydentate ligand forming a ring with the metal — more stable (chelate effect).
- **Ambidentate:** can bind through two different atoms — NO₂⁻ (N or O), SCN⁻ (S or N).
- **Coordination number:** number of donor atoms bonded to the metal.
- **Homoleptic** (one kind of ligand, [Co(NH₃)₆]³⁺) vs **heteroleptic** ([Co(NH₃)₄Cl₂]⁺).
- **Oxidation number** of the central atom from the charges.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Ex 1.** Oxidation state and CN in K₃[Fe(C₂O₄)₃]: 3(+1) + x + 3(−2) = 0 ⇒ **x = +3**; three didentate oxalates ⇒ **CN = 6**.

**Ex 2.** 1 mol of CrCl₃·5H₂O gives 2 mol AgCl. Formula: **[Cr(H₂O)₅Cl]Cl₂·H₂O**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Equating coordination number with number of ligands — count donor atoms (en counts 2).
- Counting chlorides inside the bracket as ionisable.
- Calling Mohr's salt a coordination compound.

activity.prompt: Classify each ligand by denticity.

quiz.q: Secondary valence in Werner's theory corresponds to
quiz.why: In Werner's theory the secondary (non-ionisable) valence is the number of ligand bonds to the metal, which is the coordination number.
Each ethylenediamine (en) is didentate and bonds through two N atoms, so three en gives a coordination number of 3 × 2 = 6.
NO₂⁻ is ambidentate because it can bind through either the N atom or the O atom. NH₃ is unidentate, en is didentate and EDTA is hexadentate.

quiz.q: [CoCl(NH₃)₅]Cl₂ with excess AgNO₃ gives AgCl (mol per mol)
quiz.why: In [CoCl(NH₃)₅]Cl₂ one Cl is inside the coordination sphere. The two outside Cl⁻ ions are ionisable and precipitate 2 mol of AgCl.
A heteroleptic complex has more than one kind of ligand. [Co(NH₃)₄Cl₂]⁺ has NH₃ and Cl⁻, while the others have only one type.

lessons.title: IUPAC nomenclature of coordination compounds

story.title: A name that tells the structure

scenes.text: Mohit is asked to write the formula of 'potassium hexacyanidoferrate(III)' in a test.
He breaks it apart: potassium outside; six cyanides around iron; iron in +3; '-ate' because the complex is an anion.
K₃[Fe(CN)₆] — the name encodes everything.

steps.title: Writing formulas
steps.body: Central atom first, then ligands in alphabetical order (of the ligand name/formula), all in square brackets; polyatomic ligands in parentheses; charge outside as a superscript.

steps.title: Naming rules
steps.body:
1. Name the **cation first**, then the anion (as for simple salts).
2. Within the complex, **ligands first in alphabetical order** (ignore multiplying prefixes), then the metal.
3. Anionic ligands end in **-o**: chlorido, bromido, cyanido, hydroxido, oxalato, nitrito-N (–NO₂), nitrito-O (–ONO), thiocyanato-S/N. Neutral ligands keep their names except **aqua** (H₂O), **ammine** (NH₃), **carbonyl** (CO), **nitrosyl** (NO).
4. Prefixes di-, tri-, tetra-; for complex ligand names (like ethane-1,2-diamine) use **bis-, tris-, tetrakis-** with parentheses.
5. Oxidation state of the metal in Roman numerals in parentheses.
6. If the complex is an **anion**, the metal name ends in **-ate**: cobaltate, nickelate, zincate; Latin roots for some: **ferrate** (Fe), **cuprate** (Cu), **argentate** (Ag), **aurate** (Au), **plumbate** (Pb), **stannate** (Sn).
7. Neutral complexes are named as one word, without a counter ion.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
- [Co(NH₃)₆]Cl₃ → **hexaamminecobalt(III) chloride**
- K₃[Fe(CN)₆] → **potassium hexacyanidoferrate(III)**
- [Pt(NH₃)₂Cl₂] → **diamminedichloridoplatinum(II)**
- [CoCl₂(en)₂]⁺ → **dichloridobis(ethane-1,2-diamine)cobalt(III) ion**
- K₂[Zn(OH)₄] → **potassium tetrahydroxidozincate(II)**
- [Ni(CO)₄] → **tetracarbonylnickel(0)**
- [Cr(H₂O)₅Cl]Cl₂ → **pentaaquachloridochromium(III) chloride**

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using 'ammonia' or 'water' instead of ammine and aqua.
- Writing 'iron' in an anionic complex (should be ferrate).
- Ordering ligands by charge instead of alphabetically, or alphabetising by the prefix ('di', 'tetra').

activity.prompt: Match the formula to its IUPAC name.

quiz.q: The ligand name for NH₃ is
quiz.why: The ligand NH₃ is named ammine, with a double m, in complexes. The single-m amine refers to organic amines.

quiz.q: In an anionic complex of copper, the metal is named
quiz.why: In an anionic complex the metal name ends in -ate, and copper uses its Latin root, so it becomes cuprate.
Ligands are named alphabetically (ammine before chlorido), then the metal. [Pt(NH₃)₂Cl₂] is neutral, so the metal keeps the name platinum(II).

quiz.q: Oxidation state of Fe in K₄[Fe(CN)₆] is
The prefix used before ethane-1,2-diamine for two such ligands is
quiz.why: For ligands whose own names already contain numerical prefixes, such as ethane-1,2-diamine, IUPAC uses bis, tris, tetrakis. So two such ligands are written as bis(ethane-1,2-diamine), not 'di'.

lessons.title: Isomerism in coordination compounds

scenes.text: Cisplatin, cis-[Pt(NH₃)₂Cl₂], is a life-saving anticancer drug.
Its geometrical isomer, transplatin, with exactly the same formula, is far less effective.
The arrangement of ligands in space decides how the molecule binds to DNA.

steps.title: Structural isomerism
steps.body:
- **Linkage:** ambidentate ligand binds through different atoms — [Co(NH₃)₅(NO₂)]Cl₂ (nitrito-N, yellow) vs [Co(NH₃)₅(ONO)]Cl₂ (nitrito-O, red).
- **Coordination:** ligands exchanged between cationic and anionic complexes — [Co(NH₃)₆][Cr(CN)₆] and [Cr(NH₃)₆][Co(CN)₆].
- **Ionisation:** a counter ion swaps with a ligand — [Co(NH₃)₅(SO₄)]Br and [Co(NH₃)₅Br]SO₄ (give different ions in solution).
- **Solvate (hydrate):** water inside vs outside — [Cr(H₂O)₆]Cl₃ (violet) and [Cr(H₂O)₅Cl]Cl₂·H₂O (grey-green).

steps.title: Geometrical isomerism
steps.body:
- **Square planar MA₂B₂:** cis and trans (e.g. [Pt(NH₃)₂Cl₂]).
- **Octahedral MA₄B₂:** cis and trans ([CoCl₂(NH₃)₄]⁺).
- **Octahedral MA₃B₃:** **fac** (three identical ligands on one face) and **mer** (around a meridian) — [Co(NH₃)₃(NO₂)₃].
- [MX₂(AA)₂] type (AA = en): cis and trans.
- **Tetrahedral** complexes do not show geometrical isomerism.

steps.title: Optical isomerism
steps.body:
Non-superimposable mirror images (**enantiomers**, d and l) rotate plane-polarised light equally in opposite directions. Common in octahedral complexes with didentate ligands:
- [Co(en)₃]³⁺ — optically active.
- **cis**-[CoCl₂(en)₂]⁺ — optically active; **trans** is optically inactive (has a mirror plane).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Ex 1.** Isomers of [CoCl₂(en)₂]⁺: trans (1) + cis pair d and l (2) = **3 stereoisomers**.

**Ex 2.** [Co(NH₃)₅Br]SO₄ gives a white precipitate with BaCl₂; its ionisation isomer [Co(NH₃)₅(SO₄)]Br gives a pale yellow precipitate with AgNO₃.

**Ex 3.** [Ni(CO)₄] (tetrahedral) shows **no** geometrical isomerism.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying trans-[CoCl₂(en)₂]⁺ is optically active.
- Expecting cis/trans in tetrahedral complexes.
- Confusing ionisation isomers (different ions released) with hydrate isomers (different water positions).

activity.prompt: Match each pair to its type of isomerism.

quiz.why: [Co(en)₃]³⁺ has three chelating rings arranged like a propeller. It has no plane of symmetry, so its mirror image cannot be superimposed and it is optically active. The other options are symmetric.
Facial–meridional isomerism occurs in octahedral MA₃B₃: the three identical ligands either sit on one face (fac) or around a meridian (mer).
Linkage isomers arise when a ligand can attach through different donor atoms. This needs an ambidentate ligand such as NO₂⁻ (N or O) or SCN⁻ (S or N).
In a tetrahedron all four positions are adjacent to one another, so swapping A and B positions gives the same shape. Tetrahedral MA₂B₂ therefore has no geometrical isomers.
Cisplatin, cis-[Pt(NH₃)₂Cl₂], binds to DNA in cancer cells and stops them dividing, so it is used as an anticancer drug.

lessons.title: Valence bond theory

scenes.text: [Ni(CN)₄]²⁻ is square planar and diamagnetic; [NiCl₄]²⁻ is tetrahedral and paramagnetic.
Same metal, same oxidation state, same coordination number — why different?
Valence bond theory explains it through hybridisation and electron pairing.

steps.title: Hybridisation and geometry
steps.body:
The metal uses hybrid orbitals to accept ligand electron pairs:
- CN 4: **sp³** tetrahedral; **dsp²** square planar.
- CN 6: **d²sp³** octahedral (inner orbital, uses (n−1)d) or **sp³d²** octahedral (outer orbital, uses nd).
Strong-field ligands (CN⁻, CO, often NH₃ for Co³⁺) can force pairing of d electrons, freeing inner d orbitals.

steps.title: Worked VBT cases
steps.body:
- **[Co(NH₃)₆]³⁺:** Co³⁺ 3d⁶; electrons pair into 3 orbitals; **d²sp³**, inner orbital, **diamagnetic**.
- **[CoF₆]³⁻:** no pairing; **sp³d²**, outer orbital, **4 unpaired**, paramagnetic.
- **[Ni(CN)₄]²⁻:** Ni²⁺ 3d⁸ paired into 4 orbitals; **dsp²**, square planar, **diamagnetic**.
- **[NiCl₄]²⁻:** no pairing; **sp³**, tetrahedral, **2 unpaired**.
- **[Ni(CO)₄]:** Ni(0) 3d⁸4s² → 3d¹⁰; **sp³**, tetrahedral, diamagnetic.
- **[Fe(CN)₆]³⁻:** Fe³⁺ 3d⁵ → d²sp³ with **1 unpaired**.

steps.title: Limitations of VBT
steps.body: Involves assumptions; cannot explain colour; no quantitative magnetic data beyond counting; cannot predict whether a complex is inner or outer orbital or distinguish weak and strong ligands reliably; does not explain tetrahedral vs square planar for 4-coordinate complexes in general.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting to remove 4s electrons before filling hybrid orbitals.
- Assuming every octahedral complex is d²sp³.
- Using μ to count unpaired electrons incorrectly: 1.73 BM ⇒ 1, 2.83 ⇒ 2, 3.87 ⇒ 3.

activity.prompt: Match each complex to its hybridisation (VBT).

quiz.why: [Ni(CN)₄]²⁻ is square planar. Ni²⁺ is d⁸, and strong-field CN⁻ pairs the electrons, freeing one d orbital for dsp² hybridisation.
F⁻ is a weak-field ligand and does not pair Co³⁺ (d⁶) electrons, so the outer 4d orbitals are used (sp³d²). The complex has 4 unpaired electrons and is paramagnetic.

quiz.q: Number of unpaired electrons in [Fe(CN)₆]³⁻ is
quiz.why: CN⁻ is strong-field, so Fe³⁺ (d⁵) pairs electrons as t₂g⁵. That leaves just 1 unpaired electron.
In Ni(CO)₄ nickel is Ni(0), 3d¹⁰ after CO pushes the 4s electrons in. All electrons are paired, so it is diamagnetic, and sp³ hybridisation gives a tetrahedral shape.
Valence bond theory explains geometry, hybridisation and magnetic behaviour, but it cannot explain the colours of complexes because it does not deal with excited states or d–d transitions.

lessons.title: Crystal field theory, colour and magnetism

story.title: Why ruby is red and emerald green

scenes.text: Both ruby and emerald get their colour from Cr³⁺ ions in different host crystals.
The surrounding oxygen atoms split Cr³⁺'s d orbitals by different amounts.
Different splitting means different colours absorbed — crystal field theory in a gemstone.

steps.title: Splitting of d orbitals
steps.body: Ligands are treated as point charges. In an **octahedral** field the d orbitals split into **t₂g** (dxy, dyz, dzx; lower by 0.4Δ₀) and **e_g** (dx²−y², dz²; higher by 0.6Δ₀). In a **tetrahedral** field the order is reversed (e lower, t₂ higher) and **Δt = (4/9)Δ₀** — so tetrahedral complexes are almost always high spin.

steps.title: Spectrochemical series and spin
steps.body:
Ligands in order of increasing field strength:
**I⁻ < Br⁻ < SCN⁻ < Cl⁻ < S²⁻ < F⁻ < OH⁻ < C₂O₄²⁻ < H₂O < NCS⁻ < edta⁴⁻ < NH₃ < en < CN⁻ < CO**
For d⁴–d⁷ octahedral ions, compare Δ₀ with pairing energy P:
- **Δ₀ < P** (weak field): **high spin** — e.g. d⁴ as t₂g³e_g¹.
- **Δ₀ > P** (strong field): **low spin** — d⁴ as t₂g⁴e_g⁰.

steps.title: Colour and limitations
steps.body:
Absorption of light promotes an electron t₂g → e_g; the complementary colour is seen. [Ti(H₂O)₆]³⁺ (d¹) absorbs blue-green (~498 nm) and appears **violet**. Without ligands there is no splitting: anhydrous CuSO₄ is white, hydrated is blue. [Ni(H₂O)₆]²⁺ is green; adding en gives blue/violet complexes as Δ₀ increases.
**Limitations of CFT:** treats ligands as point charges and ignores covalent bonding; cannot explain why anionic ligands like F⁻ are weaker than neutral H₂O, NH₃.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Ex 1.** [CoF₆]³⁻ (d⁶, weak field): t₂g⁴e_g² ⇒ **4 unpaired**, μ ≈ 4.90 BM. [Co(NH₃)₆]³⁺ (strong field): t₂g⁶ ⇒ **0 unpaired**.

**Ex 2.** CFSE of low-spin d⁶ octahedral: 6 × (−0.4Δ₀) = **−2.4Δ₀** (+ pairing terms).

**Ex 3.** Which absorbs light of longer wavelength: [Co(H₂O)₆]³⁺ or [Co(CN)₆]³⁻? Smaller Δ₀ with H₂O ⇒ lower energy ⇒ **[Co(H₂O)₆]³⁺** absorbs longer λ.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Putting e_g below t₂g for octahedral complexes.
- Forgetting tetrahedral splitting is reversed and smaller.
- Assuming high-spin/low-spin choice applies to d¹–d³ or d⁸–d¹⁰ octahedral ions (only one arrangement possible).

activity.prompt: Arrange these ligands from WEAKEST to STRONGEST field.

quiz.q: In an octahedral field, the lower set of d orbitals is
quiz.why: In an octahedral field the ligands approach along the axes. The t₂g orbitals point between the ligands and feel less repulsion, so they are lower in energy than e_g.

quiz.q: Δt is related to Δ₀ by
quiz.why: A tetrahedral complex has only four ligands and they do not point directly at the d orbitals, so the splitting is smaller: Δt = (4/9)Δ₀.

quiz.q: Which ligand produces the largest splitting?
quiz.why: CO is at the strong-field end of the spectrochemical series, so it causes the largest crystal field splitting. H₂O, NH₃ and Cl⁻ are weaker.

quiz.q: A d⁴ ion in a strong field has configuration
quiz.why: With a strong field (large Δ₀), electrons pair in the lower t₂g set before going to e_g, so d⁴ becomes t₂g⁴e_g⁰.
A complex shows the complementary colour of the light it absorbs. A violet appearance means it absorbs the opposite colour, blue-green, in the visible range.

lessons.title: Metal carbonyls and applications

scenes.text: The green of a neem leaf comes from chlorophyll, a magnesium complex.
Our blood is red because haemoglobin contains an iron complex that carries oxygen.
From medicines to metal extraction, coordination compounds are everywhere.

steps.title: Metal carbonyls
steps.body:
Homoleptic carbonyls: [Ni(CO)₄] tetrahedral, [Fe(CO)₅] trigonal bipyramidal, [Cr(CO)₆] octahedral, [Mn₂(CO)₁₀] and [Co₂(CO)₈] with M–M bonds.
**Synergic bonding:** CO donates a lone pair to the metal (σ bond) and the metal donates d electrons back into empty π* orbitals of CO (**π back-bonding**). Each strengthens the other, making the M–CO bond strong.

steps.title: Applications
steps.body:
- **Biology:** chlorophyll (Mg), haemoglobin (Fe), vitamin B₁₂ (cyanocobalamin, Co).
- **Analysis:** hardness of water by titration with **EDTA** (Ca²⁺, Mg²⁺); **Ni²⁺** gives a red precipitate with dimethylglyoxime.
- **Metallurgy:** Ag and Au extracted as [Ag(CN)₂]⁻ and [Au(CN)₂]⁻ then recovered with Zn; **Mond process** purifies nickel via volatile [Ni(CO)₄].
- **Catalysis:** Wilkinson's catalyst [(Ph₃P)₃RhCl] for hydrogenation of alkenes.
- **Photography:** undeveloped AgBr dissolves in hypo as [Ag(S₂O₃)₂]³⁻.
- **Medicine:** **cisplatin** (anticancer); EDTA to treat lead poisoning; chelating agents for excess Cu or Fe.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Ex 1.** In [Fe(CO)₅], oxidation state of Fe = **0**; geometry **trigonal bipyramidal** (dsp³ in VBT).

**Ex 2.** Why does EDTA estimate hardness? It forms stable 1 : 1 chelates with Ca²⁺ and Mg²⁺ — moles of EDTA used = moles of hardness ions.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking CO bonds only by σ donation.
- Assigning +2 to Ni in [Ni(CO)₄].
- Forgetting that EDTA binds metal ions 1 : 1 regardless of charge.

activity.prompt: Match the complex to its role.

quiz.why: Chlorophyll is a magnesium porphyrin complex. Iron is in haemoglobin, cobalt in vitamin B₁₂.

quiz.q: Synergic bonding in metal carbonyls involves
quiz.why: In metal carbonyls CO donates a lone pair to the metal (σ bond) and the metal gives back electrons into CO's empty π* orbitals (π back-donation). The two effects strengthen each other, which is synergic bonding.
Fe(CO)₅ has five ligands and sp³d hybridisation, giving a trigonal bipyramidal shape.

quiz.q: Hardness of water is estimated by titration with
quiz.why: EDTA forms stable chelate complexes with Ca²⁺ and Mg²⁺, so titrating water with EDTA measures its hardness.
Vitamin B₁₂ (cyanocobalamin) is a cobalt complex of a corrin ring.

sources: NCERT Class 12 Chemistry (topic reference, own wording)

questions.q: The coordination number of Fe in [Fe(C₂O₄)₃]³⁻ is
questions.why: Oxalate (C₂O₄²⁻) is didentate, using two O atoms. Three of them make 3 × 2 = 6 bonds, so the coordination number of Fe is 6.

questions.q: EDTA is a
questions.why: EDTA has two N atoms and four carboxylate O atoms that can bind, so it is hexadentate.

questions.q: IUPAC name of [Co(NH₃)₅Cl]Cl₂:
questions.why: Ligands are named alphabetically (ammine, then chlorido), then the metal. Charge: 3 + 0 − 1 = +2 balanced by 2 Cl⁻, so Co is +3. The cation keeps the name cobalt, not cobaltate.

questions.q: Assertion: [Co(en)₃]³⁺ is optically active. Reason: It has no plane of symmetry and its mirror image is non-superimposable.
options: Both true; reason does not explain
questions.why: Both are true. [Co(en)₃]³⁺ has no plane of symmetry and its mirror images do not superimpose, which is exactly why it is optically active.

questions.q: Which complex is square planar?
questions.why: Ni²⁺ with strong-field CN⁻ forms square planar dsp² [Ni(CN)₄]²⁻. [NiCl₄]²⁻ and [Zn(NH₃)₄]²⁺ are tetrahedral, and Ni(CO)₄ is tetrahedral too.

questions.q: The spin-only magnetic moment of [MnBr₄]²⁻ is 5.9 BM. Its geometry is
questions.why: 5.9 BM means 5 unpaired electrons, as in Mn²⁺ (d⁵) with no pairing. With no pairing, outer sp³ hybridisation applies, so [MnBr₄]²⁻ is tetrahedral.

questions.q: Which isomerism is shown by [Co(NH₃)₅(SCN)]²⁺ and [Co(NH₃)₅(NCS)]²⁺?
questions.why: The SCN⁻ ligand is ambidentate, binding through S in one isomer and N in the other. Isomers differing only in the donor atom are linkage isomers.

questions.q: Number of geometrical isomers of [Pt(NH₃)₂Cl₂]:
questions.why: Square planar [Pt(NH₃)₂Cl₂] can have the two Cl on the same side (cis) or opposite sides (trans), so 2 geometrical isomers.

questions.q: Case: 1 mol of a complex CoCl₃·4NH₃ precipitates 1 mol AgCl. The complex and its geometrical isomers number:
questions.why: One mole of AgCl means only one Cl⁻ is ionisable, so the formula is [Co(NH₃)₄Cl₂]Cl. The octahedral [Co(NH₃)₄Cl₂]⁺ has cis and trans forms, so 2 isomers.

questions.q: The correct order of field strength is
questions.why: The spectrochemical series of field strength is CO > CN⁻ > NH₃ > H₂O > Cl⁻, from strong-field ligands to weak-field ones.

questions.q: Assertion: Tetrahedral complexes are generally high spin. Reason: Δt is small (about 4/9 Δ₀) and usually less than the pairing energy.
options: Both true; reason does not explain
questions.why: Both are true. Δt is only about 4/9 of Δ₀, usually smaller than the pairing energy, so electrons stay unpaired and tetrahedral complexes are high spin.

questions.q: Number of unpaired electrons in [Mn(CN)₆]³⁻ (low spin) is
questions.why: Mn³⁺ is d⁴. With strong-field CN⁻ all four electrons go into t₂g (t₂g⁴), which has two paired and two unpaired electrons.

questions.q: Case: [Fe(H₂O)₆]²⁺ is paramagnetic with 4 unpaired electrons while [Fe(CN)₆]⁴⁻ is diamagnetic. This is because
options: CN⁻ is a strong-field ligand causing pairing (t₂g⁶)
questions.why: Water is weak-field, so Fe²⁺ (d⁶) is high spin with 4 unpaired electrons. CN⁻ is strong-field (Δ₀ larger than pairing energy), so all six electrons pair in t₂g and the complex is diamagnetic.

questions.q: CFSE for a high-spin d⁴ octahedral ion is
questions.why: High-spin d⁴ is t₂g³e_g¹. CFSE = 3(−0.4Δ₀) + 1(+0.6Δ₀) = −1.2Δ₀ + 0.6Δ₀ = −0.6Δ₀.

questions.q: How many stereoisomers does [CoCl₂(en)₂]⁺ have?
questions.why: [CoCl₂(en)₂]⁺ has a trans form, which is symmetric, and a cis form, which is chiral and exists as two optical isomers. That makes 3 stereoisomers.

questions.q: Which absorbs light of the shortest wavelength?
questions.why: CN⁻ is the strongest-field ligand, giving the largest Δ₀. A bigger gap means higher-energy, shorter-wavelength light is absorbed.

questions.q: In the Mond process, nickel is purified by forming
questions.why: In the Mond process impure nickel reacts with CO to form volatile [Ni(CO)₄], which is then heated to decompose and give pure nickel.

school-c12-chemistry-b.title: Class 12 Chemistry · Part B (Ch 6–10 + Revision)
school-c12-chemistry-b.description: Class 12 Chemistry, chapters 6–10: haloalkanes and haloarenes, alcohols, phenols and ethers, aldehydes, ketones and carboxylic acids, amines and biomolecules, plus Revision & Practice.

courses.title: Ch 6 · Haloalkanes and Haloarenes
courses.summary: Classification and nomenclature, nature of the C–X bond, methods of preparation (from alcohols, hydrocarbons, halogen exchange), physical properties, SN1 and SN2 mechanisms with stereochemistry, elimination and reactions with metals, reactions of haloarenes, and polyhalogen compounds with their environmental effects. Independent practice material; not affiliated with or endorsed by any board or exam body.
outcomes: Learners can name haloalkanes/haloarenes and choose a preparation method.
Learners can compare SN1 and SN2 (order, mechanism, stereochemistry, substrate reactivity).
Learners can predict major products of substitution and elimination (Zaitsev rule).
Learners can explain the low reactivity of haloarenes and describe uses and hazards of polyhalogen compounds.

lessons.title: Classification, nomenclature and the C–X bond

scenes.text: In an old lab cupboard, Rehana finds chloroform stored in a dark brown bottle, filled to the brim.
Her teacher explains: light and air slowly turn chloroform into poisonous phosgene.
Organic halogen compounds are useful and reactive — understanding the C–X bond explains both.

steps.title: Classification
steps.body:
- By number of halogens: mono-, di-, polyhalo compounds.
- **Alkyl halides:** 1°, 2°, 3° by the carbon bearing X.
- **Allylic** (X on carbon next to C=C, e.g. CH₂=CH–CH₂Cl) and **benzylic** (C₆H₅CH₂Cl) halides — sp³ C–X.
- **Vinylic** (CH₂=CHCl) and **aryl** halides (C₆H₅Cl) — X on sp² carbon.
- Dihalides: **geminal** (both X on one C, alkylidene halides) and **vicinal** (adjacent C, alkylene dihalides).

steps.title: Nomenclature
steps.body: Common names: alkyl halide (CH₃CH₂Br, ethyl bromide). IUPAC: halo-substituted alkane (bromoethane). Examples: (CH₃)₃CBr → 2-bromo-2-methylpropane; CH₂=CHCH₂Br → 3-bromoprop-1-ene; C₆H₄Cl₂ (1,4-) → 1,4-dichlorobenzene (p-dichlorobenzene).

steps.title: Nature of the C–X bond
steps.body: C–X is **polar** (C δ+, X δ−) because halogens are more electronegative. Bond length increases and bond enthalpy decreases from C–F to C–I, so **reactivity: R–I > R–Br > R–Cl > R–F**. Dipole moments: CH₃Cl (1.860 D) > CH₃F (1.847 D) > CH₃Br (1.830 D) > CH₃I (1.636 D) — F is most electronegative, but the C–F bond is very short.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Ex 1.** Classify CH₃CH(Cl)CH₃ → **2° alkyl halide** (2-chloropropane).

**Ex 2.** Classify C₆H₅CH₂CH₂Cl → **1° alkyl halide** (not benzylic — X is two carbons away from the ring).

**Ex 3.** CH₃CHCl₂ is a **geminal** dihalide (1,1-dichloroethane); ClCH₂CH₂Cl is **vicinal** (1,2-dichloroethane).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling vinyl chloride an allylic halide.
- Assuming CH₃F has the largest dipole moment.
- Numbering the chain from the end farther from the halogen.

activity.prompt: Classify each halide.

quiz.q: Which halide has X on an sp² carbon?
quiz.why: In vinyl chloride, CH₂=CHCl, the Cl is on a carbon of the C=C double bond, which is sp² hybridised. In allyl chloride, benzyl chloride and 2-chloropropane the halogen is on an sp³ carbon.
(CH₃)₃CBr has a three-carbon main chain with a methyl and bromine both on carbon 2, so it is 2-bromo-2-methylpropane. tert-Butyl bromide is the common name.
The C–X bond gets weaker down the group (C–F strongest, C–I weakest), and the weaker bond breaks more easily. So reactivity is RI > RBr > RCl > RF.

quiz.q: Highest dipole moment among methyl halides:
quiz.why: Dipole moment = charge × bond length. CH₃F has the more polar bond but a short one, so CH₃Cl, with a longer bond, has the highest dipole moment among these halides.
In geminal (gem) dihalides both halogens are on the same carbon. Vicinal dihalides have them on adjacent carbons.

lessons.title: Preparation of haloalkanes and haloarenes

scenes.text: For her project, Lavanya must make bromoethane, chlorobenzene and fluoroethane.
Each needs a different tool: an alcohol reaction, an aromatic substitution, a halogen swap.
Knowing which method fits which target is a classic board and JEE question.

steps.title: From alcohols
steps.body:
- **HX:** R–OH + HCl (ZnCl₂) → R–Cl + H₂O (Lucas reagent; works best for 3° alcohols). HBr, HI also used.
- **PX₃ / PX₅:** 3R–OH + PCl₃ → 3R–Cl + H₃PO₃; R–OH + PCl₅ → R–Cl + POCl₃ + HCl.
- **Thionyl chloride (preferred):** R–OH + SOCl₂ → R–Cl + SO₂↑ + HCl↑ — by-products are gases, so pure product.
Phenols do *not* give haloarenes this way (C–O bond in phenol has partial double-bond character).

steps.title: From hydrocarbons
steps.body:
- **Free-radical halogenation** of alkanes (Cl₂/hν): gives mixtures.
- **Electrophilic substitution** of arenes: C₆H₆ + Cl₂ (FeCl₃, dark) → C₆H₅Cl; toluene → o- and p-chlorotoluene.
- **Sandmeyer reaction:** ArN₂⁺ + CuCl/HCl → ArCl; CuBr/HBr → ArBr; ArN₂⁺ + KI → ArI.
- **Addition of HX to alkenes:** propene + HBr → **2-bromopropane** (Markovnikov); in the presence of peroxide → **1-bromopropane** (anti-Markovnikov, Kharasch effect, only for HBr). Br₂ in CCl₄ adds to give vicinal dibromides (bromine colour discharged — test for unsaturation).

steps.title: Halogen exchange
steps.body:
- **Finkelstein:** R–Cl/Br + NaI (dry acetone) → R–I + NaCl/NaBr↓ (precipitation drives the reaction).
- **Swarts:** R–Br/Cl + AgF, Hg₂F₂, CoF₂ or SbF₃ → R–F.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Ex 1.** Ethanol → chloroethane cleanly: C₂H₅OH + SOCl₂ → C₂H₅Cl + SO₂ + HCl.

**Ex 2.** Product of CH₃CH=CH₂ + HBr with benzoyl peroxide: **CH₃CH₂CH₂Br** (1-bromopropane).

**Ex 3.** Iodobenzene from aniline: diazotise (NaNO₂/HCl, 273–278 K), then add KI.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Applying the peroxide effect to HCl or HI.
- Trying to make chlorobenzene from phenol with HCl.
- Forgetting that the Finkelstein solvent must be dry acetone.

activity.prompt: Match the reaction to its name or reagent.

quiz.q: Best reagent to convert ethanol to chloroethane is
quiz.why: SOCl₂ converts the alcohol into the chloride and the by-products SO₂ and HCl escape as gases, leaving a pure product. HCl alone or Cl₂ would not do this cleanly.
By Markovnikov's rule, H adds to the carbon with more hydrogens and Br goes to the more substituted carbon, giving 2-bromopropane.
The Swarts reaction heats an alkyl chloride or bromide with a metal fluoride such as AgF or Hg₂F₂ to make alkyl fluorides.
In the Sandmeyer reaction a diazonium salt is converted to an aryl chloride or bromide using Cu(I) halides, CuCl or CuBr.

quiz.q: The peroxide effect is observed only with
quiz.why: Only HBr gives the peroxide (anti-Markovnikov) effect, because its radical chain steps are energetically favourable. HCl and HI do not follow this path, and HF is unreactive.
