lessons.title: Physical properties and nucleophilic substitution (SN1 and SN2)

scenes.text: A chemist makes a drug molecule and finds one mirror-image form heals while the other does nothing.
Whether a substitution keeps, flips or scrambles the 3-D arrangement depends on its mechanism.
SN1 and SN2 are the two main pathways — and each leaves its own fingerprint.

steps.title: Physical properties
steps.body:
- Colourless when pure; bromides and iodides darken in light.
- **Boiling points** higher than parent alkanes (polarity, larger mass); increase RCl < RBr < RI; decrease with branching for isomers.
- **Density** rises with number and mass of halogens (CH₂Cl₂ < CHCl₃ < CCl₄).
- **Very slightly soluble in water** (cannot form strong enough H-bonds to break water's H-bonds) but soluble in organic solvents.
- p-Dihalobenzenes have higher m.p. than o and m (symmetry, better packing).

steps.title: SN2 (bimolecular)
steps.body:
- Rate = k[RX][Nu⁻] — second order, **one step**.
- Nucleophile attacks from the side **opposite** the leaving group; transition state with five groups around carbon; **inversion of configuration** (Walden inversion).
- Reactivity: **CH₃X > 1° > 2° > 3°** (steric hindrance).
- Favoured by strong nucleophiles and polar aprotic solvents.

steps.title: SN1 (unimolecular)
steps.body:
- Rate = k[RX] — first order, **two steps**: slow ionisation to a **carbocation**, then fast attack by Nu⁻.
- Planar carbocation can be attacked from either side ⇒ **racemisation** (with some excess inversion).
- Reactivity: **3° > 2° > 1° > CH₃X** (carbocation stability); allylic and benzylic halides react fast (resonance-stabilised cations).
- Favoured by polar protic solvents (water, alcohols).

steps.title: Stereochemistry basics
steps.body: A carbon with four different groups is **chiral** (asymmetric); such molecules are **optically active**. **Enantiomers** are non-superimposable mirror images, rotating plane-polarised light equally but oppositely (d/+ and l/−). A 50 : 50 mixture is a **racemic mixture** (optically inactive). Example: 2-chlorobutane is chiral; 1-chlorobutane is not.

steps.title: Ambident nucleophiles
steps.body:
- KCN (ionic) → **alkyl cyanide** R–CN (attack by C); AgCN (covalent) → **isocyanide** R–NC (attack by N).
- KNO₂ → **alkyl nitrite** R–O–N=O; AgNO₂ → **nitroalkane** R–NO₂.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Ex 1.** Fastest SN2: CH₃Br, CH₃CH₂Br, (CH₃)₂CHBr, (CH₃)₃CBr? **CH₃Br** (least hindered).

**Ex 2.** Fastest SN1 in aqueous ethanol: **(CH₃)₃CBr** (most stable 3° cation).

**Ex 3.** (−)-2-bromooctane + OH⁻ by SN2 gives **(+)-octan-2-ol with inverted configuration**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying SN1 gives inversion only — it mostly racemises.
- Using 3° halides as SN2 substrates.
- Mixing KCN/AgCN products.

activity.prompt: SN1 or SN2?

quiz.why: In SN2 the nucleophile attacks from the side opposite the leaving group, so the configuration is inverted (Walden inversion).
SN1 goes through a carbocation, and the tertiary carbocation from (CH₃)₃CCl is the most stable, so this halide reacts fastest.
AgCN is mainly covalent, so the nitrogen lone pair attacks the carbon and an isocyanide (R–NC) forms. Ionic KCN gives nitriles instead.
A racemic mixture has equal amounts of two enantiomers. Their rotations cancel, so the mixture is optically inactive.

quiz.q: Haloalkanes are only slightly soluble in water because
options: they cannot form strong H-bonds with water
quiz.why: Dissolving a haloalkane needs breaking water's strong H-bonds, but the new haloalkane–water attractions are weaker and do not make up the energy. So solubility is low.
2-Chlorobutane has a carbon bonded to four different groups (H, Cl, CH₃, C₂H₅), so it is chiral. In the other compounds no carbon has four different groups.

sources: NCERT Class 12 Chemistry (topic reference, own wording)

lessons.title: Elimination and reactions with metals

scenes.text: In 1912, Victor Grignard won the Nobel Prize for a simple reagent made from a haloalkane and magnesium.
It lets chemists join carbon atoms together almost at will.
But it is so reactive that a drop of water destroys it — chemists must keep everything bone-dry.

steps.title: β-Elimination (dehydrohalogenation)
steps.body:
Heating with **alcoholic KOH** removes H from the β-carbon and X from the α-carbon to form an alkene.
**Zaitsev (Saytzeff) rule:** the major product is the **more substituted alkene** (more alkyl groups on the double-bond carbons).
2-Bromobutane + alc. KOH → **but-2-ene (major)** + but-1-ene (minor).
Substitution and elimination compete: strong bulky bases and 3° halides favour elimination; good nucleophiles and 1° halides favour substitution.

steps.title: Reactions with metals
steps.body:
- **Grignard reagent:** R–X + Mg (dry ether) → **RMgX**. The C–Mg bond is highly polar (carbon nucleophilic). With water/alcohols/any H-source: RMgX + H₂O → **R–H** + Mg(OH)X — so reagents must be dry.
- **Wurtz reaction:** 2R–X + 2Na (dry ether) → **R–R** + 2NaX (alkanes with double carbon number).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Ex 1.** 2-Bromo-2-methylbutane + alc. KOH: major product **2-methylbut-2-ene** (trisubstituted), minor 2-methylbut-1-ene.

**Ex 2.** CH₃MgBr + H₂O → **CH₄** + Mg(OH)Br.

**Ex 3.** 2CH₃CH₂Br + 2Na (dry ether) → **CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₃** (butane).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using aqueous KOH for elimination — aqueous KOH mainly substitutes (alcohol); alcoholic KOH eliminates.
- Making Grignard reagents in moist solvents.
- Expecting Wurtz to give odd-numbered alkanes cleanly from one halide (it doubles the chain).

activity.prompt: Complete the reactions.
activity.text: 2-Bromobutane with alcoholic KOH gives mainly ___-2-ene. CH₃MgBr reacts with water to give ___. The rule for the major alkene is called ___ rule.

quiz.q: Alcoholic KOH with haloalkanes mainly causes
quiz.why: Alcoholic KOH is a strong base in a non-aqueous medium and removes H and X from adjacent carbons, so elimination (dehydrohalogenation) gives an alkene. Aqueous KOH favours substitution.
Zaitsev's rule says elimination gives mainly the more substituted alkene, as it is the more stable one.
Grignard reagents react with water and acids, so they are prepared from RX and magnesium in dry (anhydrous) ether.
In the Wurtz reaction two alkyl groups from RX join with sodium in dry ether. Two CH₃ groups give CH₃–CH₃, ethane.
The R–Mg bond is strongly polar, with carbon as a carbanion. Water protonates it to give the alkane RH and Mg(OH)X.

sources: NCERT Class 12 Chemistry (topic reference, own wording)

lessons.title: Reactions of haloarenes

scenes.text: Siddharth tries to make phenol by boiling chlorobenzene with NaOH — nothing happens.
Industry needs 623 K and 300 atm for the same reaction.
The C–Cl bond in an aromatic ring is far stronger and better protected than in an alkyl chloride.

steps.title: Low reactivity towards nucleophilic substitution
steps.body:
1. **Resonance:** the lone pair on Cl delocalises into the ring, giving the C–Cl bond **partial double-bond character**.
2. **sp² carbon** is more electronegative and holds the bond more tightly (shorter bond).
3. The phenyl cation is unstable (SN1 impossible).
4. Electron-rich ring repels nucleophiles; backside attack is blocked (SN2 impossible).
Forcing conditions: C₆H₅Cl + NaOH (623 K, 300 atm) → C₆H₅ONa → phenol (Dow process).

steps.title: Effect of electron-withdrawing groups
steps.body:
–NO₂ at **ortho or para** to Cl stabilises the negative intermediate by resonance and greatly speeds substitution:
- 4-nitrochlorobenzene → 4-nitrophenol (aq. NaOH, 443 K)
- 2,4-dinitrochlorobenzene → 2,4-dinitrophenol (368 K)
- 2,4,6-trinitrochlorobenzene → picric acid (warm water)
A meta –NO₂ has little effect.

steps.title: Electrophilic substitution and metal reactions
steps.body:
Halogens are **deactivating** (−I effect) but **ortho/para directing** (+R effect). Chlorination (FeCl₃), nitration, sulphonation and Friedel–Crafts alkylation/acylation of chlorobenzene give o- and p-products (p major).
- **Wurtz–Fittig:** C₆H₅X + RX + 2Na (dry ether) → C₆H₅–R (alkylbenzene).
- **Fittig:** 2C₆H₅X + 2Na → C₆H₅–C₆H₅ (biphenyl).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Ex 1.** Chlorobenzene + CH₃Cl (anhyd. AlCl₃) → **1-chloro-2-methylbenzene + 1-chloro-4-methylbenzene** (para major).

**Ex 2.** Bromobenzene + CH₃Br + Na (dry ether) → **toluene** (Wurtz–Fittig).

**Ex 3.** Arrange for nucleophilic substitution: chlorobenzene < 4-nitrochlorobenzene < 2,4-dinitrochlorobenzene.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling halogens meta-directing because they deactivate.
- Expecting a meta nitro group to activate nucleophilic substitution.
- Confusing Fittig (aryl–aryl) with Wurtz–Fittig (aryl–alkyl).

activity.prompt: Order from LEAST to MOST reactive towards aqueous NaOH (nucleophilic substitution).

quiz.q: Haloarenes are less reactive than haloalkanes towards nucleophiles because
quiz.why: In haloarenes the lone pair on halogen is delocalised into the ring, giving the C–X bond partial double-bond character. It is stronger and shorter, so it is harder to break.
Cl withdraws electrons by the −I effect, which deactivates the ring, but donates its lone pair by +R at o/p positions, so it directs o/p.
The Fittig reaction couples two aryl halide molecules with sodium in dry ether to give a biaryl, such as biphenyl from bromobenzene.

quiz.q: Nucleophilic substitution in chlorobenzene is accelerated by –NO₂ at
quiz.why: An –NO₂ group at the ortho or para position to Cl stabilises the negative intermediate by resonance, so substitution is easier. At the meta position it cannot delocalise the charge to the carbon bearing Cl.
The Wurtz–Fittig reaction joins an aryl halide and an alkyl halide with sodium to make an alkylarene (Ar–R), such as toluene from bromobenzene and CH₃Br.

lessons.title: Polyhalogen compounds and the environment

scenes.text: In the 1980s scientists found the ozone layer over Antarctica thinning dramatically.
The culprits were freons — once-praised 'safe' refrigerants and aerosol propellants.
The Montreal Protocol (1987) phased them out; the ozone layer is slowly healing.

steps.title: Dichloromethane and chloroform
steps.body:
- **CH₂Cl₂:** solvent, paint remover, propellant in aerosols. Harms the central nervous system on exposure; direct contact burns skin and eyes.
- **CHCl₃:** solvent for fats, alkaloids, iodine; once used as an anaesthetic (replaced by safer ones). Oxidised slowly by air in light to poisonous **phosgene (COCl₂)**: 2CHCl₃ + O₂ → 2COCl₂ + 2HCl — so stored in dark bottles filled to the brim.

steps.title: Iodoform and carbon tetrachloride
steps.body:
- **CHI₃ (iodoform):** yellow solid; formerly an antiseptic (liberates iodine); objectionable smell.
- **CCl₄:** solvent, used in making refrigerants and propellants; exposure can damage the liver, nervous system; released to air it reaches the stratosphere and **depletes ozone**.

steps.title: Freons and DDT
steps.body:
- **Freons** (chlorofluorocarbons, e.g. CCl₂F₂ Freon-12): unreactive, non-toxic, non-flammable — used as refrigerants and propellants. In the stratosphere UV light breaks them into Cl radicals that destroy ozone in chain reactions.
- **DDT** (p,p'-dichlorodiphenyltrichloroethane): first chlorinated organic insecticide; Paul Müller received the 1948 Nobel Prize for discovering its insecticidal properties. Used widely against malaria-carrying mosquitoes. **Problems:** insect resistance, toxicity to fish, very **slow breakdown**, and accumulation in fatty tissues up food chains. It has been banned in many countries and restricted largely to public-health use elsewhere.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking freons are toxic at ground level — their danger is ozone destruction high up.
- Calling DDT biodegradable.
- Forgetting why chloroform is stored in dark, full bottles.

steps.title: What you can do
steps.body: Dispose of old refrigerators and ACs through authorised recyclers who recover refrigerant gases; avoid burning plastics containing chlorine; follow label instructions for any pesticide.

activity.prompt: Match the compound to its use or hazard.
pairs: Forms phosgene in air and light

quiz.q: Chloroform is stored in dark bottles to prevent formation of
quiz.why: In air and light chloroform oxidises to the very poisonous gas phosgene (COCl₂). Dark, full bottles keep light and air out.

quiz.q: Freons damage the ozone layer by releasing
quiz.why: In the stratosphere UV light breaks C–Cl bonds in freons, releasing chlorine radicals that destroy ozone in a chain reaction.

quiz.q: DDT is harmful mainly because it
options: is non-biodegradable and accumulates in fat
quiz.why: DDT does not break down easily and dissolves in fat, so it accumulates up the food chain (biomagnification), harming wildlife.
Iodoform (CHI₃) is a yellow crystalline solid with a characteristic smell, once used as an antiseptic.

quiz.q: The international agreement to phase out CFCs is the
quiz.why: The Montreal Protocol (1987) is the international agreement to phase out ozone-depleting substances like CFCs. Kyoto and Paris are about greenhouse gases.

sources: NCERT Class 12 Chemistry (topic reference, own wording)

questions.q: IUPAC name of CH₂=CHCH₂Cl:
questions.why: Number the chain from the end nearer the double bond: C1=C2, Cl on C3 ⇒ 3-chloroprop-1-ene.

questions.q: Which gives the purest alkyl chloride from an alcohol?
questions.why: SOCl₂ gives the alkyl chloride with SO₂ and HCl as gaseous by-products, so the product is easy to purify. PCl₃, PCl₅ leave phosphorus compounds, and HCl/ZnCl₂ is a weaker method.

questions.q: The order of boiling points is
questions.why: Boiling point rises with molar mass and polarisability, which increase from Cl to Br to I. So CH₃I > CH₃Br > CH₃Cl.

questions.q: Assertion: SN2 reaction of an optically active haloalkane gives a product with inverted configuration. Reason: The nucleophile attacks from the side opposite to the leaving group.
options: Both true; reason does not explain
questions.why: Both are true. In SN2 the nucleophile attacks from the back side, opposite the leaving group, which inverts the configuration (Walden inversion).

questions.q: Which reacts fastest with aqueous KOH by SN1?
questions.why: SN1 speed depends on the carbocation. The benzyl cation is stabilised by resonance with the ring, so benzyl chloride reacts fastest. Chlorobenzene and vinyl chloride barely ionise.

questions.q: The product of C₂H₅Br + KCN is mainly
questions.why: KCN is ionic, so the carbon end of the cyanide ion attacks and gives the nitrile C₂H₅CN. AgCN would give the isocyanide.

questions.q: Chlorobenzene on nitration gives mainly
questions.why: Cl is an ortho/para director, so nitration gives mainly o- and p-nitrochlorobenzene, with the para isomer in larger amount.

questions.q: Case: 2-Bromopentane is heated with alcoholic KOH. The major product is
questions.why: Alcoholic KOH causes elimination. By Zaitsev's rule the more substituted alkene, pent-2-ene, is the major product, not pent-1-ene.

questions.q: Which statement about SN1 is correct?
options: Carbocation is formed in the slow step
questions.why: SN1 is a two-step reaction in which ionisation to a carbocation is the slow, rate-determining step. The rate does not depend on the nucleophile, tertiary halides react fastest, and racemisation occurs.

questions.q: Assertion: Haloarenes are less reactive than haloalkanes in nucleophilic substitution. Reason: The C–X bond in haloarenes has partial double-bond character.
options: Both true; reason does not explain
questions.why: Both are true. Resonance gives the C–X bond partial double-bond character, so it is stronger and the halogen is harder to replace than in haloalkanes.

questions.q: Identify X: C₆H₅N₂⁺Cl⁻ + KI → X
questions.why: In the diazonium salt the group N₂⁺ leaves as nitrogen gas and iodide replaces it, giving iodobenzene, C₆H₅I.

questions.q: Case: Compound A (C₄H₉Br) is optically active. On SN2 with OH⁻ it gives B, also optically active. A is
questions.why: For SN2 to give an optically active product, A must be chiral. Only 2-bromobutane has a carbon with four different groups; the other C₄H₉Br isomers are achiral.

questions.q: Which reagent converts CH₃CH₂Cl into CH₃CH₂I?
questions.why: The Finkelstein reaction swaps Cl for I using NaI in dry acetone. NaCl is insoluble in acetone and precipitates, which drives the reaction.

questions.q: Order of SN2 reactivity: (a) 1-bromopentane (b) 2-bromopentane (c) 2-bromo-2-methylbutane
questions.why: SN2 is hindered by crowding at the carbon being attacked. So the primary halide reacts fastest, then secondary, and the tertiary one slowest: a > b > c.

questions.q: Case: An alkyl halide C₅H₁₁Br (A) reacts with alcoholic KOH to give a mixture of two isomeric alkenes, B (major) and C. Hydrogenation of both gives 2-methylbutane. A is likely
questions.why: Alcoholic KOH on 2-bromo-2-methylbutane gives 2-methylbut-2-ene (major, Zaitsev) and 2-methylbut-1-ene. Both give 2-methylbutane when hydrogenated.

questions.q: Which is NOT true for Grignard reagents?
options: Can be stored in aqueous solution
React with water to give alkanes
questions.why: Grignard reagents react with water and are destroyed, forming alkanes, so they cannot be kept in aqueous solution. They are made in dry ether and have a nucleophilic carbon.

questions.q: Case: p-Nitrochlorobenzene reacts with aqueous NaOH at 443 K while chlorobenzene needs 623 K and 300 atm. The best explanation is
options: –NO₂ stabilises the negative intermediate by resonance
questions.why: The para –NO₂ group withdraws electrons and stabilises the negatively charged intermediate by resonance, which is why substitution is far easier than in chlorobenzene.

courses.title: Ch 7 · Alcohols, Phenols and Ethers
courses.summary: Classification, nomenclature and structure; preparation of alcohols and phenols; physical properties and acidity; reactions of alcohols (O–H and C–O cleavage, dehydration, oxidation); reactions of phenols (electrophilic substitution, Kolbe, Reimer–Tiemann); methanol and ethanol; and ethers — preparation, Williamson synthesis and reactions. Independent practice material; not affiliated with or endorsed by any board or exam body.
outcomes: Learners can name and classify alcohols, phenols and ethers.
Learners can choose methods to prepare alcohols and phenols, including cumene process.
Learners can explain the acidity order of alcohols, phenols and substituted phenols.
Learners can predict products of key reactions, including dehydration mechanism, Kolbe, Reimer–Tiemann and ether cleavage.

lessons.title: Classification, nomenclature and structure

scenes.text: Kriti's hand sanitiser contains isopropyl alcohol; the dettol-like smell at the clinic comes from phenolic compounds.
A century ago, diethyl ether was used to put patients to sleep during surgery.
All three families contain C–O bonds — but their properties differ hugely.

steps.title: Classification
steps.body:
- **Alcohols:** –OH on sp³ carbon — mono-, di- (glycols), trihydric (glycerol). 1°, 2°, 3° by the carbinol carbon. Also allylic and benzylic alcohols.
- **Phenols:** –OH directly on an aromatic ring (sp² carbon).
- **Ethers:** R–O–R'; **simple/symmetrical** (C₂H₅OC₂H₅) or **mixed/unsymmetrical** (CH₃OC₂H₅, anisole C₆H₅OCH₃).

steps.title: Nomenclature
steps.body:
- Alcohols: alkan-**ol**: CH₃CH(OH)CH₃ → propan-2-ol; (CH₃)₃COH → 2-methylpropan-2-ol; HOCH₂CH₂OH → ethane-1,2-diol; glycerol → propane-1,2,3-triol.
- Phenols: cresols are methylphenols (o-cresol = 2-methylphenol); benzene-1,2-diol (catechol), 1,3-diol (resorcinol), 1,4-diol (hydroquinone).
- Ethers: alkoxyalkanes — CH₃OCH₂CH₃ → methoxyethane; C₆H₅OCH₃ → methoxybenzene (anisole).

steps.title: Structure
steps.body:
- In alcohols, O is sp³; C–O–H angle ≈ **108.9°** in methanol (lone-pair repulsion makes it less than 109.5°).
- In phenols, the C–O bond is **shorter** (136 pm vs 142 pm in methanol) because of partial double-bond character (lone pair conjugates with the ring) and sp² carbon.
- In ethers, C–O–C angle ≈ **111.7°** (bulky groups repel).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Ex 1.** CH₃CH₂CH(OH)CH₂CH₃ → **pentan-3-ol**, a 2° alcohol.

**Ex 2.** C₆H₅CH₂OH → **phenylmethanol** (benzyl alcohol) — an alcohol, *not* a phenol (OH on sp³ carbon).

**Ex 3.** C₂H₅–O–CH(CH₃)₂ → **2-ethoxypropane**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling benzyl alcohol a phenol.
- Naming ethers by the smaller group as the parent — the larger alkyl group is the parent alkane, the smaller is the alkoxy.
- Forgetting locants for diols.

activity.prompt: Alcohol, phenol or ether?

quiz.why: The longest chain containing the carbon with –OH has 3 carbons, with a methyl and –OH on carbon 2. So the name is 2-methylpropan-2-ol; tert-butanol is only a common name.
Catechol has two –OH groups on adjacent ring carbons, so it is benzene-1,2-diol. The 1,3 and 1,4 isomers are resorcinol and hydroquinone.

quiz.q: C–O bond in phenol is shorter than in methanol because of
quiz.why: In phenol the oxygen lone pair is delocalised into the ring, giving the C–O bond partial double-bond character. It is shorter than the single C–O bond of methanol.
Anisole is methyl phenyl ether, C₆H₅OCH₃, named methoxybenzene.

quiz.q: C–O–C angle in ethers is about
quiz.why: The C–O–C angle in ethers is about 111.7°, larger than the H–O–H angle in water, because the bulky alkyl groups repel each other.

sources: NCERT Class 12 Chemistry (topic reference, own wording)

lessons.title: Preparation of alcohols and phenols

story.title: From cumene to phenol and acetone

scenes.text: India's chemical plants make phenol by a clever route that starts with cumene.
The process gives a bonus: acetone, a valuable solvent, from the same reaction.
Knowing several preparation routes lets chemists pick the cheapest and cleanest.

steps.title: Alcohols
steps.body:
- **Acid-catalysed hydration of alkenes** (Markovnikov): CH₃CH=CH₂ + H₂O (H⁺) → CH₃CH(OH)CH₃. Mechanism: protonation to carbocation → water attacks → deprotonation.
- **Hydroboration–oxidation** (anti-Markovnikov, net): alkene + B₂H₆, then H₂O₂/OH⁻ → 1° alcohol (CH₃CH=CH₂ → propan-1-ol).
- **Reduction of carbonyls:** aldehydes → 1°, ketones → 2° (H₂/Pd, NaBH₄, LiAlH₄).
- **Reduction of acids/esters:** LiAlH₄ → 1° alcohols (industrially esters are hydrogenated).
- **Grignard reagents:** HCHO → 1°; other aldehydes → 2°; ketones → 3° alcohols (after hydrolysis).

steps.title: Phenols
steps.body:
- **From haloarenes:** chlorobenzene + NaOH (623 K, 300 atm) → sodium phenoxide → phenol.
- **From benzenesulphonic acid:** fuse with NaOH, then acidify.
- **From diazonium salts:** warm ArN₂⁺Cl⁻ with water → phenol + N₂.
- **From cumene (isopropylbenzene):** air oxidation → cumene hydroperoxide; dilute acid → **phenol + acetone**.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Ex 1.** CH₃MgBr + CH₃COCH₃, then H₂O → **2-methylpropan-2-ol** (3°).

**Ex 2.** CH₃CHO + C₂H₅MgBr, then H₂O → **butan-2-ol** (2°).

**Ex 3.** HCHO + C₆H₅MgBr, then H₂O → **benzyl alcohol** (1°).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Expecting hydroboration–oxidation to follow Markovnikov orientation.
- Using NaBH₄ to reduce carboxylic acids (LiAlH₄ is needed).
- Forgetting the hydrolysis step after a Grignard addition.

activity.prompt: Match the Grignard substrate with the alcohol class formed.

quiz.why: Hydroboration–oxidation adds water in anti-Markovnikov fashion, so –OH goes to the terminal carbon of propene and gives propan-1-ol.

quiz.q: Ketones react with Grignard reagents to give
quiz.why: A Grignard reagent adds its R group to the carbonyl carbon of a ketone. That carbon already has two R groups, so the product after hydrolysis is a tertiary alcohol.

quiz.q: The cumene process gives phenol and
quiz.why: In the cumene process cumene is oxidised and then treated with acid, giving phenol and acetone, the useful by-product.

quiz.q: Acid-catalysed hydration of alkenes proceeds via
quiz.why: The alkene is protonated to a carbocation, then water attacks it and a proton is lost, giving the alcohol. This is electrophilic addition via carbocations.

quiz.q: Warming benzenediazonium chloride with water gives
quiz.why: Warming the diazonium salt with water replaces the N₂⁺ group by –OH, giving phenol and releasing N₂ gas.

lessons.title: Physical properties and acidity

story.title: Why phenol burns but ethanol does not

scenes.text: A lab warning card says phenol causes skin burns, while ethanol is only drying.
Phenol is about a million times more acidic than ethanol.
The reason is resonance: the phenoxide ion spreads its negative charge over the ring.

steps.title: Physical properties
steps.body:
- **Boiling points** of alcohols and phenols are much higher than those of hydrocarbons, ethers and haloalkanes of similar mass — **intermolecular H-bonding**. They increase with chain length and decrease with branching.
- **Solubility:** lower alcohols mix with water (H-bonding); solubility falls as the hydrophobic alkyl part grows.
- Ethers have low b.p. (no O–H, so no H-bonding among themselves) but are slightly water-soluble (O accepts H-bonds).

steps.title: Acidity of alcohols
steps.body: Alcohols react with active metals (Na, K, Al) giving alkoxides and H₂: 2ROH + 2Na → 2RONa + H₂. They are **weaker acids than water**; alkyl groups (+I) destabilise the alkoxide. Order: **1° > 2° > 3°**.

steps.title: Acidity of phenols
steps.body:
Phenol (pKa ≈ 10.0) is far more acidic than ethanol (pKa ≈ 15.9) because the **phenoxide ion is resonance-stabilised** (charge delocalised to o and p positions). Phenol turns blue litmus red only weakly; it reacts with NaOH but **not with NaHCO₃**.
- **Electron-withdrawing groups** (–NO₂) at o/p increase acidity: p-nitrophenol pKa 7.1, o-nitrophenol 7.2, 2,4,6-trinitrophenol (picric acid) ≈ 0.5.
- **Electron-donating groups** (–CH₃) decrease acidity: cresols pKa ≈ 10.1–10.2.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Ex 1.** Acidity order: picric acid > 2,4-dinitrophenol > p-nitrophenol > phenol > p-cresol > ethanol.

**Ex 2.** Why does o-nitrophenol boil lower and is steam-volatile while p-nitrophenol is not? o-Nitrophenol has **intramolecular** H-bonding (no association); p-nitrophenol has **intermolecular** H-bonding (molecules associate).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying phenol reacts with NaHCO₃ (only carboxylic acids and strong phenols like picric acid do).
- Ranking 3° alcohols as most acidic.
- Forgetting that meta –NO₂ increases acidity only by the −I effect (less than o/p).

activity.prompt: Arrange from MOST acidic to LEAST acidic.

quiz.q: Alcohols have higher b.p. than ethers of similar mass due to
quiz.why: Alcohol molecules form O–H···O hydrogen bonds with each other, which need extra energy to break. Ethers have no such bonds, so alcohols boil higher.

quiz.q: Phenol is more acidic than ethanol because
quiz.why: The phenoxide ion is stabilised by delocalising its negative charge into the ring by resonance. The ethoxide ion has no such stabilisation, so phenol loses H⁺ more easily.

quiz.q: Which does NOT react with phenol?
quiz.why: Phenol is a very weak acid, weaker than carbonic acid, so it does not release CO₂ from NaHCO₃. It does react with Na, NaOH and bromine water.
Alkyl groups push electrons (+I) towards O, making the O–H bond harder to ionise. More alkyl groups make the alcohol less acidic, so 1° > 2° > 3°.
o-Nitrophenol forms an intramolecular H-bond within each molecule, so it does not associate with others and is volatile with steam. The para isomer has intermolecular H-bonds.

sources: NCERT Class 12 Chemistry (topic reference, own wording)

lessons.title: Reactions of alcohols

story.title: Lucas test in the practical exam

scenes.text: In the chemistry practical, Harsh adds Lucas reagent to three unknown alcohols and starts his stopwatch.
One turns cloudy at once, another after a few minutes, the third stays clear.
The speed of the reaction reveals whether each alcohol is 3°, 2° or 1°.

steps.title: O–H bond cleavage
steps.body:
- With active metals: alkoxides + H₂.
- **Esterification:** ROH + R'COOH ⇌ R'COOR + H₂O (conc. H₂SO₄, reversible; remove water to push forward). With acid chlorides/anhydrides: faster (pyridine removes HCl).

steps.title: C–O bond cleavage
steps.body:
- **With HX:** ROH + HX → RX + H₂O. **Lucas test** (conc. HCl + anhyd. ZnCl₂): 3° alcohols give turbidity **immediately**, 2° within about **5 minutes**, 1° **not at room temperature**.
- **With PX₃, PCl₅, SOCl₂:** alkyl halides.
- **Dehydration:** with conc. H₂SO₄ or H₃PO₄ (or Al₂O₃): 1° ethanol at 443 K → ethene; 2° and 3° need milder conditions (3° easiest). Mechanism: (1) protonation of –OH, (2) loss of water to a **carbocation** (slow), (3) loss of H⁺ from β-carbon → alkene (Zaitsev product).

steps.title: Oxidation
steps.body:
- **1° alcohol → aldehyde → carboxylic acid** with acidified KMnO₄ or K₂Cr₂O₇; to stop at the aldehyde use **PCC** (pyridinium chlorochromate) or CrO₃ in anhydrous medium.
- **2° alcohol → ketone** (CrO₃).
- **3° alcohols** resist oxidation under mild conditions (strong agents break C–C bonds).
- **Dehydrogenation** over Cu at 573 K: 1° → aldehyde, 2° → ketone, 3° → alkene (dehydration).
- Biological: ethanol is oxidised in the liver; methanol is oxidised to toxic methanal/methanoic acid.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Ex 1.** Propan-2-ol + PCC → **propanone**.

**Ex 2.** Butan-2-ol + conc. H₂SO₄ (heat) → **but-2-ene (major)** via a 2° carbocation.

**Ex 3.** Ethanol + CH₃COOH (H⁺) → **ethyl ethanoate** + water.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Writing 3° alcohol → ketone.
- Using acidified KMnO₄ when only the aldehyde is wanted.
- Forgetting that dehydration goes through a carbocation (so rearrangements are possible).

a.text: Alcohol X gives turbidity with Lucas reagent within 5 minutes. What class is X?

choices.label: Secondary (2°)
choices.feedback: Correct — 2° alcohols react in a few minutes.

a2.text: Immediate = 3°, about 5 min = 2°, no reaction at room temperature = 1°. So X is…

b.text: X (C₃H₈O) is oxidised by CrO₃. What product forms?

choices.label: Propanone (a ketone)
choices.feedback: Right — 2° alcohols give ketones; X is propan-2-ol.

b2.text: A secondary alcohol has one H on the carbinol carbon. Oxidation removes it to give…

end.text: You identified propan-2-ol from two simple tests.

quiz.why: Lucas reagent is concentrated HCl with anhydrous ZnCl₂. It is used to tell 1°, 2° and 3° alcohols apart by how fast turbidity appears.
PCC is a mild, anhydrous oxidant that stops at the aldehyde stage when it oxidises a primary alcohol, unlike KMnO₄ or K₂Cr₂O₇, which go on to the acid.
The –OH is protonated and leaves as water, giving a carbocation. Then a proton is lost to form the alkene.
Dehydration goes through a carbocation, and 3° carbocations are the most stable. So 3° alcohols dehydrate most easily, then 2°, then 1°.

quiz.q: Over hot Cu (573 K), a 3° alcohol gives
quiz.why: On hot copper at 573 K, 1° alcohols give aldehydes and 2° give ketones by losing hydrogen. A 3° alcohol has no H on the carbinol carbon, so it dehydrates to an alkene.

sources: NCERT Class 12 Chemistry (topic reference, own wording)

lessons.title: Reactions of phenols; methanol and ethanol

scenes.text: Willow bark was used for pain relief for centuries; its active compound relates to salicylic acid.
Kolbe found how to put a –COOH onto phenol using CO₂ — making salicylic acid in bulk.
Acetylating it gives aspirin, one of the most used medicines on Earth.

steps.title: Electrophilic substitution
steps.body:
–OH strongly **activates** the ring and is **o/p directing**.
- **Nitration:** dilute HNO₃ (298 K) → o- and p-nitrophenol (separated by steam distillation). Conc. HNO₃ → **2,4,6-trinitrophenol (picric acid)** (low yield; better via sulphonation first).
- **Bromination:** Br₂ in CS₂ (low temperature) → mainly **p-bromophenol** (monosubstitution). **Bromine water** → **2,4,6-tribromophenol** (white precipitate) — test for phenol.

steps.title: Named reactions and others
steps.body:
- **Kolbe's reaction:** sodium phenoxide + CO₂ (≈ 400 K, 4–7 atm), then H⁺ → **salicylic acid** (2-hydroxybenzoic acid).
- **Reimer–Tiemann:** phenol + CHCl₃ + aq. NaOH (≈ 340 K), then H⁺ → **salicylaldehyde** (2-hydroxybenzaldehyde) via a dichlorocarbene/benzal intermediate.
- **With zinc dust:** phenol → benzene.
- **Oxidation:** with chromic acid → **benzoquinone**; phenols slowly turn pink/dark in air.

steps.title: Methanol and ethanol
steps.body:
- **Methanol (wood spirit):** made from CO + 2H₂ (ZnO–Cr₂O₃, 573–673 K, 200–300 atm). Very poisonous: small amounts cause blindness, larger amounts death.
- **Ethanol:** by **fermentation** of sugars (molasses, grapes) using yeast enzymes invertase and zymase, in the absence of air. Industrial alcohol is **denatured** (CuSO₄ for colour, pyridine for foul smell) to make it unfit to drink.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Ex 1.** Phenol + 3Br₂ (aq) → **2,4,6-tribromophenol** + 3HBr.

**Ex 2.** Salicylic acid + acetic anhydride → **acetylsalicylic acid (aspirin)**.

**Ex 3.** Distinguish phenol from ethanol: phenol gives a **violet colour with neutral FeCl₃** and a white precipitate with bromine water; ethanol does neither.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Expecting monobromination of phenol in bromine water.
- Mixing Kolbe (–COOH) and Reimer–Tiemann (–CHO).
- Thinking denatured spirit is safe to drink.

activity.prompt: Match the reaction to its product.

quiz.why: The –OH group donates its lone pair into the ring (+R effect), so the ring is activated and electrophiles enter at the ortho and para positions.
In the Reimer–Tiemann reaction phenol is heated with chloroform and NaOH; dichlorocarbene is the attacking species and salicylaldehyde is formed.

quiz.q: Phenol gives with neutral FeCl₃ a
quiz.why: Phenols give a violet (or blue/green) colour with neutral FeCl₃ due to complex formation. It is a standard test for the phenolic –OH group.
Methanol is made industrially by passing CO and H₂ (1:2) over a ZnO–Cr₂O₃ catalyst at high pressure and temperature: CO + 2H₂ → CH₃OH.

quiz.q: Enzyme that converts glucose to ethanol in fermentation is
quiz.why: Zymase, an enzyme in yeast, converts glucose into ethanol and CO₂. Invertase acts earlier by converting sucrose into glucose and fructose.

sources: NCERT Class 12 Chemistry (topic reference, own wording)

lessons.title: Ethers: preparation and reactions

story.title: The ether that made surgery painless

scenes.text: In 1846, diethyl ether was publicly used as an anaesthetic in a surgery — a turning point in medicine.
Today safer anaesthetics are used, but ethers remain key solvents.
Their C–O–C link is quite unreactive — except towards strong acids like HI.

steps.title: Preparation
steps.body:
- **Dehydration of 1° alcohols** with conc. H₂SO₄ at **413 K**: 2C₂H₅OH → C₂H₅OC₂H₅ + H₂O (at 443 K ethene forms). Mechanism: SN2 attack of an alcohol on a protonated alcohol. Not suitable for 2°/3° alcohols (they give alkenes).
- **Williamson synthesis:** R–X + R'–O⁻Na⁺ → R–O–R' + NaX (SN2). Use a **1° alkyl halide**; with 3° halides elimination dominates. Example: (CH₃)₃CONa + CH₃Br → (CH₃)₃COCH₃ ✔, but (CH₃)₃CBr + CH₃ONa → alkene. For aryl ethers: phenoxide + alkyl halide (C₆H₅ONa + CH₃I → anisole).

steps.title: Reactions
steps.body:
- **Cleavage by HI** (most reactive HX): R–O–R + HI → ROH + RI; excess HI → 2RI.
- Mixed ethers: with 1°/2° groups the halide forms from the **smaller** alkyl group (SN2); with a 3° group, the halide forms on the **tertiary** carbon (SN1).
- **Alkyl aryl ethers:** C₆H₅OCH₃ + HI → **C₆H₅OH + CH₃I** (O–aryl bond is strong, so never gives C₆H₅I).
- **Electrophilic substitution in anisole** (–OCH₃ activates, o/p): bromination (Br₂ in ethanoic acid) → p-bromoanisole (major); Friedel–Crafts alkylation and acylation → o/p products; nitration (conc. H₂SO₄ + HNO₃) → o- and p-nitroanisole.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Ex 1.** Best route to 2-methoxy-2-methylpropane: **(CH₃)₃CONa + CH₃Br**.

**Ex 2.** CH₃OCH₂CH₃ + HI (1 equiv) → **CH₃I + CH₃CH₂OH**.

**Ex 3.** (CH₃)₃C–O–CH₃ + HI → **(CH₃)₃CI + CH₃OH**.

**Ex 4.** Anisole + CH₃COCl (AlCl₃) → **2- and 4-methoxyacetophenone** (para major).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using a 3° alkyl halide in Williamson synthesis.
- Predicting iodobenzene from anisole + HI.
- Heating ethanol with H₂SO₄ at 443 K and expecting ether (you get ethene).

statements.s: Williamson synthesis works best with tertiary alkyl halides.
Anisole + HI gives phenol and methyl iodide.
Ethers have higher boiling points than isomeric alcohols.
–OCH₃ is an ortho/para-directing activating group.

quiz.q: Ethanol + conc. H₂SO₄ at 413 K mainly gives
quiz.why: At about 413 K with excess ethanol, one molecule of alcohol attacks the ethyl hydrogen sulphate and gives diethyl ether. At 443 K elimination makes ethene.

quiz.q: Williamson synthesis is an example of
quiz.why: In the Williamson synthesis an alkoxide ion attacks a primary alkyl halide by the SN2 mechanism, forming an ether.
In anisole the O–CH₃ bond breaks because the O–aryl bond has partial double-bond character. So HI gives phenol and CH₃I, not iodobenzene.
The –OCH₃ group activates the ring and directs to ortho and para positions. The para product is major because it is less hindered.

quiz.q: Ethers are good solvents because they are
options: relatively unreactive and dissolve many organics
quiz.why: Ethers are relatively inert and dissolve many organic compounds. This makes them useful solvents.

sources: NCERT Class 12 Chemistry (topic reference, own wording)

questions.q: IUPAC name of CH₃CH(OH)CH₂CH₃ is
questions.why: The longest chain has four carbons and –OH is on carbon 2, so it is butan-2-ol.

questions.q: Phenol is
questions.why: Phenol is a weak acid with pKa about 10: it ionises slightly in water, and is stronger than alcohols but weaker than carboxylic acids.

questions.q: Picric acid is
questions.why: Picric acid is 2,4,6-trinitrophenol. Three nitro groups make the phenol strongly acidic.

questions.q: Assertion: Phenol is more acidic than ethanol. Reason: Phenoxide ion is stabilised by resonance.
options: Both true; reason does not explain
questions.why: Both are true. Resonance spreads the negative charge of the phenoxide ion over the ring, so phenoxide is more stable and phenol is the stronger acid.

questions.q: Which alcohol gives turbidity immediately with Lucas reagent?
questions.why: A tertiary alcohol forms a stable carbocation and reacts with Lucas reagent immediately, giving turbidity at once. Secondary ones take a few minutes and primary ones do not react at room temperature.

questions.q: Kolbe's reaction gives
questions.why: In Kolbe's reaction sodium phenoxide reacts with CO₂ and is then acidified, giving salicylic acid (o-hydroxybenzoic acid).

questions.q: Case: An alcohol C₄H₁₀O resists oxidation by acidified K₂Cr₂O₇ under mild conditions. It is
questions.why: Tertiary alcohols have no hydrogen on the carbinol carbon, so mild oxidising agents do not oxidise them. 2-Methylpropan-2-ol is the tertiary alcohol among the options.

questions.q: Product of CH₃CH₂CHO + CH₃MgBr followed by hydrolysis:
questions.why: The Grignard reagent adds CH₃ to the aldehyde carbon. After hydrolysis CH₃CH₂CHO becomes CH₃CH₂CH(OH)CH₃, which is butan-2-ol.

questions.q: Which is the strongest acid?
questions.why: An electron-withdrawing –NO₂ at the para position stabilises the phenoxide ion, so p-nitrophenol is the strongest acid. The methyl group in cresol destabilises the ion, and ethanol is least acidic.

questions.q: Assertion: Bromination of phenol in bromine water gives 2,4,6-tribromophenol. Reason: –OH strongly activates the ring at ortho and para positions.
options: Both true; reason does not explain
questions.why: Both are true. –OH strongly activates the ortho and para positions, and in bromine water Br₂ is polarised, so all three positions are substituted to give 2,4,6-tribromophenol.

questions.q: The best method to prepare tert-butyl methyl ether is
questions.why: In the Williamson synthesis a tertiary halide would eliminate, so the tertiary part must be the alkoxide and the halide should be primary: (CH₃)₃CONa + CH₃Br.

questions.q: Case: Compound A (C₇H₈O) is insoluble in NaHCO₃ but dissolves in NaOH and gives violet colour with FeCl₃. A is
questions.why: Dissolving in NaOH but not in NaHCO₃ shows a weak acid, and a violet colour with FeCl₃ shows a phenol. A cresol, CH₃C₆H₄OH, fits C₇H₈O.

questions.q: (CH₃)₃C–O–CH₂CH₃ with HI gives
questions.why: With HI, ethers with a tertiary alkyl group cleave by SN1 because the stable tertiary carbocation forms. The products are (CH₃)₃CI and ethanol.

questions.q: Dehydration of 2-methylbutan-2-ol with conc. H₂SO₄ gives mainly
questions.why: Dehydration follows Zaitsev's rule: the more substituted, more stable alkene, 2-methylbut-2-ene, is the major product.

questions.q: Which reagent converts propan-1-ol to propanal without further oxidation?
questions.why: PCC is a mild oxidant that stops at the aldehyde. KMnO₄, HNO₃ and excess dichromate oxidise further to propanoic acid.

questions.q: Case: Phenol is treated with CHCl₃/NaOH and the product is oxidised with Tollens' reagent, then acidified. The final product is
questions.why: Reimer–Tiemann gives salicylaldehyde from phenol. Tollens' reagent oxidises the –CHO to –COOH, and acidification gives salicylic acid.

questions.q: Why is o-nitrophenol more volatile than p-nitrophenol?
questions.why: o-Nitrophenol has intramolecular H-bonding, so molecules do not bind to each other. p-Nitrophenol has intermolecular H-bonds, which lowers its volatility.

courses.title: Ch 8 · Aldehydes, Ketones and Carboxylic Acids
courses.summary: Nomenclature and structure of the carbonyl group; preparation of aldehydes and ketones; nucleophilic addition and its mechanism; reduction, oxidation and distinguishing tests; aldol, Cannizzaro and haloform reactions; carboxylic acids — preparation, acidity and reactions including HVZ and decarboxylation; and uses. Independent practice material; not affiliated with or endorsed by any board or exam body.
outcomes: Learners can choose named preparations (Rosenmund, Stephen, Etard, Gattermann–Koch, Friedel–Crafts).
Learners can explain nucleophilic addition and why aldehydes are more reactive than ketones.
Learners can distinguish aldehydes, ketones and acids using Tollens', Fehling's, iodoform and NaHCO₃ tests.
Learners can predict products of aldol, Cannizzaro, Clemmensen, Wolff–Kishner, HVZ and Kolbe reactions and rank acid strengths.

lessons.title: Carbonyl compounds: nomenclature, structure and preparation

story.title: The smell of almonds and vanilla

scenes.text: Vanilla ice cream gets its flavour from vanillin; bitter almonds smell of benzaldehyde.
Lemons owe their tang partly to citral, and cinnamon to cinnamaldehyde.
All contain the carbonyl group C=O — one of the most useful groups in organic synthesis.

steps.title: Nomenclature and structure
steps.body:
- Aldehydes: alkan**al** (HCHO methanal, CH₃CHO ethanal, C₆H₅CHO benzaldehyde = benzenecarbaldehyde). Ketones: alkan**one** (CH₃COCH₃ propanone, C₆H₅COCH₃ 1-phenylethanone = acetophenone).
- The carbonyl carbon is **sp²**, trigonal planar (≈120°); C=O has one σ and one π bond and is **polar** (C δ+, O δ−) — so the carbon is electrophilic and the oxygen is a Lewis base.

steps.title: Preparation of aldehydes and ketones
steps.body:
- **Oxidation of alcohols** (1° → aldehyde with PCC; 2° → ketone) or **dehydrogenation** over Cu at 573 K.
- **Ozonolysis** of alkenes (O₃, then Zn/H₂O).
- **Hydration of alkynes** (HgSO₄/H₂SO₄): ethyne → ethanal; other alkynes → ketones.
- **Rosenmund reduction:** RCOCl + H₂ (Pd–BaSO₄, poisoned) → RCHO.
- **Stephen reaction:** RCN + SnCl₂/HCl → imine → (H₃O⁺) RCHO. **DIBAL-H** reduces nitriles and esters to aldehydes.
- **Aromatic aldehydes:** **Etard reaction** (toluene + CrO₂Cl₂ → chromium complex → benzaldehyde); toluene + CrO₃/(CH₃CO)₂O → benzylidene diacetate → hydrolysis; side-chain chlorination to benzal chloride then hydrolysis; **Gattermann–Koch** (benzene + CO + HCl, anhyd. AlCl₃/CuCl → benzaldehyde).
- **Ketones:** acyl chloride + **dialkylcadmium** (2R'COCl + R₂Cd → 2R'COR + CdCl₂); nitrile + Grignard then hydrolysis; **Friedel–Crafts acylation** (C₆H₆ + RCOCl, AlCl₃ → C₆H₅COR).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Ex 1.** CH₃CN + CH₃MgBr, then H₃O⁺ → **propanone**.

**Ex 2.** Benzoyl chloride + H₂ (Pd–BaSO₄) → **benzaldehyde**.

**Ex 3.** Propyne + H₂O (HgSO₄/H₂SO₄) → **propanone** (Markovnikov addition via enol).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting the BaSO₄ 'poison' in Rosenmund (without it the aldehyde is reduced further).
- Using Grignard + acyl chloride for ketones (it adds twice) — dialkylcadmium stops at the ketone.
- Expecting propyne hydration to give an aldehyde.

activity.prompt: Match the named reaction to its product.

quiz.q: Hybridisation of the carbonyl carbon is
quiz.why: The carbonyl carbon is joined to three atoms (two σ bonds to groups and one σ to O) in one plane, with a π bond to O, so it is sp² hybridised.

quiz.q: Hydration of ethyne with HgSO₄/H₂SO₄ gives
quiz.why: Ethyne with HgSO₄/H₂SO₄ adds water to give an unstable vinyl alcohol, which rearranges to ethanal (CH₃CHO).
The Etard reaction oxidises the methyl group of toluene to an aldehyde (benzaldehyde) using chromyl chloride, CrO₂Cl₂.

quiz.q: Ketones can be prepared from acyl chlorides using
quiz.why: Acyl chlorides react with dialkylcadmium to give ketones. Grignard reagents and LiAlH₄ are too reactive and would go further.
Acetophenone is C₆H₅COCH₃: a two-carbon ketone chain with a phenyl on C1, so its IUPAC name is 1-phenylethanone.

sources: NCERT Class 12 Chemistry (topic reference, own wording)

lessons.title: Nucleophilic addition reactions

scenes.text: A chemist needs to separate an aldehyde from a messy mixture.
She shakes it with sodium bisulphite: crystals of the addition product appear and are filtered off.
Treating the crystals with dilute acid gives back the pure aldehyde — a reversible nucleophilic addition.

steps.title: Mechanism and reactivity
steps.body:
A nucleophile attacks the electrophilic carbonyl carbon **perpendicular to the plane**; the carbon changes from sp² to sp³ giving a tetrahedral alkoxide, which is then protonated.
**Aldehydes are more reactive than ketones:** (1) steric — two bulky groups in ketones hinder attack; (2) electronic — two alkyl groups (+I) reduce the positive charge on carbon. Aromatic aldehydes are less reactive than aliphatic ones (resonance reduces δ+).

steps.title: Important additions
steps.body:
- **HCN** (base catalysed) → **cyanohydrins**.
- **NaHSO₃** → crystalline bisulphite adducts (most aldehydes, methyl ketones); used for separation/purification.
- **Grignard reagents** → alcohols after hydrolysis.
- **Alcohols** (dry HCl) → hemiacetal → **acetal** (aldehydes); ketones with ethylene glycol → cyclic **ketals** (protecting groups).
- **Ammonia derivatives** H₂N–Z (weakly acidic medium) → C=N–Z + H₂O:
  - hydroxylamine → **oxime**; hydrazine → **hydrazone**; phenylhydrazine → **phenylhydrazone**; **2,4-DNP** → 2,4-dinitrophenylhydrazone (yellow-orange precipitate, test for C=O); semicarbazide → **semicarbazone**.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Ex 1.** CH₃CHO + HCN → **CH₃CH(OH)CN** (2-hydroxypropanenitrile).

**Ex 2.** CH₃COCH₃ + NH₂OH → **(CH₃)₂C=NOH** (acetoxime) + H₂O.

**Ex 3.** Reactivity order towards HCN: HCHO > CH₃CHO > CH₃COCH₃ > C₆H₅COCH₃.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Doing addition of ammonia derivatives in strongly acidic medium (the nucleophile gets protonated) — pH should be mildly acidic.
- Ranking ketones above aldehydes in reactivity.
- Forgetting to show water lost in condensation with H₂N–Z.

activity.prompt: Match the reagent with the product type formed with a carbonyl compound.

quiz.q: Nucleophilic addition to C=O changes carbon hybridisation from
quiz.why: The carbonyl carbon is sp² before the attack. After the nucleophile adds, it has four single bonds, so it becomes sp³ (tetrahedral).

quiz.q: Which is most reactive towards nucleophiles?
quiz.why: Formaldehyde has two hydrogens and no alkyl group, so it is least hindered and its carbonyl carbon is the most positive. It is the most reactive towards nucleophiles.
2,4-DNP reacts with the C=O group of aldehydes and ketones to give a coloured (yellow, orange or red) 2,4-dinitrophenylhydrazone precipitate.

quiz.q: Acetals are formed from aldehydes with
quiz.why: An aldehyde reacts with two molecules of an alcohol in the presence of dry HCl to form a gem-dialkoxy compound, an acetal.
Weakly acidic pH activates the carbonyl without protonating all the ammonia derivative. In strong acid the nucleophile becomes unreactive, and in base the carbonyl is not activated.

lessons.title: Reduction, oxidation and reactions involving α-hydrogen

scenes.text: In the lab, Ananya warms a test tube with Tollens' reagent and an unknown liquid.
A shiny silver mirror forms on the glass — the unknown must be an aldehyde.
Aldehydes are easily oxidised; ketones are not — a simple way to tell them apart.

steps.title: Reduction
steps.body:
- **To alcohols:** NaBH₄ or LiAlH₄ (or H₂/Ni, Pt, Pd): aldehydes → 1°, ketones → 2°.
- **To hydrocarbons (C=O → CH₂):** **Clemmensen** (Zn–Hg + conc. HCl) or **Wolff–Kishner** (NH₂NH₂, then KOH in ethylene glycol, heat).

steps.title: Oxidation and tests
steps.body:
- Aldehydes are oxidised to acids by mild agents:
  - **Tollens' reagent** (ammoniacal AgNO₃) → **silver mirror** (all aldehydes, including aromatic).
  - **Fehling's solution** (Cu²⁺ tartrate complex) → **red-brown Cu₂O** precipitate (aliphatic aldehydes; aromatic aldehydes do not respond).
- Ketones need strong oxidants and break C–C bonds.
- **Haloform reaction:** compounds with **CH₃CO–** (or CH₃CH(OH)– which oxidises to it) + NaOX → haloform + carboxylate. **Iodoform test:** yellow CHI₃ precipitate (ethanal, methyl ketones, ethanol, propan-2-ol).

steps.title: α-Hydrogen reactions
steps.body:
α-H is acidic because the resulting **enolate** is resonance-stabilised.
- **Aldol reaction:** aldehydes/ketones with α-H + dilute NaOH → β-hydroxy carbonyl (aldol), which on heating loses water to an α,β-unsaturated carbonyl (**aldol condensation**). 2CH₃CHO → CH₃CH(OH)CH₂CHO (3-hydroxybutanal) → CH₃CH=CHCHO (but-2-enal).
- **Cross aldol:** two different carbonyls ⇒ mixture of four products (unless one has no α-H).
- **Cannizzaro reaction** (no α-H: HCHO, C₆H₅CHO) with **concentrated** alkali: one molecule is reduced to alcohol, another oxidised to the acid salt: 2HCHO + conc. KOH → CH₃OH + HCOOK.
- **Ring substitution:** –CHO is a **meta-directing, deactivating** group (benzaldehyde → m-nitrobenzaldehyde).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Ex 1.** Distinguish ethanal and propanone: Tollens' — ethanal gives a silver mirror, propanone does not.

**Ex 2.** Distinguish propanal and propanone: iodoform — **propanone** gives yellow CHI₃; propanal does not.

**Ex 3.** 2C₆H₅CHO + conc. NaOH → **C₆H₅CH₂OH + C₆H₅COONa**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using Fehling's test for benzaldehyde (negative).
- Applying Cannizzaro to ethanal (it has α-H — gives aldol).
- Confusing Clemmensen (acidic) and Wolff–Kishner (basic).

activity.prompt: Which compounds give a positive iodoform test?

quiz.why: The Clemmensen reduction converts C=O to CH₂ using zinc amalgam and concentrated HCl. Wolff–Kishner does the same under basic conditions with hydrazine and KOH.
Aldehydes are easily oxidised and reduce Tollens' reagent to silver. Benzaldehyde is an aldehyde, while the other options are ketones.
Cannizzaro needs an aldehyde without α-hydrogen. HCHO has none, so it undergoes Cannizzaro, whereas the other options have α-hydrogens.

quiz.q: Aldol of ethanal on heating gives
quiz.why: Two ethanal molecules form aldol (3-hydroxybutanal), which on heating loses water to give but-2-enal.
Fehling's solution is reduced by aliphatic aldehydes to give a red-brown precipitate of Cu₂O. Aromatic aldehydes and ketones do not respond.
The –CHO group withdraws electrons by resonance and induction, deactivating the ring and directing the incoming group to the meta position.

sources: NCERT Class 12 Chemistry (topic reference, own wording)

lessons.title: Carboxylic acids: nomenclature, preparation and physical properties

scenes.text: When a red ant bites Karan, it stings — formic (methanoic) acid from the ant.
His grandmother's pickles taste sour from vinegar, a dilute solution of ethanoic acid.
Both belong to the carboxylic acids, the most acidic common organic compounds.

steps.title: Nomenclature and structure
steps.body: Suffix **-oic acid**: HCOOH methanoic (formic), CH₃COOH ethanoic (acetic), C₆H₅COOH benzoic, HOOC–COOH ethanedioic (oxalic). The carboxyl carbon is sp²; the –COOH group is planar, and resonance makes the C=O less reactive than in aldehydes/ketones.

steps.title: Preparation
steps.body:
- **Oxidation of 1° alcohols and aldehydes** (KMnO₄, K₂Cr₂O₇, CrO₃).
- **Oxidation of alkylbenzenes** (KMnO₄/KOH, then acid): any alkyl side chain with a benzylic H → **benzoic acid**.
- **Hydrolysis of nitriles and amides** (H⁺ or OH⁻): RCN → RCONH₂ → RCOOH.
- **Grignard + CO₂** (dry ice), then H₃O⁺ → RCOOH (one carbon more than RX).
- **Hydrolysis of acyl halides, anhydrides and esters.**

steps.title: Physical properties
steps.body:
- Lower acids are liquids with sharp smells; higher ones waxy solids.
- **Higher boiling points** than alcohols, aldehydes and ketones of similar mass — they form **H-bonded dimers** that persist even in the vapour and in aprotic solvents.
- Lower acids (up to four carbons) mix with water; solubility falls with chain length; benzoic acid is only slightly soluble in cold water.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Ex 1.** C₆H₅CH₂CH₃ + KMnO₄/KOH (heat), then H₃O⁺ → **benzoic acid** (the ethyl chain is cut back).

**Ex 2.** CH₃CH₂MgBr + CO₂, then H₃O⁺ → **propanoic acid**.

**Ex 3.** CH₃CN + H₃O⁺ (heat) → **ethanoic acid** + NH₄⁺.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Expecting tert-butylbenzene to give benzoic acid (no benzylic H — it resists).
- Forgetting the extra carbon in the Grignard–CO₂ route.
- Thinking acids boil lower than alcohols of similar mass.

activity.prompt: Arrange in increasing boiling point (similar molar masses ~ 58–60 g/mol).

quiz.q: IUPAC name of oxalic acid is
quiz.why: Oxalic acid has two –COOH groups on a two-carbon chain, so its IUPAC name is ethanedioic acid.
Vigorous oxidation by KMnO₄ cuts any alkyl side chain with a benzylic hydrogen down to –COOH, so ethylbenzene gives benzoic acid.

quiz.q: Carboxylic acids have high b.p. because
quiz.why: Carboxylic acids form strong hydrogen-bonded dimers, so more energy is needed to separate their molecules, giving high boiling points.

quiz.q: RMgX + CO₂ followed by hydrolysis gives
quiz.why: The Grignard reagent adds to CO₂ to give RCOOMgX, and hydrolysis then gives the carboxylic acid RCOOH, with one more carbon.

quiz.q: Hydrolysis of a nitrile gives finally
quiz.why: Hydrolysis of a nitrile goes first to an amide and then to the carboxylic acid (RCN → RCONH₂ → RCOOH).

sources: NCERT Class 12 Chemistry (topic reference, own wording)

lessons.title: Acidity of carboxylic acids

story.title: Why lemon juice fizzes with baking soda

scenes.text: Shreya mixes baking soda into lemon juice and it foams up.
The acid is strong enough to push CO₂ out of bicarbonate — phenols cannot do that.
Resonance in the carboxylate ion and nearby groups decide how strong an acid is.

steps.title: Why acids are acidic
steps.body:
RCOOH ⇌ RCOO⁻ + H⁺. The **carboxylate ion** has two equivalent resonance structures; the negative charge is shared equally by two oxygen atoms (C–O bond lengths equal). This makes acids stronger than phenols (charge delocalised partly onto less electronegative carbon) and alcohols.
Test: acids liberate **CO₂ with NaHCO₃** (brisk effervescence); phenols do not.

steps.title: Effect of substituents
steps.body:
- **Electron-withdrawing groups** (–NO₂, –CN, –F, –Cl, –CF₃) increase acidity by stabilising the anion; the effect grows with number and proximity.
- **Electron-donating groups** (alkyl) decrease acidity.
- pKa values: CF₃COOH 0.23, CCl₃COOH 0.65, CHCl₂COOH 1.26, ClCH₂COOH 2.86, HCOOH 3.75, C₆H₅COOH 4.19, CH₃COOH 4.76.
- Order of halogen effect: F > Cl > Br > I (FCH₂COOH strongest).
- Benzoic acid is stronger than ethanoic acid; nitro-substituted benzoic acids are stronger still.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Ex 1.** Acidity order: CH₃COOH < ClCH₂COOH < Cl₂CHCOOH < Cl₃CCOOH.

**Ex 2.** Which is stronger: 2-chlorobutanoic or 4-chlorobutanoic acid? **2-Chlorobutanoic** — the −I effect falls with distance.

**Ex 3.** Ka from pKa: pKa = 4.76 ⇒ Ka ≈ **1.74×10⁻⁵**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking a larger pKa means a stronger acid (it is the opposite).
- Ranking ethanoic acid above methanoic acid (HCOOH is stronger; the methyl group donates electrons).
- Forgetting that EWG effects weaken with distance.

activity.prompt: Arrange in DECREASING acid strength.

quiz.q: Carboxylic acids are more acidic than phenols because
options: the carboxylate charge is shared by two O atoms
quiz.why: In the carboxylate ion the negative charge is shared equally between two O atoms by two equivalent resonance forms, which makes it more stable than the phenoxide ion.
F is the most electronegative halogen, so its −I effect is strongest and stabilises the carboxylate best. FCH₂COOH is thus the strongest acid of these.

quiz.q: A test that distinguishes benzoic acid from phenol:
quiz.why: Benzoic acid is stronger than carbonic acid and releases CO₂ from NaHCO₃ with effervescence. Phenol is too weak to do this.

quiz.q: pKa of a stronger acid is
quiz.why: pKa = −log Ka, so a larger Ka (a stronger acid) gives a smaller pKa.
Ethanoic acid has an electron-donating methyl group, which destabilises the carboxylate. Methanoic acid has only H, so its anion is more stable and it is the stronger acid.

sources: NCERT Class 12 Chemistry (topic reference, own wording)

lessons.title: Reactions and uses of carboxylic acids

scenes.text: A perfume maker heats an acid with an alcohol and a few drops of sulphuric acid.
The sharp smell of the acid turns into a sweet, fruity fragrance.
Esterification is just one of many ways a –COOH group can be transformed.

steps.title: Reactions involving O–H and C–OH
steps.body:
- With **Na** → RCOONa + H₂; with **NaOH** → salt + water; with **NaHCO₃** → salt + CO₂ + H₂O.
- **Anhydride formation:** heating with P₂O₅ or conc. H₂SO₄: 2CH₃COOH → (CH₃CO)₂O + H₂O.
- **Esterification** (Fischer, conc. H₂SO₄ or dry HCl, reversible): RCOOH + R'OH ⇌ RCOOR' + H₂O. Mechanism: protonation of C=O, attack by alcohol, proton transfer, loss of water.
- With **PCl₅, PCl₃, SOCl₂** → acyl chlorides (SOCl₂ preferred — gaseous by-products).
- With **NH₃** → ammonium salt → (heat) **amide**: CH₃COONH₄ → CH₃CONH₂ + H₂O. Phthalic acid + NH₃ (strong heating) → phthalimide.

steps.title: Reactions of the –COOH group and the chain
steps.body:
- **Reduction:** LiAlH₄ or B₂H₆ → 1° alcohol (NaBH₄ does not reduce –COOH).
- **Decarboxylation:** sodium salt + soda lime (NaOH + CaO), heat → alkane with **one carbon less**: CH₃COONa → CH₄.
- **Kolbe electrolysis:** electrolysis of aqueous sodium/potassium carboxylate → alkane R–R (2CH₃COO⁻ → C₂H₆ + 2CO₂ at the anode).
- **Hell–Volhard–Zelinsky (HVZ):** acids with α-H + Cl₂/Br₂ and **red phosphorus** → **α-halo acids**.
- **Ring substitution** in benzoic acid: –COOH is **meta-directing, deactivating**; benzoic acid does **not** undergo Friedel–Crafts reactions (deactivated ring; AlCl₃ binds –COOH).

steps.title: Uses
steps.body: Methanoic acid: rubber, textile, dyeing, leather industries. Ethanoic acid: solvent; **vinegar** in food. Hexanedioic (adipic) acid: nylon-6,6. Esters of benzoic acid: perfumery; **sodium benzoate: food preservative**. Higher fatty acids: soaps and detergents.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Ex 1.** CH₃CH₂COOH + Br₂ (red P) → **CH₃CHBrCOOH** (2-bromopropanoic acid).

**Ex 2.** CH₃CH₂COONa + NaOH/CaO (heat) → **ethane** + Na₂CO₃.

**Ex 3.** C₆H₅COOH + conc. HNO₃/H₂SO₄ → **3-nitrobenzoic acid**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using NaBH₄ to reduce acids.
- Forgetting that decarboxylation loses one carbon while Kolbe electrolysis doubles the chain (minus CO₂).
- Expecting Friedel–Crafts on benzoic acid.

activity.prompt: Match the reaction to its product from ethanoic acid (or its salt).

quiz.why: In the Hell–Volhard–Zelinsky reaction a carboxylic acid with α-hydrogen is treated with Cl₂ or Br₂ and red P, giving an α-halo acid.

quiz.q: Decarboxylation of sodium propanoate with soda lime gives
quiz.why: Heating a sodium salt of a carboxylic acid with soda lime removes CO₂. Sodium propanoate (3 C) gives ethane (2 C).

quiz.q: Which does NOT reduce carboxylic acids?
quiz.why: NaBH₄ is too mild to reduce a carboxylic acid. LiAlH₄ and diborane (B₂H₆) can.
The –COOH group is electron-withdrawing and deactivates the ring, directing the nitro group to the meta position and giving m-nitrobenzoic acid.
Sodium benzoate prevents growth of microbes, so it is used as a food preservative.

sources: NCERT Class 12 Chemistry (topic reference, own wording)

questions.q: IUPAC name of CH₃COCH₂CH₃ is
questions.why: The chain has four carbons with the C=O on carbon 2, so it is a ketone named butan-2-one.

questions.q: Tollens' reagent is
questions.why: Tollens' reagent is ammoniacal silver nitrate. Aldehydes reduce it to metallic silver, giving a silver mirror.

questions.q: Which acid is present in vinegar?
questions.why: Vinegar contains ethanoic (acetic) acid, about 5–8%.

questions.q: Assertion: Aldehydes are more reactive than ketones towards nucleophilic addition. Reason: Ketones have two alkyl groups that hinder attack and reduce the positive charge on the carbonyl carbon.
options: Both true; reason does not explain
questions.why: Both are true. Ketones have two electron-donating alkyl groups, which reduce the positive charge on carbon, and they also crowd the carbon. So aldehydes are more reactive.

questions.q: Which does not undergo aldol condensation?
questions.why: Aldol condensation needs an α-hydrogen. HCHO has no α-carbon, so it cannot undergo aldol condensation.

questions.q: Benzaldehyde + conc. NaOH gives
questions.why: Benzaldehyde has no α-hydrogen, so with concentrated NaOH it undergoes Cannizzaro: one molecule is oxidised to sodium benzoate and one is reduced to benzyl alcohol.

questions.q: Which reagent distinguishes propanal from propanone?
questions.why: Propanal is an aldehyde and reduces Tollens' reagent, giving a silver mirror. Propanone, a ketone, does not.

questions.q: Case: Compound A (C₃H₆O) gives a yellow precipitate with I₂/NaOH and does not reduce Tollens' reagent. A is
questions.why: A yellow precipitate with I₂/NaOH shows a CH₃CO– group, and no reduction of Tollens' reagent shows it is not an aldehyde. The C₃H₆O compound is propanone.

questions.q: Acidity order:
questions.why: A more electron-withdrawing group stabilises the carboxylate more. F has a stronger −I effect than Cl, and CH₃ is electron-releasing, so FCH₂COOH > ClCH₂COOH > CH₃COOH.

questions.q: Product of CH₃COCl + H₂ over Pd–BaSO₄:
questions.why: The Rosenmund reduction hydrogenates an acyl chloride over poisoned Pd–BaSO₄, stopping at the aldehyde, so CH₃COCl gives CH₃CHO.

questions.q: Assertion: Benzoic acid does not undergo Friedel–Crafts reaction. Reason: The –COOH group deactivates the ring and binds the AlCl₃ catalyst.
options: Both true; reason does not explain
questions.why: Both are true. The –COOH group deactivates the ring and also bonds with the AlCl₃ catalyst, so Friedel–Crafts does not work on benzoic acid.

questions.q: Which conversion uses Wolff–Kishner reduction?
questions.why: Wolff–Kishner reduction (hydrazine and KOH) turns a C=O group into CH₂. So acetone, CH₃COCH₃, is reduced to propane.

questions.q: Case: A (C₇H₆O) gives a silver mirror and undergoes Cannizzaro reaction but does not give Fehling's test. A is
questions.why: A silver mirror shows an aldehyde, and Cannizzaro shows no α-H. Not giving Fehling's test means it is aromatic, so A is benzaldehyde, C₆H₅CHO.

questions.q: The number of aldol products from a mixture of ethanal and propanal (simple aldol, no dehydration) is
questions.why: Ethanal and propanal each have α-H, so two self-aldol products form (ethanal + ethanal, propanal + propanal) and two cross-aldol products (each as donor with the other). That is 4 in all.

questions.q: Case: An organic acid X (C₂H₄O₂) is treated with Cl₂/red P to give Y, which with aqueous KOH and acidification gives Z (C₂H₄O₃). Z is
questions.why: X is ethanoic acid. HVZ gives chloroethanoic acid (Y), and aqueous KOH replaces Cl by OH, so after acidification Z is hydroxyethanoic (glycolic) acid, C₂H₄O₃.

questions.q: Which gives CO₂ with NaHCO₃?
questions.why: Ethanoic acid is stronger than carbonic acid, so it releases CO₂ from NaHCO₃. Phenol, ethanol and acetone are too weakly acidic to do this.

questions.q: Arrange in decreasing reactivity towards HCN: (i) HCHO (ii) CH₃CHO (iii) CH₃COCH₃ (iv) C₆H₅COC₆H₅
questions.why: Reactivity falls with more alkyl or aryl groups, which give more steric hindrance and less positive carbon. So HCHO > CH₃CHO > CH₃COCH₃ > C₆H₅COC₆H₅.

questions.q: Case: Toluene is converted to benzaldehyde without over-oxidation by
questions.why: The Etard reaction (CrO₂Cl₂, then hydrolysis) stops at benzaldehyde. Hot KMnO₄ would oxidise toluene all the way to benzoic acid.

courses.title: Ch 9 · Amines
courses.summary: Structure, classification and nomenclature of amines; preparation (reduction, ammonolysis, Gabriel synthesis, Hoffmann bromamide); physical properties and basicity in gas phase and water; chemical reactions and tests (carbylamine, nitrous acid, Hinsberg); electrophilic substitution of aniline; and diazonium salts with their reactions and coupling. Independent practice material; not affiliated with or endorsed by any board or exam body.
outcomes: Learners can name amines and classify them as 1°, 2° and 3°.
Learners can choose a preparation method, including when Gabriel and Hoffmann methods apply.
Learners can explain basicity orders using inductive, solvation, steric and resonance effects.
Learners can distinguish amines by chemical tests and use diazonium salts in synthesis.

lessons.title: Structure, classification and nomenclature

scenes.text: Walking through the fish market, Arpita notices the strong 'fishy' odour.
It comes largely from trimethylamine, a simple amine released as fish spoils.
Amines are everywhere in living things — in proteins, vitamins, hormones and medicines.

steps.title: Structure
steps.body: Amines are derivatives of NH₃ where H atoms are replaced by alkyl/aryl groups. N is **sp³** with a lone pair, so amines are **pyramidal**; C–N–C angle in trimethylamine ≈ **108°**. In aniline the lone pair is partly delocalised into the ring.

steps.title: Classification and naming
steps.body:
- **1°** RNH₂, **2°** R₂NH, **3°** R₃N (by the number of groups on N); simple (same R) or mixed.
- **Common names:** alkylamine (methylamine, ethylmethylamine).
- **IUPAC:** alkanamine: CH₃CH₂NH₂ → ethanamine; CH₃NHCH₂CH₃ → **N-methylethanamine**; (CH₃)₃N → N,N-dimethylmethanamine; H₂NCH₂CH₂NH₂ → ethane-1,2-diamine; C₆H₅NH₂ → aniline (benzenamine); C₆H₅NHCH₃ → N-methylaniline.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Ex 1.** Classify (CH₃)₂CHNH₂ → **1° amine** (propan-2-amine) — the classification is by groups on N, not by the carbon.

**Ex 2.** CH₃CH₂N(CH₃)₂ → **3° amine**, N,N-dimethylethanamine.

**Ex 3.** C₆H₅CH₂NH₂ → **phenylmethanamine** (benzylamine), an aliphatic-type 1° amine.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Classifying amines like alcohols (by the carbon) — tert-butylamine is a 1° amine.
- Forgetting the N- locant for substituents on nitrogen.
- Treating benzylamine as an aromatic amine (N is not on the ring).

activity.prompt: Classify each amine.

quiz.q: Shape of amines around N is
quiz.why: Nitrogen in amines is sp³ hybridised with three bonds and one lone pair, so its shape is pyramidal.
In tert-butylamine only one carbon group is on nitrogen (R–NH₂), so it is a primary amine, even though the carbon is tertiary.
The longer ethane chain is the parent and the methyl on N is a substituent. So the name is N-methylethanamine.

options: an aliphatic-type amine (N on side chain)
quiz.why: In benzylamine the –NH₂ is attached to the CH₂ side chain, not directly to the ring. So it behaves like an aliphatic amine, not an aromatic one.

quiz.q: C–N–C angle in trimethylamine is about
quiz.why: Nitrogen is sp³ with a lone pair, which repels the bonds slightly more, so the C–N–C angle is about 108°, a little under the tetrahedral 109.5°.

sources: NCERT Class 12 Chemistry (topic reference, own wording)

lessons.title: Preparation of amines

scenes.text: Aniline was once made in huge vats to start the synthetic dye industry.
Factories reduce nitrobenzene with scrap iron and a little hydrochloric acid.
For pure primary amines in the lab, chemists use special routes like Gabriel synthesis.

steps.title: By reduction
steps.body:
- **Nitro compounds:** H₂/Ni, Pt or Pd, or metals in acid: Sn/HCl or **Fe/HCl** (preferred industrially — FeCl₂ formed is hydrolysed, releasing HCl, so little acid is needed). C₆H₅NO₂ → C₆H₅NH₂.
- **Nitriles:** LiAlH₄ or H₂/Ni → RCH₂NH₂ (**one carbon more** than the starting halide; ascending the series).
- **Amides:** LiAlH₄ → RCH₂NH₂ (same carbon count).

steps.title: Ammonolysis of alkyl halides
steps.body: RX + NH₃ (ethanolic, sealed tube, 373 K) → RNH₃⁺X⁻ → RNH₂; but the product amine also reacts, giving a **mixture** of 1°, 2°, 3° amines and quaternary ammonium salts. Large excess of NH₃ favours 1°. Reactivity of halides: RI > RBr > RCl.

steps.title: Gabriel and Hoffmann methods
steps.body:
- **Gabriel phthalimide synthesis:** phthalimide + ethanolic KOH → potassium phthalimide; + RX → N-alkylphthalimide; alkaline hydrolysis → **pure 1° amine**. **Not for aromatic amines** (aryl halides do not undergo SN with the phthalimide anion).
- **Hoffmann bromamide degradation:** RCONH₂ + Br₂ + 4NaOH → **RNH₂** + Na₂CO₃ + 2NaBr + 2H₂O — amine with **one carbon less** than the amide (aryl/alkyl group migrates from carbonyl carbon to N).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Ex 1.** Ethanamide → methanamine: Br₂/NaOH (**Hoffmann**).

**Ex 2.** Methyl bromide → ethanamine (one carbon more): CH₃Br + KCN → CH₃CN, then LiAlH₄ → **CH₃CH₂NH₂**.

**Ex 3.** Why can't aniline be made by Gabriel synthesis? Bromobenzene does not undergo nucleophilic substitution with phthalimide anion.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using Gabriel synthesis for aniline.
- Forgetting the carbon count change: nitrile reduction +1 C (from RX), Hoffmann −1 C.
- Expecting ammonolysis to give a single amine.

activity.prompt: Match the method with its feature.

quiz.q: Hoffmann bromamide degradation of propanamide gives
quiz.why: In Hoffmann bromamide degradation an amide loses one carbon as carbonate, so propanamide (3 C) gives ethanamine (2 C).

quiz.q: Gabriel synthesis is used to prepare
quiz.why: Gabriel synthesis uses potassium phthalimide with an alkyl halide, so it gives primary aliphatic amines. Aryl halides do not react.

quiz.q: Reduction of CH₃CN with LiAlH₄ gives
quiz.why: LiAlH₄ reduces the nitrile group –C≡N to –CH₂NH₂. So CH₃CN gives CH₃CH₂NH₂, ethanamine.

quiz.q: Fe/HCl is preferred for reducing nitrobenzene because
options: FeCl₂ hydrolysis regenerates HCl, so little acid is needed
quiz.why: With Fe/HCl, FeCl₂ hydrolyses to release HCl again, so only a small amount of HCl is needed, making it economical.

options: a mixture of amines and quaternary salts
quiz.why: The amine product is itself nucleophilic and reacts again with the alkyl halide, so ammonolysis gives a mixture of 1°, 2°, 3° amines and a quaternary ammonium salt.
