lessons.title: Physical properties and basicity

story.title: Why aniline is a weak base

scenes.text: In the lab, Rohan finds that a few drops of methylamine solution turn red litmus blue strongly; aniline barely does.
In aniline, the nitrogen's lone pair is shared with the benzene ring.
Less available lone pair means weaker base — basicity is all about the lone pair.

steps.title: Physical properties
steps.body: Lower aliphatic amines are gases with fishy odour; higher ones liquids/solids. 1° and 2° amines form **intermolecular H-bonds** (3° cannot — no N–H), so b.p.: **1° > 2° > 3°** for isomers; amines boil lower than alcohols of similar mass (N–H…N weaker than O–H…O). Lower amines are water-soluble. Aniline is colourless when pure but darkens on storage (air oxidation).

steps.title: Basicity
steps.body:
Amines are Lewis bases (lone pair on N). Basicity measured by **Kb** (pKb lower ⇒ stronger base).
- **Aliphatic amines are stronger bases than NH₃** (+I effect of alkyl groups).
- **Gas phase:** 3° > 2° > 1° > NH₃ (inductive effect alone).
- **In water**, solvation (H-bonding of the ammonium ion) and steric effects also matter:
  - methyl: **(CH₃)₂NH > CH₃NH₂ > (CH₃)₃N > NH₃**
  - ethyl: **(C₂H₅)₂NH > (C₂H₅)₃N > C₂H₅NH₂ > NH₃**
- pKb values: NH₃ 4.75; CH₃NH₂ 3.38; (CH₃)₂NH 3.27; (CH₃)₃N 4.22; C₂H₅NH₂ 3.29; (C₂H₅)₂NH 3.00; (C₂H₅)₃N 3.25; C₆H₅NH₂ **9.38**.
- **Aryl amines are much weaker** — the lone pair is delocalised into the ring and the anilinium ion has fewer resonance structures. EDG (–CH₃, –OCH₃) on the ring increase, EWG (–NO₂) decrease basicity.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Ex 1.** Order of basicity in water: (C₂H₅)₂NH > (C₂H₅)₃N > C₂H₅NH₂ > NH₃ > C₆H₅NH₂.

**Ex 2.** p-Toluidine vs aniline: **p-toluidine** is more basic (–CH₃ donates electrons).

**Ex 3.** p-Nitroaniline vs aniline: **aniline** is more basic (–NO₂ withdraws electron density).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using the gas-phase order for aqueous questions.
- Thinking 3° amines have the highest boiling point (no N–H).
- Forgetting that higher pKb means a weaker base.

activity.prompt: Arrange in DECREASING basic strength in water.

quiz.q: Which has the lowest pKb in water?
quiz.why: Diethylamine has pKb about 3.00, the lowest here. A lower pKb means a stronger base, and it benefits from inductive effects, solvation and little steric crowding.

quiz.q: Aniline is a weaker base than ammonia because
options: its lone pair is delocalised into the ring
quiz.why: In aniline the nitrogen lone pair is delocalised into the benzene ring by resonance, so it is less available to accept a proton. Aniline is therefore a weaker base than ammonia.

quiz.q: Among isomeric amines, the lowest boiling is
quiz.why: Tertiary amines have no N–H bonds, so they cannot form hydrogen bonds with each other. They boil lower than isomeric primary and secondary amines.

quiz.q: In the gas phase basicity order is
quiz.why: In the gas phase there is no solvation, so only the +I effect matters. More alkyl groups mean greater basicity, so 3° > 2° > 1°.
An electron-donating methyl group increases electron density on N, making p-methylaniline more basic than aniline. The nitro group and the amide carbonyl reduce basicity.

sources: NCERT Class 12 Chemistry (topic reference, own wording)

lessons.title: Chemical reactions and tests of amines

story.title: The test with the terrible smell

scenes.text: In the practical exam, Imran warms an unknown amine with chloroform and alcoholic KOH.
A revolting smell fills the lab — isocyanide!
Only primary amines give this carbylamine test, so he has identified his compound.

steps.title: Alkylation, acylation and benzoylation
steps.body:
- **Alkylation:** RNH₂ + R'X → 2°, 3° amines and quaternary salts.
- **Acylation:** 1° and 2° amines + acid chlorides/anhydrides (pyridine removes HCl) → **amides**: C₂H₅NH₂ + CH₃COCl → C₂H₅NHCOCH₃. 3° amines do not acylate (no N–H).
- **Benzoylation** with C₆H₅COCl gives N-substituted benzamides.

steps.title: Tests
steps.body:
- **Carbylamine test (1° amines only):** RNH₂ + CHCl₃ + 3KOH (alc., heat) → **RNC** (isocyanide, foul smell) + 3KCl + 3H₂O.
- **Nitrous acid (NaNO₂ + HCl):** 1° aliphatic amines → **alcohol + N₂ gas** (brisk effervescence) via unstable diazonium salts; 1° aromatic amines at **273–278 K** → stable **arenediazonium salts**.
- **Hinsberg's reagent** (benzenesulphonyl chloride, C₆H₅SO₂Cl):
  - 1° → N-alkylbenzenesulphonamide, **soluble in alkali** (acidic N–H).
  - 2° → N,N-dialkylbenzenesulphonamide, **insoluble in alkali** (no acidic H).
  - 3° → **no reaction**.

steps.title: Electrophilic substitution in aniline
steps.body:
–NH₂ is a strong activating, **o/p-directing** group.
- **Bromination:** bromine water → **2,4,6-tribromoaniline** (white precipitate). For monosubstitution, first **acetylate** (–NHCOCH₃ is less activating), brominate → p-bromoacetanilide, then hydrolyse.
- **Nitration:** direct nitration gives tarry oxidation products and, because aniline is protonated to anilinium (meta-directing) in acid, a large amount of **meta** product (about 47% m, 51% p, 2% o). Protect by acetylation to get mainly p-nitroaniline.
- **Sulphonation:** with conc. H₂SO₄ → anilinium hydrogensulphate → (453–473 K) **sulphanilic acid** (p-aminobenzenesulphonic acid, a zwitterion).
- Aniline does **not** undergo Friedel–Crafts (it forms a salt with AlCl₃, deactivating the ring).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Ex 1.** Distinguish ethylamine and diethylamine: **carbylamine test** — only ethylamine gives the foul smell.

**Ex 2.** Product of CH₃NH₂ + HNO₂: **CH₃OH + N₂**.

**Ex 3.** p-Bromoaniline from aniline: acetylation (acetic anhydride) → bromination (Br₂/CH₃COOH) → acid/base hydrolysis.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Applying the carbylamine test to 2° amines.
- Thinking direct nitration of aniline gives only o/p products.
- Saying 3° amines react with Hinsberg's reagent.

a.text: An unknown amine reacts with Hinsberg's reagent; the product dissolves in aqueous KOH. What type is it?

choices.label: Primary amine
choices.feedback: Correct — the sulphonamide still has an acidic N–H.

a2.text: Solubility in alkali requires an acidic H on nitrogen after sulphonylation. Which class keeps one?

b.text: To confirm, which test gives a foul smell only with primary amines?

choices.label: Iodoform test
choices.feedback: That is for methyl ketones and some alcohols.

b2.text: Think of the test that turns RNH₂ into RNC…

end.text: Two tests confirm a primary amine.

quiz.why: In the carbylamine test, a primary amine with CHCl₃ and alcoholic KOH gives a foul-smelling isocyanide. It requires two N–H bonds, so only 1° amines respond.
Hinsberg's reagent is benzenesulphonyl chloride, C₆H₅SO₂Cl, used to distinguish 1°, 2° and 3° amines.
–NH₂ strongly activates the ring at ortho and para positions, so bromine water substitutes all three and gives 2,4,6-tribromoaniline.

quiz.q: Direct nitration of aniline gives significant meta product because
quiz.why: In the strongly acidic nitrating mixture aniline is protonated to anilinium ion, –NH₃⁺, which is a meta director. So a good amount of the meta product forms.
Aliphatic primary amines with nitrous acid give unstable diazonium salts that decompose to alcohols and N₂ gas.
Acylation replaces an N–H hydrogen. Tertiary amines such as (CH₃)₃N have no N–H, so they cannot be acylated.

sources: NCERT Class 12 Chemistry (topic reference, own wording)

lessons.title: Diazonium salts

scenes.text: The bright orange and yellow of many cheap dyes and indicators — like methyl orange — come from azo compounds.
They are made from diazonium salts prepared in ice-cold solutions.
A diazonium salt can also be swapped for Cl, Br, I, F, CN, OH or H — a gateway to many aromatic compounds.

steps.title: Preparation and stability
steps.body: **Diazotisation:** ArNH₂ + NaNO₂ + 2HCl (273–278 K) → **ArN₂⁺Cl⁻** + NaCl + 2H₂O. Arenediazonium salts are stable only in cold solution (resonance delocalisation over the ring); they are used immediately, never stored dry (explosive). Alkyl diazonium salts are unstable even when cold.

steps.title: Replacement of N₂ (loss of nitrogen)
steps.body:
- **Sandmeyer:** CuCl/HCl → ArCl; CuBr/HBr → ArBr; **CuCN/KCN → ArCN**.
- **Gattermann:** Cu powder + HCl/HBr → ArCl/ArBr.
- **KI** → ArI (no catalyst needed).
- **Balz–Schiemann:** HBF₄ → ArN₂⁺BF₄⁻, heat → **ArF**.
- **H₃PO₂ or ethanol** → **ArH** (replacement by hydrogen).
- **Warm water** → **ArOH** (phenol).
- **HBF₄ then NaNO₂/Cu (heat)** → ArNO₂.

steps.title: Coupling reactions (N₂ retained)
steps.body:
Diazonium ion is a weak electrophile that attacks activated rings at the para position:
- With **phenol** (mildly alkaline) → **p-hydroxyazobenzene** (orange dye).
- With **aniline** (mildly acidic) → **p-aminoazobenzene** (yellow dye).
The –N=N– group extends conjugation, giving colour (azo dyes).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Ex 1.** Benzene → fluorobenzene: nitration → reduction (Sn/HCl) → diazotisation → HBF₄, heat.

**Ex 2.** Aniline → benzonitrile: diazotise, then **CuCN/KCN**.

**Ex 3.** 1,3,5-tribromobenzene from aniline: bromine water (2,4,6-tribromoaniline) → diazotise → H₃PO₂ (removes the –N₂⁺, leaving Br at 1,3,5).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Diazotising above 278 K (the salt decomposes to phenol).
- Forgetting that fluorobenzene needs Balz–Schiemann, not Sandmeyer.
- Expecting coupling at the meta position.

activity.prompt: Match the reagent with the product from C₆H₅N₂⁺Cl⁻.

quiz.why: Diazonium salts are unstable at higher temperatures, so diazotisation is done at 273–278 K (ice-cold).

quiz.q: Sandmeyer reaction converts ArN₂⁺ to ArCl using
quiz.why: In the Sandmeyer reaction CuCl/HCl replaces N₂⁺ by Cl. In the Gattermann variant Cu powder with HCl is used.
Hypophosphorous acid, H₃PO₂, reduces the diazonium salt and replaces N₂⁺ by H, giving benzene.

quiz.q: Coupling with phenol takes place at
quiz.why: Coupling occurs at the para position of phenol, which is activated and less hindered than ortho. The product is p-hydroxyazobenzene.
The Balz–Schiemann reaction heats benzenediazonium fluoroborate (ArN₂⁺BF₄⁻) to give fluorobenzene.

sources: NCERT Class 12 Chemistry (topic reference, own wording)

questions.q: Which is a secondary amine?
questions.why: A secondary amine has two carbon groups on nitrogen and one N–H. CH₃NHC₂H₅ has a methyl and an ethyl, so it is secondary.

questions.q: IUPAC name of C₆H₅NH₂ is
questions.why: C₆H₅NH₂ is called aniline in common usage and benzenamine in IUPAC naming.

questions.q: Hoffmann bromamide degradation of benzamide gives
questions.why: Hoffmann bromamide reaction removes the carbonyl carbon. Benzamide (C₆H₅CONH₂) becomes aniline (C₆H₅NH₂), with one carbon fewer.

questions.q: Assertion: Aniline is a weaker base than ethanamine. Reason: The lone pair on N in aniline is delocalised over the benzene ring.
options: Both true; reason does not explain
questions.why: Both are true. In aniline the lone pair is delocalised into the ring, so it is less available to take a proton. In ethanamine the alkyl group pushes electrons to N, making it more basic.

questions.q: Which amine gives N₂ with nitrous acid at room temperature?
questions.why: Primary aliphatic amines react with HNO₂ to give unstable diazonium salts and release N₂ gas. CH₃NH₂ is the only primary amine in the list.

questions.q: Product of aniline + CHCl₃ + alc. KOH:
questions.why: A primary aromatic amine with CHCl₃ and alcoholic KOH gives phenyl isocyanide in the carbylamine test, recognised by its foul smell.

questions.q: The correct basicity order in water is
questions.why: In water, basicity depends on inductive effect, solvation and steric hindrance together, so the order is (CH₃)₂NH > CH₃NH₂ > (CH₃)₃N.

questions.q: Case: An amine C₃H₉N reacts with Hinsberg's reagent to give a product insoluble in alkali. The amine is
questions.why: A secondary amine reacts with Hinsberg's reagent to give a sulphonamide with no acidic N–H, which is insoluble in alkali. N-Methylethanamine (C₃H₉N) is the secondary amine among the options.

questions.q: Gabriel synthesis cannot make aniline because
options: aryl halides do not undergo nucleophilic substitution with phthalimide anion
questions.why: Gabriel synthesis needs the phthalimide anion to attack an alkyl halide by nucleophilic substitution. Aryl halides are unreactive that way, so aniline cannot be made.

questions.q: Assertion: Acetylation of aniline reduces its activating effect. Reason: The lone pair on N in acetanilide is also delocalised onto the carbonyl oxygen.
options: Both true; reason does not explain
questions.why: Both are true. In acetanilide the nitrogen lone pair is also drawn toward the carbonyl oxygen, so less is available to the ring and the activating effect falls.

questions.q: Benzenediazonium chloride + CuCN/KCN gives X; X on hydrolysis gives Y. Y is
questions.why: The diazonium salt with CuCN gives benzonitrile (X). Hydrolysis of the nitrile, via benzamide, finally gives benzoic acid.

questions.q: Case: To make m-bromoaniline from benzene, the right order is
questions.why: –NO₂ is meta-directing, so nitrate benzene first, then brominate to put Br meta to NO₂, and finally reduce –NO₂ to –NH₂ to get m-bromoaniline.

questions.q: Why does aniline not undergo Friedel–Crafts reactions?
options: It forms a salt with AlCl₃, putting + charge on N and deactivating the ring
questions.why: Aniline is a base and reacts with the Lewis acid AlCl₃ to form a salt, putting a positive charge on N. That strongly deactivates the ring, so Friedel–Crafts fails.

questions.q: The number of moles of Br₂ needed to convert 1 mol of aniline into 2,4,6-tribromoaniline is
questions.why: Each Br₂ replaces one H at an ortho or para position. Aniline has three such positions, so 3 mol of Br₂ give 2,4,6-tribromoaniline.

questions.q: Case: Compound A (C₇H₉N) dissolves in dil. HCl, gives carbylamine test, and on diazotisation and warming gives o-cresol. A is
questions.why: A dissolves in HCl and gives the carbylamine test, so it is a primary amine. Diazotisation then warming gives o-cresol, so the –NH₂ and CH₃ are ortho: o-toluidine.

questions.q: Coupling of benzenediazonium chloride with aniline gives
questions.why: Diazonium salts couple at the para position of aniline, giving the yellow dye p-aminoazobenzene (C₆H₅–N=N–C₆H₄NH₂).

questions.q: Which reagent sequence converts nitrobenzene to 1,3,5-tribromobenzene?
options: Sn/HCl; Br₂ water; NaNO₂/HCl (273 K); H₃PO₂
questions.why: Reduce nitrobenzene to aniline (Sn/HCl), tribrominate it with bromine water, diazotise (NaNO₂/HCl at 273 K), then remove N₂⁺ with H₃PO₂ to give 1,3,5-tribromobenzene.

courses.title: Ch 10 · Biomolecules
courses.summary: Carbohydrates — classification, glucose and fructose structures, D/L configuration, anomers, disaccharides and polysaccharides; proteins — amino acids, peptide bond, levels of structure and denaturation; enzymes and vitamins (extension); and nucleic acids — DNA and RNA structure and functions. Independent practice material; not affiliated with or endorsed by any board or exam body.
outcomes: Learners can classify carbohydrates and explain the open-chain and cyclic structures of glucose.
Learners can describe sucrose, maltose, lactose, starch, cellulose and glycogen.
Learners can explain amino acids, zwitterions, peptide bonds, protein structure levels and denaturation.
Learners can compare DNA and RNA in composition, structure and function.

lessons.title: Carbohydrates and the structure of glucose

scenes.text: When Aarohi eats a roti, enzymes in her saliva start breaking starch into sugars.
Her body burns glucose for energy; plants make that glucose from sunlight.
Glucose looks like a simple six-carbon sugar, but chemists needed decades to settle its exact structure.

steps.title: Classification
steps.body:
Carbohydrates are optically active **polyhydroxy aldehydes or ketones**, or compounds that hydrolyse to them.
- **Monosaccharides** (cannot be hydrolysed): glucose, fructose, ribose. **Aldoses** (–CHO) and **ketoses** (C=O).
- **Oligosaccharides** (2–10 units): disaccharides sucrose, maltose, lactose.
- **Polysaccharides:** starch, cellulose, glycogen.
- **Reducing sugars** reduce Tollens'/Fehling's (free aldehyde/ketone group): all monosaccharides, maltose, lactose. **Non-reducing:** sucrose.
- Sweet, crystalline, water-soluble ones are called **sugars**.

steps.title: Glucose: preparation and open-chain evidence
steps.body:
Prepared by boiling sucrose with dilute acid (gives glucose + fructose) or by hydrolysing starch (dilute H₂SO₄, 393 K, 2–3 bar). Evidence for C₆H₁₂O₆ as a straight-chain aldohexose:
- With **HI** (long heating) → **n-hexane** (six carbons in a chain).
- With **NH₂OH** → oxime; with **HCN** → cyanohydrin (carbonyl present).
- With **bromine water** → **gluconic acid** (carbonyl is an aldehyde).
- **Acetylation** with acetic anhydride → pentaacetate (**five –OH** groups).
- With **HNO₃** → **saccharic acid** (both ends oxidised, so one end is a 1° alcohol).
Glucose is **D-(+)-glucose**: D refers to configuration of the –OH on the lowest chiral carbon (C5) relating to D-glyceraldehyde; (+) means dextrorotatory.

steps.title: Cyclic structure
steps.body:
The open chain cannot explain: (1) **no Schiff's test** and **no NaHSO₃ addition**, (2) **pentaacetate does not react with NH₂OH**, (3) two forms, **α** and **β**, exist. So glucose exists mainly as a **six-membered ring (pyranose)** formed when the C5–OH adds to the C1 aldehyde (hemiacetal). α and β differ only at **C1** — they are **anomers**; C1 is the anomeric carbon. The ring is drawn as a **Haworth projection**.
**Fructose:** a ketohexose, **D-(−)-fructose**, with a five-membered **furanose** ring (C5–OH adds to C2 keto group).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Ex 1.** Which reaction shows glucose has an aldehyde group? **Bromine water → gluconic acid** (a mild oxidant that acts on –CHO).

**Ex 2.** Glucose + HI (prolonged heat) → **n-hexane**, proving a straight chain of six carbons.

**Ex 3.** α-D-glucose and β-D-glucose are **anomers** (differ only at C1).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking D/L tells the direction of optical rotation (that is +/−).
- Calling α and β glucose enantiomers — they are diastereomers (anomers).
- Forgetting that glucose's ring is six-membered while fructose's is five-membered.

activity.prompt: Match each reaction of glucose to what it proves.
pairs: Six carbons in a straight chain
Aldehyde is tied up in a ring

quiz.why: Glucose has six carbons and an aldehyde group (–CHO), so it is an aldohexose.
Anomers are two cyclic forms of glucose that differ only in configuration at the new chiral centre made on ring closure, the anomeric carbon C1.
In its combined form (as in sucrose) fructose has a five-membered ring, called a furanose. Glucose forms a six-membered pyranose ring.
Bromine water is a mild oxidant that converts only the –CHO group of glucose to –COOH, giving gluconic acid. Strong nitric acid would give saccharic acid.

options: configuration at the lowest chiral carbon
quiz.why: The D label shows the –OH on the chiral carbon farthest from the carbonyl is on the right in the Fischer projection, like D-glyceraldehyde. It is not about the direction of rotation.

sources: NCERT Class 12 Chemistry (topic reference, own wording)

lessons.title: Disaccharides and polysaccharides

scenes.text: Some people feel unwell after drinking milk — they cannot digest lactose, milk's sugar.
A cotton shirt is almost pure cellulose, made of glucose units, yet we cannot digest it.
A potato's starch is also glucose units — linked differently, and easy to digest.

steps.title: Disaccharides
steps.body:
Two monosaccharides joined by a **glycosidic linkage** (oxygen bridge, water lost).
- **Sucrose:** α-D-glucose (C1) + β-D-fructose (C2) — both anomeric carbons used ⇒ **non-reducing**. Sucrose is dextrorotatory, but hydrolysis gives glucose (+52.5°) and fructose (−92.4°) — net **laevorotatory**, so the product is called **invert sugar**.
- **Maltose:** two α-D-glucose units, C1 to C4 (α-1,4) — **reducing** (free C1 in second unit).
- **Lactose (milk sugar):** β-D-galactose (C1) + β-D-glucose (C4) — **reducing**.

steps.title: Polysaccharides
steps.body:
- **Starch** (plants' storage): polymer of α-glucose: **amylose** (water-soluble, 15–20%, unbranched, α-1,4) and **amylopectin** (insoluble, 80–85%, branched, α-1,4 chains with α-1,6 branches).
- **Cellulose** (plant cell walls): unbranched chains of **β-D-glucose** linked β-1,4. Humans lack the enzyme to break β-links.
- **Glycogen** (animal starch, stored in liver, muscles, brain): like amylopectin but **more highly branched**.

steps.title: Importance
steps.body: Energy sources (glucose, starch, glycogen), structural materials (cellulose in plants; chitin-like polymers elsewhere), raw materials (cotton, paper, wood), and components of nucleic acids (ribose, deoxyribose). Honey is largely glucose and fructose.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Ex 1.** Why is sucrose non-reducing? Both anomeric carbons (glucose C1, fructose C2) are in the glycosidic bond — no free hemiacetal.

**Ex 2.** Starch vs cellulose: both glucose polymers; starch has **α**-links (digestible), cellulose **β**-links (not digestible by humans).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling sucrose reducing.
- Mixing up amylose (unbranched, soluble) and amylopectin (branched, insoluble).
- Thinking cellulose is made of a different sugar from starch.

activity.prompt: Reducing or non-reducing sugar?

quiz.why: Hydrolysis of sucrose gives equal amounts of D-glucose and D-fructose, called invert sugar.
Lactose, the sugar in milk, is a disaccharide of β-D-galactose and β-D-glucose.
Cellulose is a polymer of β-D-glucose joined by β-1,4 glycosidic links, which makes it linear. Starch has α links.
Amylopectin, the main component of starch, is branched: α-1,4 links form the main chain and α-1,6 links form the branches. Amylose is the unbranched part.
Glycogen is the storage carbohydrate of animals, stored in the liver and muscles, and is structurally similar to amylopectin, so it is called animal starch.

sources: NCERT Class 12 Chemistry (topic reference, own wording)

lessons.title: Proteins

scenes.text: Saanvi boils an egg; the clear, runny white turns solid and opaque.
Heat unfolds the albumin proteins and they tangle together.
The amino-acid sequence is unchanged, but the shape — and so the function — is lost: denaturation.

steps.title: Amino acids
steps.body:
Contain –NH₂ and –COOH; in proteins they are **α-amino acids** (both on the same carbon), RCH(NH₂)COOH, with different side chains R.
- About 20 occur in proteins. **Essential** amino acids must come from diet (e.g. valine, leucine, lysine); non-essential ones can be made in the body (glycine, alanine).
- Neutral, acidic or basic depending on extra –COOH or –NH₂.
- In solution they exist as dipolar ions (**zwitterions**) H₃N⁺–CHR–COO⁻ — amphoteric, high m.p., water-soluble.
- All except glycine are optically active; natural ones are mostly L-configuration.

steps.title: Peptide bond and structure levels
steps.body:
**Peptide bond** –CO–NH– forms between –COOH of one amino acid and –NH₂ of the next (water lost). Two units: dipeptide; many: polypeptide; above ~100 residues (mass > 10 000 u) usually called a protein.
- **Fibrous proteins** (keratin, myosin): parallel chains, insoluble. **Globular proteins** (insulin, albumin): folded into spheres, water-soluble.
- **Primary structure:** sequence of amino acids.
- **Secondary:** **α-helix** (H-bonds between –NH and C=O of the same chain, right-handed coil) or **β-pleated sheet** (H-bonds between neighbouring chains).
- **Tertiary:** overall folding (H-bonds, disulphide links, van der Waals, ionic).
- **Quaternary:** arrangement of two or more subunits (e.g. haemoglobin).

steps.title: Denaturation
steps.body: Changes in temperature or pH disrupt H-bonds and other interactions, so the protein unfolds and loses biological activity; **the primary structure stays intact**. Examples: coagulation of egg white on boiling; curdling of milk (lactic acid from bacteria).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Ex 1.** Glycine + alanine can form **two** dipeptides: Gly-Ala and Ala-Gly.

**Ex 2.** Why are amino acids high-melting solids? They exist as **zwitterions** — ionic attractions in the crystal.

**Ex 3.** What is broken in denaturation? Secondary and tertiary interactions (H-bonds etc.), **not** peptide bonds.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying denaturation breaks peptide bonds.
- Mixing up α-helix (one chain) and β-sheet (side-by-side chains).
- Saying glycine is optically active (its α-carbon has two H atoms).

activity.prompt: Match the level of protein structure to its description.
pairs: Loss of shape and activity, sequence intact

quiz.why: A peptide bond is the amide link –CO–NH– formed between the –COOH of one amino acid and the –NH₂ of the next.

quiz.q: Which amino acid is optically inactive?
quiz.why: Glycine has two hydrogens on the α-carbon, so that carbon is not chiral and glycine is optically inactive. The other listed amino acids all have a chiral α-carbon.

quiz.q: Amino acids exist in water as
quiz.why: The acidic –COOH gives a proton to the basic –NH₂ in the same molecule, forming a dipolar ion, the zwitterion.
The α-helix is held in place by hydrogen bonds between the N–H of one residue and the C=O of another in the same chain.

quiz.q: Curdling of milk is an example of
quiz.why: Lactic acid from bacteria lowers the pH, changing the protein's shape so it coagulates, which is denaturation of milk protein.

lessons.title: Enzymes and vitamins (extension)

scenes.text: Long ago, sailors on months-long voyages suffered from bleeding gums and weakness — scurvy.
A ship's doctor found that citrus fruit prevented it.
We now know the missing factor was vitamin C — one of many small molecules life cannot do without.

steps.title: Enzymes
steps.body: Enzymes are biological catalysts, mostly **globular proteins**, highly **specific** for their substrates and reactions. They work best at an optimum temperature and pH (e.g. pepsin in acidic stomach), lowering activation energy greatly. Examples: **maltase** (maltose → glucose), **invertase** (sucrose → glucose + fructose), zymase (fermentation). Many need cofactors (metal ions or vitamins).

steps.title: Vitamins
steps.body:
Organic compounds needed in small amounts for normal growth and health.
- **Fat-soluble (A, D, E, K):** stored in liver and adipose tissue.
- **Water-soluble (B group, C):** must be supplied regularly in the diet (excreted in urine); **B₁₂** is an exception and can be stored in the liver.
- Deficiencies: **A** → night blindness, xerophthalmia; **B₁** → beriberi; **B₂** → cheilosis (cracked lips); **B₆** → convulsions; **B₁₂** → pernicious anaemia; **C** → scurvy (bleeding gums); **D** → rickets (children), osteomalacia (adults); **E** → fragile red blood cells, muscle weakness; **K** → increased blood-clotting time.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Ex 1.** A person who rarely sees sunlight and avoids dairy may lack vitamin **D** → bone problems.

**Ex 2.** Why must vitamin C be eaten daily? It is **water-soluble** and is not stored; excess is excreted.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying all vitamins are stored by the body.
- Thinking enzymes are consumed in reactions.
- Confusing rickets (vitamin D) with scurvy (vitamin C).

steps.title: Note on syllabus
steps.body: Some recent rationalised NCERT editions trimmed parts of this content; it remains useful for NEET and general health knowledge. Check your current syllabus. This is general education, not medical advice — see a doctor for diet or deficiency concerns.

activity.prompt: Match the vitamin to its deficiency disease.

quiz.why: Vitamins A, D, E and K dissolve in fat and are stored in the body. B-complex vitamins and C are water-soluble.
Enzymes are biological catalysts and nearly all are globular proteins.

quiz.q: Scurvy is due to deficiency of
quiz.why: Deficiency of vitamin C (ascorbic acid) causes scurvy, with bleeding gums.
Invertase hydrolyses sucrose into glucose and fructose, a process called inversion, since the optical rotation changes sign.

quiz.q: Which water-soluble vitamin can be stored in the liver?
quiz.why: Vitamin B₁₂ is an exception among water-soluble vitamins, as it is stored in the liver. The others, like C, B₁ and B₂, are largely excreted.

sources: NCERT Class 12 Chemistry (topic reference, own wording)

lessons.title: Nucleic acids

scenes.text: A DNA test can show that two people are related — or solve a crime.
DNA is a long chain carrying instructions written in just four 'letters'.
Its double helix can unzip and copy itself, passing information from cell to cell and parent to child.

steps.title: Composition
steps.body:
Nucleic acids (DNA, RNA) are polymers of **nucleotides**. On complete hydrolysis they give a **pentose sugar**, **phosphoric acid** and **nitrogenous bases**.
- **DNA:** sugar **β-D-2-deoxyribose**; bases **adenine (A), guanine (G), cytosine (C), thymine (T)**.
- **RNA:** sugar **β-D-ribose**; bases **A, G, C, uracil (U)**.
- **Nucleoside** = base + sugar (base at C1'); **nucleotide** = nucleoside + phosphate (at C5'). Nucleotides join by **phosphodiester** links between C5' and C3' of sugars.

steps.title: Structure
steps.body:
- **DNA:** a **double helix** (Watson and Crick, 1953): two antiparallel strands held by **H-bonds between complementary bases — A with T, G with C**.
- **RNA:** usually single-stranded (may fold). Types: **mRNA** (messenger), **rRNA** (ribosomal), **tRNA** (transfer).

steps.title: Functions
steps.body:
- DNA stores genetic information and undergoes **replication** — each strand serves as a template, so heredity is passed on.
- RNA carries out **protein synthesis**: DNA → mRNA (transcription) → protein on ribosomes, with tRNA bringing amino acids (translation).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Ex 1.** A DNA strand has the sequence 5'-ATGCCA-3'. Its complementary strand is **3'-TACGGT-5'**.

**Ex 2.** If DNA has 30% adenine, it has 30% thymine and therefore **20% guanine and 20% cytosine** (A = T, G = C).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Putting thymine in RNA or uracil in DNA.
- Pairing A with G.
- Calling a nucleoside a nucleotide (no phosphate in a nucleoside).

activity.prompt: DNA, RNA or both?

quiz.why: DNA contains 2-deoxyribose, which lacks the –OH on carbon 2′ that ribose in RNA has.

quiz.q: Base found in RNA but not DNA:
quiz.why: RNA contains uracil in place of thymine. Adenine, guanine and cytosine occur in both DNA and RNA.
In DNA, base pairing is A with T (two hydrogen bonds) and G with C (three hydrogen bonds). So guanine pairs with cytosine.
A nucleotide is a nucleoside (base + sugar) with a phosphate group attached.

quiz.q: The double helix model was proposed by
quiz.why: James Watson and Francis Crick proposed the double helix model of DNA in 1953.

sources: NCERT Class 12 Chemistry (topic reference, own wording)

questions.q: Which is a ketohexose?
questions.why: Fructose has six carbons with the ketone group at C2, so it is a ketohexose. Glucose and galactose are aldohexoses and ribose is an aldopentose.

questions.q: Which sugar is non-reducing?
questions.why: Sucrose is non-reducing because the glycosidic bond joins the anomeric carbons of both glucose and fructose, leaving no free aldehyde or ketone group. Lactose and maltose have a free anomeric carbon and are reducing.

questions.q: The bond linking amino acids in proteins is
questions.why: Amino acids join through the amide-type peptide bond, –CO–NH–, formed between the –COOH of one and the –NH₂ of the next. Glycosidic bonds join sugars and phosphodiester bonds join nucleotides.

questions.q: Assertion: Glucose does not give Schiff's test. Reason: The aldehyde group is mostly present as a cyclic hemiacetal.
options: Both true; reason does not explain
questions.why: Both are true. In solution glucose exists mostly as a cyclic hemiacetal with no free –CHO, so it does not restore the colour of Schiff's reagent. The reason explains the assertion.

questions.q: Number of –OH groups in glucose (open chain):
questions.why: Open-chain glucose is HOCH₂–(CHOH)₄–CHO, with one –OH on each of five carbons. This is shown by its pentaacetate, formed with acetic anhydride.

questions.q: Cellulose is a polymer of
questions.why: Cellulose is a polymer of β-D-glucose units joined by β-1,4 glycosidic links. Starch is made of α-D-glucose.

questions.q: Which vitamin deficiency causes night blindness?
questions.why: Vitamin A (retinol) is needed for the pigment in the eye's retina, so its deficiency causes night blindness.

questions.q: Case: A carbohydrate on hydrolysis gives only glucose, reduces Fehling's solution and is a disaccharide. It is
questions.why: A disaccharide that gives only glucose on hydrolysis is made of two glucose units, so it is maltose. Maltose has a free anomeric carbon, so it reduces Fehling's solution; sucrose does not.

questions.q: Invert sugar is called so because
options: the sign of optical rotation changes from + to − on hydrolysis
questions.why: Sucrose is dextrorotatory (+66.5°), but its hydrolysis gives glucose (+52.5°) and fructose (−92.4°). Fructose's stronger laevorotation makes the mixture laevorotatory, so the sign is inverted.

questions.q: Assertion: Denaturation destroys biological activity of a protein. Reason: Peptide bonds are hydrolysed during denaturation.
options: Both true; reason does not explain
questions.why: The assertion is true: denaturation changes the 2° and 3° structure and destroys activity. The reason is false, as peptide bonds stay intact, so the primary structure is unchanged.

questions.q: In amylopectin, branching occurs through
questions.why: The main chain of amylopectin has α-1,4 links, and the branches start with α-1,6 glycosidic links. That is where its branched structure comes from.

questions.q: Case: A DNA sample has 18% cytosine. Its adenine content is
questions.why: In DNA, C pairs with G, so G = 18%. A + T = 100 − 36 = 64%, and A = T, so adenine is 32%.

questions.q: Which reaction of glucose shows a straight chain of six carbons?
questions.why: Prolonged heating of glucose with HI reduces it to n-hexane, which shows that all six carbons are in an unbranched straight chain.

questions.q: The complementary strand of 5'-GATTC-3' is
questions.why: The complementary strand pairs A–T and G–C and runs antiparallel. For 5′-GATTC-3′ it reads 3′-CTAAG-5′. RNA's U does not appear in DNA.

questions.q: Case: An amino acid has pKa values 2.3 (–COOH) and 9.7 (–NH₃⁺) and no ionisable side chain. Its isoelectric point is about
questions.why: With no ionisable side chain, the isoelectric point is the average of the two pKa values: (2.3 + 9.7)/2 = 6.0.

questions.q: Number of different tripeptides that can be formed from glycine, alanine and valine, each used once:
questions.why: Using each of three different amino acids once, the number of different sequences is 3! = 3 × 2 × 1 = 6.

questions.q: α- and β-D-glucopyranose are
questions.why: α- and β-D-glucopyranose differ only in the configuration at C1, the anomeric carbon, so they are anomers.

courses.title: Revision & Practice · Class 12 Chemistry
courses.summary: Formula sheet for physical chemistry, a quick-reference summary of inorganic trends, a named-reactions and conversions sheet for organic chemistry, distinguishing tests, two mock papers with explained answers and a 25-question final mock with difficulty spread 1–5. Independent practice material; not affiliated with or endorsed by any board or exam body.
outcomes: Learners can recall all key physical-chemistry formulas with units.
Learners can recall inorganic trends of d/f-block elements and coordination compounds.
Learners can recall named reactions, reagents and distinguishing tests in organic chemistry.
Learners can solve mixed-chapter questions under time pressure.

lessons.title: Formula sheet: physical chemistry (Ch 1–3)

scenes.text: Ritika squeezes all of solutions, electrochemistry and kinetics onto one page of formulas.
For each one she writes the units and a one-line 'when to use'.
On exam day she glances at nothing — the page is in her head.

steps.title: Solutions
steps.body:
- Molarity = n/V(L); molality = n/kg solvent; x = n/Σn
- Henry: p = K_H x; Raoult: p = x₁p₁° + x₂p₂°
- RLVP: (p° − p)/p° = i x₂
- ΔT_b = iK_b m; ΔT_f = iK_f m (water: K_b 0.52, K_f 1.86 K kg mol⁻¹)
- π = iCRT (R = 0.083 L bar mol⁻¹ K⁻¹)
- M₂ = 1000Kw₂/(ΔT w₁); α(dissociation) = (i − 1)/(n − 1)

steps.title: Electrochemistry
steps.body:
- E°cell = E°cathode − E°anode
- E = E° − (0.059/n) log Q (298 K)
- ΔG° = −nFE°; log K = nE°/0.059; F = 96 500 C mol⁻¹
- κ = G*/R; G* = l/A; Λm = 1000κ/M (S cm² mol⁻¹)
- Λm = Λ°m − A√c (strong); Λ°m = ν₊λ°₊ + ν₋λ°₋
- α = Λm/Λ°m; Ka = cα²/(1 − α)
- m = MIt/(nF)

steps.title: Chemical kinetics
steps.body:
- Rate = −(1/a)d[A]/dt; rate = k[A]ˣ[B]ʸ; k units (mol L⁻¹)^(1−n) s⁻¹
- Zero order: [R] = [R]₀ − kt; t½ = [R]₀/2k
- First order: k = (2.303/t) log([R]₀/[R]); t½ = 0.693/k; 99.9% ≈ 10 t½
- Gas: k = (2.303/t) log[p₀/(2p₀ − pt)]
- Arrhenius: k = Ae^(−Ea/RT); log(k₂/k₁) = Ea(T₂ − T₁)/(2.303RT₁T₂)

steps.title: Units first
steps.body: Most errors: g vs kg, mL vs L, °C vs K, S m⁻¹ vs S cm⁻¹. Write units at every step.

quiz.q: Molality of 0.5 mol solute in 250 g water:
quiz.why: Molality = moles of solute ÷ kg of solvent = 0.5 mol ÷ 0.250 kg = 2 m.

quiz.q: van't Hoff factor of CaCl₂ (complete dissociation):
quiz.why: CaCl₂ gives one Ca²⁺ and two Cl⁻ on complete dissociation, so there are 3 particles and i = 3.

quiz.q: Units of k for zero order:
quiz.why: For zero order rate = k, so k has the same unit as the rate: mol L⁻¹ s⁻¹.
ΔG° = −nFE° = −2 × 96500 × 0.1 = −19 300 J = −19.3 kJ. A positive E° gives a negative ΔG°.

quiz.q: Charge to deposit 1 mol Al from Al³⁺:
quiz.why: Al³⁺ + 3e⁻ → Al, so 3 mol of electrons, that is 3 faradays, are needed per mole of aluminium.

quiz.q: A first-order reaction has k = 0.01 s⁻¹. t½ =
quiz.why: For a first-order reaction t½ = 0.693/k = 0.693/0.01 = 69.3 s.

lessons.title: Summary sheet: inorganic chemistry (Ch 4–5)

scenes.text: Dev used to memorise inorganic facts one by one and forget them.
Now he learns the reasons: half-filled d⁵, filled d¹⁰, lanthanoid contraction, ligand field strength.
A few reasons explain dozens of facts.

steps.title: d- and f-block
steps.body:
- Configurations: Cr 3d⁵4s¹, Cu 3d¹⁰4s¹; ions lose 4s first
- Zn, Cd, Hg not transition elements
- Mn: +2 to +7; Cu: E° = +0.34 V (only positive one in 3d series)
- Mn³⁺, Co³⁺ oxidising; Cr²⁺ reducing
- μ = √(n(n + 2)) BM: 1.73, 2.83, 3.87, 4.90, 5.92
- d⁰ and d¹⁰ ions colourless
- Catalysts: V₂O₅ (Contact), Fe (Haber), Ni (hydrogenation)
- Lanthanoids +3 (Ce⁴⁺ oxidising; Eu²⁺, Yb²⁺ reducing); contraction ⇒ Zr ≈ Hf; basicity La(OH)₃ > Lu(OH)₃
- Actinoids: all radioactive, up to +7

steps.title: Coordination compounds
steps.body:
- CN = number of donor atoms; en, ox didentate; EDTA hexadentate; NO₂⁻, SCN⁻ ambidentate
- Naming: ligands alphabetical; aqua, ammine, carbonyl; anionic complexes end '-ate' (ferrate, cuprate)
- Isomers: linkage, ionisation, coordination, hydrate; cis/trans, fac/mer; optical in [Co(en)₃]³⁺, cis-[CoCl₂(en)₂]⁺
- VBT: d²sp³ inner, sp³d² outer, dsp² square planar, sp³ tetrahedral
- Spectrochemical: I⁻ < Br⁻ < SCN⁻ < Cl⁻ < S²⁻ < F⁻ < OH⁻ < C₂O₄²⁻ < H₂O < NCS⁻ < edta⁴⁻ < NH₃ < en < CN⁻ < CO
- Δt = (4/9)Δ₀; high spin if Δ₀ < P
- Applications: EDTA (hardness), DMG (Ni²⁺), cisplatin, Mond process, Wilkinson's catalyst

steps.title: Common traps
steps.body:
- Counting ligands instead of donor atoms.
- Forgetting that tetrahedral complexes do not show geometrical isomerism.
- Mixing up oxidation state of the metal in carbonyls (zero).

activity.prompt: Match the complex with its magnetic behaviour.

quiz.why: Cr³⁺ is d³ with 3 unpaired electrons: μ = √(n(n+2)) = √15 = 3.87 BM.
Sc³⁺ is d⁰, with no d electrons for d–d transitions, so it is colourless. Ti³⁺ (d¹), Co²⁺ (d⁷) and Cu²⁺ (d⁹) are coloured.
Dimethylglyoximate (dmg) is didentate, so two dmg ligands make 2 × 2 = 4 bonds and the coordination number of Ni is 4.

quiz.q: Which ion shows linkage isomerism as a ligand?
quiz.why: SCN⁻ is ambidentate, as it can bind through S or through N, so it gives linkage isomers. NH₃, H₂O and en have only one kind of donor atom.
CO is a neutral ligand, so the oxidation state of Fe in [Fe(CO)₅] is 0.

quiz.q: Lanthanoid contraction makes the radii of Zr and Hf
quiz.why: Because of lanthanoid contraction, Zr (160 pm) and Hf (159 pm) have nearly equal radii, even though Hf lies a period below.

sources: NCERT Class 12 Chemistry (topic reference, own wording)

lessons.title: Named reactions and conversions: organic chemistry (Ch 6–10)

scenes.text: Neha draws a map: alkyl halides in the middle, arrows to alcohols, ethers, amines, nitriles, acids.
Each arrow is labelled with a reagent and a named reaction.
Conversion questions become route-finding on her map.

steps.title: Haloalkanes, alcohols, phenols, ethers
steps.body:
- Finkelstein (NaI/acetone), Swarts (AgF), Sandmeyer (CuX), Wurtz (Na/ether), Wurtz–Fittig, Fittig
- KCN → RCN, AgCN → RNC; KNO₂ → R–ONO, AgNO₂ → RNO₂
- SN2: inversion, CH₃ > 1° > 2° > 3°; SN1: racemisation, 3° > 2° > 1°
- Lucas test (3° immediate); PCC (1° → aldehyde); Cu/573 K
- Kolbe (salicylic acid), Reimer–Tiemann (salicylaldehyde), cumene process (phenol + acetone)
- Williamson: RONa + 1° RX; anisole + HI → phenol + CH₃I

steps.title: Carbonyls, acids, amines
steps.body:
- Rosenmund, Stephen, Etard, Gattermann–Koch, DIBAL-H
- Clemmensen (Zn–Hg/HCl), Wolff–Kishner (NH₂NH₂/KOH)
- Aldol (α-H, dil. base), Cannizzaro (no α-H, conc. base), haloform (CH₃CO–)
- HVZ (Cl₂/red P), Kolbe electrolysis, decarboxylation (soda lime, −1 C)
- Gabriel (1° aliphatic), Hoffmann bromamide (−1 C), Fe/HCl reduction
- Carbylamine (1° only), Hinsberg, diazotisation (273–278 K), Balz–Schiemann, H₃PO₂, coupling

steps.title: Distinguishing tests
steps.body:
- Tollens' / Fehling's: aldehydes (Fehling's: aliphatic only)
- Iodoform: CH₃CO–, CH₃CH(OH)–
- NaHCO₃: carboxylic acids
- Neutral FeCl₃: phenols (violet)
- Bromine water: phenol/aniline (white ppt), alkenes (decolourised)
- Lucas: 1°/2°/3° alcohols
- Carbylamine and Hinsberg: amine classes

steps.title: Biomolecules
steps.body:
- Glucose: aldohexose, pyranose; fructose: ketohexose, furanose; α/β anomers at C1
- Sucrose (non-reducing, invert sugar), maltose, lactose (reducing)
- Starch: amylose + amylopectin (α); cellulose (β-1,4); glycogen (highly branched)
- Protein levels 1°–4°; denaturation keeps 1° intact
- DNA: deoxyribose, A=T, G≡C; RNA: ribose, U

activity.prompt: Match the test to the compound class it identifies.

quiz.q: Conversion of ethanamide to methanamine uses
quiz.why: Hoffmann bromamide degradation shortens the chain by one carbon, so ethanamide (CH₃CONH₂) gives methanamine (CH₃NH₂).
Benzaldehyde has no α-hydrogen, so with concentrated NaOH it undergoes the Cannizzaro reaction, not aldol condensation.
Phenol with chloroform and NaOH is the Reimer–Tiemann reaction, giving mainly salicylaldehyde. Salicylic acid is made by Kolbe's reaction.

quiz.q: Which reagent converts R–COOH to R–CH₂OH?
quiz.why: LiAlH₄ is a strong hydride donor and reduces a carboxylic acid to a primary alcohol. NaBH₄ and PCC do not do this.
The Gattermann–Koch reaction formylates benzene directly, using CO and HCl with AlCl₃/CuCl, giving benzaldehyde in one step.
The glycosidic bond in sucrose uses the anomeric carbons of both glucose and fructose, so no free carbonyl is left and sucrose is non-reducing.

He marks each wrong answer: concept, formula, reagent recall or careless reading.

steps.title: How to use this mock
steps.body: Attempt the 8 questions below in 12 minutes. Afterwards read every explanation — including those you got right. Keep an error log by chapter.

steps.title: Board exam strategy
steps.body:
- Write balanced equations with conditions (catalyst, temperature) — they carry marks.
- In conversions, number the steps and name the reagent at each arrow.
- For numericals: formula → substitution with units → answer with unit.
- In mechanism questions, show curved arrows and intermediates clearly.

steps.title: JEE/NEET strategy
steps.body:
- Organic questions often test exceptions (Fehling's with benzaldehyde, Gabriel for aniline, NaBH₄ with acids).
- In inorganic, reason from configuration (d⁰, d⁵, d¹⁰) instead of memorising.
- For NEET, guess only when you can eliminate two options.

items: Formula/reaction sheet re-read for those chapters

quiz.q: 18 g glucose in 500 g water. Molality:
quiz.why: Moles of glucose = 18/180 = 0.1 mol. Molality = 0.1 ÷ 0.5 kg = 0.2 m.

quiz.q: E°cell for Zn | Zn²⁺ || Ag⁺ | Ag (E° Zn −0.76, Ag +0.80):
quiz.why: E°cell = E°cathode − E°anode = 0.80 − (−0.76) = 1.56 V, with Ag as cathode and Zn as anode.

quiz.q: A first-order reaction is 50% complete in 30 min. Time for 87.5%:
quiz.why: 50% completion takes one half-life, so t½ = 30 min. 87.5% completion leaves 12.5% = (1/2)³, which is 3 half-lives, so 90 min.
Fe³⁺ is d⁵ with 5 unpaired electrons: μ = √(5 × 7) = √35 = 5.92 BM.
In an anionic complex the metal name ends in -ate, ligands are named first, with CN⁻ as cyanido, and the oxidation state follows. So K₃[Fe(CN)₆] is potassium hexacyanidoferrate(III).
SN1 speed depends on carbocation stability, and (CH₃)₃C⁺ is a tertiary cation, the most stable of these, so (CH₃)₃CBr reacts fastest.
Propanone is a methyl ketone (CH₃CO–), so with I₂/NaOH it gives the haloform reaction: yellow iodoform (CHI₃) and sodium acetate (CH₃COONa).

quiz.q: Which is most basic in water?
quiz.why: In water, (CH₃)₂NH has the lowest pKb (about 3.0) of these, so it is the strongest base. Aniline is the weakest.

lessons.title: Mock paper 2 (mixed chapters)

scenes.text: A week before boards, Aisha takes her last mock under exam conditions.
She focuses on assertion–reason and case-based questions — her weak spot last time.
Her improved score gives her the confidence she needs.

steps.title: Instructions
steps.body: 8 questions, 12 minutes. Includes assertion–reason and case-based items.

steps.title: Assertion–reason method
steps.body: 1. Is the assertion true? 2. Is the reason true? 3. Only if both are true: does the reason *explain* the assertion?

steps.title: Case-based questions
steps.body: Read the passage once, underline data and conditions, then answer each part separately.

steps.title: Last-minute warnings
steps.body:
- 'Aqueous' vs 'molten' changes electrolysis products.
- 'Alcoholic' vs 'aqueous' KOH changes elimination vs substitution.
- 'Dilute' vs 'concentrated' NaOH changes aldol vs Cannizzaro.

activity.prompt: Compare your two mock scores. Which chapter improved most, and which needs one more pass? Write a three-day plan.
activity.hint: List chapter, topic and how many practice questions per day.

quiz.q: Assertion: Molar conductivity increases on dilution. Reason: Number of ions per unit volume increases on dilution.
options: Both true; reason does not explain
quiz.why: Ions per unit volume decrease; Λm rises because mobility/dissociation per mole increases.

quiz.q: Case: 2 g of a non-electrolyte in 100 g water lowers f.p. by 0.372 K (K_f = 1.86). Molar mass:

quiz.why: In acid hydrolysis of ethyl acetate, water is in large excess and its concentration stays almost constant, so the reaction obeys first-order kinetics although it is truly second order.
cis-[CoCl₂(en)₂]⁺ has no plane of symmetry, so it exists as two non-superimposable mirror images. The trans form is symmetric and the others lack chirality.
The –OH group strongly activates the ring, so in bromine water all ortho and para positions are brominated, forming 2,4,6-tribromophenol (white precipitate).
The –COOH group is electron-withdrawing and meta-directing, so nitration gives the meta product (m-nitrobenzoic acid).
Aniline is diazotised with NaNO₂/HCl at 273–278 K and the diazonium salt is treated with CuCN (Sandmeyer) to give benzonitrile. KCN cannot replace the –NH₂ directly.

quiz.q: DNA contains which base not found in RNA?
quiz.why: Thymine occurs only in DNA, while RNA has uracil in its place. Adenine and guanine are found in both.

questions.q: Unit of molality is
questions.why: Molality is moles of solute per kilogram of solvent, so its unit is mol/kg.

questions.q: The SHE has potential
questions.why: The standard hydrogen electrode is the reference and is assigned a potential of exactly 0 V.

questions.q: Which is a transition element?
questions.why: Cu²⁺ is d⁹, so it has an incomplete d subshell and Cu is a transition element. Zn, Cd and Hg have filled d¹⁰ in both the atom and common ion.

questions.q: Glucose is
questions.why: Glucose has six carbons with an aldehyde group, so it is an aldohexose. This makes it an aldose and a monosaccharide.

questions.q: Which aqueous solution has the lowest freezing point?
questions.why: Freezing point depression depends on i × m. K₂SO₄ gives three ions (i = 3), more than NaCl (2), glucose (1) or urea (1), so it gives the lowest freezing point.

questions.q: For aA → products, if rate doubles when [A] doubles, the order is
questions.why: If doubling [A] doubles the rate, rate ∝ [A]¹, so the reaction is first order.

questions.q: CN and oxidation state of Co in [Co(en)₂Cl₂]⁺:
questions.why: Two didentate en and two Cl⁻ give 2 × 2 + 2 = 6 bonds. Charge: x + 0 + 2(−1) = +1, so Co is +3.

questions.q: The reagent that converts propan-1-ol to propanal:
questions.why: PCC is a mild oxidant that stops at the aldehyde, so propan-1-ol gives propanal. KMnO₄/H⁺ goes on to the acid, and LiAlH₄ and Zn–Hg/HCl are reducing agents.

questions.q: Assertion: Ethers are less soluble in water than isomeric alcohols. Reason: Ethers cannot donate H-bonds to water.
options: Both true; reason does not explain
questions.why: Both are true. Alcohols have O–H and can donate hydrogen bonds to water. Ethers cannot, so they dissolve less; the reason explains the assertion.

questions.q: Λ°(CH₃COOH) from Λ°(HCl) = 426, Λ°(CH₃COONa) = 91, Λ°(NaCl) = 126 S cm² mol⁻¹:
questions.why: By Kohlrausch's law, Λ°(CH₃COOH) = Λ°(HCl) + Λ°(CH₃COONa) − Λ°(NaCl) = 426 + 91 − 126 = 391 S cm² mol⁻¹.

questions.q: Ea for a reaction whose rate constant doubles from 300 to 310 K is about
Which is the strongest acid?
questions.why: Electron-withdrawing Cl atoms stabilise the carboxylate by the −I effect. Cl₂CHCOOH has two Cl atoms, so it is a stronger acid than ClCH₂COOH, and much stronger than CH₃COOH or HCOOH.

questions.q: Which amine does not react with Hinsberg's reagent?
questions.why: Hinsberg's reagent reacts through N–H bonds. A tertiary amine like (CH₃)₃N has none, so it does not react.

questions.q: Which gives a positive iodoform test?
questions.why: The iodoform test needs a CH₃CO– or CH₃CH(OH)– group. Propan-2-ol has CH₃CH(OH)–, and I₂/NaOH oxidises it first to the methyl ketone. The others lack this group.

questions.q: Product of chlorobenzene + CH₃Cl + Na (dry ether):
questions.why: The Wurtz–Fittig reaction couples an aryl halide with an alkyl halide using sodium in dry ether. Chlorobenzene and CH₃Cl give toluene.

questions.q: Case: Copper is deposited by passing 0.5 A for 1 hour through CuSO₄. Mass deposited (M = 63.5):
Case: E for Cu | Cu²⁺ (0.01 M) || Ag⁺ (0.1 M) | Ag at 298 K, with E° = 0.46 V and Q = [Cu²⁺]/[Ag⁺]²:
questions.why: With Cu²⁺ = 0.01 M and Ag⁺ = 0.1 M, Q = 0.01/(0.1)² = 1. Since log 1 = 0, E = E° = 0.46 V.

questions.q: The high-spin d⁶ octahedral complex has how many unpaired electrons?
questions.why: A high-spin d⁶ ion in an octahedral field is t₂g⁴e_g², which has one paired set and four unpaired electrons.

questions.q: Assertion: Aryl halides are not prepared from phenols with HCl. Reason: The C–O bond in phenol has partial double-bond character.
options: Both true; reason does not explain
questions.why: Both are true. The C–O bond in phenol has partial double-bond character from resonance and is hard to break, so HCl cannot replace the –OH to give aryl halides.

questions.q: Case: A (C₂H₄O) reduces Tollens' reagent and gives a yellow precipitate with I₂/NaOH. A is
questions.why: Reducing Tollens' reagent shows an aldehyde, and a yellow iodoform precipitate shows a CH₃CO– group. Ethanal (CH₃CHO) fits C₂H₄O and has both features.

questions.q: Which pair of solutions is isotonic at the same T?
questions.why: Isotonic solutions have equal i × C. Glucose gives 0.1 × 1 = 0.1 and NaCl gives 0.05 × 2 = 0.1, so they have the same osmotic pressure.

questions.q: Case: A first-order gas reaction A → B + C starts at 0.6 atm; after 20 min total pressure is 0.9 atm. Its t½ is
questions.why: For A → B + C, total pressure = p₀ + x, so x = 0.3 and p_A = 0.6 − 0.3 = 0.3 atm, half of p₀. So t½ = 20 min.

questions.q: Number of stereoisomers of [Co(NH₃)₃Cl₃]:
questions.why: Octahedral [Co(NH₃)₃Cl₃] has facial and meridional isomers. Neither is chiral, so there are 2 stereoisomers in all.

questions.q: Case: C₇H₉N (aromatic) gives a foul smell with CHCl₃/KOH and on diazotisation then H₃PO₂ gives toluene. Possible structure:
questions.why: The foul smell with CHCl₃/KOH shows a primary amine, and deamination with H₃PO₂ giving toluene shows the amine group is on a toluene ring. So A is a toluidine (o-, m- or p-).

questions.q: A DNA sample has 22% thymine. Guanine content:
questions.why: In DNA A = T, so A = 22%. Then G + C = 100 − 44 = 56% and G = C = 28%.
